Introduction

介绍

I told my husband I was going to take a class one night a week and he went ballistic in that quiet way of his. “Do whatever you want, you always do anyway,” he told me, “but don’t expect me to be waiting for you when you get home. I’m always there for you; why can’t you be there for me?” I knew his argument didn’t make sense, but it made me feel so selfish. I asked for my registration fee back. —L IZ

我告诉丈夫我要每周抽出一个晚上去上课，他却像往常一样，用他那种安静的方式勃然大怒。“你想做什么就做什么，反正你总是这么做，”他冲我吼道，“但别指望我等你回家。我总是为你守候，为什么你不能也为我守候呢？”我知道他的话毫无道理，但却让我觉得自己太自私了。我要求他退还我的报名费。——莉兹

I was planning to spend Christmas traveling with my wife, a vacation we’d been looking forward to for months. I called my mom to tell her the news that we’d finally gotten the tickets, and she almost started to cry. “But what about Christmas dinner?” she said. “You know everyone always gets together for the holiday. If you go on that trip instead of coming, you’ll ruin the holiday for everyone. How can you do this to me? How many Christmases do you think I have left?” So of course I gave in. My wife’s going to kill me, but I don’t see how I could enjoy a vacation while I’m buried under all that guilt. — T OM

我原本计划和妻子一起旅行过圣诞节，我们盼望这次旅行已经好几个月了。我打电话告诉妈妈我们终于买到机票了，她差点哭了。“可是圣诞晚餐怎么办？”她说，“你知道大家过节都会聚在一起的。如果你不来，而是去旅行，你会毁了大家的节日。你怎么能这样对我？你觉得我还能过几个圣诞节？” 所以，我当然妥协了。我老婆肯定会杀了我的，但我实在想不出，如果我一直背负着这么大的罪恶感，怎么能好好享受假期。——汤姆

I went in to tell my boss that I had to have help or a more realistic deadline on a big project I’m doing. As soon as I mentioned that I really needed some relief, he started on me. “I know how much you want to get home to your family,” he said, “but even though they miss you now, you know they’ll appreciate that promotion we’ve been considering you for. We need a team player with real dedication for that job — that’s what I thought you were. But go ahead. Spend more time with the kids. Just remember that if those are your priorities, we might have to reconsider our plans for you.” I felt totally blindsided. Now I don’t know what to do. —K IM

我去跟老板说，我手头有个大项目，需要人帮忙或者更实际的截止日期。我刚一提我真的需要人帮忙，他就开始训斥我。“我知道你很想回家陪家人，”他说，“虽然他们现在很想你，但你也知道，他们会很感激我们一直在考虑给你的那个晋升机会。我们需要一个真正敬业、有团队精神的人来做这份工作——我觉得你就是这样的人。不过，你可以多花点时间陪陪孩子。只是你要记住，如果这是你优先考虑的事情，我们可能不得不重新考虑你的晋升计划。” 我当时完全懵了。现在我不知道该怎么办。——金

What’s going on here? Why do certain people leave us thinking “I’ve lost again. I always give in. I didn’t say what I was really feeling. Why can’t I ever get my point across? How come I can never stand up for myself?” We know we’ve been had. We know we feel frustrated and resentful, and we know we’ve given up what we want to please someone else, but we just don’t know what to do about it. Why is it that some people are able to emotionally overpower us, leaving us feeling defeated?

这到底是怎么回事？为什么有些人总是让我们觉得“我又输了。我总是妥协。我没有说出自己的真实感受。为什么我总是无法表达自己的观点？为什么我总是无法维护自己的权益？”我们知道自己被骗了。我们知道自己感到沮丧和怨恨，也知道自己为了取悦别人而放弃了自己想要的东西，但我们就是不知道该怎么办。为什么有些人能够轻易地在情感上控制我们，让我们感到彻底的失败？

The people we’re coming up against in these can’t-win situations are skillful manipulators. They swathe us in a comforting intimacy when they get what they want, but they frequently wind up threatening us in order to get their way, or burying us under a load of guilt and self-reproach when they don’t. It may seem as though they map out ways to get what they want from us, but often they’re not even aware of what they’re doing. In fact, many can appear sweet or long-suffering and not threatening at all.

在这些进退两难的困境中，我们遇到的往往是操控高手。当他们达到目的时，会用亲密无间的氛围让我们感到舒适，但一旦得逞，他们往往会威胁我们，或者让我们背负沉重的罪恶感和自责。他们似乎精心策划了各种手段来达到目的，但实际上，他们往往意识不到自己的所作所为。事实上，许多人看起来和蔼可亲、忍耐力强，完全没有威胁性。

Generally, it’s one particular person—a partner, a parent, a sibling, a friend—who manipulates us so consistently that we seem to forget everything we know about being effective adults. Though we may be skilled and successful in other parts of our lives, with these people we feel bewildered, powerless. They’ve got us wrapped around their little fingers.

通常情况下，是某个特定的人——伴侣、父母、兄弟姐妹、朋友——不断地操控我们，以至于我们似乎忘记了所有关于如何成为高效成年人的知识。尽管我们在生活的其他方面可能能力出众、事业有成，但在这些人面前，我们却感到困惑、无力。他们把我们玩弄于股掌之间。

Take my client Sarah, a court reporter. Sarah, a vivacious brunette, has been seeing a builder named Frank for almost a year. A close couple in their 30s, they got along well—until the subject of marriage came up. Then, said Sarah, “his whole demeanor toward me changed. He seemed to want me to prove myself.” It all became clear one weekend when Frank invited her up for a romantic weekend at his cabin in the mountains. “When we arrived, the place was full of tarps and paint cans, and he handed me a brush. I didn’t know what else to do, so I painted.” They worked, mostly in silence, all day, and when they finally sat down to rest, Frank pulled out a huge diamond engagement ring.

以我的客户莎拉为例，她是一名法庭速记员。莎拉是一位活泼的棕发女郎，和一位名叫弗兰克的建筑工人交往了将近一年。这对三十多岁的情侣关系亲密，相处融洽——直到他们谈到结婚。莎拉说，之后“他对我的态度完全变了。他似乎想让我证明自己。” 一切都在一个周末变得明朗起来，弗兰克邀请她去他在山里的小屋度过一个浪漫的周末。“我们到的时候，小屋里到处都是油布和油漆罐，他递给我一把刷子。我不知道还能做什么，就涂起了油漆。” 他们默默地干了一整天，最后坐下来休息时，弗兰克掏出一枚硕大的钻石订婚戒指。

“I asked him, ‘What’s going on?”’ Sarah said, “and he said he needed to know that I was a good sport, that I would pitch in and not expect him to do everything in the marriage.” Of course, that wasn’t the end of the story.

“我问他，‘到底怎么回事？’”莎拉说，“他说他需要知道我是一个能接受现实的人，我会分担家务，而不是指望他包揽婚姻中的一切。” 当然，故事并没有就此结束。

We set a date and everything, but we went up and down like a yo-yo. He kept giving me gifts, but he also kept testing me. If I didn’t want to go take care of his sister’s kids one weekend, he said I didn’t have a strong sense of family and maybe we should think about calling off the wedding. Or if I talked about expanding my business, it meant I wasn’t really committed to him. So of course I put that on hold. It went on and on, with me always giving in. But I kept telling myself what a great guy he was and that maybe he was scared of getting married and just needed to feel more secure with me.

我们定好了婚期，一切都安排好了，但之后却像坐过山车一样反反复复。他不停地送我礼物，但也不停地试探我。如果我周末不想去帮他姐姐照顾孩子，他就说我家庭观念不够强，也许我们应该考虑取消婚礼。或者，如果我谈到拓展事业，他就觉得我对他不够投入。所以，我当然就把这些都搁置了。就这样反反复复，我总是妥协。但我一直告诉自己，他是个多么好的人，也许他只是害怕结婚，需要从我这里获得安全感。

Frank’s threats were quiet, yet they were powerfully effective because they alternated with a closeness enticing enough to obscure what was really going on. And like most of us, Sarah kept coming back for more.

弗兰克的威胁悄无声息，却威力十足，因为它与一种足以掩盖真相的亲近感交替出现。而和我们大多数人一样，莎拉一次又一次地被他吸引。

She gave in to Frank’s manipulations because, in the moment, making him happy seemed to make sense—there was so much at stake. Like so many of us, Sarah felt resentful and frustrated at Frank’s threats, but she justified her capitulation to them in the name of peace.

她屈服于弗兰克的操纵，因为在当时，让他高兴似乎合情合理——事关重大。和我们许多人一样，莎拉对弗兰克的威胁感到愤恨和沮丧，但她以和平之名，为自己的屈服找到了理由。

In such relationships, we keep our focus on the other person’s needs at the expense of our own, and we relax into the temporary illusion of safety we’ve created for ourselves by giving in. We’ve avoided conflict, confrontation—and the chance of a healthy relationship.

在这样的关系中，我们总是把注意力放在对方的需求上，忽略了自己的需求，沉浸在通过妥协而为自己营造的暂时安全感幻觉中。我们逃避了冲突和对抗，也因此错失了建立健康关系的机会。

Maddening interactions like these are among the most common causes of friction in almost every relationship, yet they’re rarely identified and understood. Often these instances of manipulation get labeled miscommunication. We tell ourselves, “I’m operating from feelings and he’s operating from intellect” or “She’s just coming from a different mind-set.” But in reality, the source of friction isn’t in communication styles. It’s more in one person getting his or her way at the expense of another. These are more than simple misunderstandings—they’re power struggles.

像这样令人恼火的互动几乎是所有关系中最常见的摩擦来源之一，但却很少被识别和理解。通常，这些操控行为会被贴上“沟通不畅”的标签。我们会告诉自己：“我是凭感觉行事，他是凭理智行事”，或者“她只是思维方式不同”。但实际上，摩擦的根源不在于沟通方式，而在于一方为了达到目的不惜牺牲另一方的利益。这不仅仅是简单的误会，更是权力斗争。

Over the years I’ve searched for a way to describe these struggles and the troubling cycle of behavior they lead to, and I’ve found that people almost universally respond with a charge of recognition when I tell them that what we’re talking about here is pure and simple blackmail— emotional blackmail.

多年来，我一直在寻找一种方法来描述这些挣扎以及它们导致的令人不安的行为循环，我发现当我告诉人们我们在这里谈论的是纯粹的勒索——情感勒索时，几乎所有人都表示认同。

I realize that the term blackmail is one that conjures up sinister images of criminals, fear and extortion. Certainly it’s difficult to think of your husband, your parents, your boss, your siblings or your children in that context. Yet I’ve found that blackmail is the only term that accurately describes what’s going on. The very sharpness of the word helps us pierce the denial and confusion that cloud so many relationships, and doing that brings us to clarity.

我知道“勒索”这个词会让人联想到罪犯、恐惧和敲诈勒索等阴险的画面。当然，很难将你的丈夫、父母、老板、兄弟姐妹或孩子与这种行为联系起来。然而，我发现“勒索”是唯一能准确描述现状的词。这个词本身的尖锐性，能帮助我们刺破笼罩在许多关系中的否认和迷雾，从而让我们看清真相。

Let me reassure you: Just because there’s emotional blackmail in a close relationship doesn’t mean it’s doomed. It simply means that we need to honestly acknowledge and correct the behavior that’s causing us pain, putting these relationships back on a more solid foundation.

让我向你保证：亲密关系中出现情感勒索并不意味着这段关系就注定失败。这仅仅意味着我们需要坦诚地承认并纠正那些给我们带来痛苦的行为，从而让这些关系重新建立在更加稳固的基础之上。

WHAT IS EMOTIONAL BLACKMAIL?

什么是情感勒索？

Emotional blackmail is a powerful form of manipulation in which people close to us threaten, either directly or indirectly, to punish us if we don’t do what they want. At the heart of any kind of blackmail is one basic threat, which can be expressed in many different ways: If you don’t behave the way I want you to, you will suffer. A criminal blackmailer might threaten to use knowledge about a person’s past to ruin her reputation, or ask to be paid off in cash to hide a secret. Emotional blackmail hits closer to home. Emotional blackmailers know how much we value our relationship with them. They know our vulnerabilities. Often they know our deepest secrets. And no matter how much they care about us, when they fear they won’t get their way, they use this intimate knowledge to shape the threats that give them the payoff they want: our compliance.

情感勒索是一种强有力的操控手段，我们身边的人会直接或间接地威胁我们，如果我们不按他们的意愿行事，就会受到惩罚。任何形式的勒索，其核心都是一个基本威胁，这种威胁可以用多种方式表达：如果你不按我的意愿行事，你就会遭受惩罚。犯罪分子可能会威胁利用他人的过往经历来毁掉她的名誉，或者要求用现金来掩盖秘密。而情感勒索则更加贴近我们的生活。情感勒索者深知我们有多么重视与他们的关系。他们了解我们的弱点。他们往往知道我们最深层的秘密。无论他们多么关心我们，当他们害怕无法得逞时，他们就会利用这些私密信息来制造威胁，从而达到他们想要的目的：让我们屈服。

Knowing that we want love or approval, our blackmailers threaten to withhold it or take it away altogether, or make us feel we must earn it. For example, if you pride yourself on being generous and caring, the blackmailer might label you selfish or inconsiderate if you don’t accede to his wishes. If you value money and security, the blackmailer might attach conditions to providing them or threaten to take them away. And if you believe the blackmailer, you could fall into a pattern of letting him control your decisions and behavior.

勒索者深知我们渴望爱或认可，便会威胁不予给予，甚至彻底剥夺，或者让我们觉得必须靠自己努力才能获得。例如，如果你以慷慨和体贴为傲，勒索者可能会在你不顺从他意愿时，给你贴上自私或冷漠的标签。如果你重视金钱和安全感，勒索者可能会在提供这些时附加条件，或者威胁要剥夺它们。如果你相信了勒索者，就可能陷入一种让他控制你决定和行为的模式。

We get locked into a dance with blackmail, a dance with myriad steps, shapes and partners.

我们陷入了一场与勒索的舞蹈，一场有无数舞步、舞姿和舞伴的舞蹈。

LOST IN THE FOG

迷失在迷雾中

How do so many smart, capable people find themselves groping to understand behavior that seems so obvious? One key reason is that our blackmailers make it nearly impossible to see how they’re manipulating us, because they lay down a thick fog that obscures their actions. We’d fight back if we could, but they ensure that we literally can’t see what is happening to us. I use fog as both a metaphor for the confusion blackmailers create in us and as a lens for burning it off. FOG is a shorthand way of referring to Fear, Obligation and Guilt, the tools of the blackmailer’s trade. Blackmailers pump an engulfing FOG into their relationships, ensuring that we will feel afraid to cross them, obligated to give them their way and terribly guilty if we don’t.

为什么这么多聪明能干的人会发现自己难以理解那些看似显而易见的行为？一个关键原因是，勒索者让我们几乎无法看清他们是如何操纵我们的，因为他们会营造一种浓雾，掩盖他们的所作所为。如果我们有能力，我们一定会反抗，但他们却确保我们根本看不清自己正在遭受什么。我用“迷雾”来比喻勒索者在我们心中制造的混乱，同时也把它当作一种驱散迷雾的透镜。“迷雾”（FOG）是恐惧（Fear）、义务（Obligation）和内疚（Guilt）的缩写，这些都是勒索者惯用的伎俩。勒索者会在彼此的关系中注入一层浓重的迷雾，让我们害怕得罪他们，被迫屈从于他们的要求，如果不顺从，就会感到深深的内疚。

Because it’s so tough to cut through this FOG to recognize emotional blackmail when it’s happening to you—or even in retrospect—I’ve devised the following checklist to help you determine if you are a blackmailer’s target.

因为很难拨开迷雾，在遭遇情感勒索时（甚至事后回想起来）识别出来，所以我制定了以下清单，以帮助你确定自己是否是勒索者的目标。

Do important people in your life:

你生命中重要的人：

  • Threaten to make your life difficult if you don’t do what they want?
    他们威胁说，如果你不按他们的意愿行事，他们就让你日子不好过？
  • Constantly threaten to end the relationship if you don’t do what they want?
    如果你不按他们的意愿行事，他们就会不断威胁要结束这段关系？
  • Tell you or imply that they will neglect, hurt themselves or become depressed if you don’t do what they want?
    他们告诉你或者暗示你，如果你不按他们的意愿行事，他们就会疏于照顾自己、伤害自己或变得抑郁？
  • Always want more, no matter how much you give?
    无论付出多少，总是想要更多？
  • Regularly assume you will give in to them?
    你是否经常认为自己会向他们妥协？
  • Regularly ignore or discount your feelings and wants?
    经常忽略或轻视自己的感受和需求吗？
  • Make lavish promises that are contingent on your behavior and then rarely keep them?
    做出许多以你的行为为条件的诱人承诺，然后却很少兑现？
  • Consistently label you as selfish, bad, greedy, unfeeling or uncaring when you don’t give in to them?
    当你不向他们妥协时，他们总是给你贴上自私、坏、贪婪、冷酷无情或漠不关心的标签吗？
  • Shower you with approval when you give in to them and take it away when you don’t?
    当你顺从他们时，他们会对你赞许不已；当你拒绝他们时，他们会收回赞许？
  • Use money as a weapon to get their way?
    利用金钱作为武器来达到目的？

If you answered yes to even one of these questions, you are being emotionally blackmailed. But I want to assure you that there are many changes you can put into practice immediately to improve your situation and the way you feel.

如果你对以上任何一个问题的回答是肯定的，那么你正在遭受情感勒索。但我可以向你保证，你可以立即采取许多措施来改善你的处境和感受。

COMING TO CLARITY

弄清真相

Before we can affect change, we need to clear away our confusion about how our relationships with blackmailers are operating. We need to turn on the light. This is a vitally important step in ending emotional blackmail because, even as we work to burn off the FOG, the blackmailer is busy pumping in thick new layers. Despite all the sophistication we’ve developed in recent years about our moods, psyches and motivations, when we’re dealing with FOG, our senses are muffled, and the finely tuned sensors that usually guide us in relationships fill with static. Blackmailers can skillfully mask the pressure they’re applying to us, and often we experience it in ways that make us question our perception of what’s happening. In addition, there is frequently a vast difference between what our blackmailers do and the benign or even loving way they interpret their actions to us and themselves. We feel confused, disoriented and resentful. But we’re not alone. Emotional blackmail is a dilemma affecting millions of people.

在做出改变之前，我们需要先厘清与勒索者之间关系运作方式的迷雾。我们需要拨开迷雾，看清真相。这是终结情感勒索至关重要的一步，因为即便我们努力驱散迷雾，勒索者仍在不断地制造新的迷雾。尽管近年来我们对自身的情绪、心理和动机有了更深刻的理解，但当我们身处迷雾之中时，我们的感官却变得迟钝，那些通常指引我们处理人际关系的敏锐感知也变得杂乱无章。勒索者能够巧妙地掩盖他们施加在我们身上的压力，而我们常常会以一种让我们质疑自身认知的方式感受到这种压力。此外，勒索者的实际行为与他们向我们和他们自己所宣称的善意甚至充满爱意的解释之间，往往存在着巨大的差异。我们感到困惑、迷茫和怨恨。但我们并不孤单。情感勒索是一个影响着数百万人的困境。

Throughout this book, in dramatic case histories, you will meet people who are struggling with emotional blackmail—and finding ways to end it. These are stories about real people with real feelings and real conflicts. They’re people you’ll identify with—men and women who function with great competence, grace and effectiveness in many parts of their lives but who have fallen into the blackmail trap. If you open your heart, you can learn a great deal from them. Their stories are modern fables, teaching stories that can serve as guides and beacons on your own journey.

在这本书中，你将通过一系列引人入胜的案例，了解那些身陷情感勒索困境并努力摆脱困境的人们。这些故事讲述的是真实的人，他们有着真实的情感和真实的冲突。你会与他们产生共鸣——这些男男女女在生活的许多方面都展现出卓越的能力、优雅的风度和高效的执行力，却不幸落入了情感勒索的陷阱。如果你敞开心扉，就能从他们身上学到很多。他们的故事如同现代寓言，能够指引你前行，为你指明方向。

BLACKMAIL TAKES TWO

勒索需要两个人

In the first half of this book, I’ll show you exactly how emotional blackmail operates and why some of us are especially vulnerable to it. I’ll explain, in detail, how the blackmail transaction works and show what each party to the transaction wants, what they get and how they get it. I’ll explore the psyche of the blackmailer, a task that seems a bit daunting at first because not every blackmailer has the same style or character traits: Some are passive, some quite aggressive. Some are direct and others are extremely subtle. Some let us know precisely what the consequences will be if we displease them, others emphasize how much we are making them suffer. Yet no matter how different they appear to be on the surface, they all have major traits in common, characteristics that feed their manipulative behavior. I’ll show you how our blackmailers use FOG and their other tools, and I’ll help you understand what drives them.

本书前半部分，我将详细揭示情感勒索的运作机制，以及为何有些人特别容易受到其影响。我会详细解释勒索交易的运作方式，并阐明交易双方的诉求、所得以及获取方式。我将深入剖析勒索者的心理，这项任务乍看之下似乎有些艰巨，因为并非所有勒索者都拥有相同的风格或性格特征：有些被动，有些则咄咄逼人；有些直截了当，有些则极其隐晦；有些会明确告知我们若不悦将会面临的后果，而有些则会强调我们给他们造成了多大的痛苦。然而，无论他们表面上看起来多么不同，他们都拥有一些共同的主要特征，这些特征助长了他们的操控行为。我将向您展示勒索者如何运用“情感恐惧”（FOG）和其他手段，并帮助您理解他们的动机所在。

I’ll show how fear—fear of loss, fear of change, fear of rejection, fear of losing power—is a common ground stretching beneath those who become blackmailers. For some, these fears are rooted in a lengthy history of feeling anxious and inadequate. For others, they may be a response to more recent uncertainties and stresses that have undermined their sense of themselves as secure, competent people. I’ll demonstrate how the potential for blackmail skyrockets as fears build in the blackmailer’s life. And I’ll show how triggering events such as rejection by a lover, the loss of a job, divorce, retirement or illness can easily turn someone close to us into a blackmailer.

我将揭示恐惧——害怕失去、害怕改变、害怕被拒绝、害怕失去权力——是如何成为勒索者的共同根源。对一些人来说，这些恐惧源于长期的焦虑和无力感。对另一些人来说，这些恐惧可能是对近期不确定性和压力的反应，这些不确定性和压力削弱了他们作为安全可靠之人的自我认知。我将阐明，随着勒索者生活中恐惧的累积，勒索的可能性会急剧上升。我还会揭示，诸如被爱人拒绝、失业、离婚、退休或疾病等触发事件，是如何轻易地将我们身边亲近的人变成勒索者的。

The people close to us who use emotional blackmail are rarely individuals who wake up every morning saying “How can I destroy my victim?” Rather, they are people for whom blackmail is the ticket to feeling safe and in charge. No matter how confident they look on the outside, blackmailers are operating out of high degrees of anxiety.

我们身边那些使用情感勒索的人，很少是那种每天早上醒来就想着“我该如何摧毁我的受害者？”的人。相反，对他们来说，勒索是获得安全感和掌控感的途径。无论他们表面上看起来多么自信，勒索者内心都充满了焦虑。

But when they snap their fingers and we jump, for a moment our blackmailers can feel powerful. Emotional blackmail becomes their defense against feeling hurt and afraid.

但当他们打个响指，我们就吓得跳起来时，勒索者会瞬间感到自己无所不能。情感勒索成了他们抵御伤害和恐惧的防御机制。

THE ROLE WE PLAY

我们扮演的角色

Without our help, however, blackmail can’t take root. Remember: Blackmail takes two—this is a transaction —and our next step will be to see what we as blackmail targets contribute.

然而，没有我们的配合，勒索就无法得逞。记住：勒索需要双方参与——这是一场交易——而下一步，我们将看看作为勒索目标的我们能做出什么贡献。

Each of us brings into any relationship our own potent set of hot buttons—our stored-up resentments, regrets, insecurities, fears, angers. These are our soft spots, places that hurt when touched. Emotional blackmail can only operate when we let people know they’ve found our hot buttons and that we’ll jump when they push them. Throughout this book, we will see how our life experiences have shaped the automatic emotional responses that power our hot buttons.

我们每个人都会在任何一段关系中带入自己强烈的“敏感点”——积压已久的怨恨、悔恨、不安、恐惧和愤怒。这些是我们的软肋，触碰它们就会让我们感到疼痛。情感勒索只有在我们让别人知道他们找到了我们的“敏感点”，并且知道一旦被触碰就会立刻做出反应时，才能奏效。本书将探讨我们的人生经历如何塑造了驱动这些“敏感点”的自动情绪反应。

It’s been fascinating to me to watch as our philosophy of human behavior has evolved from one that sees us as victims to one that encourages us to take responsibility for our lives and our problems. Nowhere is that more important than in the arena of emotional blackmail. It’s easy to focus on other people’s behavior and to think that if they change, things will be fine. But what we really need to find is the commitment and courage to understand ourselves and to change the way we interact with would-be blackmailers. It’s tough to acknowledge that through capitulating, we actually teach the blackmailer how to blackmail us. But the hard truth is this: Our compliance rewards the blackmailer, and every time we reward someone for a particular action, whether we realize it or not , we’re letting them know in the strongest possible terms that they can do it again.

令我着迷的是，我们对人类行为的理解已经从视我们为受害者转变为鼓励我们为自己的人生和问题承担责任。在情感勒索领域，这一点尤为重要。我们很容易把注意力放在他人的行为上，认为只要他们改变，一切都会好起来。但我们真正需要的是找到理解自身、改变与潜在勒索者互动方式的决心和勇气。承认这一点很难：我们的屈服实际上是在教勒索者如何勒索我们。但残酷的现实是：我们的顺从助长了勒索者的气焰，每次我们因为某种行为而给予他人奖励时，无论我们是否意识到，我们都在以最强烈的语气告诉他们，他们可以再次这样做。

THE PRICE WE PAY

我们付出的代价

Emotional blackmail spreads like ivy, and its coiling tendrils can wrap around every aspect of our lives. If we’re capitulating to emotional blackmail on the job, we may come home and take it out on the kids. If we have a bad relationship with a parent, we may shower our partner with negativity. We can’t just put a conflict in a box labeled boss or husband and keep it out of the rest of our lives. We may even duplicate the dynamic that’s making us suffer and become blackmailers ourselves, taking out our frustration on someone weaker or more vulnerable than we are.

情感勒索如同常春藤般蔓延，其缠绕的触须会渗透到我们生活的方方面面。如果我们屈服于工作中的情感勒索，回家后可能会把气撒在孩子身上。如果我们与父母关系不好，可能会把负能量倾泻到伴侣身上。我们不能仅仅把冲突归咎于老板或丈夫，然后就置之不理。我们甚至可能重蹈覆辙，变成勒索者，把挫败感发泄到比我们更弱小或更易受伤害的人身上。

Many of the people who use emotional blackmail are friends, colleagues and family members with whom we have close ties that we want to preserve and strengthen. They may be people we love for the good times we’ve shared, the closeness we still occasionally manage to have and the histories we have in common. We may consider our relationships with them to be good, for the most part, but pulled off course by blackmail. It’s vital not to let the blackmail habit suck us—and everyone around us—into its vortex.

许多使用情感勒索的人都是我们关系密切的朋友、同事和家人，我们希望维系并加强这些关系。我们或许爱他们，因为我们曾一起度过美好时光，我们偶尔还能保持亲密关系，我们拥有共同的经历。我们可能认为我们与他们的关系大部分时候都很好，但却被勒索拖入了歧途。至关重要的是，不要让勒索的恶习将我们自己以及我们周围的人都卷入其中。

The price we pay when we repeatedly give in to emotional blackmail is enormous. The blackmailer’s comments and behavior keep us feeling off-balance, ashamed and guilt-ridden. We know we need to change the situation, and we repeatedly vow that we will, only to find ourselves outwitted or outmaneuvered or ambushed again. We begin to doubt our ability to keep promises to ourselves, and we lose confidence in our own effectiveness. Our sense of self-worth erodes. Perhaps worst of all, every time we capitulate to emotional blackmail, we lose contact with our integrity, the inner compass that helps us determine what our values and behavior should be. Although emotional blackmail is not heavy-duty abuse, don’t think for a moment that the stakes aren’t high. When we live with emotional blackmail, it eats away at us and escalates until it puts our most important relationships and our whole sense of self-respect in jeopardy.

当我们一次又一次屈服于情感勒索时，付出的代价是巨大的。勒索者的言行让我们感到失衡、羞愧和内疚。我们明明知道自己需要改变现状，也一次又一次地信誓旦旦地保证会改变，却总是发现自己再次被对方耍得团团转，或者被对方耍得团团转，或者再次遭到伏击。我们开始怀疑自己能否信守承诺，也开始对自己的能力失去信心。我们的自尊心逐渐被侵蚀。或许最糟糕的是，每次我们向情感勒索屈服，我们都会失去与自身正直的联系——那份指引我们判断自身价值观和行为准则的内在指南针。虽然情感勒索并非严重的虐待，但千万不要以为它的危害不大。当我们长期遭受情感勒索的折磨时，它会慢慢侵蚀我们，不断升级，最终危及我们最重要的关系和我们全部的自尊。

CHANGING UNDERSTANDING

改变理解

INTO ACTION

付诸行动

I have been a therapist for more than 25 years. In that time, I have treated many thousands of people in a variety of settings, and if there is one sweeping generalization I can make without fear of contradiction, it is that change is the scariest word in the English language. No one likes it, almost everyone is terrified of it, and most people, including me, will become exquisitely creative to avoid it. Our actions may be making us miserable, but the idea of doing anything differently is worse.

我从事心理治疗工作超过25年。这些年来，我在各种不同的环境中治疗过成千上万的人。如果说我能毫不夸张地概括一件事，那就是“改变”是英语中最可怕的词。没有人喜欢改变，几乎每个人都害怕改变，而且大多数人，包括我自己，都会想方设法逃避改变。我们的行为或许让我们痛苦不堪，但改变的想法更让我们感到恐惧。

Yet if there’s one thing I know with absolute certainty, both personally and professionally, it is this: Nothing will change in our lives until we change our own behavior. Insight won’t do it. Understanding why we do the self-defeating things we do won’t make us stop doing them. Nagging and pleading with the other person to change won’t do it. We have to act. We have to take the first step down a new road.

然而，如果说有一件事我无论在个人生活还是职业生涯中都绝对确信无疑，那就是：除非我们改变自身的行为，否则我们的生活不会有任何改变。洞察力无济于事。理解我们为何会做出那些自我挫败的行为并不能让我们停止它们。唠叨和恳求他人改变也无济于事。我们必须行动起来。我们必须迈出踏上新道路的第一步。

A NEW VOCABULARY OF CHOICES

新的选择词汇

All my books have been solution-oriented, and in the second part of this book I will take you step by step through the wide range of choices you have when someone targets you for emotional blackmail. Though we often operate with a constricted view of the choices available to us, we generally have far more options than we realize. And having choice empowers us. I will show you strategies for standing fast in the face of blackmail even when you feel intimidated or afraid, and I’ll help you feel good about yourself as you do. I’ll provide checklists, simple exercises, practice scenarios and specific nondefensive communication techniques. These are techniques I’ve taught and refined over the past 25 years—and they work!

我的所有著作都以解决问题为导向，本书第二部分将一步步引导你了解在遭遇情感勒索时，你可以采取的各种应对措施。虽然我们常常对可选项的认知存在局限，但实际上我们拥有的选择远比我们意识到的要多。而拥有选择权能赋予我们力量。我会向你展示如何在面对勒索时坚定立场，即使你感到害怕或恐惧，并帮助你从中获得自信。我会提供清单、简单练习、情景模拟以及具体的非防御性沟通技巧。这些技巧是我在过去25年中教授和完善的——而且它们行之有效！

Equally important, I will guide you through the vitally important ethical, moral and psychological questions we all struggle with in the face of emotional blackmail, questions like:

同样重要的是，我将引导你思考在面对情感勒索时，我们所有人都会遇到的至关重要的伦理、道德和心理问题，例如：

  • When am I being selfish and when am I being true to my own wants and priorities?
    我什么时候是在自私，什么时候又是在忠于自己的愿望和优先事项？
  • How much can I do or give without feeling resentful or depressed?
    我究竟能做到什么程度，付出多少而不感到怨恨或沮丧？
  • If I give in to the blackmailer, am I violating my integrity?
    如果我向勒索者屈服，我是否违背了自己的正直原则？

I will give you the tools to determine, instance by instance, where your responsibilities to other people begin and end—one of the most important keys to freeing yourself from manipulation.

我将教你如何逐一确定你对他人的责任范围——这是摆脱操控的最重要关键之一。

One of the greatest gifts of this book will be to help you reduce and manage the feelings of guilt that your blackmailers have inspired in you. I will show you how to tolerate the inevitable discomfort that results when you start to change your behavior in the service of breaking free from guilt you don’t deserve. I’ll show you how guilt diminishes the more you act in healthy, self-affirming ways. And I’ll show you that without guilt, the blackmailer is impotent.

这本书最大的价值之一，就是帮助你减轻和控制勒索者在你心中激起的愧疚感。我会告诉你，当你开始改变自己的行为，摆脱这种你不应该承受的愧疚感时，如何忍受随之而来的不适。我会告诉你，当你更多地以健康、积极的方式行事时，愧疚感就会逐渐减轻。我还会告诉你，没有愧疚感，勒索者就无能为力。

I will accompany you through the process of making the major internal shifts that will enable you to abandon your automatic reactions to emotional blackmail and replace them with conscious, positive choices about how far you’re willing to go to accommodate someone at the expense of your own well-being.

我将陪伴你完成重大的内在转变过程，使你能够放弃对情感勒索的自动反应，并用有意识的、积极的选择来取代它们，从而决定你愿意为了迎合他人而牺牲自身福祉到什么程度。

As I help you resist blackmail, I’ll also help you decide when an instance of blackmail is not worth going to the mat about, and even when complying with a blackmailer can actually be smart strategy. In a few extreme cases, the only healthy recourse is to break off from a blackmailer completely, and I’ll deal with why and how to do that when all else has failed.

在我帮助你抵制勒索的同时，我也会帮助你判断何时不值得为之据理力争，甚至在顺从勒索者有时反而是明智之举。在少数极端情况下，唯一明智的做法是彻底断绝与勒索者的关系，我会解释为什么以及如何在其他所有方法都无效时做到这一点。

When we finally gain the understanding and behavioral skills that can free us from the deadening cycle of emotional blackmail, we release incredible excitement and energy.

当我们最终获得能够使我们摆脱情感勒索这种令人窒息的循环的理解和行为技能时，我们会释放出难以置信的兴奋和能量。

“I was able to say no to my boyfriend and realize that his demands were irrational,” my patient Maggie reported to me. “I didn’t do anything to hurt him, even though he would like to pretend I did. And for the first time, I didn’t go beat myself up and call him back 10 minutes later to apologize or give in.”

“我终于能够对男友说‘不’，并且意识到他的要求是不合理的，”我的病人玛吉告诉我。“我没有做任何伤害他的事，尽管他想假装是我伤害了他。而且，我第一次没有自责，也没有在10分钟后打电话给他道歉或妥协。”

I wrote this book for everyone who is struggling to stay close to a lover, parent, colleague or friend who’s strangling an important and otherwise good relationship with the twisted vine of manipulation.

我写这本书是为了帮助所有正在努力与爱人、父母、同事或朋友保持亲密关系的人，这些人正被扭曲的操控手段扼杀着一段重要且原本良好的关系。

Please understand that although I can’t be right there with you as you travel through this process, I will provide moral support every step of the way as you take these sometimes difficult but life-changing actions. I will help you through the important work of building new and healthy relationships—not only with the blackmailers in your life, but also with yourself.

请理解，虽然我无法全程陪伴您走过这段历程，但我会在您采取这些有时艰难却意义非凡的行动时，给予您每一步的精神支持。我会帮助您建立新的、健康的人际关系——不仅是与那些勒索您的人，更是与您自己的关系。

It takes real courage to confront emotional blackmail. This book will give you the power to do it.

对抗情感勒索需要真正的勇气。这本书将赋予你这种力量。

# ↩

Part I

第一部分

Understanding the Blackmail Transaction

了解勒索交易

# ↩

1

Diagnosis: Emotional Blackmail

诊断：情感勒索

The world of emotional blackmail is confusing. While some emotional blackmailers are clear in their threats, others may send us mixed signals, acting kindly much of the time and resorting to blackmail only occasionally. All this makes it difficult to see when a pattern of manipulation is developing in a relationship.

情感勒索的世界令人困惑。有些情感勒索者威胁直白，而另一些则会发出模棱两可的信号，大部分时间表现得和善，只有偶尔才会诉诸勒索。所有这些都使得我们很难察觉一段关系中是否正在形成某种操控模式。

Certainly there are forceful, unambiguous blackmailers who consistently make direct threats about what will happen if you don’t go along with them and spell out the consequences of noncompliance in no uncertain terms: “If you leave me you’ll never see your kids again.” “If you don’t support my project, I’ll hold up your recommendation until you do.” Clear threat, no question of intent.

当然，确实存在一些咄咄逼人、毫不含糊的勒索者，他们会不断直接威胁你，如果你不顺从他们，就会发生什么，并且会毫不含糊地阐明不服从的后果：“如果你离开我，你就再也见不到你的孩子了。”“如果你不支持我的项目，我就扣留你的推荐信，直到你支持为止。”威胁很明确，意图毋庸置疑。

More often, however, emotional blackmail is far more subtle and occurs in the context of a relationship where much is good and positive. We know what the other person is like at his best, and we let our memories of positive experiences overshadow our nagging feeling that something is wrong. Emotional blackmail creeps up on us, edging quietly over the line from normal, acceptable behavior into transactions that are first tinged, then permeated with elements that compromise our well-being.

然而，情感勒索往往更加隐蔽，发生在看似和谐美好的关系之中。我们了解对方最好的一面，因此常常让美好的回忆掩盖内心深处挥之不去的疑虑。情感勒索悄然滋生，逐渐越过正常、可接受行为的界限，最终演变成一种带有损害我们身心健康的隐患的交易。

Before we can label anyone’s behavior emotional blackmail, it has to have certain components. We can make the diagnosis much as a doctor would determine that a person has a physical ailment: by looking at the symptoms. In the example that follows, you’ll see a couple in a love relationship, but the symptoms hold true whether the partners in a conflict are friends, business colleagues or family members. The issues may differ, but the tactics and actions will be the same—and clearly recognizable.

在我们能够将任何人的行为贴上“情感勒索”的标签之前，它必须具备某些要素。我们可以像医生诊断身体疾病一样进行诊断：通过观察症状。在下面的例子中，你会看到一对情侣，但无论冲突双方是朋友、同事还是家人，这些症状都适用。问题可能不同，但策略和行为却相同——而且很容易识别。

THE SIX DEADLY SYMPTOMS

六种致命症状

A young couple I know, Jim and Helen, have been together for just over a year. Helen, a professor of literature at a community college, has huge brown eyes and a broad, perfect smile. She was introduced to Jim at a party, and Jim seemed delightful. Tall and soft-spoken, he’s a successful songwriter. The couple share a great affection for each other. However, for Helen the ease of being with Jim has been draining away. In fact, their relationship has progressed through the six stages of emotional blackmail.

我认识的一对年轻情侣，吉姆和海伦，在一起一年多了。海伦是社区大学的文学教授，她有一双棕色的大眼睛和灿烂的笑容。她在一次聚会上认识了吉姆，吉姆看起来非常讨人喜欢。他身材高大，说话轻声细语，是一位成功的词曲作家。这对情侣彼此深爱着对方。然而，对海伦来说，和吉姆在一起的轻松自在感正在逐渐消失。事实上，他们的关系已经经历了情感勒索的六个阶段。

To give you a clear idea of what the six emotional blackmail symptoms look and feel like, let’s walk through a simplified version of a conflict that came up between Jim and Helen. You’ll notice that some of the symptoms describe Jim’s behavior, and some focus on Helen’s.

为了让你更清楚地了解情感勒索的六种症状，我们来看一个简化版的吉姆和海伦之间的冲突案例。你会注意到，有些症状描述的是吉姆的行为，有些则侧重于海伦的行为。

1: A demand. Jim wants something from Helen. He suggests to her that they’ve been spending so much time with each other, they might as well move in together. “I practically live here already,” he tells her. “Let’s just make it official.” Her apartment is huge, and half his things are there, he adds, so it’ll be a simple transition.

1：吉姆提出了一个要求。他想从海伦那里得到些什么。他建议说，他们最近相处的时间这么多，不如干脆搬到一起住。“我实际上已经住在这里了，”他告诉她，“不如就正式确定下来吧。”他还补充说，她的公寓很大，而且他一半的东西都在里面，所以过渡起来会很轻松。

Sometimes blackmailers don’t verbalize what they want as clearly as Jim did, but instead make us figure it out. Jim might make his point indirectly, perhaps sulking after a friend’s wedding, then letting Helen extract from him, “I wish we could be closer; I get so lonely sometimes,” and eventually saying that he’d like to move in.

有时候，勒索者不会像吉姆那样直白地表达自己的意图，而是让我们自己去揣摩。吉姆可能会用间接的方式表明自己的意思，比如在朋友的婚礼后闷闷不乐，然后让海伦套出一句：“我希望我们能更亲近些；我有时候真的很孤独。”最后，吉姆会说他想搬过来住。

At first blush, Jim’s suggestion sounds loving, and not like a demand at all, but it soon becomes clear that he is set in his course of action and is not willing to discuss or change it.

乍一看，吉姆的建议听起来像是出于爱意，一点也不像是一种要求，但很快就会发现，他已经下定决心，不愿讨论或改变。

2: Resistance. Helen feels uncomfortable about Jim’s moving in and expresses her unwillingness by telling him that she’s not ready for that kind of change in the relationship. She cares deeply for him, but she wants him to have his own place.

2：抵触情绪。海伦对吉姆搬进来感到不自在，她告诉吉姆，她还没准备好接受这种关系上的改变。她很在乎吉姆，但她希望他能有自己的住处。

If she were a less direct person, Helen might resist in other ways. She could withdraw and become less affectionate, or tell him that she’s decided to repaint and he’ll have to take his things home until the job is done. However she expresses her resistance, the message is clear. The answer is no.

如果海伦性格不那么直接，她可能会用其他方式拒绝。她可能会疏远他，变得冷淡，或者告诉他她决定重新粉刷墙壁，他得把东西搬回家，等工程完工后再搬。无论她用什么方式表达拒绝，意思都很明确：答案是否定的。

3: Pressure. When he sees that Helen isn’t giving him the response he wants, Jim does not try to understand her feelings. Rather, he pushes her to change her mind. At first he acts as if he’s willing to talk over the issue with her, but the discussion becomes one-sided and turns into a lecture. He transforms Helen’s statement of resistance into a statement of her deficiencies, and he casts his own desires and demands in the most positive terms: “I only want what’s best for us. I only want to give to you. When two people love each other, they should want to share their lives. Why don’t you want to share yourself with me? If you weren’t so self-centered, you could open up your life a little.”

3：施压。当吉姆发现海伦没有给他想要的回应时，他并没有试图理解她的感受，而是强迫她改变主意。起初，他表现得好像愿意和她好好谈谈，但讨论很快就变成了单方面的说教。他把海伦的抗拒解读成对她缺点的指责，并用最积极的措辞来表达自己的欲望和要求：“我只想对我们好。我只想为你付出。两个人相爱，就应该想要分享彼此的生活。你为什么不愿意和我分享你自己呢？如果你不那么以自我为中心，你就能敞开心扉一些。”

Then he turns on the charm and asks, “Don’t you love me enough to want me here all the time?” Another blackmailer might turn up the pressure by adamantly insisting that his moving in would improve the relationship and bring them closer. Whatever the style, pressure will come into play, though it may be cloaked in benevolent terms—for example, Jim’s letting Helen know how much her reluctance is paining him.

然后他会使出浑身解数，问道：“难道你不够爱我，不想让我一直待在你身边吗？”另一个勒索者可能会加大施压，坚持认为他搬进来会改善彼此的关系，让两人更加亲密。无论采用何种方式，施压都会奏效，尽管它可能披着善意的外衣——例如，吉姆让海伦知道她的不情愿让他多么痛苦。

4: Threats. As Jim continues to hit a wall of resistance, he lets Helen know there will be consequences if she doesn’t give him what he wants. Blackmailers may threaten to cause us pain or unhappiness. They may let us know how much we’re making them suffer. They may also try to tantalize us with promises of what they’ll give us, or how much they’ll love us, if we go along with them. Jim works on Helen with veiled threats: “If you can’t make this kind of commitment to me after all we’ve meant to each other, maybe it’s time for us to see other people.” He doesn’t directly threaten to end the relationship, but the implication is impossible for Helen to miss.

4：威胁。吉姆屡屡碰壁，海伦开始警告他，如果她不满足他的要求，将会面临后果。勒索者可能会威胁要让我们痛苦或不快乐。他们可能会让我们知道我们让他们承受了多少痛苦。他们也可能用各种承诺来诱惑我们，比如如果我们顺从他们，他们会给我们什么，或者他们会多么爱我们。吉姆用隐晦的威胁来对付海伦：“如果我们彼此如此重要，你却不能对我做出这样的承诺，也许我们该各自寻找新的伴侣了。”他没有直接威胁要结束这段关系，但海伦不可能听不懂他话里的意思。

5: Compliance. Helen doesn’t want to lose Jim, and tells herself that perhaps she’s been wrong to say he can’t move in, despite her continuing uneasy feelings. She and Jim only talk superficially about her concerns, and Jim makes no attempt to allay them. A couple of months later, Helen stops resisting, and Jim moves in.

5：顺从。海伦不想失去吉姆，尽管她内心仍然感到不安，但她还是告诉自己，也许当初阻止吉姆搬进来是错的。她和吉姆只是浅尝辄止地谈了谈她的担忧，吉姆也没有试图消除她的疑虑。几个月后，海伦不再抗拒，吉姆搬了进来。

6: Repetition. Jim’s victory ushers in a quiescent period. Now that he’s gotten his way, he removes the pressure, and the relationship appears to stabilize. Helen is still uncomfortable about how things have turned out, but she’s also relieved to have the pressure off and to regain Jim’s love and approval. Jim has seen that pressuring Helen and making her feel guilty is a sure way to get what he wants. And Helen has seen that the fastest way to end Jim’s pressure tactics is to give in. The groundwork is laid for a pattern of demands, pressure and capitulation.

第六章：重复。吉姆的胜利带来了一段平静期。既然他已经如愿以偿，他便不再施加压力，两人的关系似乎也趋于稳定。海伦仍然对事情的最终结果感到不安，但她也松了一口气，因为压力消失了，她重新获得了吉姆的爱和认可。吉姆已经明白，向海伦施压并让她感到内疚是达到目的的捷径。而海伦也明白，摆脱吉姆施压的最快方法就是屈服。这就为接下来的索取、施压和妥协的模式埋下了伏笔。

These six characteristics are at the heart of the emotional blackmail syndrome, and we will be returning to them and exploring them more deeply throughout this book.

这六个特征是情感勒索综合症的核心，我们将在本书中反复提及并更深入地探讨它们。

IF IT’S SO CLEAR, WHY DON’T WE SEE IT?

如果这么清楚，为什么我们看不见？

These symptoms seem so clear, and so troubling, that you’d think alarm bells would go off when they begin to appear. But often we’re immersed in emotional blackmail before we recognize that it’s entangled us. In part this happens because emotional blackmail takes to extremes behavior that we use and encounter all the time: manipulation.

这些症状如此明显，又如此令人不安，你可能会觉得它们一出现就应该敲响警钟。但很多时候，我们深陷情感勒索的泥潭，却浑然不觉自己已被它缠身。部分原因是，情感勒索将我们日常生活中经常使用和遇到的行为——操纵——推向了极端。

Many forms of manipulation aren’t troublesome at all. We all manipulate one another at times, and we all get manipulated. We’ve learned to play a multitude of games to maneuver people into doing what we’d like. One of my favorites is “Gee, I wish someone would open the window,” as opposed to “Could you please open the window?”

许多操纵手段其实根本无伤大雅。我们有时都会操纵别人，有时也会被别人操纵。我们学会了玩各种各样的游戏，以此来操控别人做我们想做的事。我最喜欢的一种说法是“哎，真希望有人能打开窗户”，而不是“你能帮我打开窗户吗？”

It’s amazing how hard it is for many of us to be direct even about minor things, much less when there’s a lot at stake and we want something significant. Why not just ask? Because asking is risky. What if the other person says no? Letting people know what we want in a direct and clear way is something few of us do. We’re afraid to put ourselves on the line by telling the other person what we want or how we’re feeling. What if we end up feeling angry—or worse yet, rejected? If we don’t actually ask, then if the other person says no, it’s not really a no, right? We can explain away any discomfort.

令人惊讶的是，我们很多人即使是小事也很难直言不讳，更何况是事关重大、我们想要得到重要的东西时。为什么不直接问呢？因为问了就意味着冒险。万一对方拒绝了怎么办？很少有人会直接、清晰地表达自己的需求。我们害怕冒险，不敢告诉对方我们想要什么或感受如何。万一我们最终感到生气——或者更糟，被拒绝了怎么办？如果我们不开口问，那么即使对方拒绝了，也算不上真正的拒绝，对吗？我们可以找各种理由来掩饰任何不适。

We can also avoid appearing too aggressive or too needy if we don’t make an outright request. It’s easier to find indirect ways to signal people in hopes that they’ll read between the lines and figure out what we want: “The dog looks like he needs to go out [hint, hint].”

如果我们不直接提出要求，也能避免显得过于咄咄逼人或过于依赖。更容易找到间接的方式来暗示别人，希望他们能领会言外之意，明白我们的意思：“狗狗看起来需要出去一下[暗示]。”

Sometimes we even do this without words. Obvious or subtle hints—a sigh, a pout, what’s known as “that look,” we all use them, and we’re all on the receiving end, even in the best of relationships. But there is a clear point where everyday manipulation turns into something far more harmful. Manipulation becomes emotional blackmail when it is used repeatedly to coerce us into complying with the blackmailer’s demands, at the expense of our own wishes and well-being.

有时我们甚至无需言语就能做到这一点。无论是明显的暗示还是微妙的举动——叹息、撅嘴、那种所谓的“眼神”，我们都使用过，也都曾是接收者，即使在最亲密的关系中也是如此。但日常的操控一旦达到临界点，就会演变成更具危害性的行为。当操控被反复用于胁迫我们屈从于勒索者的要求，而牺牲我们自身的意愿和福祉时，它就变成了情感勒索。

THE RIGHT TO SET LIMITS

设定限制的权利

When we’re talking about emotional blackmail, we’re automatically talking about conflict, power and rights. When one person wants something and the other doesn’t, how hard can each reasonably push? When does another person’s pressure go too far? This is fuzzy territory since we now put so much emphasis on expressing feelings and setting limits. Remember, it’s important that we not label every conflict or expression of strong feelings or especially instances of healthy limit-setting as emotional blackmail.

当我们谈论情感勒索时，我们自然而然地会想到冲突、权力和权利。当一方想要某样东西而另一方不想要时，双方各自可以合理地施加多大的压力？对方施加的压力何时会过分？由于我们现在非常重视表达感受和设定界限，这方面的界限变得模糊不清。请记住，我们不应该把每一次冲突、每一次强烈情感的表达，尤其是健康的界限设定都贴上情感勒索的标签。

To help you discern the distinctions more clearly, I’d like to show you several situations that involve appropriate limit-setting, then let you see what they look like when they’ve crossed the line into emotional blackmail.

为了帮助你更清楚地辨别其中的区别，我想向你展示几个涉及适当设定界限的情况，然后再让你看看当他们越过界限变成情感勒索时会是什么样子。

No Blackmail Here

这里没有勒索

Not long after she sold a photography book she’d been working on for almost a year, my friend Denise related a situation that had come up between her and Amy, a friend who’d been her colleague at an ad agency until they’d both decided to freelance. Denise wondered if Amy was emotionally blackmailing her.

我的朋友丹妮丝花了近一年时间制作的摄影集终于售出后不久，她就跟我讲了她和艾米之间发生的一件事。艾米是她以前在广告公司共事的同事，后来两人都决定做自由职业者。丹妮丝怀疑艾米是不是在情感上勒索她。

As Denise told me,

正如丹妮丝告诉我的那样，

From the beginning, we’d, always been able to talk about anything. We’ve spent hours comparing notes about the struggles of being on our own and the challenges of life after downsizing—both of us started out working for big companies, and both of us sometimes miss it. We talk a lot about the scariness of being on our own, and we do lots of supportive things for each other. We were really close until I told her about working on this book.

从一开始，我们就能无话不谈。我们花了很多时间交流独居的艰辛和裁员后的挑战——我们俩都曾在大公司工作过，有时也会怀念那段时光。我们经常谈论独居的恐惧，也互相扶持。在我们认识之前，我们关系非常亲密，直到我告诉她我在写这本书。

She sounded happy for me, but soon after, she called me up and told me, “You know, I’m feeling kind of jealous. I’m working so hard right now and not much is happening. I’d appreciate it if you just didn’t talk about your work and how excited you are for awhile — it’s a sore spot with me.” So—I said OK. And as though nothing had happened, we switched gears and started talking about what she’s working on.

她听起来为我高兴，但没过多久，她就打电话给我说：“你知道吗，我有点嫉妒你。我现在这么努力工作，却没什么进展。如果你能暂时别再谈论你的工作和你的兴奋之情，我会很感激的——这让我有点难受。”于是，我说好。然后就好像什么都没发生过一样，我们转换了话题，开始聊起她正在做的事情。

Now, if I even mention something about the book, she’ll stop the conversation and say, “It would be best if you and I didn’t talk about that.” It’s beginning to feel like a strain, but I like her, and I’m trying to adjust to playing by her rules.

现在，只要我稍微提起那本书，她就会打断谈话，说：“我们最好别谈这个。” 这让我感觉有点吃力，但我喜欢她，所以我正在努力适应她的规则。

At first blush it may appear that Amy is pressuring Denise in order to get her own way and controlling the interaction between them by deciding what is and isn’t OK to talk about. But in reality, Amy is honestly acknowledging her feelings and taking good care of herself by setting limits on how much she can hear of Denise’s good news. Amy has the right to do that. It’s only human to be envious when someone gets something we want for ourselves, especially if we’re at a low spot in our lives. There are times when all of us want to avoid certain topics, and like Amy, we have a right to set limits. Denise also has the right to decide that she doesn’t like the limits Amy has set and to express her discomfort, or to spend less time with Amy.

乍一看，艾米似乎是在给丹妮丝施加压力，以达到自己的目的，并通过决定哪些话题可以谈论、哪些话题不可以谈论来控制她们之间的互动。但实际上，艾米只是坦诚地承认自己的感受，并通过限制自己能听到多少丹妮丝的好消息来好好照顾自己。艾米有权利这样做。当别人得到我们想要的东西时，感到羡慕是很正常的，尤其是在我们人生低谷的时候。我们每个人都会有想要回避某些话题的时候，就像艾米一样，我们有权设定界限。丹妮丝也有权利不喜欢艾米设定的界限，并表达她的不适，或者减少与艾米相处的时间。

In this situation, Amy has made no threat, either direct or indirect, about what she will do if Denise doesn’t honor her request. There’s also no real pressure, just a statement of needs and feelings. Yes, there’s a conflict. Yes, Denise is uncomfortable with the change in the relationship. Yes, there are some powerful feelings here. But no, this isn’t emotional blackmail.

在这种情况下，艾米既没有直接威胁丹妮丝，也没有间接威胁她如果不满足她的要求会怎么样。她也没有施加任何真正的压力，只是表达了自己的需求和感受。没错，她们之间存在冲突。没错，丹妮丝对这种关系的变化感到不舒服。没错，她们的情感非常强烈。但是，这并非情感勒索。

Crossing the Line

越界

Now let’s look at the same situation and add the component of emotional blackmail. I think you’ll see how the atmosphere and the scenario change. Say that on hearing Denise’s news, Amy’s response is something like this: “I’m so glad to hear about your book project! I know you’ll have a ton of work. Wouldn’t it be great if we could work together on it? I could be your assistant.”

现在我们来看同样的情况，但这次加上情感勒索的因素。我想你会发现气氛和情境会发生怎样的变化。假设艾米听到丹妮丝的消息后，她的反应是这样的：“我很高兴听到你的新书计划！我知道你肯定会非常忙碌。如果我们能一起合作，那该多好啊！我可以做你的助理。”

When Denise says she doesn’t need that kind of help, Amy says, “I thought you were my friend. You know things are rough for me right now. It was tough enough breaking up with Roger, and on top of that, you know how bad the money’s been since I got that huge tax bill. I’ve been so depressed I can hardly work. I thought you were the kind of person who’d help a friend in need.”

当丹妮丝说她不需要那种帮助时，艾米说：“我以为你是我的朋友。你知道我现在处境艰难。和罗杰分手已经够难受了，再加上你也知道自从我收到那笔巨额税单后，我的经济状况有多糟糕。我一直很沮丧，几乎无法工作。我以为你是那种会在朋友需要帮助时伸出援手的人。”

As she meets continuing resistance, Amy turns up the pressure, appealing to Denise’s generosity. “I can’t see how it would hurt you to share your good fortune with me,” she says. “You know I would do the same for you.” She begins to label Denise selfish and greedy, and emphasizes the bleakness of her own situation. At the same time, she threatens to cut off the friendship if she can’t become Denise’s assistant. Finally, Denise gives in.

面对持续的阻力，艾米加大了施压，恳求丹妮丝慷慨大方。“我不明白，你跟我分享你的好运会有什么损失，”她说，“你知道我也会为你这么做的。”她开始指责丹妮丝自私贪婪，并强调自己处境的艰难。与此同时，她威胁说，如果不能成为丹妮丝的助理，她就断绝这段友谊。最终，丹妮丝妥协了。

This scenario contains all the elements of emotional blackmail: a demand, resistance, pressure, threats and compliance. And it’s a scenario just ripe to be repeated.

这种情况包含了情感勒索的所有要素：要求、抵抗、施压、威胁和屈服。而且，这种情景极易重演。

ONE CONFLICT, TWO SOLUTIONS

一个冲突，两种解决方案

Asking someone to refrain from talking about a touchy subject is fairly innocuous. But what if the conflict involves something more serious: a partner’s affair, another person’s drinking problem, someone’s dishonesty at work? In such cases, people may say terrible things to each other, and setting limits may begin to sound like emotional blackmail because feelings are so strong. Yet even here, there’s a sharp distinction between appropriate limit-setting and emotional blackmail. Again, let’s contrast a couple of similar situations.

要求别人不要谈论敏感话题本身并无不妥。但如果冲突涉及更严重的问题呢？比如伴侣出轨、他人酗酒、工作中的不诚实行为？在这种情况下，人们可能会互相说出伤人的话，而设定界限听起来就像是情感勒索，因为情绪如此强烈。然而，即使在这种情况下，恰当的界限设定和情感勒索之间也存在着明显的区别。让我们再次对比几种类似的情况。

The Affair

婚外情

I’ve known my friend Jack and his wife, Michelle, for years, and I’ve always admired their marriage. There’s a large age difference between the two—Jack is 15 years older—but the two of them, both musicians in the symphony, seem to have a rare kind of intimacy. One night, Jack offered to drive me to a meeting of the opera group we both belong to, and on the way home we had a chance to talk. “What makes it work between you two?” I asked. “Who gave you the secret of a perfect marriage?”

我认识我的朋友杰克和他的妻子米歇尔很多年了，我一直很欣赏他们的婚姻。他们俩年龄差距很大——杰克比米歇尔大15岁——但他们都是交响乐团的乐手，彼此之间似乎有一种难得的亲密感。一天晚上，杰克提出开车送我去参加我们共同所属的歌剧小组的聚会，回家的路上我们聊了起来。“你们俩的婚姻秘诀是什么？”我问。“是谁告诉你们婚姻美满的秘诀？”

Jack’s answer wasn’t what I’d expected.

杰克的回答出乎我的意料。

To tell you the truth, things haven’t always been so perfect. At least I haven’t been. I’m going to tell you something very few people know. Three years ago, I did a stupid thing. I started seeing a young woman who was playing with the orchestra as a guest violinist. The affair was short, but I felt guilty as hell. It was dumb. Thoughtless. I couldn’t stand keeping that secret from Michelle, and I knew that I could never be genuinely close to her again unless I confessed. So I made the decision that it was best for me to tell her and risk whatever followed.

说实话，事情并非一直都这么完美。至少对我来说并非如此。我要告诉你一件鲜为人知的事。三年前，我做了件蠢事。我开始和一个在乐团担任客座小提琴手的年轻女子交往。这段婚外情很短暂，但我却为此感到无比愧疚。这太愚蠢了，太不经大脑了。我无法忍受对米歇尔隐瞒这件事，我知道如果我不坦白，就永远无法再和她亲近。所以我决定，对我来说最好的选择就是告诉她，并承担随之而来的一切后果。

At first I thought she was going to kill me. She barely spoke to me for a couple of weeks, and I moved downstairs into the den. But then she surprised me. She said she’d been thinking, and she realized that we needed a plan if we were going to be together for the rest of our lives. She said she was mad as hell, but she wanted to offer me a deal: She’d let the subject drop and she wouldn’t keep rubbing my nose in what I’d done or use it as a club when she wanted something from me. But if I didn’t recommit to her in an exclusive relationship and knock off the crap and go to counseling with her, there was no way we were going to make it together. And if I couldn’t make those commitments, she wouldn’t be able to stay in the marriage, because she wasn’t going to live with insecurity and uncertainty and suspicion.

起初我以为她要杀了我。她好几个星期几乎没跟我说话，我搬下楼去了书房。但后来她却出乎我的意料。她说她一直在思考，意识到如果我们想共度余生，就必须制定一个计划。她说她气疯了，但她想跟我做个交易：她会不再提起这件事，不会再拿我做过的事来烦我，也不会在她想从我这里得到什么的时候拿这件事当把柄。但如果我不重新承诺和她保持专属关系，不再胡闹，并且和她一起去做咨询，我们就没法继续下去了。如果我做不到这些承诺，她也无法继续这段婚姻，因为她无法忍受生活在不安、不确定和猜疑之中。

I told Jack he was fortunate to be dealing with Michelle because she set limits in a healthy way, a process I’ll outline here and discuss in greater depth in the second half of the book. In dealing with Jack, Michelle:

我告诉杰克，他很幸运能和米歇尔相处，因为她能以一种健康的方式设定界限，我将在下文中概述这个过程，并在本书后半部分进行更深入的探讨。在与杰克相处的过程中，米歇尔：

  • Defined her position
    明确了她的立场
  • Stated what she needed
    她说明了自己的需求
  • Laid out what she would and wouldn’t accept
    她列出了自己能够接受和不能接受的条件。
  • Gave Jack the choice of saying yes or no
    让杰克自己选择说“是”或“否”。

Also, she insisted on therapy for both of them.

此外，她坚持要求他们两人都接受心理治疗。

All of us have the right to let others know when their actions are unacceptable to us, just as Michelle did. We all have a basic right not to live with poison in our relationships, whether it’s dishonesty or addictions or any form of abuse.

就像米歇尔一样，我们每个人都有权告诉他人，当他们的行为令我们无法接受时，我们有权表达出来。我们都有基本的权利，不受人际关系中毒毒害的影响，无论是欺骗、成瘾还是任何形式的虐待。

If someone confronts us fairly about something we’ve done, the words and feelings may be strong, but if there are no threats and no pressure, there is no blackmail. Appropriate limit-setting isn’t about coercion, pressure or repeatedly characterizing the other person as flawed. It’s a statement of what kind of behavior we will and won’t allow into our lives.

如果有人就我们的所作所为坦诚地指出我们的错误，言辞和情绪或许会很激烈，但如果没有威胁和压力，就不存在敲诈勒索。恰当的界限设定并非胁迫、施压或反复指责对方的缺点，而是表明我们允许和不允许哪些行为进入我们的生活。

A Blackmailer’s Approach

勒索者的手段

Contrast Michelle’s way of dealing with this crisis with that of a couple I saw as clients a couple of years ago. Stephanie and Bob’s marriage was on the brink, and they came into my office barely speaking to one another. An attractive couple in their late 30s, Bob is a tax attorney with an active practice, and Stephanie sells real estate. Since it was Bob’s idea that they come to see me, I asked him to start the session.

米歇尔处理这场危机的方式，与我几年前接待的一对客户夫妇截然不同。斯蒂芬妮和鲍勃的婚姻岌岌可危，他们走进我的办公室时几乎不说话。这对夫妇相貌堂堂，都年近四十，鲍勃是一位业务繁忙的税务律师，斯蒂芬妮则从事房地产销售。由于是鲍勃提议来找我，所以我请他先开始咨询。

He began,

他开口说道：

I don’t know how much more I can take. I made a horrible mistake 18 months ago and it’s destroying us. I had a short affair with a woman I met on a business trip. I’m totally to blame. This never should’ve happened. But it did. And I’m doing my best to find ways to make it up to Stephanie because I love her and I want to stay with her. We have a good life, two beautiful kids. But my God I’m being treated like a mass murderer. She just won’t let go of it.

我不知道自己还能承受多久。18个月前我犯了个可怕的错误，它正在摧毁我们。我在一次出差中认识了一个女人，并和她发生了短暂的婚外情。这一切都是我的错。这本不该发生。但它还是发生了。我正在尽我所能地想办法弥补斯蒂芬妮，因为我爱她，我想和她在一起。我们生活美满，有两个可爱的孩子。但是天哪，她现在把我当成一个杀人犯。她就是不肯放手。

Now she brings it up every time she wants something. She dictates when her parents will come and stay with us, something as silly as which movie we’re going to see, what I have to buy her to make her happy. Right now she wants to go to Europe at a time when I have a big case coming up, and there’s no way I can take off. I’d love it if she went and took a friend, but she wants what she wants when she wants it. I’m supposed to drop everything and go right then. It’s like I have to because I betrayed her. She’ll say, “You owe me. If you live to a thousand you can’t make up what you did to me.” If I don’t give her her way all the time, she’s going to remind me of what a rat I was. She even put a Post-it on the medicine cabinet saying “cheater.” How can I not give in to her? I’m afraid she’ll leave me if I don’t. It’s true. I was a cheater and I feel awful about it. But I can’t go on like this. How do we get out of this swamp?

现在她每次想要什么东西都要提这件事。她管着她父母什么时候来我们家住，就连看什么电影这种小事都要管，还得我给她买什么东西才能让她开心。现在她想去欧洲，而我马上要处理一个大案子，根本没法走。要是她带个朋友一起去就好了，但她想要什么就一定要立刻得到。好像我应该放下一切马上就去似的。好像我背叛了她，所以不得不去似的。她会说：“你欠我的。就算你活到一千岁也弥补不了你对我的伤害。”如果我不一直顺着她，她就会一直提醒我我以前有多卑鄙。她甚至在药柜上贴了张便签，上面写着“骗子”。我怎么能不答应她呢？我怕如果我不答应她，她会离开我。真的。我作弊了，我为此感到非常愧疚。但我不能再这样下去了。我们该如何摆脱这种困境？

Stephanie, like Michelle, had a right to be angry. But her response to Bob was punitive and controlling. In fact, it was blackmail. Frightened and insecure after she learned of Bob’s affair, Stephanie erroneously believed that she could bind him to her by making him feel so guilty that he would do whatever she wanted. She continually defined him as morally inferior and unworthy, using his transgression as a weapon. Her threat was clear and constant: “If I don’t get what I want, I will make you miserable.” Her message: “I am in control now.”

和米歇尔一样，斯蒂芬妮有理由生气。但她对鲍勃的回应却是惩罚性的、控制性的。事实上，这是一种敲诈勒索。得知鲍勃出轨后，斯蒂芬妮感到恐惧和不安，她错误地认为可以通过让鲍勃感到深深的罪恶感来控制他，让他言听计从。她不断地将鲍勃定义为道德败坏、不值得被爱的人，并将他的过错当作武器。她的威胁清晰而持续：“如果我得不到我想要的，我会让你痛苦不堪。” 她传递的信息是：“现在我说了算。”

A crisis such as an affair can be an experience full of both danger and opportunity. It’s also one of those complex life situations that’s rife with potential for blackmail. Michelle used her experience as a chance to refocus her relationship with Jack and to define what she expected of him, herself and their marriage. But Stephanie got mired in rage and revenge.

婚外情这样的危机既充满危险，也蕴藏机遇。它也是人生中复杂且容易被勒索的局面之一。米歇尔利用这段经历重新审视了她与杰克的关系，并明确了她对杰克、对她自己以及对他们婚姻的期望。但斯蒂芬妮却深陷于愤怒和复仇的泥潭。

The possibilities for hurt or healing exist in any situation in which we’ve chosen to maintain a relationship after a serious transgression: a betrayal by a colleague, a damaging rift in a family, a discovery that we’ve been deceived by a friend. But if both parties are coming from a position of goodwill and truly want to resolve whatever crisis is impairing the relationship, there is no place for emotional blackmail.

在任何情况下，当我们选择在经历严重过错后维持一段关系时，都存在着伤害或治愈的可能性：例如同事的背叛、家庭的破裂、发现自己被朋友欺骗等等。但如果双方都出于善意，真心想要解决任何损害关系的危机，那么情感勒索就毫无立足之地。

WHAT’S THE REAL MOTIVE?

真正的动机是什么？

How can we know if someone is more interested in winning or in resolving the problem? They’re not going to tell us. They’re certainly not going to come out and say, “I don’t care what you want, I’m only trying to get my way.” In an emotionally intense situation, our perceptions get clouded, a condition that gets worse when we’re feeling pressured. The following list will help you diagnose emotional blackmail by allowing you to clarify the intentions and goals behind the other person’s behavior.

我们如何才能知道对方更在意的是赢还是解决问题？他们不会直接告诉我们。他们当然不会直截了当地说：“我不在乎你想要什么，我只想按我的方式来。” 在情绪紧张的情况下，我们的感知会变得模糊，而当我们感到压力时，这种情况会更加严重。以下清单将帮助你识别情感勒索，让你能够厘清对方行为背后的意图和目标。

If people genuinely want to resolve a conflict with you in a fair and caring way, they will:

如果人们真心想以公平和关怀的方式与你解决冲突，他们会：

  • Talk openly about the conflict with you
    坦诚地和你谈谈冲突。
  • Find out about your feelings and concerns
    了解你的感受和担忧
  • Find out why you are resisting what they want
    找出你为什么抗拒他们想要的东西。
  • Accept responsibility for their part of the conflict
    承担他们在冲突中所应承担的责任

As we saw with Michelle and Jack, you can be angry with someone without trying to beat them up emotionally. Disagreements, even strong ones, don’t have to be mixed with insults or negative judgments.

正如我们从米歇尔和杰克的例子中所看到的，你可以对某人生气，但不必在情感上攻击他们。即使是激烈的分歧，也不必夹杂着侮辱或负面评价。

If someone’s primary goal is to win, he or she will:

如果某人的主要目标是获胜，那么他或她会：

  • Try to control you
    试着控制你
  • Ignore your protests
    别理会你的抗议
  • Insist that his or her character and motives are superior to yours
    坚持认为他或她的品格和动机都优于你。
  • Avoid taking any responsibility for the problems between you
    避免承担你们之间任何问题的责任。

When you see that other people are trying to get their way regardless of the cost to you, you’re looking at the bottom-line behavior of the emotional blackmailer.

当你看到其他人不顾你的利益也要达到目的时，你看到的就是情感勒索者的底线行为。

FROM FLEXIBLE TO FROZEN

从可弯曲到冷冻

In looking at situations that might be drifting into emotional blackmail, as well as probing for symptoms and motives, I ask another question: How much flexibility do I have, and allow, in this relationship?

在审视可能正在演变成情感勒索的情况，以及探究其症状和动机时，我会问自己另一个问题：在这段关系中，我拥有多少灵活性，允许多少灵活性？

When emotional blackmail begins to seep into a relationship, we feel a major shift in the atmosphere that surrounds us. As we saw with Stephanie and Bob, the relationship gets stuck. Threats and pressure become a regular part of our everyday interactions. A chill sets in, and we lose much of the flexibility that allows us to navigate smoothly through the rough spots.

当情感勒索开始渗透到一段关系中时，我们会感到周围的气氛发生了巨大的变化。正如我们在斯蒂芬妮和鲍勃的例子中看到的，这段关系陷入了僵局。威胁和压力成了日常互动的一部分。一种寒意袭来，我们失去了许多原本可以用来轻松应对困境的灵活性。

When flexibility is there, we can easily take it for granted. Every day, without much trouble or trauma, we negotiate the myriad details of our existences—what restaurant to eat in, what movie to go to, what color to paint the living room or where to hold the office picnic. Actually, in many cases, the outcome doesn’t matter too much, and the person with the strongest preference usually wins by default. But despite normal disagreements and manipulation, there’s a rhythm of give and take, a sense of balance and fairness. We can give in to many things with little negative effect and replenish our egos and energies quickly. At the same time, we also expect others to give us our way from time to time.

当拥有灵活性时，我们很容易将其视为理所当然。每天，我们都能轻松地处理生活中的无数细节——去哪家餐厅吃饭、看哪部电影、客厅刷什么颜色，或者公司野餐在哪里举行。事实上，在很多情况下，结果并不那么重要，通常情况下，意愿最强烈的人会不由自主地胜出。但即便存在正常的争执和博弈，其中也存在着一种互惠互利的节奏，一种平衡和公平感。我们可以对很多事情做出让步，而不会产生太大的负面影响，并迅速恢复我们的自尊和精力。与此同时，我们也希望别人时不时地顺从我们。

When the willingness to compromise begins to disappear, the status quo becomes the template for the future. It’s as though we’re not allowed to change, or move away from a role that may not always fit. We’re frozen.

当妥协的意愿开始消失时，现状就成了未来的模板。仿佛我们被禁止改变，或者放弃一个可能并不总是适合自己的角色。我们被冻结了。

When I was a kid, my friends and I used to play a game called freeze tag in which the object was to escape being touched by the person who was It. If you were tagged, you had to freeze in place and not move until the game was over. A lawn where the game was in progress wound up looking like a sculpture garden, scattered with kids holding themselves in odd, shocked-looking positions. Emotional blackmail is a lot like freeze tag, but it’s not a game anymore. Once blackmail has touched a relationship, it becomes rigid, stuck in patterns of demands and capitulation. We’re not allowed to adjust our stances or change positions.

小时候，我和朋友们常玩一种叫“冻结捉迷藏”的游戏，目标是躲开“捉人者”的触碰。如果被抓住了，就必须一动不动地待在原地，直到游戏结束。游戏进行时，草坪上到处都是孩子们摆出各种奇特、惊恐的姿势，活像一座雕塑花园。情感勒索很像“冻结捉迷藏”，但它不再是游戏了。一旦勒索渗透到一段关系中，它就会变得僵化，陷入索取和屈服的循环模式。我们被禁止调整立场或改变位置。

Allen is a bright, funny man who owns a small furniture company. But he was grim the first time he came to see me as he described his problems with his new wife, Jo.

艾伦是个聪明风趣的人，拥有一家小型家具公司。但他第一次来见我时，神情阴郁，向我倾诉他和新婚妻子乔之间的问题。

“I thought Jo was just what I wanted—she’s gorgeous, she’s got a great sense of humor, she’s smart,” he began.

“我觉得乔正是我想要的那种人——她很漂亮，很有幽默感，也很聪明，”他说道。

“Sounds good to me,” I said. “So why the long face?”

“听起来不错，”我说。“那你为什么愁眉苦脸的呢？”

I just don’t know if this is going to work. I know she loves me, but I don’t like what’s happening to us. If I suggest that we spend any time apart—my friends are always bugging me to go to movies or hang out after work—she acts really hurt. She looks at me with those big sad eyes and says, “What’s the matter? You’re bored with me? You don’t want to be with me anymore? I thought you were wild about me.” If I start to make plans, she pouts, pleads with me and lets me know how unhappy I’m making her in no uncertain terms. I didn’t know she was so needy. I’m fine if she wants to go off with her friends, but she wants to do less and less of that. It’s like she wants to be in my pocket. One time I actually got brave enough to go out with my friends anyway, and she wouldn’t speak to me for the rest of the week. I thought she was the one — she’s great—but I’m feeling a lot of resentment. We have such a good relationship in so many ways. But dammit, she sure likes to get her own way.

我不知道这段感情还能不能继续下去。我知道她爱我，但我并不喜欢我们现在的关系。如果我提议我们分开一段时间——我的朋友们总是缠着我下班后去看电影或者一起出去玩——她就会装出一副很受伤的样子。她会用那双可怜兮兮的大眼睛看着我，问：“怎么了？你觉得我无聊了吗？你不想和我在一起了吗？我还以为你很爱我呢。”如果我开始计划约会，她就会撅嘴，苦苦哀求，毫不含糊地告诉我我让她有多不开心。我以前不知道她这么黏人。如果她想和朋友们出去玩，我没意见，但她越来越不想这么做了。感觉她好像想把我牢牢地控制住。有一次，我鼓起勇气还是和朋友们出去了，结果她整整一个星期都没理我。我原以为她就是我的真命天女——她真的很好——但我现在却感到非常怨恨。我们在很多方面都相处得很好。但该死的，她总是喜欢随心所欲。

Often when needy, dependent people get into relationships, they panic when their partner wants to enjoy activities apart from them. They experience abandonment fears and rejection anxiety, and rather than talking about those fears, they hide them. They’re adults, after all, and “supposed” to be independent, not feeling like scared little kids. As Jo saw Allen wanting more freedom, instead of being able to talk about her feelings, she expressed them indirectly. She made Allen feel guilty when he wanted to do a perfectly normal thing like going out by himself.

通常情况下，依赖性强的人一旦进入恋爱关系，当伴侣想要独自享受一些活动时，他们就会感到恐慌。他们会感到被抛弃的恐惧和被拒绝的焦虑，但与其说出来，不如把这些恐惧藏在心底。毕竟，他们是成年人，理应独立，而不是像胆小的小孩一样。乔看到艾伦想要更多自由，却无法直接表达自己的感受，而是选择了间接的方式。当艾伦想要独自外出这种完全正常的事情时，她却让他感到内疚。

Allen was doing his best to understand her.

艾伦竭尽全力去理解她。

She had a tough time as a kid, so I know why she’s so needy. I don’t blame her for feeling insecure. Some days it feels great to have a woman who wants me so much she won’t let me out of her sight. But to tell you the truth, it’s starting to get me down. She gets what she wants by making me feel so damn guilty all the time. And I feel like a wimp always giving in to her.

她小时候过得很艰难，所以我明白她为什么这么需要人照顾。我不怪她缺乏安全感。有时候，有个女人如此渴望我，寸步不离地跟着我，这种感觉确实很棒。但说实话，这开始让我感到沮丧。她总是让我感到内疚，以此来达到她的目的。而我总是对她百依百顺，觉得自己像个懦夫。

Though he didn’t want to admit it to himself, Allen realized that behind Jo’s pleading looks and those charming, loving-sounding statements, there was a demand, backed up by well-placed pressure. Jo expected him to spend all his free time with her—that was the only role she willingly allowed him to take. He wasn’t allowed to have activities or interests of his own. But Allen did something that many targets of emotional blackmail do, particularly at the beginning: He gave Jo the benefit of the doubt and rationalized away her clinginess because of his compassion for her difficult childhood and his deep feelings for her now.

尽管艾伦不愿承认，但他意识到，在乔恳求的眼神和那些动听甜言蜜语的背后，隐藏着一种要求，以及精心设计的施压。乔希望他把所有空闲时间都花在她身上——这是她唯一心甘情愿让他扮演的角色。他不被允许拥有自己的活动或兴趣。但艾伦做了许多情感勒索的受害者都会做的事，尤其是在一开始：他选择相信乔，并因为同情她坎坷的童年以及自己对她深厚的感情而为她的依赖辩解。

He also did what many people do when they are pressured by neediness or possessiveness: He misinterpreted it as a sign of how much she cared about him. As we will see throughout this book, understanding and compassion get you nowhere with an emotional blackmailer. In fact, they only add fuel to the blackmail flames.

他也像许多人一样，在被依赖或占有欲驱使时，会做出同样的选择：他误以为这是她对他的关心。正如我们将在本书中看到的，对付情感勒索者，理解和同情毫无用处。事实上，它们只会火上浇油，助长勒索之火。

Once you discern the symptoms of emotional blackmail in any relationship, you may feel as though a rug’s been pulled out from under you. Suddenly you realize you don’t really know your lover, or your parent, or your brother, or your boss, or your friend. Something’s been lost. There’s little room for compromise or flexibility. There’s no balance of power, no sense that one of you gets your way one time, the other the next. Where no “payment” was previously required for love and respect, being in the good graces of blackmailers increasingly depends on giving them their way.

一旦你察觉到任何关系中存在情感勒索的迹象，你可能会感觉就像脚下的地毯被抽走了一样。你突然意识到，你其实并不了解你的爱人、父母、兄弟姐妹、老板或朋友。有些东西已经失去了。妥协和灵活变通的空间变得很小。权力不再平衡，不再是轮流占便宜的感觉。以前，爱和尊重不需要任何“代价”，而现在，要想博得勒索者的欢心，就越来越依赖于顺从他们。

# ↩

2

The Four Faces of Blackmail

勒索的四种面孔

“If you really loved me . . .”

“如果你真的爱我……”

“Don’t leave me or I’ll . . .”

“别离开我，否则我会……”

“You’re the only one who can help me . . .”

“只有你能帮我……”

“I could make things easy for you if you’d just . . .”

“如果你愿意的话，我可以帮你把事情办得轻松些……”

In blackmail-speak, all of these statements are ways of putting a demand on the table. Yet they appear to be markedly different because each reflects a singular blackmail type. When we look closely at emotional blackmail, what seems to be one kind of behavior splits into four varieties, distinct as the bands of color that appear when you pass a beam of light through a prism.

在勒索的语境中，所有这些说法都是提出要求的方式。然而，它们表面上看起来截然不同，因为每一种都反映了一种特定的勒索类型。当我们仔细观察情感勒索时，看似同一种行为实际上可以细分为四种类型，就像光束穿过棱镜时呈现出的色带一样，彼此之间差异显著。

Punishers, who let us know exactly what they want—and the consequences we’ll face if we don’t give it to them—are the most glaring. They may express themselves aggressively, or they may smoulder in silence, but either way, the anger they feel when thwarted is always aimed directly at us. Self-punishers, who occupy the second category, turn the threats inward, emphasizing what they’ll do to themselves if they don’t get their way. Sufferers are talented blamers and guilt-peddlers who often make us figure out what they want, and always conclude that it is up to us to ensure that they get it. Tantalizers put us through a series of tests and hold out a promise of something wonderful if we’ll just give them their way.

惩罚者会毫不掩饰地告诉我们他们想要什么，以及如果我们不满足他们将会面临的后果，这类人最为显眼。他们可能表现得咄咄逼人，也可能默默地暗暗发火，但无论哪种方式，当他们的愿望落空时，他们的怒火总是直接指向我们。自我惩罚者属于第二类，他们会将威胁转向自身，强调如果得不到满足，他们会如何惩罚自己。受苦者擅长指责和制造罪恶感，他们常常让我们自己去揣摩他们的意图，并最终得出结论：确保他们得到满足是我们的责任。诱惑者会让我们经历一系列考验，并许诺如果我们顺从他们，就会得到美好的回报。

Each type of blackmailer operates with a different vocabulary, and each gives a peculiar spin to the demands, pressure, threats and negative judgments that go into blackmail. These differences can make blackmail difficult to detect, even when you think you’re savvy enough to recognize it. If you think all birds look like eagles, you might be shocked when someone tells you the swan that just floated by was a bird, too. The same kind of cognitive dissonance occurs when an unexpected form of emotional blackmail appears in your life.

每种类型的勒索者都使用不同的语言，他们对勒索中的要求、施压、威胁和负面评价也都有着各自独特的解读。这些差异使得勒索难以察觉，即使你自认为足够精明，能够识别它。如果你认为所有的鸟都长得像鹰，那么当有人告诉你刚才游过的天鹅也是鸟时，你可能会感到震惊。当生活中出现意想不到的情感勒索时，也会产生类似的认知失调。

But once you understand the four faces of blackmail, you can begin to see the danger signs in another person’s actions and develop an early-warning system that can help you to predict, prepare for and even prevent emotional blackmail.

但是，一旦你了解了勒索的四种面孔，你就可以开始看到他人行为中的危险信号，并建立一个预警系统，帮助你预测、准备甚至预防情感勒索。

THE PUNISHER

惩罚者

I’ve begun this field guide to the blackmail quartet with the most blatant blackmailers—the punishers—not because they’re necessarily the most prevalent but because they’re the most obvious. It’s impossible to be unaware that you’ve crossed punishers, because any perceived resistance incurs immediate anger. They may express that anger aggressively, with direct threats—I call this group the active punishers—or unleash a smouldering fury, the mode of passive punishers. Whatever their style, punishers want relationships in which the balance of power is totally one-sided: “My way or the highway” is the punisher’s motto. No matter what you feel or need, punishers override you. They cancel you out.

我之所以从最明目张胆的勒索者——惩罚者——开始这篇勒索四重奏指南，并非因为他们最普遍，而是因为他们最显而易见。你不可能意识不到自己得罪了惩罚者，因为任何被他们察觉的反抗都会立即激怒他们。他们可能会以咄咄逼人的方式表达愤怒，直接发出威胁——我称这类人为主动惩罚者——或者释放一种暗流涌动的怒火，这是被动惩罚者的惯用伎俩。无论他们采用何种方式，惩罚者都渴望建立一种权力完全一边倒的关系：“要么听我的，要么滚蛋”是惩罚者的座右铭。无论你的感受或需求是什么，惩罚者都会凌驾于你之上。他们会彻底否定你。

Active Punishers

积极惩罚者

“If you go back to work, I’ll leave you.”

“如果你回去工作，我就离开你。”

“If you don’t take over the family business, I’ll cut you out of my will.”

“如果你不接管家族企业，我就把你从遗嘱里除名。”

“If you try to divorce me, you’ll never see your kids again.”

“如果你要跟我离婚，你再也见不到你的孩子了。”

“If you won’t accept this overtime, you can forget about asking for a promotion.”

“如果你不接受加班，就别想要求升职了。”

These statements are strong—and they’re scary. They’re also highly effective because they give us a sharp picture of what will happen if we don’t give aggressive punishers their way. They can make our lives miserable, or at the very least unpleasant. Punishers may not always realize the full impact of their words or notice how often they threaten to disapprove of us, let others know how terrible we are or take away something that is important to us. Punishers may not carry through on a threat 19 times out of 20, and they may be quite pleasant in the calms between storms, but because the threatened consequences can be serious, we live in fear of the one time the active punisher follows through.

这些话掷地有声，令人胆寒。它们之所以如此有效，是因为它们清晰地描绘出，如果我们不顺从那些咄咄逼人的惩罚者，将会发生什么。他们会让我们的生活苦不堪言，或者至少会让我们感到不快。惩罚者可能并不总是意识到自己话语的全部影响，或者注意到他们有多少次威胁要否定我们、让别人知道我们有多糟糕，或者夺走对我们重要的东西。惩罚者或许二十次里有十九次都不会真的付诸行动，在风平浪静的时候他们可能表现得相当和善，但正因为威胁的后果可能很严重，我们才生活在恐惧之中，害怕他们真的会付诸行动。

Liz, a thin, dark-eyed woman with a low, quiet voice, came to see me, as so many women have over the years, for help in figuring out if there was anything she could salvage of a romance that had become a cold and emotionally abusive marriage. She had met Michael at a training session for computer salespeople several years out of high school, and as they worked on a team project, she’d been impressed by his authoritative way with people and his ability to cut to the core of any problem. His good looks only sweetened the package.

莉兹身材纤瘦，黑眼睛，声音低沉轻柔。像这些年来许多女性一样，她来找我寻求帮助，想知道自己那段已经变成冷漠且充满情感虐待的婚姻是否还有挽回的余地。高中毕业几年后，她在一次电脑销售员培训会上认识了迈克尔。在一次团队项目中，她被迈克尔权威的待人方式和直击问题核心的能力所折服。他英俊的外表更是锦上添花。

Michael seemed terrific in the beginning. He was caring and responsible, and there are still a lot of good times. So it took me a long time to see what a control freak he was. Within a year after we were married, I was pregnant with the twins, and I settled right into the routines and demands of motherhood. When the twins were finally in school, I thought I’d better head back to school myself. In our field, you have to either keep up or get out. But Michael believes that mothers of school-age kids belong at home. Period. He’s swatted me down every time I’ve asked for his ideas about what we can do about day care and tuition.

起初，迈克尔看起来很棒。他体贴又负责，我们之间也有很多美好的时光。所以，我花了很长时间才发现他是个控制狂。结婚不到一年，我就怀上了双胞胎，很快就适应了为人母的各种日常琐事和挑战。等到双胞胎终于上学后，我觉得我也应该重返校园。在我们这个行业，要么跟上时代，要么就得退出。但迈克尔认为，学龄儿童的母亲就应该待在家里。就这么简单。每次我问他关于托儿所和学费的问题，他都会一口回绝。

I got so frustrated that I told him I didn’t know if I wanted to stay in a marriage with him. And that’s when things got crazy. He told me that if I leave him, he’ll get all the money and leave me out on the street. He was like a total stranger. “You like living in a nice house? You like your lifestyle?” he said to me. “You just think about filing for divorce and I’ll see you out on the curb like a bag lady. And once my lawyer gets through with you, they’ll never let you near the kids again. So knock off the crap about divorce and behave yourself.” I have no way of knowing if he’s full of hot air or if he’d go that far to hurt me. So I told my lawyer to stop everything and I canceled the divorce proceedings. Right now I just hate him, and I don’t know what to do.

我实在太沮丧了，就告诉他我不知道自己是否还想继续这段婚姻。事情就此变得一发不可收拾。他威胁我说，如果我离开他，他会拿走所有的钱，把我赶出家门。他就像个陌生人一样。“你喜欢住这么好的房子吗？你喜欢现在的生活方式吗？”他问我，“你要是敢提离婚，我就让你像个流浪汉一样流落街头。等我的律师把你处理完，他们就再也不会让你靠近孩子了。所以别再胡扯什么离婚了，老实点。” 我不知道他是不是在吹牛，还是真的会做出这种事来伤害我。所以我让我的律师停止一切，取消了离婚程序。现在我恨透了他，不知道该怎么办。

As Liz found, there is no more fertile ground for punishers than marital difficulty, the end of a love relationship or a divorce. Perhaps the most powerful blackmailers are individuals like Michael, who at times of overwhelming stress and pain can threaten to make their target’s life even more miserable by cutting off financial resources or contact with the children—and who pour on any other punishment they can think of.

正如莉兹所发现的，没有什么比婚姻危机、恋情破裂或离婚更能滋生惩罚者的温床了。也许最厉害的勒索者就是像迈克尔这样的人，他们在承受着巨大的压力和痛苦时，会威胁要切断受害者的经济来源或剥夺其与孩子的联系，从而让受害者的生活更加痛苦——并且还会施加他们能想到的任何其他惩罚。

People trying to deal with punishers are always between a rock and a hard place. If they resist and try to hold their ground, they run the risk that the punisher will actually carry through on the threat. If they capitulate, or at least buy some time, they find themselves swimming in a cauldron of rage: rage at the blackmailer for creating such an oppressive and constricting situation, and at themselves for not having the guts to put up a fight.

面对勒索者，人们总是进退两难。如果他们反抗并坚持立场，勒索者很可能真的会兑现威胁。如果他们屈服，或者至少争取一些时间，他们就会发现自己陷入愤怒的漩涡：既愤怒于勒索者制造了如此压迫和束缚的局面，又愤怒于自己没有勇气反抗。

Kids R Us

儿童反斗城

It’s not surprising that many of the people who’ve mastered the art of turning otherwise competent adults into children are parents. Often our parents need to maintain control over us long after we’ve left the nest, feeling it is their job to help determine whom we should marry, how we should raise our children, where we should live and how. They can wield enormous power because of our loyalty to them as well as our lifelong fear of incurring their disapproval. That fear can loom large when parents turn up the pressure on us, using wills or the promise of money to cement their authority and our obedience.

许多擅长把原本能力出众的成年人变成孩子的人都是父母，这并不令人惊讶。即便我们早已离家独立，父母仍然需要对我们保持控制，因为他们觉得有责任决定我们应该和谁结婚、如何养育子女、在哪里生活以及如何生活。他们之所以能拥有如此巨大的权力，是因为我们对他们的忠诚，以及我们终生害怕遭到他们的反对。当父母加大对我们施加的压力，利用遗嘱或金钱承诺来巩固他们的权威和我们的服从时，这种恐惧感会更加强烈。

My client Josh, a 32-year-old furniture designer, has met the love of his life, an enthusiastic businesswoman named Beth. He’s wildly happy, and there’s only one problem: his father, Paul.

我的客户乔什是一位32岁的家具设计师，他遇到了此生挚爱——一位热情洋溢的女商人贝丝。他欣喜若狂，但只有一个问题：他的父亲保罗。

My dad has always been devout — we’re Catholic—and everyone has always married within the church. Just my luck, I fell in love with a Jewish girl I met playing racquetball! I tried to talk to Dad about it, but he went crazy. If I marry Beth, he’s threatened not to co-sign the loan for my business, which I’ve built all my plans on, and to cut me out of his will. And you know what? He might do it. I can’t bring Beth home or even mention her, and it’s ridiculous. There’s no point in talking to Dad about this — I’ve tried. He makes the pronouncement that this subject is not to be discussed again and walks out of the room. I keep asking myself, Am I for sale? How much is my soul worth? Am I supposed to stop seeing my family, or is it better to go on lying to them and pretending Beth doesn’t exist? This is killing me. It’s more than money — I’ve always been close to my family, and now I can’t go home without lying.

我爸一直很虔诚——我们是天主教徒——而且我们家一直都是在教堂里结婚的。真是倒霉，我居然爱上了一个打壁球时认识的犹太女孩！我试着跟爸爸谈这件事，但他却勃然大怒。他威胁说，如果我娶了贝丝，他就不给我公司贷款做担保，而我所有的计划都寄托在这个公司上，他还威胁要把我从遗嘱里除名。你知道吗？他真有可能这么做。我不能把贝丝带回家，甚至不能提起她，这太荒谬了。跟爸爸谈这件事根本没用——我已经试过了。他宣布以后不能再谈这个话题，然后就走出了房间。我一直在问自己，我是不是可以被出卖？我的灵魂值多少钱？我应该从此不再见家人吗？还是继续对他们撒谎，假装贝丝不存在更好？这快把我逼疯了。这不仅仅是钱的问题——我一直和家人关系很亲密，现在不撒谎就没法回家了。

Parents who are punishers often make their children choose between them and other people they love, setting up a situation in which any choice is seen as betrayal. And their blackmailed children often cling to the fantasy that if they give up a “flawed” partner for the sake of making peace in the family this time, next time they’ll be able to find someone who passes the test. Of course, it is just a fantasy. Parents using this kind of blackmail will inevitably find a flaw in the next person, and the next, and in anyone who represents a threat to their control.

那些喜欢惩罚孩子的父母常常逼迫孩子在自己和其他所爱之人之间做出选择，从而制造出一种任何选择都被视为背叛的局面。而那些被勒索的孩子往往会抱有一种幻想：如果这次为了家庭和睦而放弃一个“有缺陷”的伴侣，下次就能找到一个“合格”的人。当然，这仅仅是幻想。使用这种勒索手段的父母，必然会在下一个人身上找到缺陷，再下一个，以及任何对他们的控制构成威胁的人身上都找到缺陷。

Josh bent over backward trying to placate Paul while at the same time holding on to what he wanted for himself. No matter which way he looked, he could see only choices that compromised his integrity. He could give in to his father, which wasn’t an acceptable option—he had no intention of giving up Beth—or he could pretend to go along and live a lie.

乔什竭尽全力安抚保罗，同时又坚守着自己的利益。无论他怎么想，看到的都只有违背他原则的选择。他可以向父亲妥协，但这绝不是他能接受的——他绝不会放弃贝丝——或者他也可以假装顺从，活在谎言之中。

As we maneuver to avoid the wrath of punishers and the aggressive way they manipulate us, we may find ourselves doing things that amaze us—lying, keeping secrets, sneaking around—to maintain the illusion of obeying them. Behaving as though we’re still rebellious teenagers, and violating our own standards, adds to what may already be a significant load of self-reproach born out of the failure to stand up to the blackmailer.

为了躲避惩罚者的怒火和他们咄咄逼人的操控，我们可能会做出一些令自己都感到惊讶的事情——撒谎、保守秘密、偷偷摸摸——以维持服从他们的假象。这种如同叛逆少年般的行为，违背了我们自身的准则，无疑会加重我们因未能挺身反抗勒索者而产生的沉重自责。

The Silent Treatment

冷战

Punishers needn’t be articulate, or even speak, to get their message across. As compelling as the blackmailers we’ve seen so far are the sulkers and nontalkers who retreat behind unverbalized anger.

惩罚者无需能言善辩，甚至无需开口，就能传达他们的信息。正如我们目前所见的勒索者一样，那些默默生闷气、沉默寡言，将怒火藏于无声愤怒背后的人，也同样令人信服。

Jim, the songwriter we met in the last chapter , revealed himself as a silent punisher soon after he moved in with Helen, and her description of his style of pressuring her is a prime example of this style of blackmail.

我们在上一章中认识的作曲家吉姆，在搬去和海伦同住后不久，就展现出他沉默的惩罚者本性，而海伦对他的施压方式的描述，正是这种敲诈勒索方式的典型例子。

I don’t know what to do about Jim. When he gets upset with me, he clams up and goes a million miles away. I know he’s mad, but he won’t talk it out. The other night, I got home late with a pounding headache. My classes had been grueling, and my department head needed a staffing report from me to submit with his budget—no rest for the weary. Jim made me dinner, lit some candles and gave me a fabulous welcome home, and I was really touched. He’s such a sweet man. When he wanted to cuddle on the couch later on, I knew what was coming—he wanted to make love. Ordinarily, that would be a treat.
