But my head was still pounding, I was still thinking about things I hadn’t done at work, and I felt about as sexy as a paper bag. I tried to tell him as nicely as I could that this was not a good time for me, and could I have a rain check. But he took it all wrong. He didn’t yell, he didn’t even say a word. He tightened his jaw, gave me one of those dark looks of his and walked away. Next thing I knew, the den door slammed shut and the stereo was blaring from inside.

我不知道该怎么对付吉姆。他一生我的气，就闭口不谈，仿佛消失得无影无踪。我知道他生气了，但他就是不肯好好沟通。前几天晚上，我头痛欲裂地回到家。课程安排得满满当当，系主任还要我提交一份人员配置报告，好跟他的预算一起交上去——真是累得够呛。吉姆给我做了晚饭，点了蜡烛，热情地欢迎我回家，我真的很感动。他真是个贴心的人。后来他想在沙发上和我依偎一会儿，我知道接下来会发生什么——他想和我亲热。平时，这当然是件好事。但我当时头痛得厉害，脑子里还想着工作上没做完的事情，感觉自己一点魅力都没有。我尽量委婉地告诉他，我现在不方便，能不能改天再约。但他完全误解了我的意思。他没吼叫，甚至一句话也没说。他咬紧牙关，狠狠地瞪了我一眼，然后转身就走。我还没反应过来，书房的门就砰的一声关上了，里面的音响开得震天响。

The hard, cold silence of these punishers is difficult for almost anyone to bear, and we’d almost sell our souls to avoid having to live with it. “Say anything,” we plead. “Yell at me. Anything is better than this silence.” Usually, the more we try to get sulkers to tell us what’s wrong, the more they withdraw and withhold, terrified of confronting us or their own anger.

这些惩罚者冷酷无情的沉默几乎无人能忍受，我们几乎愿意出卖灵魂来逃避。“说点什么吧，”我们恳求道，“冲我吼叫。任何事都比这沉默好。” 通常，我们越是想让闷闷不乐的人说出发生了什么，他们就越是退缩、越是隐瞒，害怕面对我们，也害怕面对自己的怒火。

I didn’t know what to do. I felt this horrible pang of guilt. He’d been so romantic, and I was so cold. So I went in and tried talking to him. He sat there and looked right through me, then he said, “Don’t talk to me.” I had to do something to make up. So I put on a white satin nightgown, went back into the den, put my arms around his neck and told him how sorry I was. We ended up making love right there. It sounds kind of sexy, but it wasn’t at all for me. I still had this headache, I felt so tense I could’ve snapped in two, and it was awful. But I guess I was desperate to get him to talk to me. I couldn’t stand the silent treatment one more time.

我不知道该怎么办。我感到一阵强烈的内疚。他那么浪漫，而我却那么冷漠。于是我走进去，试着和他说话。他坐在那里，眼神空洞地看着我，然后说：“别跟我说话。”我必须做点什么来弥补。所以我穿上一件白色缎面睡衣，回到书房，搂住他的脖子，告诉他我有多么抱歉。我们最后就在那里发生了关系。听起来好像很性感，但对我来说却完全不是。我仍然头痛欲裂，感觉浑身紧绷，仿佛随时都会崩溃，真是糟糕透了。但我猜我当时是太渴望他跟我说话了。我再也无法忍受他的冷暴力了。

Silent punishers barricade themselves behind an impenetrable facade and deflect any responsibility for their feelings onto us. Like Helen, we’re in turmoil when someone is punishing us this way. We can feel their anger silently building, and we know that we are its target. They trap us in a pressure cooker of stress and tension, and most of us, like Helen, will quickly give in to them because it’s the fastest way we know to find relief.

沉默的惩罚者把自己封闭在坚不可摧的外表之下，并将他们感受的责任全部推卸给我们。就像海伦一样，当有人这样惩罚我们时，我们内心充满煎熬。我们能感受到他们怒火的暗流涌动，也知道自己是他们发泄的对象。他们把我们困在压力和紧张的漩涡中，而我们大多数人，就像海伦一样，会很快屈服于他们，因为这是我们所知的最快获得解脱的方式。

Double Punishment

双重惩罚

When you have a dual relationship—your lover is your boss, or your best friend is your business partner—the potential for punishment rises exponentially. A punisher can, and often will, carry any turmoil from one relationship into the other.

当你身处双重关系——比如你的爱人是你的老板，或者你的挚友是你的事业伙伴——惩罚的可能性会呈指数级增长。惩罚者可以，而且往往会，将一段关系中的任何冲突带到另一段关系中。

My client Sherry is 28, an ambitious, model-pretty woman who was extremely agitated when she first came to me, trying to break off a romance with the man she works for. Sherry decided to become a secretary to get an inside look at the film business and quickly became assistant to the head of a special-effects house, a volatile 52-year-old filmmaker named Charles. Charles, like Sherry, had an Ivy League education, and they share a love for obscure silent movies and modern art. Sherry was immediately attracted to a man who would take her seriously. Their conversations are lively, and because of her position Charles makes her privy to the inner workings of his business and deal-making. He’s been grooming her for months to become his operations manager, a position from which she can participate in meetings with clients and help shape the business.

我的客户雪莉今年28岁，是一位雄心勃勃、容貌姣好的女性。她第一次来找我时情绪非常激动，试图结束与她老板的恋情。雪莉决定先做秘书，以便深入了解电影行业，很快就成为了特效公司老板查尔斯的助理。查尔斯是一位脾气暴躁的52岁电影人。和雪莉一样，查尔斯也毕业于常春藤盟校，他们都热爱冷门默片和现代艺术。雪莉立刻被查尔斯认真对待她的态度所吸引。他们的谈话生动有趣，由于雪莉的职位，查尔斯让她了解他公司内部的运作和交易细节。几个月来，查尔斯一直在培养她成为运营经理，让她能够参与客户会议，并帮助公司制定发展战略。

Sherry’s friends warned her not to get involved with her boss, particularly since he’s married, but Charles was more interesting to her than men her age, and though she wasn’t initially attracted to him, the long hours and the intensity of their work together pulled them close. The building sexual tension between them finally culminated in an intense romantic relationship.

雪莉的朋友们警告她不要和老板查尔斯交往，尤其因为他已婚。但查尔斯比同龄男人更吸引她，虽然她一开始并没有被他吸引，但长时间的工作和高强度的工作环境让他们逐渐亲近。两人之间不断滋生的性张力最终发展成了一段热烈的恋情。

I know, I know. Rule number one is never, ever have an affair with your boss. But Charles is a remarkable man. No one ever got to me in the way he does. I loved seeing how his mind works, and also his worldliness. He has so much to teach, and I felt like I won the prize of being his star student. I loved the intimacy, knowing how much we share. I know we have the same vision for the company. He can’t talk to his wife about his work — she’s an alcoholic, and she’s floating off in space somewhere. Even before we got romantically involved, he was saying that once she got stable enough to stand on her own two feet, he was going to leave her. So I jumped in.

我知道，我知道。第一条规则就是永远、永远不要和老板搞婚外情。但查尔斯是个了不起的人。从来没有人像他那样影响过我。我喜欢看他思考问题的方式，也喜欢他的见多识广。他有很多东西可以教，我觉得自己很幸运能成为他最得意的学生。我喜欢这种亲密感，因为我们有很多共同点。我知道我们对公司有着相同的愿景。他没法和妻子谈论工作——她是个酒鬼，而且她现在就像在宇宙中漂浮一样。甚至在我们发展出恋情之前，他就说过，等她能独立生活后，他就会离开她。所以我就主动出击了。

The romance was heady, the sex satisfying, the job experience rewarding. But two years passed, and Charles made no move to separate from his wife. As time went on, Sherry could see that there was no end in sight for his marriage.

这段恋情令人陶醉，性生活美满，工作经历也颇有成就感。然而两年过去了，查尔斯却丝毫没有要和妻子分居的迹象。随着时间的推移，雪莉意识到，他的婚姻似乎看不到尽头。

After two years of broken promises it finally sunk in that Charles was perfectly content to have a wife and a mistress, and I didn’t like seeing myself permanently in that role. I want to have a real family someday. We were having dinner, and he started telling me about the Paris vacation he was planning to take with his wife and daughter. He knew how much I love Paris, and how we’d talked about getting married there, and I knew then that I’d been living in Fantasy Land. I was a wreck trying to deal with that realization, and finally I told Charles that I wanted to move our relationship back to that close, nonsexual place where we’d started. It would be sad, but we’d both be able to get on with real life.

两年来，他屡次食言，我终于明白查尔斯完全满足于拥有妻子和情妇，而我并不想永远扮演这样的角色。我渴望拥有一个真正的家庭。我们一起吃晚饭时，他开始跟我讲他计划和妻子女儿去巴黎度假。他知道我有多爱巴黎，也知道我们曾经讨论过在那里结婚，那一刻我才意识到，我一直活在幻想世界里。我崩溃了，难以接受这个事实，最终我告诉查尔斯，我想让我们的关系回到最初那种亲密无间、没有性关系的状态。我知道这会很伤感，但我们都能继续过好自己的生活。

Charles had been so generous and kind to me that I was shocked by how out-of-character his response was. He told me that if I stopped seeing him, I could kiss him—and my job — good-bye. I don’t know if I can deal with this breakup and unemployment at the same time. I’m finally close to a job I love, and I’m afraid he’s going to slam the door in my face. But staying with him would be like prostitution. I couldn’t look myself in the eye. I can’t believe I’m even considering it.

查尔斯对我那么慷慨善良，他的反应如此反常，让我震惊不已。他告诉我，如果我不再和他来往，我就得和他——还有我的工作——说再见了。我不知道自己能不能同时承受分手和失业的双重打击。我好不容易找到了一份心仪的工作，却害怕他会把我拒之门外。但继续和他在一起就像卖淫一样。我简直不敢面对自己。我真不敢相信自己竟然会考虑这种事。

Charles was facing loss of a passionate relationship that probably made him feel young and alive, and when he saw that he might lose it, he became desperate and lashed out in the hope of hanging on. That response was a shock to Sherry, but in the white heat of the end of a love affair, it wasn’t at all atypical.

查尔斯即将失去一段炽热的感情，这段感情或许让他感觉年轻而充满活力。当他意识到自己可能失去这段感情时，他变得绝望，并做出过激的行为，希望能挽回这段关系。这种反应令雪莉震惊，但在一段恋情走向终结的激烈冲突中，这其实并不罕见。

Sherry was left to face something that people, especially women, have had to deal with for years. It’s always perilous to become intimately involved with a person who’s in a position of power over you. If a rift opens in the relationship, you may discover, as Sherry did, that the stress and disappointment can trigger a punitive response from someone who has been an integral part of the fabric of your life. But as we’ll see later, Sherry wasn’t backed into a corner as much as she thought. There were options available to her, which we will explore later in this book.

雪莉不得不面对一个人们，尤其是女性，多年来一直不得不面对的问题。与一个对你拥有权力的人建立亲密关系总是充满风险。如果这段关系出现裂痕，你可能会像雪莉一样发现，压力和失望会引发那个曾经是你生命中不可或缺的人的惩罚性反应。但正如我们稍后会看到的，雪莉并没有她想象中那么走投无路。她还有其他选择，我们将在本书后面探讨这些选择。

Their Blind Spots—and Ours

他们的盲点——以及我们的盲点

The closer the relationship, the higher the stakes—and the more vulnerable we are to punishers. We don’t want to walk away from people we care deeply about and with whom we have longtime, or even lifelong, bonds—or, in instances like Sherry’s, people we depend on for our paychecks as well. We’ll often go to great lengths to avoid standing up to such people. We allow ourselves to believe our punishers and to let our most useful insights about their actions fall into a black hole. Josh, for example, simply couldn’t see that while his father insisted he had Josh’s best interests in mind, his demands were totally self-centered and had little to do with Josh’s feelings. The demands of punishers rarely do.

关系越亲密，风险就越高——我们也越容易受到惩罚者的伤害。我们不愿离开那些我们深爱的人，那些与我们有着长期甚至终生情谊的人——或者，像雪莉那样，那些我们赖以谋生的人。我们常常会竭尽全力避免与这些人对抗。我们让自己相信那些惩罚者的话，任由我们对他们行为最有价值的洞察化为乌有。例如，乔什根本看不出来，尽管他父亲坚称一切都是为了他好，但父亲的要求却完全以自我为中心，与乔什的感受毫无关系。惩罚者的要求很少会真正顾及乔什的感受。

When blackmail escalates, the threatened consequences of not acceding to a punisher can be alarming: Abandonment. Emotional cutoff. Withdrawal of money or other resources. Explosive anger directed at us. And, at the most terrifying extreme, threats of physical harm. The darkest threats, of course, turn into emotional abuse as they escalate into intimidation, and one person seizes total control.

当勒索升级时，不屈服于惩罚的后果可能令人震惊：被抛弃、情感断绝、撤回金钱或其他资源、对我们爆发怒火，以及最可怕的极端情况——人身伤害的威胁。当然，最阴险的威胁会演变成精神虐待，最终演变成恐吓，一方完全掌控局面。

Obviously, in the heat of emotional blackmail, blinded by the intensity of their own needs, punishers seem to be oblivious to our feelings and not terribly introspective about their own behavior. They genuinely believe in the correctness of what they’re doing and the rightness of what they want. Confronting punishers can take tremendous inner resources, but it can be done. With tools and guidance, all of the punishers’ targets we’ve met were able to reclaim their adult confidence and were finally able to say—and to show—that they wouldn’t be blackmailed anymore.

显然，在情绪勒索的狂热驱使下，施虐者被自身强烈的欲望蒙蔽了双眼，似乎对我们的感受漠不关心，也很少反思自己的行为。他们真心相信自己所作所为的正确性，以及自己想要的东西的正当性。对抗施虐者需要耗费巨大的内在力量，但这并非不可能。通过一些方法和指导，我们遇到的所有被施虐者伤害过的人都重拾了成年人的自信，最终能够坚定地表达——并且用行动证明——他们不会再被勒索。

THE SELF-PUNISHER

自我惩罚者

We’ve all met the little six-year-old terror who signals a tantrum by announcing loudly, “If you don’t let me stay up and watch videos I’ll hold my breath until I turn blue!” Adult self-punishers are a bit more sophisticated, but the principle is the same. They inform us that if we don’t do what they want us to do, they’ll be upset and maybe even unable to function. They may vow to do something to screw up their lives, or even hurt themselves, because they know that the way they can manipulate us the most successfully is to threaten to undermine their own health or happiness. “Don’t argue with me or I’ll get sick or depressed.” “Make me happy or I’ll quit my job.” “If you don’t do X, I’ll stop eating, stop sleeping, drink or take drugs. I’ll ruin my life.” “If you leave me, I’ll kill myself.” These are the self-punisher’s threats.

我们都见过那种六岁左右的小恶魔，他们会大声嚷嚷着：“如果你不让我熬夜看视频，我就憋气憋到脸色发青！”以此来宣告自己要发脾气了。成年人的自我惩罚方式则更复杂一些，但原理是一样的。他们会告诉我们，如果我们不按他们说的做，他们就会难过，甚至可能无法正常生活。他们可能会扬言要毁掉自己的生活，甚至伤害自己，因为他们知道，操纵我们最有效的方法就是威胁要损害自己的健康或幸福。“别跟我吵架，不然我会生病或抑郁。”“让我开心点，不然我就辞职。”“如果你不做X，我就不吃饭、不睡觉、喝酒或吸毒。我会毁掉自己的人生。”“如果你离开我，我就自杀。”这些都是自我惩罚者的威胁。

Allen, the businessman we met in Chapter 1 , slowly began to realize that his new wife, Jo, was blackmailing him by describing what would befall her if she didn’t get her way. Over time, her incessant demands on his time and her unwillingness to seek out independent activities had begun to feel increasingly oppressive to him.

我们在第一章中认识的商人艾伦，渐渐意识到他的新婚妻子乔正在勒索他，她威胁说如果自己不顺心就会有不好的下场。随着时间的推移，乔不断地占用他的时间，并且不愿意去做任何自己想做的事情，这让他越来越感到难以忍受。

I’m not sure I’m ready to do anything drastic, but nothing seems to get through to her. I’ve tried to talk to her about the fact that things aren’t working, but she refuses to have that conversation. She gets quiet, and sometimes I’ll see her eyes start to tear up a little. Then she goes into the bedroom and locks the door. I plead with her to come out, and eventually she starts to talk—or should I say turn on the blame machine.

我不确定自己是否准备好采取任何激烈的措施，但她似乎什么都听不进去。我试着和她谈谈我们之间出了问题，但她拒绝沟通。她会变得沉默寡言，有时我会看到她的眼眶微微泛红。然后她会走进卧室，把门锁上。我恳求她出来，最终她开始说话——或者应该说，开始指责我。

This last time, all I wanted to do was go up to my sister’s cabin in Oregon and hang out with her. You’d think I was leaving the planet with no forwarding address. “You know I won’t sleep when you’re not here and I won’t be able to work,” she told me. “I need to have you with me. And this is a really stressful time for me. You know I count on you to help me gear up for the big sales season. If you’re not here to keep me organized, everything will fall apart. I couldn’t possibly do everything I need to under that kind of pressure. Don’t you care that I need you? Is that what you want, to screw up my whole life so you can go off for a week?”

上次，我只想去俄勒冈州姐姐的小木屋和她待一会儿。你肯定以为我要离开地球，连个新地址都没留。“你知道你不在的时候我睡不着觉，也没法工作，”她跟我说。“我需要你陪着我。现在我压力真的很大。你知道我指望着你帮我为销售旺季做准备。如果你不在，没人帮我安排，一切都会乱套。在这种压力下，我根本不可能完成所有该做的事情。你难道不在乎我需要你吗？你就是想把我的生活搞得一团糟，然后自己出去玩一个星期吗？”

I said to her, “For chrissake, it’s not the end of the world. I just want to spend some time with my sister.” But in her mind, I was abandoning her. I canceled the trip. I’m pretending I never wanted to go. It might not be so bad. She’s been so sweet and affectionate since I said I’d stay home that it feels like another honeymoon. But I have these moments when I feel like I just can’t breathe.

我对她说：“我的天哪，这又不是世界末日。我只是想陪陪我妹妹。” 但在她看来，我是在抛弃她。我取消了行程。我假装自己从来没想过要去。也许也没那么糟。自从我说要待在家里之后，她就一直对我那么温柔体贴，感觉就像又过了一次蜜月。但我还是会时不时地感到喘不过气来。

High drama, hysteria and an air of crisis (precipitated by you —of course) surround self-punishers, who are often excessively needy and dependent. They tend to fuse and enmesh themselves with those around them, and often have a real struggle taking responsibility for their own lives. If they turn to blackmail, they justify their demands by making every difficulty, real or imagined, your fault. In fact, they have an incredible talent for making you feel responsible for what happens to them. Where punishers turn their targets into children, self-punishers cast their targets in the role of the grown-up—the only adult in the relationship. We’re the ones who are supposed to come running when they cry, comfort them when they’re upset, figure out what’s making them uncomfortable and fix it. We’re the competent ones who can save them from themselves, rescue them from their helplessness, protect their fragile beings.

自我惩罚者总是被一种戏剧化、歇斯底里和危机感（当然，这一切都是你造成的）所包围，他们往往过度依赖他人。他们倾向于与周围的人融合，难以承担起自己生活的责任。如果他们诉诸勒索，他们会把所有困难，无论真实存在还是臆想出来的，都归咎于你，以此来为自己的要求辩护。事实上，他们非常擅长让你觉得他们遭遇的一切都是你的错。惩罚者把受害者当作孩子，而自我惩罚者则把受害者塑造成成年人——关系中唯一的成年人。我们才是应该在他们哭泣时奔向他们，在他们难过时安慰他们，找出让他们感到不舒服的原因并解决问题的人。我们才是能够拯救他们于水火之中，让他们摆脱无助，保护他们脆弱心灵的能手。

You’ll Ruin My Recovery

你会毁了我的康复

One of the calls I got most frequently on my radio program was from middle-aged parents desperate to know how to deal with an adult child who was abusing drugs, refusing to work or go to school and draining the family’s resources. Whenever the parents tried to change the situation, the threats came thick and fast. “OK. I’ll leave. And I’ll bet you’ll enjoy seeing me out on the street. You never loved me anyhow.” “I’ll just become a prostitute and then you’ll be happy.” The intimidated parent would agree to maintain the status quo, even though it was destructive for everyone.

我在广播节目中接到最多的电话之一，是来自中年父母的，他们焦急地想知道如何应对吸毒、拒绝工作或上学、耗尽家庭资源的成年子女。每当父母试图改变现状时，威胁便接踵而至。“好吧，我走。我敢打赌，你会很乐意看到我流落街头。反正你从来就没爱过我。”“我就去当妓女，这样你们就满意了。” 受到恐吓的父母只能同意维持现状，即使这对所有人都有害。

My client Karen, a retired nurse in her late 50s, is working hard in therapy on her relationship with her daughter Melanie. To help Melanie overcome a serious drug dependency, Karen paid for an expensive rehab program, sought counseling for herself as well as joining Al-Anon and encouraged Melanie to enter a training program at the hospital where she used to work. Karen didn’t expect gratitude, but she didn’t expect blackmail, either.

我的客户凯伦是一位年近六十的退休护士，她正在努力通过心理治疗改善与女儿梅兰妮的关系。为了帮助梅兰妮克服严重的毒瘾，凯伦自费为她支付了昂贵的戒毒费用，自己也接受了心理咨询，并加入了匿名戒毒互助会（Al-Anon），还鼓励梅兰妮参加她以前工作过的医院的培训项目。凯伦并不期待梅兰妮的感激，但她也没想到会遭到勒索。

Melanie is a great kid, and I’m proud of what she’s done to turn her life around. But we fight all the time about money. When she got married to Pete, they wanted to buy a house, and they asked me to loan them the money for a down payment. You know what a nurse’s pension looks like. I would’ve loved to help them out, but I didn’t have savings to draw on unless I emptied out my retirement account, and I was scared to do that. It’s all I have for the future. But the message from Mel was, Why should I have money and she have to do without? She had to have that house.

梅兰妮是个很棒的孩子，我为她努力改变自己的人生而感到骄傲。但我们总是因为钱吵架。她和皮特结婚后，他们想买房子，就问我能不能借钱给他们付首付。你知道护士的养老金有多少。我很想帮他们，但我没有积蓄，除非我把退休账户里的钱都取出来，但我又不敢这么做。那是我唯一的未来保障。但梅兰妮的想法是，凭什么我能有钱，而她却要挨饿？她非得买那套房子不可。

I worry because I think her sobriety is still a little shaky, and she’s not that strong yet. So it’s kind of, you know, If you’re not careful with me, I’m liable to go back to using and drinking. The threat is, If you don’t treat me the way I want to be treated, I’ll start drinking again. I have no choice—I have to help pay for that house.

我担心，因为我觉得她戒酒的决心还不太稳固，意志力也不够强。所以，你知道，如果你不小心管着我，我可能又会开始吸毒喝酒。我的威胁是，如果你不按我希望的方式对待我，我就会重新开始喝酒。我别无选择——我得帮着付房贷。

Karen’s statement that she had no choice is one I hear often from targets of blackmail, and it reflects the sense of victimization that targets feel. Karen actually had several choices, but it would take some work for her to be able to see and use them. Melanie’s threat to go off the wagon went straight for Karen’s jugular. As I pointed out to Karen, it was a strong-arm tactic that didn’t mesh at all with her description of Melanie as weak, the label that many self-punishers use for camouflage.

凯伦声称自己别无选择，这种说法我经常从勒索受害者那里听到，它反映了受害者普遍存在的受害感。事实上，凯伦有很多选择，但她需要花些时间才能看到并运用这些选择。梅兰妮威胁要复吸，这直击凯伦的要害。正如我向凯伦指出的那样，这是一种强硬手段，与她之前对梅兰妮软弱的描述完全不符——许多自我惩罚者都用“软弱”这个词来掩饰自己的真实想法。

The Ultimate Self-Punishment

终极自我惩罚

The ultimate threat self-punishers can make is frightening in the extreme: It’s a suggestion that they will kill themselves. This threat, never to be taken lightly, may be used almost habitually by a self-punisher who finds that it gets results. Our deep fear is that after years of hearing someone cry wolf, we’ll come home someday and find an ambulance crew tending to them.

自我惩罚者所能发出的终极威胁极其可怕：他们会暗示自己会自杀。这种威胁绝不可轻视，但对于那些发现它有效的自我惩罚者来说，他们可能会几乎习以为常地使用这种威胁。我们内心深处的恐惧是，多年来我们一直听到有人发出“狼来了”的威胁，而有一天我们回家时却发现救护人员正在照顾他们。

Eve is a young, attractive artist who is living with Elliot, a prominent painter in his 40s. Their relationship was strong when it began, but once she moved in with him, what had seemed like romantic devotion turned out to be a smothering dependency. She’d seen his mood swings when they were dating, but she’d always attributed them to his “sensitive artistic temperament,” and she was completely unprepared to deal with his recurrent depressions, and what appeared to be a possible addiction to sleeping pills. Their relationship has become increasingly distant. The sex is gone, and so is the closeness. Eve works as Elliot’s assistant, and he supports her financially, yet he opposes her every attempt to build her own career. He even insists that when she shows her work, it must appear with his.

伊芙是一位年轻貌美的女艺术家，她与四十多岁的著名画家埃利奥特同居。起初，他们的关系十分亲密，但自从伊芙搬进埃利奥特的住所后，原本看似浪漫的爱情却变成了令人窒息的依赖。恋爱时，伊芙就察觉到埃利奥特情绪波动，但她一直将其归咎于他“敏感的艺术家气质”。然而，她完全没有做好应对埃利奥特反复发作的抑郁症以及他似乎对安眠药上瘾的准备。他们的关系日渐疏远，性生活消失殆尽，亲密感也荡然无存。伊芙担任埃利奥特的助理，埃利奥特在经济上支持她，但他却百般阻挠她发展自己的事业。他甚至坚持，伊芙的作品必须与他的作品一同展出。

I finally realized that I have to leave in order to build any kind of life for myself, but every time I make a move to do it, be threatens to take an overdose of sleeping pills. I almost laughed the first time. I said I wanted to take a drawing workshop and he said, “I might as well die then.” He’s such a drama queen I thought he was teasing. But he keeps saying things like “I can’t make it without you” and “If you leave me, I can’t promise that I’ll go on alone.” It’s not funny anymore — it’s terrifying. I feel such love and empathy for his suffering, but at the same time this rage. Why in the world would he put me in a position like this? All I wanted to do was take a class.

我终于意识到，为了建立属于自己的生活，我必须离开。但每次我有所行动，他都威胁要服药自杀。第一次听到这话时，我差点笑出声来。我说我想去参加一个绘画工作坊，他却说：“那我干脆死了算了。” 他真是个戏精，我当时以为他是在开玩笑。但他却总是说些诸如“没有你我活不下去”和“如果你离开我，我不敢保证自己能独自生活下去”之类的话。这不再好笑了——而是令人恐惧。我对他的痛苦感同身受，同时也感到无比愤怒。他为什么要让我陷入这种境地？我只是想去上个课而已。

Typical of this form of blackmail, Elliot’s threats play on Eve’s strong feelings of responsibility. “He’s been so good to me. I can’t find the strength to leave him. If he did anything to himself, I would never forgive myself,” Eve said. And then she added with total conviction, “I would die of guilt.”

这种勒索手段的典型之处在于，埃利奥特的威胁利用了伊芙强烈的责任感。“他对我这么好。我实在没有勇气离开他。如果他伤害了自己，我永远都不会原谅自己，”伊芙说道。然后她语气坚定地补充道：“我会愧疚而死。”

Most self-punishers don’t go as far as Elliot did, though self-punishment can escalate to this level. As I emphasized to Eve, staying with someone is no guarantee that you can save them. Ultimately, the decision to be self-destructive is theirs, not yours. Certainly you can direct a suicidal person to support and resources. But if you remain because you feel that it’s your duty to protect them from themselves, you’re almost ensuring that whenever they want to strengthen control over you, they will pull out this terrifying form of emotional blackmail.

大多数自虐者不会像艾略特那样走极端，尽管自虐行为也可能升级到这种程度。正如我向伊芙强调的那样，留在一个人身边并不能保证你能拯救他。归根结底，自毁的决定是他们自己的，而不是你的。当然，你可以引导有自杀倾向的人寻求帮助和资源。但如果你因为觉得有义务保护他们而留下，那么你几乎是在确保，每当他们想要加强对你的控制时，他们就会使出这种可怕的情感勒索手段。

THE SUFFERER

受苦者

The image of the sufferer is etched into our culture in a familiar picture: A sour-faced woman sits in a dim apartment, waiting for one of her children to call. “How am I?” she says when the phone finally rings. “You’re asking me how am I? You don’t call me, you don’t visit. You’ve forgotten your own mother. I may as well stick my head in the oven for all you care about me.”

受苦者的形象在我们文化中根深蒂固，一幅熟悉的画面跃然纸上：一位面容愁容满面的女人坐在昏暗的公寓里，等待着孩子的电话。“我怎么样？”电话终于响起时，她问道。“你问我怎么样？你不给我打电话，也不来看我。你连自己的母亲都忘了。你根本不在乎我，我干脆把头伸进烤箱算了。”

Sufferers take the position that if they feel miserable, sick, unhappy or are just plain unlucky, there’s only one solution: our giving them what they want—even if they haven’t told us what it is. They don’t threaten us or themselves with harm. Instead, they let us know in no uncertain terms, If you don’t do what I want, I will suffer, and it will be your fault. This last part of the accusation, “it will be your fault,” is often unspoken but, as we’ll see, can work magic on the conscience of a sufferer’s target.

受害者会认为，如果他们感到痛苦、生病、不快乐，或者只是运气不好，唯一的解决办法就是满足他们的愿望——即使他们没有告诉我们他们想要什么。他们不会威胁我们或他们自己。相反，他们会毫不含糊地告诉我们：如果你不按我说的做，我会受苦，而且都是你的错。这最后一句“都是你的错”通常是隐晦的，但正如我们将看到的，它能对受害者的良心产生神奇的影响。

An Award-Winning Performance

一场获奖演出

Sufferers are preoccupied with how awful they feel, and often they’ll interpret your inability to read their mind as proof that you don’t care enough about them. If you really loved them, you’d be able to figure out what’s bothering them without a single verbal clue. The parlor game they’ve mastered is “Guess What You Did to Me.”

患者总是沉浸在糟糕的感受中，他们常常会把你无法读懂他们的心思解读为你不够关心他们的证据。如果你真的爱他们，即使他们一言不发，你也能明白他们烦恼的原因。他们最擅长的游戏就是“猜猜你对我做了什么”。

Depressed, mute and often teary-eyed, many sufferers pull away when they don’t get what they want, but they don’t let us know why. They’ll tell us what they want on their own timetable, after letting us twist for hours, even weeks, in anxiety or concern.

许多患者情绪低落、沉默寡言，常常泪眼婆娑。当他们的愿望得不到满足时，他们会选择逃避，但却不告诉我们原因。他们会在自己的节奏下告诉我们他们想要什么，而在此之前，他们会让我们焦虑不安地煎熬数小时甚至数周。

My client Patty, a 43-year-old government worker, told me that whenever she disagreed with her husband, Joe, he would dramatically take to his bed.

我的客户帕蒂，一位 43 岁的政府工作人员，告诉我，每当她和丈夫乔意见不合时，乔就会戏剧性地躺在床上。

He’ll hardly ever come out and tell me what he wants and on the rare days when he does, if I disagree at all, he gets sad or downcast and goes out for a walk. He has the saddest eyes in the world. We used to have these nondisagreement disagreements when his mother wanted to come over—usually at the most inconvenient time. I gave up fighting that because I felt so guilty when I saw Joe looking so sad.

他几乎从不直接告诉我他想要什么，就算偶尔开口，如果我稍有异议，他就会难过沮丧，然后出去散步。他的眼神忧郁得可怕。以前他妈妈想来的时候，我们经常会因为这种“非争执”而产生分歧——而且他妈妈总是挑最不方便的时间来。后来我放弃了和他争辩，因为看到乔那么难过，我心里很愧疚。

This is typical. He’ll let out an exaggerated sigh, and when I ask what’s wrong he gives me a pained look and says, “Nothing.” Then I have to figure out what crime I’ve committed this time. I sit on the bed and tell him I’m sorry if I’ve done something to upset him, but couldn’t he at least tell me what it is? And after an hour or so I’ll get the answer to what I did. One time, I had told him I didn’t think we could afford the new computer he wanted! How could I be so insensitive and stingy? So of course I told him to go ahead and get it—and surprise, surprise, he cheered right up.

这很常见。他会夸张地叹口气，我问他怎么了，他会一脸痛苦地看着我，说：“没事。” 然后我就得琢磨这次我又犯了什么错。我坐在床上，跟他说如果我做了什么让他不高兴的事，我很抱歉，但他至少应该告诉我到底是什么吧？过一个小时左右，我才能知道我到底做错了什么。有一次，我跟他说我觉得我们买不起他想要的那台新电脑！我怎么能这么冷漠又吝啬呢？所以，我当然让他去买——结果，你猜怎么着，他立马就高兴起来了。

Joe wasn’t comfortable sitting down and talking about the computer with Patty. So he made his point another way—he used all the theatrics he could summon to give her the message that she had upset him, made him feel sick, given him a headache. He was flattened by depression because of how “bad” she was. Sufferers look in the mirror and see a victim. They rarely take responsibility for clearing the air or asking for what they want.

乔不愿坐下来和帕蒂谈论电脑问题。于是他换了一种方式表达自己的观点——他使出浑身解数，用各种夸张的表演方式告诉她，她让他心烦意乱，恶心反胃，头疼欲裂。她“太糟糕”了，让他陷入了深深的抑郁。受苦的人照镜子时看到的都是受害者。他们很少主动承担责任，澄清误会，或者提出自己的诉求。

Sufferers may look weak on the surface, but they are actually a quiet form of tyrant. They may not yell or make scenes, yet their behavior hurts, mystifies and enrages us.

患者表面上看起来很软弱，但实际上却是一种沉默的暴君。他们或许不会大喊大叫或制造事端，但他们的行为却会伤害我们、让我们困惑，甚至让我们愤怒。

The Victim of Circumstance

环境的受害者

Not all suffering is done in silence. Some sufferers happily share the details of their plights with us and, like their silent cousins, expect us to make everything better. If they’re not thriving, we’re not giving them something vital to their happiness.

并非所有的苦难都默默承受。有些受苦的人乐于与我们分享他们的困境，并且像那些沉默的同胞一样，期待我们能让他们的生活好转。如果他们无法过上幸福的生活，那就是我们没有给予他们幸福所必需的东西。

My client Zoe is 57, a striking and confident account executive for a large ad agency. She came to see me because of problems she was having with a colleague at work.

我的客户佐伊今年57岁，是一位魅力四射、自信满满的大型广告公司客户经理。她来找我是因为她和一位同事在工作中遇到了一些问题。

Tess is the youngest person on the staff, and she forgets that it’s taken most of us years of doing shitty little jobs and paying our dues to get to where we are. She thinks she should be able to walk right in, with almost 15 years’ less experience than the rest of us, and take on the big jobs. I’ve tried explaining this to her, but the girl’s nothing but impatient. Then she started having trouble with our boss and got paranoid about losing her job. Every day she’d come into my office and practically hyperventilate going down the list of what had gone wrong: Dale, one of the partners, hates her copy. She hasn’t been able to get through to a valuable client and she thinks he’s avoiding her. Her computer doesn’t work. And, oh yeah, the dog ate her homework. Sometimes she could see how funny it sounded, but the insecurity was always right there.

泰丝是公司里最年轻的员工，她忘了我们大多数人都是白手起家，做了好几年的琐碎工作，一步一个脚印才走到今天这一步的。她觉得自己应该能轻而易举地接手大活儿，尽管她比我们其他人少了将近15年的经验。我试着跟她解释过，但她一点儿也不耐烦。后来她开始跟老板闹矛盾，担心丢掉工作。她每天都跑到我办公室，几乎喘不过气来，把所有不顺心的事都一股脑儿地列举出来：合伙人之一的戴尔不喜欢她写的稿子；她联系不上一个重要的客户，觉得客户在躲着她；她的电脑坏了；哦，对了，她的作业被狗吃了。有时候她自己也觉得这些抱怨听起来挺可笑的，但她内心的不安却始终挥之不去。

She says she’s so depressed she can hardly get out of bed in the morning, she’s started chain-smoking, she seems to be losing weight. . . . I tried to reassure her, and I thought I was succeeding, but then there was a twist that’s making me really uncomfortable. She started pressuring me to put her on my team for a big new project. “I’m going to get fired if you don’t,” she told me. “Dale hates me, but he trusts you, and if you’d just help me get on his good side, I know that would change everything.” Every day it was, “I’m going to get fired if you don’t do this teeny favor for me,” and “I’m so worried and tormented. You have to help me out.”

她说她抑郁得早上都起不了床，开始疯狂抽烟，而且好像还在消瘦……我试着安慰她，以为效果不错，但后来事情出现了转折，让我很不舒服。她开始逼我让她加入我的团队，负责一个新项目。“你要是不让她加入，我就要被炒鱿鱼了，”她告诉我。“戴尔讨厌我，但他信任你，如果你能帮我讨好他，我知道一切都会改变。”她每天都说：“你要是不帮我这个小忙，我就要被炒鱿鱼了。”“我好担心好痛苦，你一定要帮帮我。”

The fact is, I don’t think she’s got enough skills yet to pull her weight with the rest of us, but I put her on the project anyway because it seemed almost selfish not to. She really got to me—I bought her idea that it was just me standing between her and a major depression. Not that her job problems had anything to do with her attitude at all. Now I’m worried that I’m going to have to push everyone harder because essentially we’re a person short—Tess can’t cut it. I felt like such a mentor when I told her she was on. Not anymore. I feel used. You’re not going to believe this, but she wants me to give her more responsibility, even though she’s struggling with what she’s got. I want to help her—I can see my younger self in her in some ways—but this is getting out of hand, and it’s going to hurt my own reputation if I don’t put a stop to it.

事实上，我觉得她目前的能力还不足以胜任我们其他人的工作，但我还是让她参与了这个项目，因为不让她参与似乎有点自私。她真的让我信以为真——我当时觉得，只有我才能阻止她陷入严重的抑郁。当然，她的态度和她的工作问题完全无关。现在我担心，因为人手不够，我不得不对每个人都更加严格——Tess 根本无法胜任。当初告诉她她加入项目时，我感觉自己像个导师。现在不是了。我觉得自己被利用了。你可能不信，但她竟然想让我给她更多责任，尽管她连自己现在的工作都做不好。我想帮她——在某些方面，我能从她身上看到年轻时的自己——但这事儿越来越离谱了，如果我不阻止她，我的名声也会受损。

Sufferers like Tess tell us how the cards are stacked against them, the fates have conspired to keep them down. Their theme song might be the old blues tune that goes “If it wasn’t for bad luck, I wouldn’t have no luck at all.” All they need is one little break to turn things around. They often have a certain underdog charm that can be appealing. Of course, these sufferers let us know that if they don’t get a break—that is, if we don’t give it to them—they’ll fail. And that failure, which they can evoke in excruciating detail, will be on our head. They effectively activate our rescuer-caretaker instinct. The problem is, if we give them the “just one break” that they ask for, they’ll almost certainly be back for more. Becoming a caretaker to a sufferer is a full-time job, not a stop-gap measure.

像苔丝这样的患者会告诉我们，他们处境艰难，命运似乎在合谋将他们击垮。他们的主题曲或许就是那首老蓝调：“要不是运气不好，我根本就没运气。”他们需要的仅仅是一个转机，就能扭转乾坤。他们身上往往有一种不屈不挠的魅力，令人动容。当然，这些患者也让我们明白，如果他们得不到喘息的机会——也就是说，如果我们不给他们机会——他们就会失败。而他们能把失败的细节描述得淋漓尽致，最终的责任都会落在我们身上。他们有效地激发了我们内心深处的拯救者和照顾者的本能。问题是，如果我们真的给了他们“哪怕一次机会”，他们几乎肯定会再次回来寻求帮助。照顾患者是一项全职工作，而不是权宜之计。

THE TANTALIZER

诱人者

Tantalizers are the most subtle blackmailers. They encourage us and promise love or money or career advancement—the proverbial carrot at the end of the stick—and then make it clear that unless we behave as they want us to, we don’t get the prize. The rewards sound juicy, but they turn to dust anytime we get near them. Our desire for what’s being promised can be so strong that we endure numerous encounters with forgotten and never-materializing rewards before we realize that we’re being emotionally blackmailed.

诱惑者是最狡猾的勒索者。他们用爱情、金钱或事业晋升等诱饵来引诱我们，就像胡萝卜加大棒一样，然后明确表示，如果我们不按他们的意愿行事，就得不到这些好处。这些奖励听起来很诱人，但只要我们稍稍靠近，它们就会化为乌有。我们对承诺的渴望如此强烈，以至于在意识到自己正遭受情感勒索之前，我们会经历无数次与那些早已被遗忘或永远不会兑现的奖励擦肩而过。

Over lunch one afternoon, my friend Julie told me about her run-in with a tantalizer, the boyfriend she’d been so excited about the last time we got together. Alex, a wealthy twice-divorced businessman, had been dating Julie, who’s an aspiring screenwriter, for seven months. When they met, Julie was running a small freelance writing business from her home and working on screenplays at night. “Your scripts are excellent,” Alex had told Julie early on, and, says Julie, he was ever-encouraging.

一天下午吃午饭时，我的朋友朱莉跟我讲了她和那个“撩妹高手”的遭遇。上次我们见面时，她还对这个男友赞不绝口。亚历克斯是个离过两次婚的富商，和梦想成为编剧的朱莉交往了七个月。他们相识时，朱莉在家经营着一家小型自由撰稿公司，晚上则埋头创作剧本。“你的剧本很棒，”亚历克斯很早就对朱莉这么说过，朱莉说，他一直都很鼓励她。

He said be bad a couple of producer friends who were looking for—how did he put it?—intelligent work, just like mine. There was supposed to be a weekend party and he said he’d introduce us. I’d been working so hard, this chance was thrilling. Then came the bait and switch. “Don’t invite any of those bohemian friends of yours,” he told me. “I think they’re holding you back.”

他说他有几个制作人朋友，正在寻找——他是怎么说的来着？——像我这样的“有深度的工作”。周末有个派对，他说他会介绍我们认识。我一直很努力，这个机会让我兴奋不已。结果他却出尔反尔。“别邀请你那些不拘一格的朋友，”他告诉我，“我觉得他们会拖你后腿。”

When she balked, there were no meetings with Alex’s influential friends, just more delicious promises. He gave her expensive gifts—a new computer to replace her ancient word processor, day-care help for her seven-year-old son, Trevor. But each came accompanied by a new hoop for her to jump through. He could open more doors for her if she’d help him arrange more social events at his house. Surely she could give up writing at night so she could entertain with him—it was for her own good.

当她犹豫不决时，亚历克斯并没有安排她与那些有影响力的朋友见面，而是抛出了更多诱人的承诺。他送给她昂贵的礼物——一台新电脑取代她那台老旧的文字处理机，还安排人照看她七岁的儿子特雷弗。但每一份礼物都附带着新的条件。如果她帮他安排更多在他家举办的社交活动，他就能为她打开更多的大门。她当然可以放弃晚上写作，以便能陪他招待客人——这都是为了她好。

Attached to Alex, and ambitious enough to thirst for what he had to offer, Julie tried to go along. Then came what was to be the final hoop.

朱莉依恋亚历克斯，又野心勃勃地渴望得到他所能提供的一切，于是她试图顺从他。然后，最后一个障碍出现了。

He said he’d been thinking about how much better things would be if Trevor went to live with his father for a while. I’d have more time to work, and I could focus on my career. “It would just be temporary,” he said. And then he said something about how I couldn’t be on the mommy track when I was so close to making it big.

他说他一直在想，如果特雷弗暂时和他父亲一起生活，情况会好得多。那样我就能有更多时间工作，也能专注于我的事业。“这只是暂时的，”他说。然后他又说，我眼看就要功成名就了，不能再走“妈妈”这条路了。

That woke Julie up, and soon after, she broke off her relationship with Alex. It was impossible for her not to see the relationship for what it was—a never-ending series of tests and demands. A typical tantalizer, Alex was full of gifts and promises, all accompanied by conditions for Julie’s behavior: “I will help you if. . . .” “I will ease the way for your career if. . . .” And finally, Julie realized that the testing would never end. Every time she got close to the carrot, Alex pulled it away. Tantalizers offer nothing with a free heart. Every seductively wrapped package has a web of strings attached.

这让朱莉幡然醒悟，不久之后，她便与亚历克斯分手了。她无法再看清这段关系的本质——一场永无止境的考验和索取。亚历克斯是个典型的诱惑者，他满口都是礼物和承诺，但所有这些都附带着对朱莉行为的条件：“如果你……我就帮你。”“如果你……我就帮你铺平职业道路。”最终，朱莉意识到，这场考验永无止境。每次她即将触及那根胡萝卜时，亚历克斯都会把它抽走。诱惑者从不真心付出。每一个精心包装的诱人礼物背后都隐藏着一张密密麻麻的陷阱。

The Price of Admission

入场费

Sometimes what tantalizers offer is less tangible than the material rewards Alex dangled before Julie. Many tantalizers traffic in emotional payoffs, castles in the air full of love, acceptance, family closeness and healed wounds. Admission to this rich, unblemished fantasy requires only one thing: giving in to what the tantalizer wants.

有时，诱惑者提供的远不如亚历克斯在朱莉面前晃动的物质回报那样触手可及。许多诱惑者兜售的是情感上的回报，是充满爱、接纳、家庭亲密和治愈创伤的空中楼阁。进入这美好而纯粹的幻想世界，只需要一件事：屈服于诱惑者的欲望。

My client Jan is an attractive businesswoman in her 50s who’s been divorced for eight years and has two grown sons. She’s built a successful jewelry business and is now enjoying the fruits of her hard work and creativity. But her relationship with her sister is a great source of pain for her.

我的客户简是一位魅力四射的五十多岁女商人，离婚八年，有两个已成年的儿子。她一手打造了一家成功的珠宝公司，如今正享受着辛勤工作和创造力带来的成果。然而，她与妹妹的关系却给她带来了巨大的痛苦。

My sister, Carol, and I have had a rocky relationship from the get-go. Our parents set us up to be really competitive with one another and were always playing favorites. I was my mother’s favorite, and my sister was my father’s. But it was Dad who had the money. He was tightfisted with me, but he always indulged Carol. She knew exactly how to play him. My father was a control freak and couldn’t bear to have anyone stand up to him. He set unreasonable rules for us about curfews and dating, and I was constantly locking horns with him. But not Carol. She played the obedient daughter to the hilt, and raked in the rewards. She had a Jaguar for her sixteenth birthday, trips to Europe, the best schools, everything. But she never learned to be self-reliant, whereas I learned early on that if I was going to get anything, I would have to get it for myself.

我和姐姐卡罗尔的关系从一开始就很紧张。父母从小就培养我们之间的竞争意识，而且总是偏袒一方。我是母亲的掌上明珠，姐姐则是父亲的宠儿。但真正有钱的是父亲。他对我吝啬，却对卡罗尔百依百顺。卡罗尔深谙如何利用父亲。父亲是个控制狂，容不得任何人反抗。他给我们制定了诸多不合理的规矩，比如门禁时间和约会，我总是和他针锋相对。但卡罗尔却截然不同。她扮演着听话女儿的角色，并因此获得了丰厚的回报。十六岁生日时，她收到了一辆捷豹，还去了欧洲旅行，就读最好的学校，一切都那么完美。但她从未学会独立，而我从小就明白，想要得到什么，就必须靠自己争取。

When my father died, he continued to play favorites even from the grave. He left most of his money to Carol and practically nothing to me. I was hurt and upset when Carol wouldn’t share even a small portion of her inheritance, and what little relationship we had deteriorated almost totally. For the next several years we rarely spoke or saw each other, and finally we stopped speaking altogether. The bottom line is that Carol and I just don’t like each other very much.

父亲去世后，他依然偏袒子女，即便死后也未曾改变。他把大部分遗产都留给了卡罗尔，几乎没给我留什么。卡罗尔连一小部分遗产都不肯分给我，这让我既伤心又难过，我们之间原本就微不足道的关系也几乎彻底破裂。接下来的几年里，我们很少说话，也很少见面，最终彻底断了联系。总之，我和卡罗尔彼此都不喜欢对方。

One day last month, out of the blue, I get a call from her. She’s crying and she wants to borrow $1,000 from me so they can put food on the table. Her husband is a total screw-up with everything he touches, and he’d lost all their money with crazy investments. Carol pawned her jewelry, and they borrowed money from my mother to keep their house out of foreclosure. It was a mess. Meanwhile, they didn’t tone down their lifestyle one bit. They have a valuable art collection, and even a Ferrari.

上个月的一天，我突然接到她的电话。她哭着说想从我这儿借1000美元，好让他们能吃饱饭。她丈夫是个彻头彻尾的失败者，什么事都搞砸了，疯狂的投资把家里的钱全赔光了。卡罗尔把首饰都典当了，他们还向我妈借钱才保住了房子，免于被银行收回。家里一团糟。与此同时，他们的生活方式却丝毫没有改变。他们收藏了不少名贵的艺术品，甚至还有一辆法拉利。

When Carol saw that I was really resisting, she pulled out all the stops: “I have no one else to turn to.” “I don’t know what else to do—I thought you could turn to your family when you’re in trouble”—suddenly I’m family again.

卡罗尔见我真的在抗拒，就使出了浑身解数：“我没有其他人可以依靠了。”“我不知道还能怎么办——我以为你遇到麻烦的时候可以向家人求助”——突然间，我又成了家人。

At first Carol was a classic sufferer, letting Jan know how awful things were for her and that it was within Jan’s power to fix them. When she heard Jan’s resistance, she switched gears and held out a special carrot.

起初，卡罗尔表现得像个典型的受害者，她告诉简她的处境有多糟糕，并说简有能力解决这一切。但当她听到简的抵触情绪后，她改变了策略，抛出了一个特别的诱饵。

Her voice suddenly got sweet and she said, “You know, I’d love to have you start coming to dinner and over for the holidays. It’ll be like the old days.” She tapped right into that fantasy I cherish of smiling faces around a beautiful holiday table. My mom is alone now, and I’m not with anyone. Carol’s the one who has the intact family, a husband and teenage children. I always get a little sad around the holidays because there’s so much distance between us. In my head I know I have friends who I’m closer to than any of my family, but when the Christmas lights go up on Hollywood Boulevard, I get this yearning for the happy family. In my head, I know we’ve never had that, and we’re never going to have it, but in my heart I’d give anything if we could. I have to admit that I was plenty tempted by Carol’s “invitation,” and I really struggled to figure out the right thing to do.

她的声音突然变得甜美起来，她说：“你知道吗，我真希望你能来我家吃晚饭，过节的时候也过来。就像以前那样。”她的话触动了我内心深处对美好节日餐桌旁大家欢声笑语的渴望。现在我妈妈孤身一人，我也没有伴侣。卡罗尔拥有一个完整的家庭，丈夫和十几岁的孩子。每到节日，我都会感到有些伤感，因为我们之间相隔太远。我知道我的朋友比我的家人更亲近，但每当好莱坞大道上的圣诞彩灯亮起时，我都会无比渴望拥有一个幸福的家庭。我知道我们从未拥有过，也永远不会拥有，但我内心深处却无比渴望。我必须承认，卡罗尔的“邀请”确实让我心动不已，我纠结了很久，不知该如何回应。

Carol made it seem that admission to the family fold could be had for a mere $1,000—a minuscule amount for something Jan held so dear. But of course, the price Jan would pay if she gave in to her sister’s pressure would be far higher. She’d have to violate her own integrity by enabling Carol to perpetuate her patterns of overspending and financial irresponsibility, and she’d also have to trust someone who had a history of deceiving her.

卡罗尔让简觉得，只要花1000美元就能融入这个家庭——对于简如此珍视的东西来说，这简直是九牛一毛。但当然，如果简屈服于姐姐的压力，她付出的代价将远不止于此。她不仅要违背自己的原则，纵容卡罗尔继续挥霍无度、不负责任的理财方式，还要信任一个曾经欺骗过她的人。

Yet the temptation Jan felt was real. The fantasy of the good family that Carol conjured for her is hard to resist—a good family is something we all yearn for, something many of us didn’t get. The desire for it is strong, and the possibility of getting it pulls us like a magnet. Ultimately, however, I was able to show Jan that if she didn’t have the kind of family she wanted by this point in her life, she probably wasn’t going to get it. Carol had painted a beautiful picture for her, but it wasn’t real. You can’t write a check for a thousand or a million or 10 million dollars and buy closeness, no matter what blackmailers might insist.

然而，简感受到的诱惑是真实的。卡罗尔为她描绘的美好家庭的幻想难以抗拒——美好的家庭是我们每个人都渴望的，也是许多人未能拥有的。这种渴望如此强烈，而拥有它的可能性就像磁铁一样吸引着我们。但最终，我还是让简明白，如果她到了这个年纪还没有拥有自己想要的家庭，那她可能永远也无法拥有了。卡罗尔为她描绘了一幅美好的蓝图，但这并非现实。无论勒索者如何哄骗，你都无法用一张一千美元、一百万美元甚至一千万美元的支票买到亲密关系。

All the forces that were working on Jan—her guilt; the temptation to look like the successful, adequate one; the tantalizing promise of family that Carol held before her—tapped a deeply vulnerable place within her. But as we’ll see, her experience with this profound instance of emotional blackmail was a turning point that helped her find the ability to withstand a coercive form of manipulation.

所有作用于简身上的因素——她的内疚感；想要表现得成功、称职的诱惑；卡罗尔在她面前描绘的诱人的家庭蓝图——都触动了她内心深处最脆弱的地方。但正如我们将看到的，这次深刻的情感勒索经历成为了她人生的转折点，帮助她学会了如何抵御这种胁迫性的操控。

WHATEVER WORKS

什么有效就用什么。

There are no firm boundaries between the styles of blackmail, and as you’ve seen, many blackmailers combine them, or use more than one. They might take Carol’s tack and switch back and forth from suffering to offering up the tantalizing fantasy of a troubled family that could be magically mended—if. . . .

勒索手段之间并没有明确的界限，正如你所看到的，许多勒索者会将多种手段结合起来，或者使用不止一种。他们可能会像卡罗尔那样，一会儿装可怜，一会儿又抛出一个诱人的幻想：一个问题重重的家庭可以被神奇地修复——如果……

Every style of emotional blackmail wreaks havoc with our well-being. It’s easiest to pay attention to the punishers, whose tactics seem the most destructive. But don’t for a minute discount the corrosive effects of the quieter types, the ones who are more like termites than tornadoes. Silent or dramatic, both can bring the house down.

每一种情感勒索都会严重损害我们的身心健康。我们最容易关注那些施虐者，因为他们的手段似乎最具破坏性。但千万不要低估那些看似温和、如同白蚁而非龙卷风般悄无声息的情感勒索者的腐蚀性影响。无论是沉默寡言还是咄咄逼人，他们都足以摧毁一切。

Most emotional blackmailers are not monsters. As we’ll see, they’re rarely driven by malice but rather by some demons of their own, which we will explore in Chapter 5 . Because they are usually people who have an important place in our lives, people we may still want to look to as protectors or supporters, I know that recognizing them as blackmailers can be extremely painful. It’s not easy to look closely at behavior we may have tried to forgive or ignore and see how it’s affected us. But it’s a vital step if we hope to put a troubled relationship back on solid ground.

大多数情感勒索者并非恶魔。正如我们将看到的，他们很少是出于恶意，而是被自身某些心魔所驱使，我们将在第五章探讨这些心魔。因为他们通常是我们生活中重要的人，是我们仍然希望视为保护者或支持者的人，我知道，意识到他们是勒索者会非常痛苦。仔细审视那些我们可能试图原谅或忽视的行为，并看清它对我们的影响，并非易事。但如果我们希望修复一段岌岌可危的关系，这是至关重要的一步。

# ↩

3

A Blinding FOG

浓雾

Emotional blackmail flourishes in a fog that spreads just below the surface of our understanding, like a bank of clouds under an airplane. As we descend into the blackmail zone, a thick mist of emotions swirls around us, and we lose our ability to think clearly about what the blackmailer is doing, or what we are doing in response. Our judgment becomes hazy.

情感勒索如同飞机下方的一层云雾，在我们理解力的表层之下蔓延开来，滋生于迷雾之中。一旦我们落入勒索的圈套，浓厚的情感迷雾便会笼罩我们，使我们无法清晰地思考勒索者正在做什么，也无法判断我们该如何应对。我们的判断力变得模糊不清。

As I’ve mentioned, I use FOG as an acronym for fear, obligation and guilt, the three feeling states that all blackmailers, no matter what their style, work to intensify in us. I think it’s an apt metaphor for the atmosphere that surrounds all emotional blackmail. FOG is penetrating, disorienting, and it obscures everything but the pounding discomfort it produces. In the midst of FOG we’re desperate to know: How did I get into this? How do I get out? How do I make these difficult feelings stop?

正如我之前提到的，我用“FOG”来指代恐惧（Fear）、义务（Obsignity）和内疚（Guilt）。所有勒索者，无论他们的手法如何，都会竭力加剧我们内心的这三种感受。我认为这恰如其分地隐喻了所有情感勒索所营造的氛围。“FOG”具有渗透性，令人迷失方向，它遮蔽了一切，只留下它带来的剧烈不适感。身处“FOG”之中，我们迫切地想要知道：我怎么会陷入这种境地？我该如何摆脱？我该如何消除这些痛苦的感受？

We’re no strangers to this trio of emotions. We all live with a host of fears, large and small. We all have obligations, and if we have a conscience, we realize that we’re interconnected with the people in our lives and have responsibilities to our families and communities. We all live with a certain amount of guilt. We wish we could turn back the clock and undo an action that hurt someone. We regret things left undone. These emotions are central to being in the world with other people, and for the most part, we’re able to coexist with them and not let them overpower us.

我们对这三种情绪并不陌生。我们都生活在各种各样的恐惧之中，无论大小。我们都肩负着责任，如果我们还有良知，就会意识到我们与生活中的人息息相关，对家庭和社区负有责任。我们都或多或少地感到内疚。我们希望能够回到过去，弥补曾经伤害过别人的行为。我们后悔那些未完成的事情。这些情绪对于我们与他人共处这个世界至关重要，而且大多数时候，我们都能与它们和谐共处，不被它们所控制。

But blackmailers turn up the volume, blasting us until we’re so uncomfortable we will do almost anything—even something that is not in our best interests—to return these feelings to a more tolerable level. Their FOG-inducing tactics prompt responses that are almost as automatic as covering our ears when a siren shrieks past. There’s little thinking on our part, only reacting, and that’s the key to effective emotional blackmail. When blackmailers pressure us, there is practically no time between feeling emotional discomfort and acting to get relief.

但勒索者会加大力度，不断轰炸我们，直到我们感到极度不适，以至于我们几乎会不惜一切代价——哪怕是违背自身利益的事情——来缓解这种不适感。他们制造的“情绪迷雾”策略会引发我们几乎是下意识的反应，就像听到警笛声时本能地捂住耳朵一样。我们几乎没有思考，只是本能地做出反应，而这正是情感勒索奏效的关键。当勒索者向我们施压时，从感受到情绪不适到采取行动寻求缓解，几乎没有任何延迟。

Even though it may sound as if this is a well-thought-out process, most blackmailers create FOG without any conscious design.

虽然这听起来像是一个经过深思熟虑的过程，但大多数勒索者制造迷雾并没有任何有意识的设计。

FOG sets in motion an elaborate, unseen chain reaction, and before we can interrupt it, we need to understand how it works. The best way to begin is to look closely at FOG’s component parts. Though I’ll be describing them individually, don’t expect these feelings to be neatly separated—they lap over, swirl together and work in combination. Remember, too, that there are as many different sources of fear, obligation and guilt as there are people, and obviously, I can’t illustrate every one. The words and actions that trigger these feelings in you may be different from the ones I describe below, but the effects are the same. They all help weave the matrix of discomfort that pushes us to give in to blackmail.

恐惧、责任和内疚会引发一系列复杂而隐秘的连锁反应，在我们能够阻止它之前，我们需要了解它的运作机制。最好的方法是仔细观察恐惧的组成部分。虽然我会逐一描述它们，但不要指望这些感觉是泾渭分明的——它们相互交织、相互影响、相互作用。还要记住，恐惧、责任和内疚的来源因人而异，显然我不可能一一列举。引发你这些感觉的言语和行为可能与我下面描述的有所不同，但其结果却是一样的。它们共同编织出一个令人不安的矩阵，驱使我们屈服于勒索。

THE REAL F-WORD: FEAR

真正的“F”字：恐惧

Blackmailers build their conscious and unconscious strategies on the information we give them about what we fear. They notice what we run away from, see what makes us nervous, observe when our bodies go rigid in response to something we’re experiencing. It’s not that they’re taking notes and actively filing them away for later use against us—we all absorb this knowledge about the people we’re close to. In emotional blackmail, fear works a transformation on the blackmailer, too—a process I’ll discuss in depth in Chapter 5 . In the simplest terms, the blackmailers’ fear of not getting what they want becomes so intense that they become tightly focused, able to see the outcome they want in exquisite detail but unable to take their eyes off their goal long enough to see how their actions are affecting us.

勒索者会根据我们透露的恐惧信息，制定有意识和无意识的策略。他们会留意我们逃避什么，观察什么会让我们紧张，以及我们身体在经历某些事情时会如何僵硬。这并非是他们刻意记录并储存起来以备日后对付我们——我们都会不自觉地吸收身边人的这些信息。在情感勒索中，恐惧也会对勒索者产生影响——我将在第五章深入探讨这一过程。简而言之，勒索者害怕得不到想要的东西，这种恐惧会变得异常强烈，以至于他们变得异常专注，能够清晰地看到自己想要的结果，却无法将目光从目标上移开，从而忽略了他们的行为对我们造成的影响。

At that point, the information they’ve gathered about us in the course of a relationship becomes ammunition for driving home a deal that’s fed on both sides by fear. The terms they offer are tailor-made for us: do things my way and I won’t [fill in the blank]:

那时，他们在交往过程中收集到的关于我们的信息就成了他们达成协议的筹码，而这项协议的背后是双方的恐惧。他们提出的条件是专门为我们量身定制的：按我的方式做，我就不[此处省略]。

  • Leave you
    离开你
  • Disapprove of you
    不赞同你
  • Stop loving you
    别再爱你了
  • Yell at you
    冲你大喊
  • Make you miserable
    让你痛苦不堪
  • Confront you
    质问你
  • Fire you
    解雇你

Whatever the specifics, they’ll be shaped to fit the contours of the fears we’ve made apparent. In fact, one of the most painful parts of emotional blackmail is that it violates the trust that has allowed us to reveal ourselves and develop a more than superficial relationship with the blackmailer. In the situations that follow, watch the way the blackmailers zero in on the fears that will get the strongest response.

无论具体情况如何，他们都会根据我们所表现出的恐惧来塑造勒索者的意图。事实上，情感勒索最痛苦的地方之一在于，它破坏了我们与勒索者之间建立的信任，正是这种信任让我们袒露心扉，并与勒索者发展出超越表面的关系。在接下来的情境中，请留意勒索者是如何精准地利用那些最能激起我们强烈反应的恐惧的。

The Most Basic Fear

最基本的恐惧

Our first encounter with fear comes in infancy, when we literally cannot survive without the goodwill of our caretakers. This helplessness creates abandonment terrors that some people never outgrow. We humans are tribal animals, and the idea of being cut off from the support and affection of those we love and depend on can be almost unbearable. That makes fear of abandonment one of our most potent, pervasive and easily triggered fears.

我们与恐惧的最初接触发生在婴儿时期，那时我们离不开照料者的关爱。这种无助感会造成被遗弃的恐惧，有些人终其一生都无法摆脱。人类是群居动物，被我们所爱和依赖的人的关爱和支持所切断，这种想法几乎令人难以忍受。因此，被遗弃的恐惧是我们最强烈、最普遍、也最容易被触发的恐惧之一。

Lynn, an IRS investigator in her late 40s, married Jeff, a 45-year-old carpenter, five years ago. She came to me because she had accumulated a long list of resentments and bad feelings about him, and she wanted to see if she could find a way to improve their relationship. Jeff quit his job after the two got married. They agreed that because of Lynn’s salary, they could afford to let Jeff devote all of his time to maintaining their home, a small ranch near Los Angeles. But the setup is a constant source of friction between them.

琳恩是一位年近五十的国税局调查员，五年前嫁给了45岁的木匠杰夫。她来找我是因为她对杰夫积攒了许多怨恨和不满，她想看看能否找到改善两人关系的方法。婚后，杰夫辞去了工作。他们商定，琳恩的收入足以让杰夫全身心投入到家务中，打理他们在洛杉矶附近的小农场。但这种安排却成了他们之间摩擦不断的根源。

Jeff and I don’t have the most equal relationship. I make the money and he spends it. No, that’s not fair. I work outside the home and he takes care of the ranch—the house, the animals, the property, me. I really like that sometimes, but I’d feel better if he could just make an effort and find some work. The fact is, most of the money we have between us is what I make, but he’s always finding ways to run through it, and I’m a pushover when he wants something.

我和杰夫的关系并不平等。我挣钱，他花钱。不，这不公平。我在外面工作，他负责照料农场——房子、牲畜、土地，还有我。有时候我挺喜欢这样，但如果他能努力找份工作，我会更开心。事实上，我们俩的大部分钱都是我挣的，但他总能想方设法花光，而我只要他想要什么，就总是心软。

We’ve been arguing lately about cash flow and our priorities, and in the past few months he’s started to sulk when we can’t agree—or when I don’t agree with him. I’ll hear the screen door slam, and he’ll yell back something like “I’m going out,” then take off for the barn. He knows I can’t stand it when he withdraws from me. I’m always following him around the house—if he goes into the other room I practically feel abandoned. When my first marriage broke up, the thing I hated most was the loneliness of coming home to an empty house, and I don’t ever want to feel like that again. I’ve told Jeff about it—and he used to be patient with me, knowing I like to be physically close to him. So it makes me crazy when he stalks off.

最近我们一直在争论现金流和优先事项，过去几个月里，只要我们意见不合——或者我不同意他的观点——他就会生闷气。我会听到纱门砰地一声关上，然后他会吼一声“我出去了”，接着就冲进谷仓。他知道我受不了他冷落我。我总是跟着他走来走去——如果他去了另一个房间，我感觉自己就像被抛弃了一样。第一次婚姻破裂时，我最痛恨的就是回到空荡荡的家后那种孤独感，我再也不想经历那种感觉了。我跟杰夫说过这件事——他以前很耐心，因为他知道我喜欢和他亲近。所以他现在这样一走了之，真的让我很抓狂。

The first thing that happens is that I start thinking he’s mad at me, so he’s going to leave. Intellectually, I know it’s crazy. We’re having some bad times, but we really love each other, and he’s not going anywhere. But this is scaring me. I can’t not say what’s on my mind, but I’m going nuts with these fights.

首先，我开始觉得他生我的气了，所以要离开。理智上我知道这很荒谬。我们之间确实有些不愉快，但我们真的很爱彼此，他也不会离开。但这真的让我很害怕。我无法控制自己不去想这些，但这些争吵快把我逼疯了。

Lynn thought of being alone as falling into what she called a black hole, a well of depression that swallows her up when she’s by herself. The black hole is the most frightening thing she can imagine, and each time Jeff withdrew, it loomed large in front of her.

琳恩觉得独处就像掉进一个黑洞，一个让她独自一人时便会吞噬她的抑郁深渊。这个黑洞是她能想象到的最可怕的东西，每次杰夫离开，它就仿佛在她眼前不断逼近。

We had a major crisis when his old truck died and he started hinting around about how great it would be to have a new one. He could do so much more with a new truck, maybe pick up jobs on the other ranches around the valley. When I told him that I didn’t think we could afford it, he was fuming. I hated fighting, but I felt that the money just wasn’t there, and I kept telling him so. After a few days of this, he said money was the only thing I cared about, I didn’t appreciate all the work he did to make my life pleasant and happy, and maybe I’d appreciate him more if he left me on my own for awhile. Then he took off and didn’t come home for four days. I was crazy with worry. I tracked him down at his brother’s, and I begged him to come back. He said he wouldn’t unless I respected him for what he was and started showing it.

他的旧卡车坏了，我们家陷入了一场大危机。他开始到处暗示说，要是能有辆新卡车该多好。有了新卡车，他就能做更多的事情，比如去山谷周围的其他牧场接活儿。我告诉他我觉得我们负担不起，他气得火冒三丈。我讨厌争吵，但我觉得我们确实没钱，所以我一直跟他说。这样折腾了几天后，他说我眼里只有钱，不感激他为了让我的生活舒适快乐所做的一切，还说如果他让我一个人待一段时间，我或许会更感激他。然后他就走了，四天都没回家。我担心得要命。我到他哥哥家找到了他，求他回来。他说除非我尊重他，并且开始用行动来证明这一点，否则他不会回来。

Jeff reacted like a wounded animal, full of defensiveness about his status in the relationship and humiliated by the constant reminders of how financially dependent he was. Despite how much we’ve evolved socially over the past few decades, relationships like Jeff and Lynn’s are still outside the traditional norm, and Jeff, like many men whose partners earn more than they do, felt that he was in a tenuous position—one that he had to justify and protect. The couple had agreed to their financial arrangement, but in Jeff’s view, Lynn changed signals whenever he wanted something. Suddenly it was not OK that he was not bringing in any money, and he was off balance, swinging at Lynn to regain his equilibrium.

杰夫的反应就像一只受伤的野兽，他对自己在这段关系中的地位充满防御心理，并且因为不断被提醒经济上依赖对方而感到羞辱。尽管过去几十年里社会发生了巨大的变化，但像杰夫和琳恩这样的关系仍然不符合传统规范。杰夫和许多伴侣收入高于自己的男性一样，感到自己处境岌岌可危——他必须证明自己的价值并维护这种地位。这对伴侣已经就财务安排达成一致，但在杰夫看来，琳恩总是在他想要什么的时候改变主意。突然间，他觉得自己没有收入是不对的，这让他失去了平衡，于是他开始攻击琳恩，试图重新获得平衡。

For her part, Lynn had gone from being confused and scared to a state of panic. Intimate relationships bring up our most potent fears because it is there that we feel the most vulnerable. We may function at a high level in the rest of our lives, only to turn to jelly at any rejection or perceived rejection by a partner.

琳恩的情绪则从困惑和恐惧迅速恶化到恐慌。亲密关系会唤起我们内心最深层的恐惧，因为在亲密关系中，我们会感到最脆弱。我们或许在其他方面表现得游刃有余，但一旦遭到伴侣的拒绝或感受到拒绝，就会瞬间崩溃。

After all my pleading, Jeff finally came home, but he wasn’t talking much, and the tension was so thick I had to do something. I couldn’t stand it. My parents had been like that — distant and angry and silent, all that fake politeness—and I always hated it. I swore I would never live like that with anyone. So I had to cut through the bad feelings. I thought about it, and I asked myself, What’s more important—Jeff or the money?

在我苦苦哀求之后，杰夫终于回家了，但他一句话也不说，气氛紧张得令人窒息，我必须做点什么。我受不了了。我的父母也曾是这样——疏远、愤怒、沉默，满嘴虚伪的礼貌——我一直很讨厌这样。我发誓我绝不会和任何人过那样的生活。所以我必须克服这种糟糕的感觉。我仔细想了想，问自己：杰夫和钱，哪个更重要？

Soon Jeff was driving a brand-new truck. Whether he’d expected the truck or not, now that he had it he felt as though he’d gained a little equality in the relationship, and he knew what it had taken to get Lynn to agree. Though he didn’t consciously formulate a strategy of playing on her fear of anger, silence and abandonment, when he felt he wasn’t getting what he needed and deserved, he played his trump cards. A pattern developed: Every time Jeff withdrew, Lynn gave in. Jeff had learned that if Lynn became afraid, all he had to do was upset her with his moods and she would give him what she wanted—not that he was a bad guy, not that he was trying to hurt her, but that what he was doing was working.

很快，杰夫就开上了一辆崭新的卡车。不管他是否预料到会得到这辆卡车，现在有了它，他感觉自己在这段关系中获得了些许平等，也明白了当初是如何让琳同意的。虽然他并非有意利用琳对愤怒、沉默和被抛弃的恐惧来达到目的，但当他觉得自己没有得到应有的、需要的东西时，他就会使出杀手锏。一种模式逐渐形成：每次杰夫退缩，琳就会妥协。杰夫明白，如果琳感到害怕，他只需要用自己的情绪惹她生气，她就会给他想要的东西——这并不是说他是个坏人，也不是说他想伤害她，而是说他这么做奏效了。

Because Jeff’s blackmail seems to be all about money, Lynn sometimes sounds like an accountant trying fit her feelings onto a balance sheet as she scrambles to avoid facing the terror inside the black hole. And she makes herself crazy obsessing and ruminating:

因为杰夫的勒索似乎完全是为了钱，琳恩有时听起来就像个会计师，试图把自己的感受塞进资产负债表里，拼命逃避面对黑洞般的恐惧。她沉迷于此，反复思索，最终把自己逼疯了：

I’m really nuts about him, but I wonder if I’d be better off without him. Is it just costing me too much money to stay with him? He’s completely dependent on me.

我真的非常爱他，但我又在想，离开他我会不会过得更好。是不是跟他在一起让我花费太多钱？他完全依赖我。

She talks more reluctantly about her emotional dependence on him:

她越来越不情愿地谈起自己对他的情感依赖：

How could I think about breaking up and starting all over again with someone else? I’m so afraid of going back into that depressed place I was in before we got married.

我怎么能想着分手，然后和别人重新开始呢？我好害怕再回到结婚前那种抑郁的状态。

I pointed out to Lynn that she was throwing the baby out with the bath water. Yes, there was a financial friction between them, but her fear of abandonment was so blinding that she lost her ability to look at the relationship objectively whenever Jeff blackmailed her. Instead of trying to work out a healthy compromise, Lynn flipped into automatic pilot and resentfully capitulated.

我指出琳恩这是因噎废食。没错，他们之间确实存在经济摩擦，但她对被抛弃的恐惧蒙蔽了双眼，以至于每当杰夫勒索她时，她都无法客观地看待这段关系。琳恩没有努力寻求合理的妥协方案，而是像进入了自动驾驶模式一样，心怀怨恨地屈服了。

Fear moves us into black-and-white—even catastrophic—thinking. Lynn was sure that if she confronted Jeff, he’d abandon her, and that left her with only two options: give him what he wanted, or choose to break up with him, which would get rid of the blackmail but leave her alone and back in the “black hole.” I told Lynn that she had another choice: Together we could deal with the aspect of the relationship that was causing them both so much trouble in the present and work to alleviate her abandonment fears.

恐惧会让我们陷入非黑即白——甚至是灾难性的——思维模式。琳恩确信，如果她和杰夫对质，他就会抛弃她，这样她就只剩下两个选择：要么满足他的要求，要么选择分手，分手虽然能摆脱勒索，但也会让她孤身一人，再次陷入“黑洞”。我告诉琳恩，她还有另一种选择：我们可以一起处理这段关系中目前给他们双方都带来诸多困扰的问题，并努力减轻她被抛弃的恐惧。

Fear of Anger

对愤怒的恐惧

Anger seems to magnetize fear, pulling it quickly to the surface and activating the fight/flight reaction in our bodies. It’s an emotion that few of us can express or experience in a comfortable way because we associate it with conflict, loss and even violence. This discomfort is reasonable and protective, leading us to duck or run when explosive anger threatens to take a physical form and harm us. But in all relationships except significantly abusive ones, anger is just another emotion—not good and not bad. We’ve built up so much anxiety and apprehension about our own and other people’s anger, however, that it can dramatically affect our ability to stand up to blackmail.

愤怒似乎会吸引恐惧，迅速将其拉到表面，激活我们身体的战斗或逃跑反应。很少有人能自在地表达或体验这种情绪，因为我们常常将其与冲突、失去甚至暴力联系在一起。这种不适感合情合理，也是一种保护机制，促使我们在愤怒爆发、可能以暴力形式伤害我们时选择躲避或逃跑。但在除严重虐待关系之外的所有关系中，愤怒只是一种情绪——既非善也非恶。然而，我们对自身和他人的愤怒积累了太多的焦虑和担忧，以至于它会严重影响我们抵御勒索的能力。

For many of us, this emotion seems so dangerous that we’re afraid of it in any form, and we fear not only other people’s anger but our own. Over the years, I’ve heard thousands of people express their fears that if they get angry they’ll hurt someone, lose control or fall into a million pieces. Just the hint of anger in another person’s voice frequently sparks fears of rejection, disapproval or abandonment and, in the extreme, visions of violence or harm.

对我们许多人来说，这种情绪似乎如此危险，以至于我们害怕它以任何形式出现，我们不仅害怕别人的愤怒，也害怕自己的愤怒。多年来，我听过成千上万的人表达他们的恐惧：如果他们生气，就会伤害别人、失去控制，或者崩溃。仅仅是别人语气中一丝愤怒，就常常会引发对被拒绝、被否定或被抛弃的恐惧，在极端情况下，甚至会引发暴力或伤害的画面。

My client Josh, the furniture maker we met in the last chapter, feels pushed to the wall by his father’s angry disapproval of the woman he loves—and frozen by his father’s anger. “All I have to do is try to talk to him about it and his whole demeanor changes,” Josh said. “I see him tense up, and his voice goes up 20 decibels. When I see that look on his face and hear that roar coming out of his mouth, even though I’m four inches taller, I’m still scared of the guy.”

我的客户乔什，就是我们在上一章里认识的那位家具匠，他因为父亲对他所爱之人的强烈反对而感到走投无路，父亲的怒火也让他噤若寒蝉。“我只要试着跟他谈谈这件事，他的态度就完全变了，”乔什说，“我看到他浑身紧绷，声音也提高了20分贝。每次看到他那副表情，听到他那咆哮般的怒吼，即便我比他高四英寸，我还是会害怕他。”

Parents have a remarkable ability to reactivate our childhood fears. As Josh recalled:

父母有一种神奇的能力，能重新唤起我们童年的恐惧。正如乔希回忆的那样：

When I was a kid, my father used to yell so loud when he got angry that I was afraid the house would come down on us. It’s ridiculous, but I still have the same feeling when he’s upset with me, though he’s mellowed over the years. I act like he’s still that scary guy he was when I was a kid.

小时候，我爸一生气就吼得震天响，我都怕房子塌下来砸到我们。现在想想真是可笑，虽然他这些年脾气温和多了，但他生我气的时候，我还是会有同样的感觉。我还是会把他当成我小时候那个可怕的人。

The events and feelings we experienced as children are alive within us and often reappear when there is turmoil and stress. Though the adult part of ourselves may know that these things took place decades ago, to the part inside all of us that is not adult, it’s as though they happened yesterday. Emotional memory can keep us locked into old ways of fearful acting and reacting, even when there’s nothing in our current reality to justify the fear.

童年时期的经历和感受鲜活地存在于我们内心，常常在动荡和压力之下重现。虽然我们成年后的认知或许明白这些事发生在几十年前，但对于我们内心深处尚未成熟的那部分而言，却仿佛就发生在昨天。情感记忆会让我们固守旧有的恐惧行为模式，即便当下的现实中没有任何理由让我们产生恐惧。

Conditioned Reflexes

条件反射

Sometimes we react to the mere suggestion of the behavior we fear. “All dad has to do is get red in the face and draw his eyebrows together and I back off,” Josh said. “It’s not like he even has to yell anymore.”

有时候，我们仅仅对某种我们害怕的行为有所反应。“爸爸只要脸涨得通红，眉毛一皱，我就退缩了，”乔什说。“他现在甚至都不用吼叫了。”

Many of you took a beginning psychology class in high school or college, and chances are you remember the story of the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov and his experiments with dogs, the classic demonstration of what’s known as conditioned reflex. Pavlov was studying the digestive process of dogs, which begins with the natural response of salivating when they see food. He noticed, though, that if he rang a bell as he presented food to them, the dogs soon began to associate the sound of the bell with food and would salivate at the mere sound of it—no food required. In much the same way, the targets of emotional blackmail exhibit conditioned reflexes whenever they have been through an event that’s created significant fear in them.

你们当中许多人在高中或大学都上过心理学入门课，很可能还记得俄国生理学家伊万·巴甫洛夫和他用狗做的实验，那是条件反射的经典演示。巴甫洛夫研究的是狗的消化过程，狗看到食物时会自然分泌唾液。但他注意到，如果他在给狗喂食的同时摇铃，狗很快就会把铃声和食物联系起来，仅仅听到铃声就会分泌唾液——无需食物。同样地，情感勒索的受害者在经历过让他们感到极度恐惧的事件后，也会表现出条件反射。

It might be that a husband makes good on his threat to leave his wife and takes off for a short time; an adult child becomes angry with something her parents have done and stops talking to them for several days; a woman’s friend becomes upset, crying and yelling at her. Even if a reconciliation has taken place, the traumatic event is not forgotten. It becomes a symbol of the pain, and by evoking it, a blackmailer refreshes our original feeling of fear, applying enough pressure to make us give in.

或许丈夫真的兑现了离开妻子的威胁，短暂离家；或许成年子女因为父母的某些行为而生气，几天不跟他们说话；或许女人的朋友情绪激动，哭着对她大喊大叫。即使最终和解，这段创伤经历也难以忘怀。它成了痛苦的象征，勒索者正是利用这段经历，重新唤起我们最初的恐惧，施加足够的压力，迫使我们屈服。

For Josh, all it took was an angry look from Paul. He quickly settled on his best course of action: He’d lie. He’d keep seeing Beth but pretend to his father that he’d broken up with her. It was an expedient solution, but Josh’s quest to avoid anger cost him dearly. As we’ll see people doing throughout this book, Josh is playing a dangerous game called Peace at Any Price. The price for Josh? His own self-respect and the physical and emotional costs of letting anger build, both within him and in his relationship with his father.

对乔什来说，保罗一个愤怒的眼神就足以让他彻底崩溃。他迅速决定了最佳方案：撒谎。他会继续和贝丝见面，但假装已经和她分手。这虽然是个权宜之计，但乔什为了避免愤怒而付出了惨痛的代价。正如我们在本书中会看到的那样，乔什正在玩一场名为“不惜一切代价换取和平”的危险游戏。而乔什的代价是什么呢？是他自身的自尊，以及任由愤怒在他内心和与父亲的关系中不断积聚所带来的身心痛苦。

Fear flourishes in the dark, unexamined but vividly imagined. Our bodies and the primitive parts of our brains read it as a reason to run away, and often that’s what we do, avoiding what we fear because deep inside we believe that’s the only way to survive. In fact, as you will see, our emotional well-being depends on doing just the opposite—facing and confronting what we fear the most.

恐惧在黑暗中滋生，未经审视却又被生动地想象出来。我们的身体和大脑的原始本能会将其解读为逃跑的理由，而我们也常常真的这么做，逃避恐惧，因为在内心深处，我们相信这是唯一的生存之道。事实上，正如你将看到的，我们的情绪健康恰恰取决于我们反其道而行之——直面并对抗我们最恐惧的事物。

OBLIGATION

义务

We all come into our adult lives with well-established rules and values regarding how much of ourselves we owe to other people and how much of our behavior ought to be determined by such ideals as duty, obedience, loyalty, altruism and self-sacrifice. We all have deeply ingrained ideas about these values, and often we think they’re our own ideas, but actually they were shaped by the influence of our parents, our religious backgrounds, the prevailing beliefs of society, the media and the people we’re close to.

我们每个人步入成年生活时，都已形成一套根深蒂固的规则和价值观，这些规则和价值观关乎我们对他人应尽的责任，以及我们的行为应在多大程度上受到诸如责任、服从、忠诚、利他主义和自我牺牲等理想的约束。我们对这些价值观有着根深蒂固的观念，我们常常认为这些观念源于自身，但实际上，它们是由我们的父母、宗教背景、社会主流观念、媒体以及我们身边亲近的人的影响所塑造的。

Often our ideas about duty and obligation are reasonable, and they form an ethical and moral foundation for our lives that I wouldn’t suggest being without. But all too often, our attempt to weigh our responsibility to ourselves against the indebtedness we feel to others falls out of balance. We go overboard for the sake of duty.

我们对责任和义务的理解通常是合理的，它们构成了我们生活的伦理道德基础，我并不认为我们应该放弃这些基础。但很多时候，我们试图权衡对自己的责任和对他人的责任时，却往往失衡。我们为了履行责任而做得过火。

Blackmailers never hesitate to put our sense of obligation to the test, emphasizing how much they’ve given up, how much they’ve done for their targets, how much we owe them. They may even use reinforcements from religion and social traditions to emphasize how much their targets should feel indebted to them.

勒索者从不犹豫地考验我们的义务感，他们会强调自己为受害者付出了多少，做了多少，以及我们欠他们多少。他们甚至会利用宗教和社会传统来强化受害者对他们的感激之情。

  • “A good daughter should spend time with her mother.”
    “好女儿应该多花时间陪伴母亲。”
  • “I work my ass off for this family, and the least you can do is be there when I get home.”
    “我为了这个家拼命工作，你们至少应该在我回家的时候陪着我。”
  • “Honor (and obey!) your father.”
    “要孝敬（并服从！）你的父亲。”
  • “The boss is always right.”
    老板永远是对的。
  • “I stood by you when you were going out with that jerk and needed support. All I’m asking now is that you loan me $2,000. I’m your best friend!”
    “你跟那个混蛋交往的时候，我一直站在你这边，支持你。我现在只求你借我2000美元。我是你最好的朋友！”

They push far beyond the limits of a give-and-take relationship, letting us know that, like it or not, it’s nothing less than our responsibility to do what they ask. These expectations are especially confusing if the blackmailer has been generous to us. But love and willingness can quickly fall out of the equation when replaced by obligation and an enforced sense of duty.

他们远远超出了互惠互利关系的范畴，让我们明白，不管我们愿不愿意，都必须按照他们的要求去做。如果勒索者之前对我们很慷慨，这种要求就尤其令人困惑。但当爱和意愿被义务和被迫的责任感所取代时，它们很快就会消失殆尽。

A client I saw several years ago remains in my mind as the epitome of the blackmail target manipulated through obligation and duty. Maria, a 37-year-old hospital administrator who was married to a well-known surgeon, described herself as one of those people who’s always there for you. She’d come over at four in the morning if you were depressed and needed company, and she couldn’t do enough for the people around her, because she loved the satisfaction of giving.

几年前我遇到的一位客户，至今仍让我记忆犹新，她堪称利用责任和义务进行敲诈勒索的典型案例。玛丽亚，一位37岁的医院行政人员，嫁给了一位知名的外科医生。她自称是那种永远乐于助人的人。如果你心情低落，需要陪伴，她会在凌晨四点过来。她总是竭尽所能地帮助身边的人，因为她享受付出带来的满足感。

Her husband, Jay, took full advantage of those traits during their stormy marriage.

在他们充满波折的婚姻中，她的丈夫杰伊充分利用了她的这些特质。

I’m from a generation where getting married, having kids and being the good, devoted wife is the most important job a woman can have and Jay probably married me because of it. I love my work at the hospital, but my home — that’s the center of my world. I took a seminar at my church that taught me something I always carry with me: It takes one person to make a relationship work. If you give your all and ask for God’s help, you can ride with all the waves that come up. As a woman, I’m serious about what I owe my family, and Jay knows that very, very well.

我这一代人认为，结婚生子、做一个贤良贤惠的妻子是女人最重要的事，杰伊大概也是因为这个才娶我的。我热爱在医院的工作，但我的家——那才是我世界的中心。我参加过教会的一个研讨会，从中我学到了一条我一直铭记于心的道理：维系一段感情，需要两个人共同努力。如果你全心全意付出，并祈求上帝的帮助，你就能经受住人生中的各种风浪。作为一名女性，我非常重视自己对家庭的责任，杰伊对此也心知肚明。

Jay tapped Maria’s sense of obligation for years, emphasizing—and probably believing—that no matter what else he did, he was a good provider, holding up his end of the marriage bargain.

多年来，杰伊利用玛丽亚的责任感，强调——而且可能也相信——无论他做了什么，他都是一个好养家糊口的人，履行了他在婚姻契约中的责任。

People always thought that we were the perfect couple, but what people didn’t realize was that Jay was a compulsive womanizer. Before we got married he used to tell me about his sexual exploits and brag about how many women were chasing him or had a crush on him. I didn’t really want to hear about them, but it made me feel good to know that with all the women he could have had, he chose me. Now I know just how naive that belief was.

人们总是觉得我们是天造地设的一对，但他们不知道的是，杰伊是个花花公子。结婚前，他经常跟我讲他的风流韵事，吹嘘有多少女人追求他、暗恋他。我其实并不想听这些，但知道他那么多女人可以选择，却偏偏选择了我，这让我感觉很好。现在我才知道，当初的想法有多么天真。

I’m not sure just how many affairs he had after we got married, but I know there were several. Out-of-town conventions, late nights at the office, frequently getting his stories mixed up and his growing indifference to me were all signs. Then came the phone calls from “friends” who saw him with another woman. My gut told me that people weren’t making this up, but it took me a long time to confront him. So many conflicting things were racing through my mind. I felt I owed him — he’d worked hard for us.

我不确定我们结婚后他到底出轨了多少次，但我知道肯定不止一次。他经常去外地参加会议，在办公室加班到深夜，经常把事情说得一团糟，而且对我越来越冷淡，这些都是迹象。后来，一些“朋友”打电话来说看到他和别的女人在一起。我的直觉告诉我，他们说的不是空话，但我花了很长时间才鼓起勇气和他摊牌。当时我脑子里一片混乱，各种矛盾的想法交织在一起。我觉得我亏欠他——他为了我们付出了很多。

Jay took the offensive in pressuring Maria to stay with him no matter what—because it was her duty.

杰伊采取了主动策略，向玛丽亚施压，让她无论如何都要留在他身边——因为这是她的责任。

He denied everything, of course. “How dare you believe some malicious gossip,” he told me. “All I’ve done is work and sacrifice to see that this family only had the best. There were plenty of times that I didn’t want to stay late at the hospital, but I did it for you—and now you’re holding it against me. How can you think of leaving and breaking up the family? Just look around at what you have compared to other women. I can’t believe you don’t appreciate what it took to get this.” By the time he was through with me, I had to agree—I did owe him loyalty and trust. And my kids. I love my kids so much. How could I do that to them—they love their dad. How could I split the family apart?

他当然否认了一切。“你怎么敢相信那些恶意的流言蜚语？”他冲我吼道，“我所做的一切都是努力工作、牺牲奉献，只为了让这个家过上最好的生活。很多时候我都不想在医院待到很晚，但我都为了你坚持了下来——现在你却因此怨恨我。你怎么能想到离开，拆散这个家？看看你现在拥有的，再看看其他女人拥有的。我真不敢相信你竟然不明白我为了得到这一切付出了多少。”他跟我说完之后，我不得不承认——我的确欠他忠诚和信任。还有我的孩子们。我那么爱我的孩子们。我怎么能那样对他们——他们爱他们的爸爸。我怎么能拆散这个家呢？

Then he put his hands on my shoulders and whispered in my ear: “Put on that black dress I like so much and I’ll take you to dinner. And I don’t want to hear the word divorce again. This is all just gossip that shouldn’t concern you.” I felt so confused I pasted on a smile, put on that dress and went out with him like nothing had happened.

然后他把手搭在我的肩膀上，在我耳边低语：“穿上那件我特别喜欢的黑色连衣裙，我带你去吃饭。还有，我不想再听到‘离婚’这个词。这些都只是流言蜚语，跟你没关系。” 我当时感觉很迷茫，只好强颜欢笑，穿上那件连衣裙，装作什么都没发生一样跟他出去了。

Jay knew exactly where Maria’s most sensitive spots were, and to reach them he described the consequences of any potential breakup in terms that would speak directly to her sense of duty to her family. Not only would she be abandoning her hard-working husband, he told her, but she’d also be dooming her children to a life of neglect and unhappiness.

杰伊非常清楚玛丽亚的痛点在哪里，为了触动她的痛点，他用直击她家庭责任感的话语，描述了任何潜在分手后果。他告诉她，她不仅会抛弃辛勤工作的丈夫，还会让孩子们过上被忽视和不幸的生活。

Reluctance to break up a family keeps many people in relationships that have gone sour. No one wants to traumatize or uproot their children or have to deal with their pain and confusion. Some blackmail targets feel so passionately about their obligation to their children that they will make what they mistakenly see as a noble sacrifice and give up their right to have a good life. Though Maria was miserable, the thought of shattering her family horrified her, and kept her paralyzed.

不愿拆散家庭让许多人继续维持着已经破裂的关系。没有人愿意让孩子遭受创伤或被迫离开熟悉的环境，也不愿面对他们的痛苦和困惑。一些被勒索的对象对子女的责任感如此强烈，以至于他们会做出他们误以为是高尚的牺牲，放弃自己拥有美好生活的权利。尽管玛丽亚很痛苦，但想到要拆散自己的家庭，她就感到恐惧，以至于动弹不得。

Maria’s sense of obligation was so powerful that it almost defined her. She was proud of it, and she instinctively defended herself against suggestions that she hadn’t lived up to her own standards. Exaggeration followed exaggeration as Jay twisted what duty and responsibility really mean, blowing them up to such a size that they completely overshadowed his own infidelity. As Jay defined it, Maria’s obligation to him was all-encompassing. His obligation to her stopped where he wanted it to—in this case, at the idea of remaining faithful to her. In his martyred how-can-you-do-this-to-me stance, he gave little thought to how he could have done this to her, and to his children, whose lives had already been affected by the stresses his affairs had brought into the house. How nice it would be if blackmailers were as sensitive to our feelings as they want us to be to theirs.

玛丽亚的责任感如此强烈，几乎定义了她。她为此感到自豪，并本能地反驳任何关于她未能达到自身标准的质疑。杰伊不断夸大其词，扭曲了责任和义务的真正含义，将它们无限放大，以至于完全掩盖了他自己的不忠。在杰伊看来，玛丽亚对他的义务是无所不包的。而他对她的义务却止于他想要止步的地方——在这个例子中，止于对她保持忠诚。他摆出一副受害者的姿态，仿佛在说“你怎么能这样对我”，却很少去想自己对她，以及对他的孩子们——他们的生活早已因他的婚外情给家庭带来的压力而受到影响——又造成了怎样的伤害。如果勒索者也能像他们希望我们体谅他们一样体谅我们的感受，那该有多好啊。

Jay refused to do anything about his role in the disintegration of their relationship, claiming he was too busy—and there was no need. He hadn’t done anything wrong, and if Maria was unhappy, she should go get “fixed” so they could go back to the way things had been.

杰伊拒绝为自己在两人关系破裂中所扮演的角色承担任何责任，声称自己太忙了——而且根本没必要。他没做错任何事，如果玛丽亚不开心，她应该去做“治疗”，这样他们就能回到以前的样子了。

I reminded Maria that no matter what position Jay—or for that matter, anyone else—took, she had an obligation to care for herself as well as to look after others. Maria’s self-negating willingness to go along with Jay was not coming from a sense of self-respect or an exploration of her choices—it was an automatic reaction to emotional blackmail.

我提醒玛丽亚，无论杰伊——或者任何人——采取什么立场，她都有义务照顾好自己，也要照顾好他人。玛丽亚违背自身意愿地顺从杰伊，并非出于自尊或对自身选择的探索，而是对情感勒索的本能反应。

As so often happens with people who are easily manipulated through obligation, Maria remembered to do what was best for everybody except herself. Most of us have a terrible time defining our boundaries, where our obligations to others begin and end. And when our sense of obligation is stronger than our sense of self-respect and self-caring, blackmailers quickly learn how to take advantage.

玛丽亚常常因为责任感而受人摆布，她总是想着做对所有人都有利的事，唯独忽略了自己。我们大多数人都很难界定自己的界限，分不清对他人的义务从何开始，又到何时结束。而当我们的责任感凌驾于自尊和自我关爱之上时，勒索者很快就会找到可乘之机。

The Everlasting IOU

永恒的欠条

Some blackmailers look selectively at the past to find a reason why we owe them whatever they want. Memory, as employed by a blackmailer, becomes the Obligation Channel, with nonstop replays of the blackmailer’s good and generous behavior toward us.

有些勒索者会选择性地回顾过去，寻找我们欠他们任何东西的理由。在勒索者眼中，记忆变成了“义务通道”，不断重现他们过去对我们的好意和慷慨。

When we receive a kindness from a blackmailer, it’s not soon forgotten. More like an open-ended loan than a gift, it’s always got payments attached—with interest—and we can never seem to get out of the red. The emphasis is on the blackmailer’s sacrifices, made not with an open heart but with the intention of scoring points, accumulating markers that can be called in.

当我们收到勒索者的“好意”时，这种好意并不会轻易被遗忘。与其说是礼物，不如说更像是一笔无底线的贷款，它总是附带利息，而且我们似乎永远无法摆脱债务。重点在于勒索者的“牺牲”，这些牺牲并非出于真心，而是为了博取关注，积累可以随时动用的筹码。

When the Target of Blackmail Becomes the Blackmailer

当勒索对象变成勒索者

Early in my work with Lynn, I found that she had struck back at Jeff by returning his blackmail with some blackmail of her own.

在我与琳恩共事的早期，我发现她对杰夫进行了反击，以自己的一些勒索手段回击了他的勒索。

I asked Jeff to come in for a joint session, and I’ll let him describe what happened:

我请杰夫来参加一次联合会议，下面由他来描述会议内容：

I’ve gotten to the point where I have to get away from her for a few days. I’d never heard her spell out what she thinks this relationship is about until she called me at my brother’s after our fight about the truck. She cried and cried, and finally she started yelling something like “If you really loved me, you never would have done this to me. How can you be so selfish? The only person you think about is you, and it’s all take, take, take. You know who makes the money around here. You know who writes the checks. After all I’ve done for you, how dare you leave me like this. If you ever so much as stop speaking to me again, the money will stop so fast it’ll make your head spin.” That’s when I knew we were in trouble. We were both so scared afterward about what was happening to us that we decided to get into therapy.

我已经到了不得不离开她几天的地步了。直到我们因为卡车吵架后，她在我哥哥家给我打电话，我才第一次听到她把这段感情说得这么清楚。她哭个不停，最后开始大喊大叫，大概是这样的：“如果你真的爱我，就不会这样对我。你怎么能这么自私？你满脑子想的都是你自己，只想着索取、索取、索取。你知道谁是家里的顶梁柱，谁是发工资的人。我为你做了那么多，你竟然敢这样离开我。你要是再敢不跟我说话，我的钱就会立刻断供，让你晕头转向。” 那一刻我就知道我们麻烦大了。事后我们俩都非常害怕，不知道发生了什么，于是决定去看心理医生。

Like many blackmailers, Lynn zeroed in on Jeff’s sense of how much he owed her, at the same time making a string of negative moral judgments about his character and motives. She did everything she could to coerce Jeff to stay, going beyond emphasizing his obligation to her and trying to make him as afraid as he’d made her. She had given up her power as she frantically hunted for him and begged him to come back, and to regain it she shifted into the blackmailer’s role, where she could call the shots.

和许多勒索者一样，琳恩精准地抓住了杰夫欠她情的心理，同时对他的人品和动机做出了一系列负面的道德评判。她想尽一切办法胁迫杰夫留下，不仅强调他对她的义务，还试图让他像她一样感到恐惧。在她疯狂地寻找他、恳求他回来的时候，她已经失去了主动权；为了重新夺回主动权，她转而扮演勒索者的角色，掌控一切。

It’s not uncommon for two people in any relationship to change roles, alternately playing both target and blackmailer.
