One person may blackmail more than the other, but rarely is blackmail completely one-sided. We may be the target of blackmail in one relationship and turn right around to become the blackmailer in another. For example, if your boss is using emotional blackmail on you at work, the frustration and resentments you feel and either can’t or won’t express directly to him may cause you to use the same tactics on your partner or children to regain some sense of control. Or, as in Lynn and Jeff’s case, the shift may occur within one relationship, with the target changing hats and blackmailing the blackmailer.

在任何关系中，两个人互换角色并不罕见，他们轮流扮演受害者和勒索者的角色。一方可能比另一方更频繁地进行勒索，但勒索很少是完全单方面的。我们可能在一段关系中是勒索的受害者，却在另一段关系中立刻变成勒索者。例如，如果你的老板在工作中对你进行情感勒索，你感受到的挫败感和怨恨，以及你无法或不愿直接向他表达的情绪，可能会导致你对伴侣或孩子使用同样的手段来重新获得一些控制感。或者，就像琳恩和杰夫的例子一样，这种转变可能发生在同一段关系中，受害者反过来勒索勒索者。

Obligation is a particularly tough feeling to keep in proportion in our lives. Too little and we shirk our responsibilities. Too much—as when Lynn started “billing” for every contribution to the relationship—and we’re pressed flat beneath the weight of inescapable debts and the inevitable resentment they produce. Blackmail is quick to follow.

在我们的生活中，保持适度的责任感尤其困难。责任感太低，我们会逃避责任；责任感太高——就像琳恩开始对这段关系的每一项付出都“收费”一样——我们会被无法摆脱的债务压得喘不过气来，随之而来的必然是怨恨。勒索也很快就会发生。

GUILT

有罪

Guilt is an essential part of being a feeling, responsible person. It’s a tool of the conscience that, in its undistorted form, registers discomfort and self-reproach if we’ve done something to violate our personal or social code of ethics. Guilt helps to keep our moral compass working, and because it feels so painful, it dominates our attention until we do something to relieve it. To avoid guilt, we try to avoid doing harm to someone else.

内疚是成为一个有感情、有责任感的人不可或缺的一部分。它是良知的工具，在未经扭曲的状态下，当我们做了违反个人或社会道德准则的事情时，它会让我们感到不适和自责。内疚有助于我们保持道德准则的正确性，而且由于它带来的痛苦感，它会一直占据我们的注意力，直到我们采取行动来缓解这种痛苦。为了避免内疚，我们会尽量避免伤害他人。

We trust this active gauge of our behavior, and we believe that whenever we feel it, it’s because we’ve stepped out of bounds and willfully violated the rules we’ve set for ourselves about what’s acceptable in our dealings with other people. Sometimes that’s true, and our feelings of guilt are a natural, appropriate response to having done something hurtful, illegal, cruel, abusive or dishonest.

我们信任这种对自身行为的积极感知，并且相信每当我们感受到这种感觉时，都是因为我们越界了，故意违反了自己设定的与人交往的可接受行为准则。有时确实如此，当我们做了伤害他人、违法、残忍、虐待或不诚实的事情后，感到内疚是一种自然而恰当的反应。

Guilty feelings are woven through our lives if we have a conscience. Unfortunately, our sense of guilt can easily give us false readings about the impact of our actions. Like an oversensitive car alarm that’s supposed to alert us to a crime but winds up going off whenever a truck rolls by, our guilt sensors can go haywire. When this happens, we experience not only the appropriate guilt I described above but also what I call undeserved guilt.

如果我们有良知，内疚感就会贯穿我们的一生。不幸的是，这种内疚感很容易让我们对自身行为的影响产生错误的判断。就像一个过于灵敏的汽车警报器，本应提醒我们注意犯罪，结果却在卡车经过时也响个不停一样，我们的内疚感也会失灵。当这种情况发生时，我们不仅会体验到我上面描述的那种合理的内疚感，还会体验到我所说的“不应有的内疚感”。

In undeserved guilt, the remorse we feel has little to do with identifying and correcting harmful behavior. This kind of guilt, which makes up a large part of the blackmailer’s FOG, is layered with blame, accusations and paralyzing self-flagellation. In simple terms, the process that produces undeserved guilt looks like this:

在不应有的内疚感中，我们感受到的悔恨与识别和纠正有害行为几乎无关。这种内疚感构成了勒索者心理迷雾（FOG）的重要组成部分，它夹杂着责备、指责和令人麻痹的自我鞭笞。简而言之，产生不应有的内疚感的过程如下：

  1. I act.
    我演戏。
  2. The other person gets upset.
    对方会生气。
  3. I take full responsibility for the other person’s upset, whether I had anything to do with it or not.
    无论这件事是否与我有关，我都会对对方的沮丧负全部责任。
  4. I feel guilty.
    我感到内疚。
  5. I will do anything to make reparations so that I can feel better.
    为了弥补过错，让自己感觉好一些，我愿意做任何事。

More specifically:

更具体地说：

  1. I tell a friend I can’t go to a movie with her this evening.
    我告诉朋友我今晚不能和她一起去看电影了。
  2. She gets upset.
    她生气了。
  3. I feel horrible and believe it’s my fault she’s upset. I feel like a bad person.
    我感觉糟透了，觉得她难过都是我的错。我觉得自己是个坏人。
  4. I cancel my other plans so we can go to the movie together. She feels better, and I feel better because she feels better.
    我取消了其他安排，这样我们就可以一起去看电影了。她感觉好多了，因为她感觉好多了，我也感觉好多了。

Undeserved guilt may have nothing at all to do with our harming someone else, but it has everything to do with believing that we did. Emotional blackmailers encourage us to take global responsibility for their complaints and unhappiness, doing all they can to reprogram the basic and necessary mechanisms of appropriate guilt into an undeserved-guilt production line where the lights continually flash guilty, guilty, guilty.

不应有的内疚感可能与我们是否伤害过他人毫无关系，但却与我们认为自己伤害了他人息息相关。情感勒索者会诱使我们为他们的抱怨和不快承担全部责任，竭尽所能地将我们原本必要的、恰当的内疚机制改造成一条“不应有的内疚”生产线，让“内疚”的指示灯不停地闪烁。

The effect is strong. All of us want to believe that we’re good people, and the guilt that blackmailers evoke attacks our sense of ourselves as loving, worthwhile people. We feel responsible for the blackmailers’ pain, and we believe them when they tell us that we’re compounding their misery by not accommodating their wishes.

这种影响非常强烈。我们都想相信自己是好人，而勒索者引发的罪恶感会动摇我们作为有爱心、有价值的人的自我认知。我们会觉得自己要为勒索者的痛苦负责，当他们说我们不满足他们的要求会加剧他们的痛苦时，我们也会相信他们。

The Name of the Game Is Blame

游戏规则就是互相指责

One of the fastest ways for blackmailers to create undeserved guilt is to use blame, actively attributing whatever upset or problems they’re having to their targets. Since our guilt system is put on alert by situations that cause us to ask, Have I harmed someone?, most of us feel pangs of guilt anytime someone directly accuses us of hurting them—whether we’ve done anything to deserve the feeling or not. Sometimes we’re able to short-circuit the guilt reaction by seeing that there’s no connection between the accusation and reality, but many times we apologize first and double-check the blackmailer’s logic later—if we check it out at all.

勒索者制造无端愧疚感的最快方法之一就是推卸责任，主动将自身遇到的任何不快或问题归咎于受害者。由于我们的内疚系统会在我们反思“我是否伤害了别人？”时被触发，因此，当有人直接指责我们伤害他们时，我们大多数人都会感到内疚——无论我们是否真的做了什么值得这种感觉的事情。有时，我们能够通过意识到指控与事实不符来消除内疚感，但很多时候，我们会先道歉，然后再去核实勒索者的逻辑——如果我们真的会去核实的话。

We often talk about guilt-peddling, but I think it’s more accurate to talk about blame-peddling. Like turn-of-the-century pushcart salesmen, emotional blackmailers who peddle blame bombard us with a sales pitch aimed at getting our attention. Though the details vary, one phrase, often unspoken but always just under the surface, serves as the blame peddler’s slogan: It’s all your fault. It’s the hook that makes us buy what they’re selling.

我们常说“兜售愧疚感”，但我认为用“兜售指责”来形容更为准确。就像世纪之交的推车小贩一样，那些兜售指责的情感勒索者会用各种推销话术来吸引我们的注意力。虽然具体手法各有不同，但有一句话——通常不说出口，却总是潜藏在字里行间——成了他们兜售指责的口号：都是你的错。正是这句话，让我们乖乖掏钱购买他们兜售的东西。

  • I’m in a lousy mood (and it’s all your fault).
    我心情很差（这都是你的错）。
  • I have a bad cold (and it’s all your fault).
    我得了重感冒（这都是你的错）。
  • I know I drink too much (and it’s all your fault).
    我知道我喝太多酒了（这都是你的错）。
  • I had a bad day at work (and it’s all your fault).
    我今天工作不顺（这都是你的错）。

When you see a list like this, the pitch sounds absurd. Chances are good that these complaints had nothing to do with the much-maligned you. But often we don’t recognize the confusing messages for what they are, because most of us have a tendency to take the blame for something when a person we care about is upset. The blackmailer is only too happy to explain to us how and why we bear all the responsibility for a situation and why they bear little or none. We buy the blame, and our guilt flows freely. We’re ripe for the relief that comes from giving in to the blackmailer.

当你看到这样的清单时，你会觉得这套说辞荒谬至极。这些抱怨很可能与你这个饱受诟病的人毫无关系。但我们常常无法认清这些令人困惑的信息的本质，因为当我们在乎的人感到不快时，我们大多数人都会倾向于承担责任。勒索者会非常乐意向我们解释，为什么所有责任都由我们承担，而他们却几乎不用承担任何责任。我们接受了这些指责，内疚感油然而生。我们很容易从向勒索者屈服中获得解脱。

ENTWINING THREADS

交织的线

It’s impossible to separate the emotions that form the FOG within us as emotional blackmailers set the stage for manipulation. Where you find one element of the FOG, the others are almost certainly close by.

我们无法将构成内心迷雾的各种情绪割裂开来，因为情感勒索者正是以此为跳板进行操控。当你发现迷雾中的某一部分时，其他部分几乎肯定也近在咫尺。

With Maria, for example, obligation and guilt were tightly bound together. Few of us can contemplate not fulfilling what we consider to be our obligations without feeling guilty, and Maria was no exception.

例如，对玛丽亚来说，义务和愧疚紧密相连。我们当中很少有人能想象自己不履行应尽的义务而不感到愧疚，玛丽亚也不例外。

Jay hammered home to me that if we broke up, it would be totally my fault. I’d lie in bed thinking about what it would mean to fail as a wife and mother, and I felt guilty as hell. I’d have to say I was almost paralyzed for a long time. I couldn’t bear the thought of letting down the kids—my God, they don’t deserve to have their lives torn apart or ruined. Anything good I’d ever done seemed to be completely erased by the thought of breaking up the family. I could hardly speak the word divorce because it made me feel so selfish.

杰伊反复强调，如果我们分手，那完全是我的错。我躺在床上，想着如果我作为妻子和母亲失败了会是什么感觉，我感到无比愧疚。说实话，那段时间我几乎麻木了。我无法忍受让孩子们失望——天哪，他们不应该承受这样的痛苦，他们的生活不应该被彻底摧毁。想到家庭破裂，我曾经做的一切好事似乎都荡然无存。我甚至都说不出“离婚”这个词，因为它让我觉得自己太自私了。

Once again, Maria put herself last, and Jay knew that he could count on her to keep doing it. Although Jay’s actions gave her good reason for feeling angry and wounded, those feelings were overshadowed by her ever-growing sense of guilt.

玛丽亚又一次把自己的利益放在最后，杰伊知道她还会继续这样做。尽管杰伊的行为让她有充分的理由感到愤怒和受伤，但这些情绪很快就被她日益增长的内疚感所掩盖。

Like Maria, many people go through the motions of everyday interactions with a blackmailer who’s plying them with guilt, but the resentment and even self-loathing that build in them are corrosive. With little fun or true intimacy, what looks like a marriage or a friendship becomes a hollow framework.

和玛丽亚一样，许多人每天都机械地应付着勒索者，对方不断用愧疚感操控他们，但内心积聚的怨恨甚至自我厌恶却具有腐蚀性。缺乏乐趣和真正的亲密感，看似婚姻或友谊的关系最终会变成空洞的框架。

NO STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS

无诉讼时效限制

Once blackmailers see that their target’s guilt can serve them, time becomes irrelevant. If there’s no recent incident to peg their guilt and blame-peddling on, one from the past will do just fine. There’s no point at which a guilt-producing event is allowed to diminish and reparations are considered fully made. Blackmail targets discover that whatever their real or imagined transgression may be, there is no statute of limitations—no point after which an ancient “crime” ceases to be an issue, or a punishable offense.

一旦勒索者发现利用受害者的罪责为自己谋利，时间就变得无关紧要了。如果没有近期发生的事件可以用来证明他们的罪责，那么过去的某个事件也完全可以。没有任何时间点允许罪责的减轻，也没有任何时间点允许赔偿被视为已经完全完成。勒索的受害者会发现，无论他们犯下的是真实的还是想象的罪行，都没有诉讼时效——没有任何时间点会让古老的“罪行”不再构成问题或不再需要受到惩罚。

Karen, the nurse we met in Chapter 2 , was kept in a fog of guilt by her daughter, Melanie, who never let her forget an accident that occurred in her childhood.

我们在第二章中认识的护士凯伦，一直被她的女儿梅兰妮折磨得内疚不已，梅兰妮从未让她忘记童年时发生的一起事故。

It goes back a long way. My husband, Melanie’s dad, was killed in a car accident when Melanie was little. Melanie was in the car—she was seriously injured and her face was scarred. I paid for plastic surgery for her and she looks fine, but she’s still self-conscious about a few remaining marks on her forehead. And of course I paid for years of therapy because I know how tough all of this was for her.

这要追溯到很久以前。我的丈夫，也就是梅兰妮的父亲，在梅兰妮很小的时候死于一场车祸。当时梅兰妮也在车里——她受了重伤，脸上留下了疤痕。我为她做了整形手术，她现在看起来不错，但她仍然对额头上残留的几道疤痕感到自卑。当然，我也支付了她多年的心理治疗费用，因为我知道这一切对她来说有多么艰难。

It’s taken me a long time to work through my guilt about that night. I know it was the other driver’s fault—but if only we hadn’t turned down that street . . . If only we had waited until the next day to leave the way my husband wanted to. . . . If only . . . Melanie has her own version of why I’m the villain of the story. She never fails to remind me that we were going on a camping trip because I insisted I needed some R&R. If I hadn’t just been thinking of myself and getting away from the office for a few days, the car wouldn’t have been where it was and the accident wouldn’t have happened. I know it’s irrational, but it feeds right into my own guilt and I end up giving her whatever she wants.

我花了很长时间才摆脱那天晚上的愧疚感。我知道是对方司机的错——但如果我们当初没有拐进那条街……如果我们等到第二天再按我丈夫的意愿离开……如果……梅兰妮有她自己一套说辞，认为我是故事里的罪魁祸首。她总是提醒我，我们去露营是因为我坚持说我需要好好放松一下。如果我当时不是只想着自己，想着离开办公室几天，车就不会停在那里，事故也不会发生。我知道这很不理智，但这只会加剧我的愧疚感，最终我总是会满足她的所有要求。

No matter what Karen did to ease the sting of her guilt, however, Melanie never let her forget it for long. Karen found, as all blackmail targets inevitably do, that giving in once or twice doesn’t end the blackmail, it only intensifies the demands.

无论凯伦如何努力减轻内心的愧疚，梅兰妮都从未让她真正忘记这件事。凯伦最终发现，就像所有被勒索的人一样，妥协一两次并不能结束勒索，只会让对方变本加厉。

Sometimes I wonder—do I have to keep making up for this for the rest of my life? I’ve tried to help her, but nothing’s enough. I know I’m not to blame for her troubles, but everything seems to come down to that one moment when some drunken bastard rammed into our car.

有时我会想——难道我这辈子都要一直弥补这件事吗？我尽力帮助她，但一切都远远不够。我知道她的困境不怪我，但一切似乎都源于那个醉鬼撞上我们车的那一刻。

Karen’s guilt is fused with a sense of obligation to her daughter. To Karen, this continuing sense of guilt means that she’ll always owe Melanie for what happened to her, even though it was not Karen’s fault, and until Karen sees what’s going on, she will always capitulate to Melanie’s demands in an effort to repay her for her pain.

凯伦的内疚感与对女儿的责任感交织在一起。对凯伦来说，这种挥之不去的内疚意味着她永远亏欠梅兰妮，即使那并非凯伦的错。在凯伦真正明白真相之前，她会一直屈从于梅兰妮的要求，试图以此来弥补她带给她的痛苦。

WHEN APPROPRIATE GUILT GETS OUT OF HAND

当适当的愧疚感失控时

Even if the guilt we feel is appropriate, an emotional blackmailer will not let us forget what we’ve done or allow our guilt to serve its function of helping to correct our behavior and serving as a teacher for the future. Bob, the lawyer we met in Chapter 1 , knew that he’d violated the trust of his wife, Stephanie, by having an affair, and he wanted desperately to make amends and find a way to allow the relationship to heal. But Stephanie had been badly hurt, and she insisted on reminding him of his offenses. Bob struggled to deal with what had now become lingering, inappropriate guilt.

即使我们感到内疚是合理的，情感勒索者也不会让我们忘记自己做过的事，也不会让内疚发挥其应有的作用——帮助我们改正行为，并为未来树立榜样。我们在第一章中遇到的律师鲍勃，知道自己出轨辜负了妻子斯蒂芬妮的信任，他迫切地想要弥补过错，找到修复这段关系的方法。但斯蒂芬妮受到了极大的伤害，她坚持要提醒他过去的罪行。鲍勃努力应对着这种挥之不去的、不恰当的内疚感。

I don’t know what else I can do to make things up to her. I have to go out to make a living, and I can’t spend all my time reassuring her. I don’t know how to make her feel safe again, and she won’t let me know what it’ll take. She won’t let go of it, though. I made her suffer, so she’s going to make sure I suffer as much or more. Jesus, even criminals get out of jail eventually, but I’m doing life with no chance of parole.

我不知道还能做些什么来弥补她。我得出去谋生，不可能把所有时间都花在安抚她身上。我不知道该怎么让她重新感到安全，她也不肯告诉我需要付出什么代价。但她就是不肯放手。我让她受了苦，所以她一定要让我受同样的苦，甚至更苦。天哪，就算罪犯最终也能出狱，但我却要终身监禁，没有假释的可能。

Stephanie had every right to be angry and hurt, but she was keeping herself and Bob suspended in time and using his guilt to control him. As long as guilt dominated their interactions, there was no chance for healing. Until Stephanie and Bob both learned how to handle this volatile emotion, neither of them was able to see a way out of the emotional blackmail that had put their marriage in a deep freeze.

斯蒂芬妮完全有理由感到愤怒和受伤，但她却让自己和鲍勃的感情停滞不前，并利用他的内疚感来控制他。只要内疚感主导着他们的互动，就永远没有治愈的可能。除非斯蒂芬妮和鲍勃都学会如何处理这种难以控制的情绪，否则他们都无法摆脱这种让他们的婚姻陷入僵局的情感勒索。

Guilt is the blackmailer’s neutron bomb. It can leave relationships standing, but it wears away the trust and intimacy that make us want to be in them.

内疚感是勒索者的致命武器。它或许能让关系维持下去，但会逐渐侵蚀信任和亲密感，而正是这些让我们渴望维系这段关系。

BEFOGGED AND BEWILDERED

困惑和迷茫

Many years ago, I lived in a beach community where, several times during the year, the fog rolls in late in the day and lingers through the night. One evening, as I was coming home late from work, the fog was particularly heavy, and I drove through my neighborhood straining to see. I was relieved when I reached my street and saw my driveway. But for some reason, I couldn’t get my garage door opener to work. When I got out of the car to check it, I realized that I’d pulled into the driveway of the house next door. I simply couldn’t see what I was doing until I’d done it.

很多年前，我住在海边的一个社区，那里一年中总有几次会在傍晚时分起雾，一直持续到深夜。一天晚上，我下班回家很晚，雾气特别浓，我开车穿过社区，努力看清路。终于到了我家门口，看到车道时，我松了一口气。但不知怎么的，车库门遥控器却打不开。我下车查看时，才发现自己开进了隔壁家的车道。直到开进去之后，我才意识到自己犯了个大错。

My experience that night was identical to what happens when we travel through the FOG of emotional blackmail. Even if our bearings are good, the FOG that emotional blackmailers create adds a new dimension that disorients us in the midst of even the most familiar situations and relationships.

我当晚的经历与我们身处情感勒索迷雾之中时的感受如出一辙。即便我们原本方向正确，情感勒索者制造的迷雾也会增添新的维度，即使在最熟悉的处境和关系中，也会让我们迷失方向。

We can’t have emotional stability if FOG controls our lives. It dismantles our sense of perspective, warps our personal histories and muddies our understanding of what’s happening around us. FOG bypasses our thought processes and goes straight for our emotional reflexes. Suddenly we’re floored, and we don’t know what hit us. Score: blackmailer 100, target 0.

如果“迷雾”（FOG）控制了我们的生活，我们就无法拥有情绪稳定。它会瓦解我们的视角，扭曲我们的个人经历，并模糊我们对周围事物的理解。“迷雾”绕过我们的思考过程，直击我们的情绪反应。突然间，我们被击倒在地，不知所措。比分：勒索者100分，受害者0分。

# ↩

4

Tools of the Trade

行业工具

How do our blackmailers create FOG in our relationships with them? How do they maneuver us into putting aside our own best interests as we fall into the frustrating pattern of demand-pressure-compliance? We can begin to see how the process works by looking more closely at the strategies blackmailers consistently use—their own specialized tools of the trade.

勒索者是如何在我们与他们的关系中制造迷雾的？他们是如何操纵我们，让我们在陷入“索取-施压-屈服”这种令人沮丧的模式时，放弃自身利益的？我们可以通过仔细研究勒索者惯用的策略——他们特有的“行骗工具”——来了解这一过程的运作方式。

Singly and in combination, these devices heighten one or more elements of the FOG, magnifying the pressure within us to find relief by saying yes to the blackmailer’s requests. They also help blackmailers justify their actions, both to themselves and to us. This element is crucial, because it helps cloak the blackmail in acceptable, even noble, reasons for being. Like parents who punish their children while saying “I’m only doing this for your own good,” blackmailers are expert rationalizers, and they use their tools to persuade us that the blackmail somehow serves us.

这些手段单独或组合使用，都会加剧“迷雾”中的一个或多个要素，放大我们内心寻求解脱的压力，迫使我们答应勒索者的要求。它们也帮助勒索者为自己的行为辩解，既向自己解释，也向我们解释。这一点至关重要，因为它能将勒索行为包装成合情合理、甚至高尚的理由。就像父母一边惩罚孩子一边说“我这样做都是为了你好”一样，勒索者是辩解高手，他们利用各种手段让我们相信，勒索行为在某种程度上对我们有益。

The tools are a constant that runs through the endlessly varied scenarios of emotional blackmail, and all blackmailers, no matter what their style, use one or more of them.

这些工具是贯穿情感勒索无穷无尽的场景的不变元素，所有勒索者，无论其风格如何，都会使用其中一种或多种工具。

THE SPIN

旋转

Blackmailers see our conflicts with them as reflections of how misguided and off-base we are, while they describe themselves as wise and well-intentioned. In the most simplistic terms, we’re the bad guys, and they’re the ones in the white hats. In politics, this process of running events through the good-guy/bad-guy filter is called “spin,” and emotional blackmailers are the original spin doctors, masters of putting a halo around their own character and motives and splattering ours with serious doubts, or even blacker mud.

勒索者将我们与他们的冲突视为我们误入歧途、偏离正轨的体现，而他们则自诩睿智且心怀善意。简单来说，我们是坏人，他们是正义的一方。在政治领域，这种将事件通过善恶二元论来解读的过程被称为“舆论操控”，而情感勒索者正是舆论操控的鼻祖，他们擅长为自己的品格和动机披上光环，同时又让我们蒙上严重的疑点，甚至抹黑我们的形象。

The Spin Doctor

公关专家

I had a call one day from a woman named Margaret, who told me that her marriage was in serious trouble and wanted to see if there was a way to salvage it. We made an appointment, and when she came in, I was struck by her charm and graceful bearing. Margaret was in her early 40s and had been divorced for five years when she met her new husband at a singles group of the church they both attended. After a short, intense courtship, Margaret and Cal got married. They’d been together about a year when she came to see me.

有一天，我接到一个名叫玛格丽特的女士的电话。她告诉我她的婚姻岌岌可危，想看看是否还有挽救的办法。我们约好时间见面，她一来，我就被她的魅力和优雅气质深深吸引。玛格丽特四十出头，离婚五年后，她在他们共同参加的教会单身小组中认识了现在的丈夫卡尔。经过短暂而热烈的交往，玛格丽特和卡尔步入了婚姻的殿堂。他们在一起大约一年后，玛格丽特来找我咨询。

I’m so confused and depressed. I need some answers here—I don’t know if I’m right or he is. I really thought I’d hit the jackpot this time. Cal is good-looking, successful and I thought really kind and caring. The fact that we met at church was important to me because it meant we had similar values and beliefs. So imagine my shock when about eight months into the marriage he announces that he wants me to participate in group sex with him—and he’s been doing it for years. He said he loved me so much he wanted to share it with me.

我感到非常困惑和沮丧。我需要一些答案——我不知道是我错了还是他错了。我真的以为这次会找到真爱。卡尔长相英俊，事业有成，而且我觉得他非常善良体贴。我们在教堂相遇对我来说很重要，因为这意味着我们拥有相似的价值观和信仰。所以，你能想象我有多震惊吗？结婚大约八个月后，他突然宣布他想让我和他一起参与群交——而且他已经这样做了好几年了。他说他非常爱我，所以想和我分享这一切。

I told him there was no way I would do such a thing—-the idea revolted me—and he acted genuinely shocked. He said he’d always loved my sensuality, and he wanted to introduce me to something that would really enrich my life. He said that he knew he was taking a risk by bringing it up, but it was proof of his love for me that he wanted to share everything with me. And doing it with him would be proof of my love for him.

我告诉他我绝对不会做那种事——这个想法让我感到恶心——他装出一副很震惊的样子。他说他一直很欣赏我的性感，想让我体验一些真正能丰富我人生的东西。他说他知道提出这件事是有风险的，但他想和我分享一切，这证明了他对我的爱。而和他一起做这件事，也将证明我对他的爱。

When I said no way, he acted really hurt and kind of angry. He said he’d badly misjudged me. He thought I was liberal, open-minded and loving, and he had no idea I was such a prude and a puritan—that wasn’t the kind of woman he had fallen in love with. And then he really stuck the knife in. He said that if I didn’t do it, there were plenty of his old girlfriends who would.

当我断然拒绝时，他装出一副受伤又有点生气的样子。他说他完全误会我了。他以为我思想开放、热情友善，却没想到我竟然如此保守保守——他爱上的根本不是这种女人。然后他话锋一转，狠狠地打击了我。他说，如果我不答应，他有很多前女友会答应。

Like all spin doctors, Cal was interpreting his desires in glowingly positive terms and describing Margaret’s resistance as darkly negative. Blackmailers let us know that they ought to win because the outcome they want is more loving, more open, more mature. It’s what’s best. They are entitled to it. At the same time—and sometimes in the most polite way—they call us selfish, uptight, immature, foolish, ungrateful, weak. Any resistance on our parts is transformed from an indication of our needs to evidence of our flaws.

和所有公关高手一样，卡尔用溢美之词包装自己的欲望，却把玛格丽特的反抗描绘成阴暗的负面情绪。勒索者让我们明白，他们理应获胜，因为他们想要的结果更充满爱、更开放、更成熟。这才是最好的。他们理应得到它。与此同时——有时甚至以最礼貌的方式——他们却指责我们自私、拘谨、不成熟、愚蠢、忘恩负义、软弱。我们任何的反抗，都被扭曲成了我们自身缺陷的证据，而非我们需求的体现。

Cal even implied he had been misled or deceived by Margaret’s earlier behavior. But she could change that assessment by going along with him, an act that would prove she was the open, sensuous woman he wanted her to be.

卡尔甚至暗示他之前被玛格丽特的行为误导或欺骗了。但如果她顺从他，就能改变他的看法，证明她就是他想要的那种开放、性感的女人。

Confusing Labels

令人困惑的标签

I’m focusing on the labels Cal used on Margaret because the spin involves applying adjectives—positive ones to the blackmailer and the compliant target, negative ones to the person who resists. Cal interpreted his differences with Margaret as an indication that something was wrong with her and then proceeded to use labels that reinforced his position. The experience is disorienting. Blackmailers’ labels are so different from the ones we’d choose that before long we doubt the labels we give to things ourselves, and we begin to internalize the blackmailers’ questions about our perceptions, our character, our worth, our desirability, our values. We’re trapped in a dense FOG of the worst kind, as Margaret told me:

我之所以关注卡尔给玛格丽特贴的标签，是因为这种歪曲事实的方式在于运用形容词——用积极的形容词形容勒索者和顺从的受害者，用消极的形容词形容反抗者。卡尔将他与玛格丽特的分歧解读为她自身存在问题的迹象，然后开始使用各种标签来强化自己的观点。这种经历令人迷失方向。勒索者使用的标签与我们自己选择的标签截然不同，以至于我们很快就会怀疑自己赋予事物的标签，并开始内化勒索者对我们认知、性格、价值、吸引力和价值观的质疑。正如玛格丽特告诉我的那样，我们被困在一种最糟糕的浓雾之中：

I couldn’t make myself see how Cal could be so different from the man I thought I’d married. How could I have been so wrong about him? I couldn’t believe it. In the most rational way you can imagine, he made it seem as though I’d led him to believe I’d do anything with him, and he kept saying how good it would be for us as a couple. It was easier for me to think I was missing something and that if I could just understand Cal’s ideas about group sex it wouldn’t seem so outrageous to me. I really struggled with it. I thought, Maybe I am uptight. Maybe I am a little prudish. Maybe I just don’t get it. I began to think there was something wrong with me and I’d been making a big deal about nothing.

我实在无法理解，卡尔怎么会和我以为嫁的那个男人如此不同。我怎么会对他看得这么错？我简直不敢相信。他用你能想象到的最理性的方式，让我感觉好像是我让他误以为我会跟他做任何事，他还一直说这对我们夫妻关系有多么好。我宁愿相信自己错过了什么，如果我能理解卡尔对群交的看法，这一切对我来说就不会那么离谱了。我真的为此纠结不已。我想，也许是我太保守了。也许是我有点儿矜持。也许我只是不理解。我开始怀疑是不是自己有问题，是不是我小题大做了。

Margaret had been certain that for her—and the marriage—group sex couldn’t have any positive effects, but as Cal kept talking, she began to doubt herself. When the spin is effective, it confuses us about what’s harmful or healthful and makes us question what we see going on between ourself and the blackmailer. We buy into the spin because we want our friends, lovers, bosses and family members to be right and good, not mean, unfeeling or oppressive. We want to trust the other person instead of acknowledging that he or she is manipulating us by labeling us in ways that make us feel ashamed or inadequate.

玛格丽特一直确信，对她自己以及这段婚姻而言，群交绝不会有任何积极作用，但随着卡尔的喋喋不休，她开始动摇了。当这种歪曲事实的伎俩奏效时，它会让我们对有害和有益的事物产生混淆，并让我们质疑自己与勒索者之间究竟发生了什么。我们之所以会相信这种歪曲事实，是因为我们希望自己的朋友、爱人、老板和家人都是正确善良的，而不是刻薄、冷酷或压迫的。我们想要信任对方，而不是承认他或她正在通过给我们贴标签来操纵我们，让我们感到羞耻或自卑。

Margaret tried hard to make the situation fit logically into the picture she had envisioned of her life with Cal. Surely there was something she hadn’t yet comprehended, an interpretation that would make Cal’s demand seem acceptable. If her concerns were valid, what did that say about their marriage, about him? These were frightening questions, and on some level Margaret didn’t want to face them. She didn’t want to admit to herself that she’d made a mistake about him. It was less painful for her to buy Cal’s version of reality than to confront the uncomfortable truths about him and their relationship.

玛格丽特努力想让眼前的状况符合她对与卡尔共同生活的设想。她确信，肯定有什么她尚未理解的地方，某种解释能让卡尔的要求显得合情合理。如果她的担忧不无道理，那又说明他们的婚姻出了什么问题？说明卡尔这个人又出了什么问题？这些问题令她感到恐惧，在某种程度上，玛格丽特并不想面对它们。她不想承认自己当初对他的看法是错误的。对她来说，接受卡尔的说法远比直面关于他和他们关系的那些令人不安的真相要容易得多。

Cal, as well as inducing Margaret’s self-doubt, leaned heavily on her sense of obligation. In his spin, it was her duty as a wife to participate in group sex with him—he didn’t want a wife who denied him that. Imagine how surprised and vulnerable she must have felt when he threatened to replace her with someone who would accommodate his “reasonable” request.

卡尔不仅让玛格丽特产生自我怀疑，还利用了她的责任感。在他看来，作为妻子，她有义务和他一起参与群交——他不想要一个拒绝他的妻子。想象一下，当他威胁要找个愿意满足他“合理”要求的人来取代她时，她该是多么惊讶和脆弱。

Unfortunately, Margaret gave in.

可惜，玛格丽特最终还是妥协了。

I can’t believe I buckled under to his pressure and agreed to try it if it meant that much to him. I’m so ashamed. I hated every minute. I feel dirty and angry and terribly depressed.

我简直不敢相信自己竟然屈服于他的压力，答应尝试，就因为这对他来说意义重大。我感到无比羞愧。我恨透了每一分钟。我感到肮脏、愤怒，而且极度沮丧。

The FOG was so thick, and Margaret had been pushed so far off center, that it was hardly a surprise she wound up acting in ways she never would have considered otherwise.

迷雾如此浓重，玛格丽特也被推离了中心，所以她最终做出一些她原本绝不会考虑的事情也就不足为奇了。

Making Us “Bad”

使我们“变坏”

In addition to discrediting the perceptions of their targets, many blackmailers turn up the pressure by challenging our character, motives and worth. This type of spin tactic is popular in family conflicts, especially those in which parents are clinging to control of their adult children. Love and respect are equated with total obedience, and when that’s not forthcoming it’s as though a betrayal has taken place. The party line of the blackmailer, repeated with infinite variations, is You are only doing this to hurt me. You care nothing for my feelings.

除了诋毁受害者的形象，许多勒索者还会通过质疑受害者的品格、动机和价值来施加压力。这种歪曲事实的伎俩在家庭冲突中十分常见，尤其是在父母试图控制成年子女的情况下。爱和尊重被等同于绝对服从，一旦得不到这种服从，就好像遭到了背叛。勒索者反复使用的那套说辞，尽管变化无穷，却总是：“你这么做只是为了伤害我。你根本不在乎我的感受。”

When Josh fell in love with Beth and began thinking of marrying outside his religion, he knew his parents would be upset, but he didn’t count on the all-out attack his father launched in an effort to get him back in line.

当乔什爱上贝丝并开始考虑与非宗教人士结婚时，他知道父母会生气，但他没想到父亲会发起全面攻击，试图让他回到正轨。

I couldn’t believe what Dad was saying. You’d think I had created some kind of conspiracy to wreck his life. Why was I torturing him? Why was I driving a spike into his heart? Overnight I went from being a good son to the biggest screwup in the family.

我简直不敢相信爸爸说的话。你肯定会觉得我策划了什么阴谋来毁掉他的人生。我为什么要折磨他？我为什么要往他心脏上扎针？一夜之间，我从一个好儿子变成了家里最大的败家子。

Josh had been away from his parents for several years, but like most people who hear a parent say “You’ve hurt me,” or “You’ve disappointed me,” Josh felt the impact of those statements like a punch in the stomach.

乔什已经离开父母好几年了，但就像大多数人听到父母说“你伤害了我”或“你让我失望了”时一样，乔什感觉这些话就像一记重拳击中了他的腹部。

Such words, coming from someone we’re close to, cling to us, affecting the inner gyroscope that guides our actions and leaving us with a wobbly sense of ourselves. Obviously, we might be labeled heartless, worthless or selfish in any relationship with a blackmailer, but those labels are especially difficult to withstand when they’re coming from a parent, whom we spent our formative years regarding as a repository of wisdom and righteousness. Parents who use the spin against us can wipe out our confidence almost faster than anyone else.

这样的话语，出自亲近之人之口，会如影随形，影响我们内心的判断，让我们对自己产生动摇。诚然，在任何与勒索者的关系中，我们都可能被贴上冷酷无情、一文不值或自私自利的标签，但当这些标签来自父母时，尤其难以承受。在我们成长的岁月里，父母一直是我们智慧和正义的化身。父母利用这种歪曲事实来攻击我们，几乎比任何人都更能迅速地摧毁我们的自信。

PATHOLOGIZING

病理化

Some blackmailers tell us that we’re resisting them only because we’re ill or crazy. In the therapy business, this is called pathologizing, and much as I hate using psychiatric jargon, the word pathologizing describes this activity to a T. Pathology comes from the Greek word pathos, which refers to suffering or deep feeling, but the current connotation of the word is “disease.” Pathologizing is a way of making us appear “sick” when we don’t go along with a blackmailer. Blackmailers accuse us of being neurotic, warped, hysterical. And most wrenching, they dissolve the trust that’s accumulated in a relationship by lining up all the unhappy events we’ve shared with them and throwing them back in our faces to prove that we caused these things to happen because we were such emotional cripples.

有些勒索者会说，我们之所以反抗，是因为我们生病或精神失常。在心理治疗领域，这被称为“病理化”。虽然我很讨厌使用精神病学术语，但“病理化”这个词确实完美地描述了这种行为。“病理”一词源于希腊语“pathos”，指的是痛苦或深切的感受，但其现代含义是“疾病”。当我们不顺从勒索者时，“病理化”就是一种让我们看起来像“病人”的方式。勒索者会指责我们神经质、精神扭曲、歇斯底里。最令人痛心的是，他们会把我们曾经经历过的所有不愉快的事情一一列举出来，然后反过来攻击我们，以此证明是我们情感上的缺陷才导致了这些事情的发生，从而瓦解我们之间建立起来的信任关系。

Because the experience of being pathologized by blackmailers can be a devastating blow to our confidence and sense of self, it’s an especially toxic—and effective—tool.

因为被勒索者病态化的经历会对我们的自信和自我意识造成毁灭性的打击，所以它是一种特别有害——而且非常有效——的工具。

When Love Is a Demand

当爱成为一种要求

Pathologizing often arises in love relationships when there’s an imbalance of desires. One person wants more than the other—more love, more time, more attention, more commitment—and when it’s not forthcoming, he or she tries to get it from us by questioning our ability to love. Many of us will go to great lengths to prove that we are loving and lovable, and many of us have the erroneous belief that “If somebody loves me, I’m supposed to love them, too—or there’s something wrong with me.”

在恋爱关系中，当双方欲望不平衡时，往往会出现病态化的倾向。一方想要更多——更多的爱、更多的时间、更多的关注、更多的承诺——而当这些需求得不到满足时，他或她就会质疑我们爱的能力，试图从我们身上榨取这些。我们中的许多人会竭尽全力证明自己充满爱心且值得被爱，而我们中的许多人也错误地认为“如果有人爱我，我也应该爱他们——否则就是我自身有问题”。

My client Roger, a screenwriter in his mid-30s, faced a blizzard of pathologizing when he decided he needed some independence from Alice, an actress he’d met at a 12-Step meeting eight months earlier.

我的客户罗杰是一位三十多岁的编剧，当他决定需要摆脱艾丽丝——一位他在八个月前的十二步互助会上认识的女演员——的束缚时，他遭遇了铺天盖地的病态解读。

I have the feeling that Alice is more devoted to me than anyone I’ve ever known. It was an incredible high to spend time with her right after we met. She’d come over and sit on my bed reading drafts of my work and raving about them. She seemed to appreciate what I was trying to do, and to love it as well as me. I fell for her hard. She’s seen every movie ever made, she’s funny, she’s gorgeous and she thinks we were meant to be together.

我感觉爱丽丝比我认识的任何人都更爱我。我们刚认识的时候，和她在一起的时光简直令人陶醉。她会过来坐在我的床上，读我的作品草稿，然后赞不绝口。她似乎很欣赏我的创作，也像我一样热爱我的作品。我深深地爱上了她。她看过所有电影，她风趣幽默，美艳动人，而且她认为我们注定要在一起。

But after only a couple of months, she was pushing for us to live together. She kept saying how thrilled she was that we’d found each other and that she knew we’d transform each other’s lives. All I needed to do was surrender my resistance — let go and let God guide us into a great relationship. She said she knew I might be reluctant because of the bad breakup I’d had with my ex last year, but I had to face my fears, not run away from them. It sounded good, but it felt way too fast.

但仅仅几个月后，她就开始催促我们同居。她不停地说我们能找到彼此让她多么高兴，并坚信我们会改变彼此的人生。她觉得我只需要放下抗拒——放手，让上帝指引我们走向一段美好的关系。她说她知道我可能因为去年和前任糟糕的分手经历而有所顾虑，但我必须直面恐惧，而不是逃避。听起来不错，但感觉进展得太快了。

Alice and Roger spent a lot of time talking about the personal 12-Step work they were doing, and they supported one another with it. But Alice liked to play therapist, especially when Roger talked about his fear that their relationship was moving too fast. He was trying to control things, she told him, and he needed to stop resisting. Even at this early stage, Alice tended to define Roger’s hesitation as leftover neurotic behavior from his drinking days, though he’d been sober for eleven years. And Roger took her feedback to heart. Despite the nagging sense that he was in over his head with Alice, he decided that maybe she was right. He told Alice she could move in.

爱丽丝和罗杰花了很多时间谈论他们正在进行的十二步戒瘾互助小组活动，并互相支持。但爱丽丝喜欢扮演心理咨询师的角色，尤其是在罗杰谈到他担心两人关系发展太快的时候。她告诉他，他试图控制一切，需要停止抗拒。即使在这段关系的初期，爱丽丝也倾向于将罗杰的犹豫归咎于他酗酒时期遗留下来的神经质行为，尽管他已经戒酒十一年了。罗杰把她的反馈放在心上。尽管他隐隐觉得爱丽丝对他来说有点难以驾驭，但他还是决定也许她是对的。他告诉爱丽丝，她可以搬进来和他一起住。

She was so clear about our future, and I was just trying to take things one step at a time—but when someone loves you like that, they seem to get this huge surge of energy, and you get swept up in it. I’ll admit it made me kind of tense, but I’m coping. In the past couple of months, though, she’s started talking about having a baby. She’s 35, and the woman has got serious baby lust. She says we wouldn’t have to get married, but this would be the perfect chance to express all of our love and creativity. She’s been reading me baby books and pulling out pictures of me as a kid to see what the baby will look like. It’s too much. I don’t know if I want to spend the rest of my life with her, or if I ever want to be someone’s father. I need space to work and write.

她对我们的未来规划得非常清晰，而我只想一步一步来——但当有人如此爱你时，他们似乎会迸发出巨大的能量，而你也会被卷入其中。我承认这让我有点紧张，但我还能应付。然而，在过去的几个月里，她开始谈论要孩子。她35岁了，这女人对孩子的渴望简直到了痴迷的地步。她说我们不必结婚，但这会是表达我们所有爱和创造力的绝佳机会。她一直在给我读育儿书籍，还翻出我小时候的照片，看看孩子会是什么样子。这一切都让我感到不知所措。我不知道我是否想和她共度余生，也不知道我是否想成为别人的父亲。我需要空间来工作和写作。

It’s not that I don’t like her and think she’s great, but I’ve got to sort things out. I’m not sure I feel for her what she seems to feel for me — I’m just not sure. So I said I needed to live by myself for awhile to get some perspective.

不是我不喜欢她，也不是我觉得她很优秀，只是我得好好理清思绪。我不确定我对她的感觉是否和她对我的感觉一样——我真的不确定。所以我说我需要一个人住一段时间，好好想想。

Roger’s resistance to Alice’s plans triggered a furious response.

罗杰对爱丽丝计划的抵制引发了强烈的反抗。

She said something like “I’m afraid of you when you talk this way. You said you loved me, but from what you just told me, I have to think that you’re a fabulous liar. I know you’re afraid of getting close to me after the mess you made of your last relationship, but I thought you were ready to start living in the present instead of the past. I know I’m an intense person, but I thought I’d met my match. I guess I can’t be mad at you, but I pity you. You’re too afraid of life to ever experience love. You’re only comfortable with your little screenplay fantasies. Face it, you’re a dry drunk just like your womanizer father.”

她大概是这么说的：“你这样说话，我真怕你。你说你爱我，但听你刚才说的，我觉得你是个撒谎高手。我知道你上次把感情搞得一团糟，所以害怕和我亲近，但我以为你已经准备好活在当下，而不是沉湎于过去。我知道我性格比较强烈，但我以为我遇到了对手。我想我不能生你的气，但我很同情你。你太害怕生活，所以永远无法体验爱情。你只沉浸在你那些不切实际的幻想里。面对现实吧，你跟你那个花花公子父亲一样，是个只会喝酒的酒鬼。”

Then, with a nervous laugh, Roger said:

然后，罗杰紧张地笑了笑，说道：

I keep replaying it in my mind and wondering if she’s right. I do have a rough time establishing relationships. Maybe I don’t know how to be with someone who really loves me.

我一直在脑海里反复回想这件事，想知道她说的是不是真的。我的确不擅长建立人际关系。也许我不知道该如何与真正爱我的人相处。

I told Roger that he’d overlooked something many people forget: There’s nothing “wrong” with you just because you don’t want someone as much as they want you. Like many pathologizers, Alice misused the word love. Her actions were full of dependency, desperation and the need to possess Roger totally, none of which has anything to do with mature love. But to her the pressure was justified in the name of her grand, overpowering passion for him—and if Roger couldn’t match her intensity, the only explanation she could live with was that he must have some horrendous psychological problem.

我告诉罗杰，他忽略了很多人都会忘记的一点：你对某人的渴望不如对方对你那样强烈，这并不代表你“有问题”。像许多喜欢把事情病态化的人一样，爱丽丝滥用了“爱”这个词。她的行为充满了依赖、绝望和想要完全占有罗杰的欲望，这些都与成熟的爱毫无关系。但在她看来，这种压力是合理的，因为她对罗杰有着强烈而难以抑制的激情——如果罗杰无法回应她的热情，她唯一能接受的解释就是他一定有严重的心理问题。

As she reacted to Roger’s request for more space, Alice used a tactic that most pathologizers rely on: throwing back in Roger’s face uncomfortable things that he’d confided to her about himself and his family. Roger had told her about his dad, who had given up drinking only to replace it with a compulsion for womanizing, and Alice knew that, like many of us, Roger strongly feared “turning into my father.” Secrets, fears or confidences we’ve shared with a pathologizer become easy-to-grab weapons in a conflict. Painful life events—divorces, child custody battles, abortions—that we have described at intimate moments are all used as proof of our instability. For Roger, Alice’s “evidence” that his hard-won sobriety was somehow tainted was cause for alarm.

当罗杰要求更多空间时，爱丽丝采用了大多数病态化者惯用的伎俩：把罗杰之前向她吐露的关于自己和家人的尴尬往事翻出来。罗杰曾告诉她，他的父亲戒了酒，却又沉迷于拈花惹草。爱丽丝知道，和我们许多人一样，罗杰非常害怕“变成我父亲那样”。我们与病态化者分享的秘密、恐惧或倾诉，在冲突中很容易被对方利用。那些我们在私密时刻描述的痛苦经历——离婚、子女监护权争夺、堕胎——都会被用来证明我们情绪不稳定。对罗杰来说，爱丽丝所谓的“证据”——他来之不易的戒酒之路似乎受到了某种玷污——让他感到恐慌。

Emotional blackmailers often accuse us of being unable to love or maintain friendships simply because we don’t feel as close to them, as friends or lovers, as they feel we should. It’s a variety of pathologizing that many of us are vulnerable to especially if we see intimate relationships as the litmus test of mental health. Though it’s a stretch for blackmailers to argue that if a relationship isn’t working, it’s because we are sick or damaged, lines like this go straight to the heart, and often they succeed.

情感勒索者常常指责我们无法去爱或维持友谊，仅仅因为我们与他们之间的关系不够亲密，无论是朋友还是恋人，都达不到他们期望的程度。这种病态化的思维方式，我们很多人都容易受到影响，尤其当我们把亲密关系视为心理健康的试金石时。虽然勒索者认为一段关系失败是因为我们生病或有缺陷的说法有些牵强，但这类话往往直击人心，而且常常奏效。

What’s Wrong with You?

你这人怎么回事？

Not all pathologizers overtly label a person as sick. This tool has more subtle guises. My client Catherine sought me out, her confidence shaken, after having repeated run-ins with her former therapist.

并非所有病理学家都会直接给一个人贴上“病人”的标签。这种做法还有更隐蔽的伪装。我的客户凯瑟琳在与前任治疗师多次发生冲突后，信心受挫，前来寻求我的帮助。

I was ready to go part-time at my accounting job and work on getting my MBA, and I was feeling pretty anxious about that. But mainly, I had recently had a bad experience with a guy, and I wanted to understand what happened. So I decided to go see a therapist that my friend Lanie was enthusiastic about.

我当时准备把会计工作转为兼职，同时攻读MBA，对此我感到非常焦虑。但更主要的原因是，我最近和一位男士有过一段不愉快的经历，我想弄明白到底发生了什么。所以我决定去看一位心理咨询师，我的朋友莱妮对她赞不绝口。

There was something forbidding about Rhonda from the first, but I figured it would just take time to get used to this new kind of relationship. It seemed to me that she was always getting in little digs at me, though. One of her favorite things was to clip articles out of the paper about successful women who had it all and give them to me at the beginning of the session for “inspiration.” It made me feel like shit. The message was, “Here’s the way you should be, and if you do what I tell you to do, you’ll get there.”

从一开始就觉得朗达有点难以接近，但我寻思着只是需要时间来适应这种新的关系。不过，我觉得她总是暗地里挖苦我。她最喜欢做的事之一就是从报纸上剪下一些关于事业有成、拥有一切的女性的文章，在每次咨询开始时给我，说是要“激励”我。这让我感觉糟透了。她传递的信息是：“你应该这样，如果你听我的，你就能达到那种境界。”

She kept bringing up my joining one of her therapy groups, but I didn’t have any interest in that. Maybe she was right that it would do me a world of good, but my god, I had so many hours to put into my master’s program and working that I didn’t have any time. Rhonda saw it another way. She said that I was being stubborn and controlling and that was why I was having problems in my life.

她一直劝我参加她组织的治疗小组，但我一点兴趣都没有。也许她说的没错，那对我的确大有裨益，但天哪，我得把所有时间都投入到硕士课程和工作中，根本没空。朗达却有不同的看法。她说我固执又控制欲强，这才是导致我生活出现问题的根源。

Pathologizing is especially persuasive when it comes from an authority figure—a doctor, professor, lawyer or therapist. Our relationships with these people are based on trust, and we tend to cloak professionals in a mantle of wisdom that some don’t deserve. We assume that they will treat us with openness and integrity. But we’ve all met authorities who seem to believe that their license to practice puts their opinions and actions beyond reproach. They may never come out and say “You are deficient,” but with a gesture, a harsh or critical tone of voice or a set jaw, they convey that you are and that your position is wrong.

当权威人士——医生、教授、律师或治疗师——提出病理化观点时，这种观点尤其具有说服力。我们与这些人的关系建立在信任之上，我们往往会给专业人士披上一层智慧的外衣，尽管有些人并不配得上这份光环。我们理所当然地认为他们会以开放和正直的态度对待我们。但我们都遇到过一些权威人士，他们似乎认为，凭借执业资格，他们的观点和行为就凌驾于一切之上。他们或许不会直接说“你有问题”，但一个手势、一种严厉或批评的语气，或者紧咬的牙关，就能传递出你确实有问题，而且你的立场是错误的信息。

It was clear from her tone, her body language and her whole attitude that she was upset with me—and that felt awful. I was afraid she might get mad at me. And that would be the final confirmation of the fact that I wasn’t OK. After all, your therapist is the arbiter of what’s right and wrong, and if your therapist doesn’t like you or disapproves of you, then there’s really something wrong with you. Also, I’ve always been scared of anger, harsh words. When you’re dealing with someone in a position of authority, that gets multiplied by ten.

从她的语气、肢体语言和整体态度来看，她显然对我生气了——这种感觉糟透了。我害怕她会对我发火。而那将最终证实我的确有问题。毕竟，治疗师是评判对错的仲裁者，如果你的治疗师不喜欢你或不认可你，那就说明你真的有问题。而且，我一直很害怕愤怒和恶语相向。当你面对的是一个权威人士时，这种恐惧感会被放大十倍。

Arrogantly, “authorities” like Rhonda indicate that they are not to be challenged. They tell us that they’re looking out for our best interests, and by resisting them we’re proving how obstinate, ill-informed or insecure we are. They are the experts, even when it comes to our deepest knowledge of ourselves, and we aren’t allowed to question their advice or their interpretations of a situation.

像朗达这样的“权威人士”傲慢地表示，不容挑战。他们声称一切都是为了我们好，而我们反抗他们，就等于证明自己多么固执、无知或缺乏安全感。他们自诩为专家，甚至连我们最深层的自我认知都掌握在他们手中，我们无权质疑他们的建议或对情况的解读。

Dangerous Secrets

危险的秘密

Many families that have “shameful” secrets of child abuse, alcoholism, emotional illness and suicide tacitly agree to keep the facts hidden and never discuss them. But when one person changes the signals by pulling out of the family system that survives on denial and secrecy, it’s typical for family members to brand that person crazy, unforgiving or a family wrecker for daring to discuss their hidden and long-denied history. I saw this kind of pathologizing frequently during the years I specialized in working with adults who had been sexually and/or physically abused as children. As my clients began to get healthier, they wanted and needed to talk about their experiences, but some families fought hard to keep them from breaking the silence.

许多家庭都隐藏着诸如虐童、酗酒、精神疾病和自杀等“不可告人的”秘密，他们默许将真相隐藏起来，从不讨论。然而，当有人打破这种以否认和保密维系的家庭体系时，家庭成员往往会给这个人贴上“疯子”、“铁石心肠”或“家庭破坏者”的标签，只因他胆敢谈论自己长期否认的隐秘过往。在我专门为童年时期遭受性虐待和/或身体虐待的成年人提供咨询的那些年里，我经常看到这种病态化的现象。随着我的客户逐渐恢复健康，他们渴望也需要倾诉自己的经历，但有些家庭却竭力阻止他们打破沉默。

It’s axiomatic that the more troubled the family, the more it tries to block its members when they try to become healthy again. And all too often, the blackmail works. Threats of abandonment, exile, punishment, retaliation and total disapproval or contempt can crush the resolve of the person whose brave attempt to recover has been pathologized as selfish, unnecessary and destructive.

家庭问题越多，就越会阻挠家庭成员重获健康，这几乎是不言而喻的。而且，这种勒索往往奏效。遗弃、放逐、惩罚、报复以及彻底否定或蔑视的威胁，足以摧毁那些勇敢尝试康复却被贴上自私、不必要且具有破坏性标签的人的决心。

Roberta, a 30-year-old telemarketing executive, still lives with injuries to her neck and bones that she suffered as a child at the hands of her abusive father. When we met, she had been hospitalized for depression in a facility where I was on staff. One of the first things she told me is that she couldn’t bear to keep holding in the family secret of abuse.

罗伯塔今年30岁，是一名电话销售主管。她童年时遭受父亲虐待，颈部和骨骼至今仍留有伤痕。我们相识时，她因抑郁症住院治疗，而我当时就在她工作的这家机构工作。她告诉我的第一件事就是，她无法继续保守这个关于家庭虐待的秘密。

As Roberta began to deal with her childhood, she looked to her mother for confirmation of what she’d seen and experienced, but instead of the understanding she had hoped for, she was met with pathologizing.

当罗伯塔开始面对自己的童年时，她向母亲寻求对她所见所闻的确认，但她所希望的理解并没有得到回应，反而被母亲的病态化对待。

I tried approaching my mom about six months ago and telling her that I found out that I still have some old injuries from Dad’s beatings. And she totally blew me away. She told me I was making it sound like my dad had killed me or something. And I said, “Do you remember when Dad got me by the hair and swung me around and threw me on the ground?”

大约六个月前，我试着跟妈妈说，我发现自己身上还有一些以前被爸爸打过的伤痕。她的反应让我大吃一惊。她说我好像把我说得好像爸爸杀了我似的。我说：“你还记得爸爸揪着我的头发把我甩来甩去，然后扔到地上吗？”

She looked at me as if I was an alien from outer space. She said, “Oh my God, where are you getting all this from? What are those doctors telling you over there? Have you been brainwashed?” And I said, “Mom, you were standing there most of the times when I got hit—in the doorway watching.” She flipped out. She could not handle it. She said I was making everything up and she thought I was out of my mind. How could I talk about my father like that? She said she couldn’t stand to talk to me until I got help and stopped needing to tell such terrible lies. It was devastating.

她看着我，仿佛我是个外星人。她说：“我的天哪，你这些话都是从哪儿听来的？那边的医生都跟你说了些什么？你是不是被洗脑了？” 我说：“妈，我挨打的时候，你大部分时间都站在门口看着。” 她彻底崩溃了。她无法接受。她说我全是编造的，她觉得我疯了。我怎么能那样说我父亲？她说，除非我接受治疗，不再编造这些可怕的谎言，否则她根本没法跟我说话。这对我来说简直是晴天霹雳。

Roberta’s mother found her daughter’s memories so threatening that she not only denied them, she also pressured Roberta to deny them herself and threatened to cut off contact until Roberta stopped upsetting the family. Healthy attempts like Roberta’s to disclose and discuss what had happened to her are frequently given an almost sinister cast by other family members, labeled “fiction” and “exaggeration” and the product of a sick mind. We may desperately need to express the truth of what’s happened to us, but it takes determination, preparation and support to counter the pervasive pathologizing that goes along with long-term abuse or deep problems within a family.

罗伯塔的母亲觉得女儿的回忆对她构成了威胁，不仅否认，还强迫罗伯塔也否认，并威胁要断绝联系，直到罗伯塔不再让家人感到不安。像罗伯塔这样出于健康原因想要倾诉和讨论自己遭遇的事情，往往会被其他家庭成员贴上“虚构”、“夸大”和“病态心理”的标签，甚至被解读为邪恶的产物。我们或许迫切需要表达自己遭遇的真相，但这需要决心、准备和支持，才能对抗伴随长期虐待或家庭深层问题而来的根深蒂固的病态化思维。

Pathologizing targets an area that’s hard for us to defend. It would be easy for most of us to defend ourselves against criticism of our skills and accomplishments because we’re surrounded by solid external confirmations of what we can do. But when a blackmailer tells us that we are somehow psychologically deficient, we may accept their description as rational feedback. We know we can’t be completely objective about ourselves, and many of us are terrified that we have unknown demons inside. Pathologizers play on that fear.

病理化攻击的目标恰恰是我们难以捍卫的领域。对于大多数人来说，面对对其技能和成就的批评，我们很容易就能为自己辩护，因为我们身边充斥着对我们能力的有力肯定。但当勒索者声称我们在心理上存在某种缺陷时，我们却可能将其视为合理的反馈。我们知道自己无法完全客观地看待自己，而且许多人都害怕自己内心深处藏着未知的恶魔。病理化者正是利用了这种恐惧。

Like the spin, pathologizing makes us unsure about our memories, our judgment, our intelligence and our character. But with pathologizing, the stakes are even higher. This tool can make us doubt our very sanity.

与歪曲事实一样，将问题病理化也会让我们对自己的记忆、判断力、智力和性格产生怀疑。但病理化的危害更大。这种做法甚至会让我们怀疑自己的理智。

ENLISTING ALLIES

争取盟友

When single-handed attempts at blackmail aren’t effective, many emotional blackmailers call in the reinforcements. They bring in other people—family members, friends, ministers—to help make their case for them and to prove that they’re right. In this way, they double- or triple-team their targets. Blackmailers round up anyone they know the target cares about and respects, and faced with this solid front, the target may feel outnumbered, overpowered.

当单枪匹马的勒索尝试无效时，许多情感勒索者会寻求帮手。他们会找来其他人——家人、朋友、牧师——来帮助他们为自己辩护，证明自己是对的。这样一来，他们就能对目标人物进行双人甚至三人围攻。勒索者会召集所有目标人物关心和尊重的人，面对如此强大的攻势，目标人物可能会感到寡不敌众，无力招架。

One evening shortly after I began working with Roberta, I saw this tool in action. Roberta’s parents showed up for a family counseling session with Roberta’s brother and two sisters, all of whom were eager to show their solidarity with their parents. When I asked them how they felt about Roberta’s desire to speak openly about her father’s abuse, I noticed how they closed ranks. The siblings looked at each other, and finally her older brother, Al, began to speak.

在我开始与罗伯塔合作不久后的一个晚上，我亲眼目睹了这种方法的运用。罗伯塔的父母带着她的弟弟和两个妹妹来参加家庭咨询，他们都急于表达对父母的支持。当我问他们对罗伯塔想要公开谈论父亲虐待行为有何感想时，我注意到他们团结一致。兄弟姐妹们互相看了看，最后，她的哥哥阿尔开口说话了。

Mom called and asked us if we’d come in and let you know the truth about what happened in our family because we’re a good family, and Roberta’s just trying to destroy us. You know how sick she’s been—look at her, in and out of the hospital for depression, suicide attempts. . . . It wouldn’t surprise me if she’s hearing voices or something.

妈妈打电话问我们愿不愿意过来，把我们家发生的事告诉你们，因为我们家是好家庭，罗伯塔却想毁了我们。你们也知道她病得有多厉害——看看她，抑郁症反复住院，还试图自杀……如果她出现幻听什么的，我一点也不觉得奇怪。

He smiled, looking around the room as his parents and siblings nodded.

他微笑着环顾四周，他的父母和兄弟姐妹都点了点头。

She’s always had big problems. We all want to help her get better, but we can’t let her tell horror stories about us. She’s made up this abuse thing, and a lot of people seem to believe it. We just want to clear our name and see that she gets the help she needs.

她一直都有很大的问题。我们都想帮她好起来，但我们不能让她编造关于我们的可怕故事。她捏造了虐待我们的事情，而且很多人似乎都相信了。我们只想澄清事实，也想确保她能得到需要的帮助。

Roberta had had a hard enough time holding on to what she knew in the face of her mother’s denial, and now her task was even more difficult. She was facing a whole roomful of blackmailers who wanted her to keep her mouth shut. And their full-court press let the “traitor” know that she would be welcomed back into the fold only if she’d be quiet, so everyone could resume a way of behaving that, despite being destructive to all of them, was familiar, and therefore comfortable.

面对母亲的否认，罗伯塔原本就很难坚守自己的认知，如今更是难上加难。她面前坐满了勒索者，他们都想让她闭嘴。他们的全力逼迫让这位“叛徒”明白，只有保持沉默，大家才能重回正轨——尽管这种做法对他们所有人都有害，但却是他们熟悉且舒适的。

Bringing in Fresh Troops

引入新兵

My client Maria, the hospital administrator we met in the last chapter , provides another compelling example of this kind of double-teaming. When she discovered her husband’s extramarital affairs and told him that she was thinking of leaving him, he tried everything to persuade her to change her mind—including enlisting his relatives.

我在上一章中提到的那位医院行政主管玛丽亚，就是我委托人，她为这种“双管齐下”的局面提供了另一个令人信服的例子。当她发现丈夫有婚外情并告诉他自己正在考虑离开他时，他想尽一切办法劝她改变主意——甚至动用了亲戚。

He saw that threats and charm and all the things that had worked for him in the past weren’t working anymore, so he brought in the heavy artillery—his parents. I was crazy about my in-laws. His father was a doctor, too, and his mother was a gentle soul who had been wonderful to me from the day I met her. So when Jay’s dad called and suggested that we have a family conference at their house, I was hesitant about it, but I felt I owed him that consideration.

他发现威胁、魅力以及过去那些对他有效的手段现在都不管用了，于是他祭出了重磅武器——他的父母。我非常喜欢我的岳父岳母。他的父亲也是一名医生，他的母亲是一位温柔善良的人，从我认识她的第一天起就对我很好。所以当杰伊的父亲打电话来建议我们去他们家开个家庭会议时，我有些犹豫，但我觉得我应该体谅他。

From the moment I walked into their house, I knew I’d made a mistake. Jay had gotten there early and had obviously been talking about how unreasonable I was being. How could they possibly be objective about their golden boy, and how could they be fair to me?

从我踏进他们家门的那一刻起，我就知道自己犯了个错误。杰伊很早就到了，显然一直在说我有多么不讲理。他们怎么可能客观地看待他们的掌上明珠，又怎么可能公平地对待我呢？

Maria’s concern was well founded. There was no way that Jay’s parents could be objective in this situation, and what happened next was no surprise.

玛丽亚的担忧不无道理。杰伊的父母在这种情况下根本不可能保持客观，接下来发生的事情也在意料之中。

For over an hour, they talked about how all marriages go through bumpy times, and you can’t walk away at the first sign of trouble. They said Jay had agreed to spend more time at home and to cut down his hours at the hospital, and that should solve our little disagreement. Now if I would just stop using the word divorce, nobody would have to know anything about it. They asked me if I really wanted the breakup of the family on my conscience, especially knowing how much Jay loved me. They said it was breaking their hearts to see him suffering, and didn’t I know what this would do to the children? How could I bear to make so many people unhappy when my husband was doing so much to provide a good future for me?

他们聊了一个多小时，说所有的婚姻都会经历坎坷，不能一遇到问题就立刻离开。他们说杰伊已经同意多花时间待在家里，减少在医院的工作时间，这样应该就能解决我们的小分歧了。如果我不再提“离婚”这个词，那就没人会知道了。他们问我，我真的想让家庭破裂的阴影一直萦绕在心头吗？尤其是我知道杰伊有多爱我。他们说看到他受苦，他们心如刀绞，难道我不知道这会对孩子们造成什么影响吗？我的丈夫为了给我创造美好的未来付出了那么多，我怎么忍心让这么多人不开心呢？

When I asked them if Jay had told them about his extramarital affairs, I could tell from their reaction that he hadn’t. They looked so uncomfortable I thought maybe they’d understand a little better why I’m so unhappy being with their son. Then his father said the most incredible thing. He said, “That’s not a good reason to break up a family! Family comes first. You can’t break down at the first sign of trouble and throw it all away. Think about the kids—our grandchildren.” That stung!

当我问他们杰伊是否告诉过他们他的婚外情时，从他们的反应来看，他显然没有。他们看起来很不自在，我想他们或许能更理解我为什么和他们的儿子在一起这么难受。然后他父亲说了一句最不可思议的话。他说：“这不是拆散家庭的好理由！家庭至上。你不能一遇到麻烦就崩溃，把一切都毁掉。想想孩子们——想想我们的孙子孙女们。” 这话真让我难受！

Now, instead of having one person twisting her arm, Maria had three, and it took all her inner resources to hold her ground against them. The message from all of them was the same—it was as though Jay himself had written the script—but hearing Jay’s words from other people she loved and trusted made those words carry even more weight.

现在，玛丽亚面对的不是一个人，而是三个人，她竭尽全力才抵挡住他们的攻势。他们说的话都一样——仿佛杰伊亲自写的剧本——但从她爱和信任的人口中听到杰伊的话，让她觉得这些话更有分量。

Calling on a Higher Authority

诉诸更高权威

When friends and family aren’t sufficient reinforcement for emotional blackmailers, they may turn to a higher authority such as the Bible, or other outside sources of knowledge or expertise, to shore up their positions. This form of pressure may sound as simple as “My therapist says you’re being bitchy” or “I took a course where they told us . . .” or “Dear Abby says. . . .”

当亲朋好友不足以支撑情感勒索者的说法时，他们可能会诉诸更高的权威，例如《圣经》或其他外部知识或专业信息来源，以巩固自己的立场。这种压力可能听起来很简单，比如“我的心理咨询师说你太刻薄了”、“我上过一个课，他们告诉我们……”或者“亲爱的艾比说……”

Wisdom resonates differently in each of us, and none of us can claim a monopoly on it, but we can count on blackmailers to insist, by pulling selective quotes, comments, teachings and writings from a host of sources, that there is just one truth: theirs.

智慧在我们每个人身上产生的共鸣都不同，我们谁也不能垄断智慧，但我们可以预料到，勒索者会通过断章取义地引用各种来源的引语、评论、教义和著作，来坚持认为只有一种真理：那就是他们的真理。

NEGATIVE COMPARISONS

负面比较

“Why can’t you be like . . .” Those five words pack an emotional punch that connects powerfully with our sense of self-doubt, our fear that we don’t measure up. Blackmailers often hold up another person as a model, a flawless ideal against which we’ll fall short. That person would have no problem satisfying the blackmailer’s demands—so why can’t we?

“为什么你不能像……”这五个字蕴含着强烈的情感冲击，它触动了我们内心深处的自我怀疑，触及了我们害怕自己达不到对方标准的恐惧。勒索者常常会把另一个人当作榜样，一个完美无瑕的理想，而我们则远远无法企及。那个人满足勒索者的要求轻而易举——那么，为什么我们做不到呢？

“Look at your sister—she’s willing to help with the business.”

“看看你妹妹——她很乐意帮忙打理生意。”

“Frank doesn’t seem to be having any trouble meeting deadlines—maybe you could get some pointers from him.”

“弗兰克似乎在按时完成任务方面没有任何问题——也许你可以向他请教一些经验。”

“You don’t see Mona abandoning her husband when the going gets rough.”

“你见过莫娜在丈夫遇到困难时抛弃他吗？”

Negative comparisons make us feel suddenly deficient. We’re not as good, not as loyal, not as accomplished as so-and-so, and we feel anxious and guilty about it. So anxious, in fact, that we may be willing to give in to blackmailers to prove that they’re wrong about us.

负面比较会让我们突然觉得自己不够好。我们不如某某优秀、不够忠诚、不够成功，为此我们会感到焦虑和内疚。事实上，这种焦虑如此强烈，以至于我们可能愿意向勒索者屈服，以证明他们对我们的评价是错误的。

My client Leigh is a stockbroker whose mother, Ellen, has a black belt in negative comparisons, and Leigh has felt the pressure in a variety of forms over the years.

我的客户 Leigh 是一名股票经纪人，她的母亲 Ellen 非常擅长负面比较，多年来 Leigh 也感受到了各种形式的压力。

When my dad died, Mom was totally helpless. All her life she’d had men taking care of her, and when Dad died she turned to me to take over her life for her.

父亲去世后，母亲彻底失去了自理能力。她一生都由男人照顾，父亲去世后，她只能依靠我来接管她的生活。

I found out fast that I was supposed to (a) spend an enormous amount of time with Mom and (b) find her a lawyer, find her an accountant and do a lot of things that she was perfectly capable of doing for herself. But she’s good at playing helpless, and I immediately jumped in. I have an easy time doing all those things, so it wasn’t a problem for me. The myth is that you’re going to get love and approval for this. But what really happens is that you can’t do anything to please a woman like her. So of course the accountant charged her too much, and the lawyer was a no-good so-and-so, and I was a criminal for having to skip dinner with her because I promised my son I’d coach him for the play he’s in.

我很快就发现，我应该（a）花大量时间陪妈妈，（b）帮她找律师、找会计，做很多她自己完全能做的事情。但她很擅长装可怜，所以我立刻就帮她做了。这些事对我来说轻而易举，所以对我来说不是问题。人们常说这样做会得到她的爱和认可，但事实是，你做什么都无法取悦像她这样的女人。所以，会计当然会漫天要价，律师当然是个庸才，而我因为答应儿子要指导他排练话剧，不得不错过和她一起吃晚饭，就成了罪人。

If what I did wasn’t exactly perfect, I sure heard about it. And anytime I started to pull away, she started leaning on my cousin Caroline. Pretty soon it was “Caroline wants to be with me all the time. Look at what a good daughter she is to me—more of a real daughter than my own.” I wonder if she had any idea how deeply those words hurt and how guilty they made me feel. I found myself spending much more time with her than I wanted to, trying to fix her problems, just to avoid being compared to Caroline.

如果我做的事不够完美，她肯定会说个不停。每当我试图疏远她时，她就开始依赖我的表妹卡罗琳。很快，她就说：“卡罗琳总是想和我待在一起。你看她对我多好——比我的亲生女儿还像。” 我不知道她是否明白这些话有多伤人，让我多么内疚。为了避免被拿来和卡罗琳比较，我发现自己花在她身上的时间远远超过了我的预期，我努力帮她解决问题。

The person we’re being compared to seems to get all the love and approval we want for ourselves, and it’s only natural that we react competitively and try to get into that position ourselves. For Leigh, there was no end to the comparisons, and no way to measure up.

我们总是拿来和别人比较，而那个人似乎总能得到我们渴望的所有爱和认可，所以我们自然会产生竞争心理，努力争取达到那样的地位。对莉来说，这种比较永无止境，她也永远无法超越对方。

Dangerous Pressure

危险压力

In the workplace, negative comparisons create an atmosphere like that in an unhealthy family, fostering envy and competitiveness. We may find ourselves trying to measure up to the impossible standards set by a paternalistic boss who, by pitting workers against each other, creates “sibling rivalries” among co-workers.

在职场中，负面比较会营造出一种类似不健康家庭的氛围，滋生嫉妒和竞争。我们可能会发现自己试图达到家长式老板设定的不可能的标准，而这位老板通过挑拨员工之间的关系，在同事之间制造出“手足相残”的局面。

When my client Kim first came to see me, she was under intense pressure from a boss who used negative comparisons to “motivate” her. Kim, who is in her mid-30s, had the misfortune of being hired to replace Miranda, a legendary magazine editor who was about to retire.

我的客户金第一次来找我时，她承受着巨大的压力，她的老板用负面比较来“激励”她。金当时三十多岁，不幸的是，她被聘来接替即将退休的传奇杂志编辑米兰达的职位。

I’m pretty efficient, and I have a lot of good ideas. I work well with writers, and I used to love what I do. But my boss is pushing me harder than anyone else on the staff, and he’s constantly comparing me to Miranda. It’s like I can never do enough. If I make four assignments in a week, my boss, Ken, says something like “That’s great. Miranda used to do it in a slow week. Her record was eight or nine.” If I say I need to leave on time one night instead of putting in my usual 10 or 11 hours, he’ll talk about how the work ethic will be dead without Miranda. She’s legendary for practically living at the office.

我工作效率很高，也有很多好点子。我和作家们合作很愉快，而且我以前很喜欢我的工作。但是我的老板对我的要求比公司里的任何人都高，他总是拿我和米兰达比较。感觉我永远都做得不够好。如果我一周完成了四个任务，我的老板肯就会说：“太棒了。米兰达以前在工作不忙的时候都能做到。她的最高纪录是八九个。”如果我说我某天晚上需要准时下班，而不是像往常一样工作十个小时或十一个小时，他就会说没有米兰达，公司的工作氛围就完了。她可是出了名的“办公室常客”。

I believe that Miranda was brilliant—but she drinks like a fish, she has no family and lives for her work. The thing is, I’m trying to compete with her—and I do have a life. I need to spend time with my kids and my husband, and I do work at my temple, that’s really important to me. But Ken’s always after me to do more, and sometimes when he says I could be the next Miranda if I take on just one more project, I fall for it. He’s got me coming and going. If I don’t do what he wants, he says I don’t measure up to her. And then he’ll also say that I have the talent to be a star like her—if I do the extra work he wants. He says I shouldn’t think of it as extra work, I should think of it as job security.

我相信米兰达才华横溢——但她嗜酒如命，没有家庭，生活重心全在工作上。问题是，我试图和她竞争——但我也有自己的生活。我需要陪伴孩子和丈夫，而且我还在寺庙工作，这对我来说非常重要。但肯总是催着我多做些事，有时他说如果我再接一个项目，就能成为下一个米兰达，我就信以为真了。他让我进进出出。如果我不按他说的做，他就说我不如她。然后他又会说，如果我做他要求的额外工作，我有成为像她一样明星的天赋。他说我不应该把这些工作看作是额外的工作，而应该看作是工作保障。

My family’s going crazy because I’m not there, I’m getting exhausted, I’m starting to get pains in my arms and my neck from being at the computer so much—and worst of all, I’m questioning my own competence. But I feel like I have to measure up to the Miranda standard, like I won’t be good enough until I do.

我不在家，家人都快疯了；我精疲力竭，长时间对着电脑，胳膊和脖子都开始疼了——最糟糕的是，我开始怀疑自己的能力。但我感觉自己必须达到米兰达的标准，好像只有达到那个标准，我才算合格。

When we think about pressure in the workplace, we tend to pay the most attention to overt pressure—like getting fired. But the workplace can reactivate many of the same feelings and relationships that we have within our families, and the same dynamics come into play. Such issues as competition, envy, sibling rivalry and wanting to please authority figures can also drive us to our limits and beyond. The danger is that in trying to measure up to a tough standard set by someone with vastly different needs, talents and circumstances, we can find ourselves sacrificing our families, our outside interests and even our health to our jobs.

当我们想到职场压力时，往往最关注的是显而易见的压力——比如被解雇。但职场会重新激活许多我们在家庭中拥有的情感和关系，同样的动态也会在其中发挥作用。诸如竞争、嫉妒、手足之争以及取悦权威人士等问题，都可能将我们逼到极限，甚至超越极限。危险在于，为了达到一个由与我们有着截然不同的需求、才能和境遇的人设定的苛刻标准，我们可能会发现自己为了工作牺牲了家庭、业余爱好，甚至健康。

We’re often quite definite, at first, about what we need and why we’re resisting an emotional blackmailer. But the blackmailers’ tools erode whatever clarity we have and persuade us that we really don’t know what we want. Using these behavioral strategies, the blackmailer can almost always get our compliance—hardly surprising, considering that a person who resists is likely to be spun around, criticized, ganged up on or found wanting. Yes, this sounds dire, but it’s all learned behavior that we have helped teach. And as we’ll see, just as we’ve effectively handed blackmailers their tools, we can also take them away or render them useless.

起初，我们往往对自己的需求以及为何要抵制情感勒索者非常清楚。但勒索者的手段会逐渐瓦解我们原本清晰的认知，让我们误以为自己根本不知道自己想要什么。利用这些行为策略，勒索者几乎总能让我们屈服——考虑到反抗者很可能被牵着鼻子走、遭到批评、被孤立或被指责能力不足，这也就不足为奇了。没错，这听起来很糟糕，但这都是我们后天习得的行为。正如我们将看到的，我们既然已经有效地将工具交给了勒索者，我们也可以夺走它们，或者让它们失效。

# ↩

5

The Inner World of the Blackmailer

勒索者的内心世界

Emotional blackmailers hate to lose. They take the old adage “It doesn’t matter if you win or lose, it’s how you play the game” and turn it on its head to read “It doesn’t matter how you play the game as long as you do not lose.” To an emotional blackmailer, keeping your trust doesn’t count, respecting your feelings doesn’t count, being fair doesn’t count. The ground rules that allow for healthy give-and-take go out the window. In the midst of what we thought was a solid relationship it’s as though someone yelled “Everyone for himself!” and the other person jumped to take advantage of us while our guard was down.

情感勒索者最怕输。他们把“输赢并不重要，重要的是过程”这句老话颠倒过来，变成了“只要不输，过程并不重要”。在情感勒索者眼里，信任无关紧要，尊重你的感受无关紧要，公平公正也无关紧要。那些维系健康互惠的原则荡然无存。在我们以为稳固的关系中，仿佛有人突然喊出“各人自扫门前雪！”，对方趁我们放松警惕，趁机占我们便宜。

Why is winning so important to blackmailers, we ask ourselves. Why are they doing this to us? Why do they need to get their way so badly that they’ll punish us if they don’t?

我们不禁要问，为什么对勒索者来说，胜利如此重要？他们为什么要这样对我们？为什么他们如此渴望达到目的，以至于如果不成功就要惩罚我们？

THE FRUSTRATION CONNECTION

挫折感的联系

As we struggle to understand what turns the people close to us into emotional bullies, we need to return to the place the blackmail began—the moment when the blackmailer wanted something from us and our words or actions said no.

当我们努力理解是什么让身边的人变成情感上的欺凌者时，我们需要回到勒索开始的地方——勒索者想要从我们这里得到什么，而我们的言语或行为拒绝的那一刻。

There’s nothing wrong with wanting. It’s fine to want, to ask and to try to figure out how to get what you want. It’s OK to plead or reason and even to beg and whine a little—as long as we let a firm no mean no. Accepting no as an answer may not be easy, and the other person may get upset or angry for a time, but if the relationship is working, the storm will pass and we’ll try to negotiate a resolution or compromise.

有愿望并没有错。想要、提出要求、努力想办法得到自己想要的东西，这些都是正常的。恳求、讲道理，甚至稍微哀求或抱怨一下，都没关系——只要我们让对方坚定的“不”就是“不”。接受“不”的答案或许并不容易，对方可能会生气或难过一阵子，但如果彼此关系良好，风波终会过去，我们会尝试协商出一个解决方案或妥协方案。

As we’ve seen throughout this book, however, that’s just the opposite of what happens with a blackmailer. Frustration becomes the trigger not for negotiation but for pressure and threats. Blackmailers cannot tolerate frustration.

然而，正如我们在本书中看到的，勒索者的情况恰恰相反。挫折感不会促使他们进行谈判，而是会引发施压和威胁。勒索者无法容忍挫折感。

It’s hard to understand why they make such a big deal of this. After all, many of us have faced plenty of disappointments without becoming bullies to feel better. We accept disappointment as a temporary setback, and we go on. But in the psyche of blackmailers, frustration symbolizes something far beyond being blocked or disappointed, and when they encounter it they can’t just regroup or shift gears. To the blackmailer, frustration is connected to deep, resonant fears of loss and deprivation, and they experience it as a warning that unless they take immediate action they’ll face intolerable consequences.

很难理解他们为何对此事如此大惊小怪。毕竟，我们很多人都经历过不少失望，却从未因此而变成欺凌者来寻求慰藉。我们把失望当作暂时的挫折，然后继续前行。但在勒索者的心理中，挫折远不止是受阻或失望那么简单，当他们遭遇挫折时，无法简单地重整旗鼓或转换策略。对勒索者而言，挫折与内心深处对失去和匮乏的恐惧紧密相连，他们将其视为一种警告：除非立即采取行动，否则将面临无法承受的后果。

FROM FRUSTRATION TO DEPRIVATION

从挫败到匮乏

On the surface, blackmailers appear to be just like everybody else, and they’re often highly effective in many areas of their lives. But in many ways, the inner world of the blackmailer resembles Depression-era America—that terrible time when many hard-working people saw their lives unravel and their security replaced with sweeping deprivation. If you know people who lived through that era, you’ve probably noticed how many of them still hoard and pinch every penny, bracing for another shock, another loss, as they try to reassure themselves that they’ll never have to face pain like that again.

表面上看，勒索者似乎和普通人没什么两样，而且往往在生活的很多方面都非常成功。但在很多方面，勒索者的内心世界却与大萧条时期的美国如出一辙——那段可怕的岁月里，许多辛勤工作的人们眼睁睁地看着自己的生活崩塌，安全感被彻底的匮乏所取代。如果你认识经历过那个时代的人，你可能已经注意到，他们中的许多人至今仍然节衣缩食，小心翼翼地省吃俭用，时刻准备着迎接下一次的打击和损失，同时又试图安慰自己，他们再也不会经历那样的痛苦了。

Emotional blackmailers—no matter what their style or preferred tools—operate from a similar sort of deprivation mentality, but we may not glimpse it until something happens to shake their sense of stability and stimulate their fear of deprivation. Just as some people can interpret a headache as a sure sign of a brain tumor, blackmailers see resistance as a symptom of something much graver. Even mild frustration is viewed as potentially catastrophic, and they believe that unless they respond to it aggressively, the world—or you—will keep them from getting something they vitally need. A deprivation tape starts to play in their heads:

情感勒索者——无论他们的手法或惯用手段如何——都基于一种类似的匮乏心态，但我们可能要等到某些事情动摇了他们的稳定感，并激发了他们对匮乏的恐惧时，才会察觉到这一点。就像有些人会把头痛解读为脑瘤的征兆一样，勒索者会将反抗视为更严重问题的征兆。即使是轻微的挫折也会被视为潜在的灾难，他们认为，除非他们采取激进的回应，否则这个世界——或者你——就会阻止他们获得他们迫切需要的东西。一段关于匮乏的录音带开始在他们的脑海中播放：

  • This isn’t going to work out.
    这行不通。
  • I never get what I want.
    我从来得不到我想要的东西。
  • I don’t trust other people to care about what I want.
    我不相信别人会关心我的想法。
  • I don’t have what it takes to get what I need.
    我没有得到我需要的东西的能力。
  • I don’t know if I can stand it if I lose something I want.
    我不知道如果失去自己想要的东西，我能不能承受得住。
  • Nobody cares about me as much as I care about them.
    没有人像我关心他们那样关心我。
  • I always lose anyone I care about.
    我总是失去所有我在乎的人。

With these thoughts cycling through their minds in an endless loop, blackmailers believe they haven’t got a chance of prevailing—unless they play hardball. That belief is the common denominator underlying all emotional blackmail.

这些念头在他们脑海中不断循环，勒索者认为自己毫无胜算——除非他们采取强硬手段。这种想法是所有情感勒索的共同根源。

DEPRIVATION AND DEPENDENCY

匮乏与依赖

For some blackmailers, these convictions are rooted in a lengthy history of feeling anxious and insecure, and if we look far enough back in their lives, we can often find important connections between incidents in their childhoods and some of their adult fears of deprivation.

对于一些敲诈者来说，这些信念源于他们长期以来的焦虑和不安全感，如果我们追溯他们的人生足够久远，我们常常可以发现他们童年时期的某些事件与他们成年后对匮乏的恐惧之间存在着重要的联系。

Allen, the businessman whose wife used blackmail to keep him from making plans that didn’t include her, began to see some of the underpinnings of her behavior when Jo became especially moody around the anniversary of her father’s death.

艾伦是一位商人，他的妻子曾用勒索手段阻止他制定任何没有她参与的计划。在她父亲的忌日前后，乔变得格外喜怒无常，艾伦开始意识到妻子这种行为背后的一些原因。

I asked her if I could do anything to cheer her up, and she pulled out some pictures I’d never seen from her junior high graduation. Her father had died two nights before the photos were taken, and she looked like a scared little girl trying to put on a smiling face. It turned out that she had to handle everything after his death—calling the relatives, making funeral arrangements, even getting herself ready for the big ceremony at school because she was giving a speech that her father had helped her write. She had to keep herself together because everyone else in her family fell apart. I asked her mom about this recently, and she said that Jo didn’t even cry very much. She just kind of retreated into her room.

我问她有没有什么办法能让她开心起来，她拿出几张我从未见过的初中毕业照。照片拍摄前两天晚上她父亲去世了，照片里的她看起来像个惊恐的小女孩，努力挤出一丝笑容。后来才知道，父亲去世后，所有的事情都得由她一个人来处理——给亲戚打电话、安排葬礼，甚至还要准备学校的毕业典礼，因为她要在典礼上发表一篇父亲曾帮她写好的演讲稿。她必须强忍着悲痛，因为家里其他人都崩溃了。最近我问过她妈妈这件事，她说乔其实很少哭，只是把自己关在房间里。

Jo told me that she’d never loved anyone as much as she loved her father, and then suddenly he was gone. I think she’s always been afraid I’ll leave, too, and her holding on is a way to keep me.

乔告诉我，她从未像爱她父亲那样爱过任何人，然后父亲突然就走了。我想她一直害怕我也会离开，所以她才如此执着地留住我。

Emotional blackmail is the only way Jo knows to cope with a world she doesn’t trust, a world she is certain will rob her of what she loves. People who have faced major deprivation and loss in childhood often become needy and overly dependent as adults to keep from feeling rejected, abandoned or ignored.

情感勒索是乔唯一能用来应对她不信任的世界的方式，她确信这个世界会夺走她所爱的一切。童年时期遭受过重大匮乏和失去的人，成年后往往会变得极度依赖他人，以此来避免被拒绝、被抛弃或被忽视的感觉。

Jo had done well at school and felt cherished by her father, but none of that was enough to protect her. The profound sense of childhood helplessness stayed with her, and as an adult she tried to make up for it by developing elaborate strategies to keep herself from experiencing pain of that magnitude again. She learned to cling fiercely to friends and lovers, but she’d never found an appropriate way to express her fear that, no matter what she did, they would be taken from her.

乔在学校成绩优异，也深受父亲宠爱，但这一切都无法保护她。童年时期那种深深的无助感一直伴随着她，长大后，她试图通过精心设计的策略来弥补这种缺失，避免再次经历如此巨大的痛苦。她学会了紧紧抓住朋友和爱人不放，但她始终找不到合适的方式来表达自己的恐惧：无论她做什么，他们终究都会离她而去。

When she married Allen, her fears escalated. Instead of being able to enjoy their relationship, she became frightened any time his plans didn’t include her. She convinced herself that if she could keep him with her all the time, she could not only keep from losing him but also regain some of the security she’d lost when her father died. She had a core belief common to many emotional blackmailers: I don’t trust that I’m going to get what I need, so I have to give myself every advantage. That justified all the clinging and all of the blackmail.

嫁给艾伦后，她的恐惧与日俱增。她非但没有享受婚姻生活，反而只要艾伦的计划中没有她，她就感到害怕。她不断说服自己，如果能一直把他留在身边，不仅能避免失去他，还能找回父亲去世后失去的安全感。她有着许多情感勒索者共有的核心信念：我不相信自己能得到想要的东西，所以我必须竭尽全力让自己占尽优势。这为她所有的依赖和勒索行为都提供了借口。

A MIX OF CAUSES

多种原因

The primary roots of Jo’s deprivation were fairly easy to trace, but bear in mind that human behavior is complex, shaped by a variety of physiological and psychological factors. Often it defies any single explanation. We’re born with particular temperaments and genetic predispositions—our own unique circuitry—and these elements interact with how we’re treated and what we learn about ourselves and our relationships to others, shaping our inner and outer lives.

乔的匮乏感根源很容易追溯，但请记住，人类行为十分复杂，受多种生理和心理因素的影响。很多时候，任何单一的解释都难以奏效。我们生来就具有特定的气质和遗传倾向——我们独特的内在回路——这些因素会与我们受到的待遇、我们对自身以及与他人关系的认知相互作用，从而塑造我们的内心世界和外在生活。

Eve, whose artist boyfriend, Elliot, was hypersensitive to frustration and frequently threatened to harm himself when he felt endangered, once told me about a conversation she’d had with Elliot’s sister.

伊芙的艺术家男友艾略特对挫折非常敏感，当他感到自身安全受到威胁时，经常会威胁要伤害自己。伊芙曾告诉我她和艾略特的妹妹的一次谈话。

She laughed when I asked her if she knew why he was always throwing tantrums. She said he’d been that way since he was born. Even when he was a baby, if the bottle wasn’t right in his mouth or he was wet for two seconds, he’d yell the house down. When he was a little older, he was a terror with his tantrums. She said it’s just how he’s wired—he was the most demanding, needy child she’s ever seen.

当我问她知不知道他为什么总是发脾气时，她笑了。她说他从出生起就是这样。即使是婴儿时期，奶瓶没含好，或者身上沾了点水，他都会嚎啕大哭，吵得屋子都塌了。再大一点，他发脾气的时候简直是个小恶魔。她说他天生就是这样——他是她见过的最黏人、最需要照顾的孩子。

That child grew up to be a demanding, needy adult who continued to throw tantrums to get what he wanted. A large part of Elliot’s basic temperament was present in infancy, including his low frustration threshold.

那个孩子长大后成了一个要求苛刻、依赖性强的成年人，他总是通过发脾气来达到自己的目的。埃利奥特性格中的大部分特征，包括他极低的挫折容忍度，早在婴儿时期就已经显现出来。

Complementing or reinforcing such genetic factors, of course, are powerful messages from our caretakers and society about who we are and how we are supposed to behave. Defining experiences in childhood, adolescence and even our adult lives create potent beliefs and feelings that often resurface, especially in conflict or when we’re under stress. We revert to those old patterns because they’re familiar, and even though they may cause us pain, they provide reassuring structure and predictability. We also believe that even if the old behavior didn’t work for us before, when we repeat it this time we’ll get it right.

当然，除了遗传因素之外，来自照护者和社会的关于我们是谁以及我们应该如何行事的强有力信息也发挥着补充或强化作用。童年、青少年时期乃至成年生活中的重要经历会形成根深蒂固的信念和感受，这些信念和感受往往会再次浮现，尤其是在冲突或压力之下。我们会回到那些旧有的模式，因为它们熟悉，即使它们可能会给我们带来痛苦，但它们也能提供令人安心的结构和可预测性。我们还相信，即使过去的行为方式对我们无效，这一次重复它也会是正确的。

Like Jo, many blackmailers have a fantasy that the helplessness and inadequacy they felt as children will vanish, and now, as adults, they’ll magically be able to “fix” a bad situation or an unhappy parent or guarantee the security they long for. They believe they can compensate for some of the frustrations of the past by changing the current reality.

和乔一样，许多勒索者都幻想，他们童年时感受到的无助和不足会消失，如今作为成年人，他们就能神奇地“解决”糟糕的局面、让不快乐的父母开心，或者保证他们渴望的安全感。他们相信，改变现状可以弥补过去的一些挫折。

WHEN A CRISIS IS THE CATALYST

当危机成为催化剂

The inability to tolerate frustration can also be a response to fairly recent uncertainties and stresses. The potential for blackmail rises dramatically during such crises as a separation or divorce, loss of a job, illness and retirement, which undermine blackmailers’ sense of themselves as valuable people. Most of the time they aren’t even consciously aware of their newly activated fears. All they can see is what they want right now and how they’ll get it.

无法忍受挫折也可能是对近期不确定性和压力的一种反应。在诸如分居或离婚、失业、疾病和退休等危机期间，勒索的可能性会急剧上升，因为这些危机削弱了勒索者自我价值的认知。大多数时候，他们甚至没有意识到自己新近产生的恐惧。他们满脑子想的都是眼前的欲望以及如何得到它。

For Stephanie, the precipitating crisis was her husband’s confession of his brief affair. Bob was working hard to get the marriage back on stable ground and attending therapy regularly, but Stephanie remained adamant about her right to keep Bob in line with healthy doses of emotional blackmail. After a year of her anger and retaliation, Bob was almost ready to give up. I told him it would be a good idea for her to come in for a joint consultation, and she agreed.

对斯蒂芬妮来说，引发危机的导火索是她丈夫坦白了短暂的婚外情。鲍勃努力想让婚姻重回正轨，并定期接受心理治疗，但斯蒂芬妮仍然坚持认为她有权用情感勒索来控制鲍勃。在经历了她一年的愤怒和报复之后，鲍勃几乎要放弃了。我建议他最好和斯蒂芬妮一起来做个咨询，她同意了。

You of all people should understand. I’ve read all your books and you talk a lot about how you can’t let people roll over you and how you have to confront them and set limits. I have every right to be mad, and Bob deserves some payback for what he did.

你最应该明白。我读过你所有的书，你经常谈到不能任人欺凌，必须勇敢地面对他们，划清界限。我有充分的理由生气，鲍勃也应该为他所做的一切付出代价。

I told Stephanie that she was indeed entitled to feel angry, hurt, betrayed and shocked, and I didn’t want to discount her pain in any way. But, I told her, there is a big difference between confrontation and emotional blackmail. While she might be getting satisfaction from playing the avenging, wronged wife and punishing Bob, her marriage was going down the tubes.

我告诉斯蒂芬妮，她当然有理由感到愤怒、受伤、被背叛和震惊，我绝不会轻视她的痛苦。但是，我告诉她，对抗和情感勒索之间有着天壤之别。虽然她扮演复仇的受害妻子，惩罚鲍勃，可能从中获得某种快感，但她的婚姻却正在走向破裂。

Stephanie became noticeably less defensive as the session went on, and as she tearfully described how she’d felt when she found out about Bob’s affair, another layer emerged, shedding considerable light on why it was so difficult for her to let go of her need for revenge.

随着谈话的进行，斯蒂芬妮的防备心明显降低了。当她泪流满面地描述自己发现鲍勃出轨时的感受时，她内心的另一层面也浮现出来，这充分说明了为什么她很难放下复仇的念头。

This wasn’t the first time I gave my heart and soul to a man who let me down, and Bob knew that. How could he even think of seeing someone else when he knew how devastated I was when my first husband cheated on me? It nearly killed me. What am I supposed to do now? How can I ever trust him again? I have never felt so unattractive, so humiliated, so . . . so inadequate in my life!

这并非我第一次全心全意地爱上一个让我失望的男人，鲍勃也知道这一点。他怎么能想到去见别人呢？他明明知道我被前夫背叛时有多么痛苦，几乎要了我的命。我现在该怎么办？我还能再次信任他吗？我这辈子从未觉得自己如此没有魅力，如此屈辱，如此……如此无能！

Stephanie was not only coping with what Bob had done, which would have been difficult enough, but also with the pain of the experience with her first husband. Drained of trust in Bob and of confidence in herself, she struck back through punishing emotional blackmail, the one way she felt she could regain control over the emotional chaos inside her.

斯蒂芬妮不仅要承受鲍勃的所作所为带来的痛苦（这本身就已十分艰难），还要面对与前夫婚姻带来的伤痛。她对鲍勃彻底失去了信任，也对自己失去了信心，于是她采取了严厉的情感勒索手段进行反击，因为她觉得这是唯一能让她重新掌控内心混乱情绪的方法。

While issues from Stephanie’s childhood had probably played a part in her reactions, we focused on the parallels in her adult life. When Stephanie saw how much the pain she’d brought from her former marriage was jeopardizing what could once again be a good relationship with Bob, she agreed to see a colleague of mine. She and Bob are both working hard, and they have been able to use this crisis as a catalyst for opening up new areas of communication and exploration. I think they’ll make it.
