虽然斯蒂芬妮童年的经历可能对她的反应有所影响，但我们更关注的是她成年生活中的相似之处。当斯蒂芬妮意识到她从前一段婚姻中带来的痛苦正在危及她与鲍勃之间可能再次建立的良好关系时，她同意接受我一位同事的咨询。她和鲍勃都在努力，并且他们已经能够将这场危机转化为契机，开辟新的沟通和探索领域。我相信他们最终会成功的。

A CHARMED LIFE

迷人的生活

Some of the most puzzling blackmailers are the ones who seem to have it all and want more. It seems incongruous to suggest that they’re motivated by deprivation because they seem to have had so few encounters with it. But often, people who have been overprotected and indulged have had little opportunity to develop confidence in their ability to handle any kind of loss. At the first hint that they might be deprived, they panic, and shore themselves up with blackmail.

有些勒索者最令人费解，他们似乎拥有一切，却还想要更多。说他们是因为匮乏感而勒索，似乎有些矛盾，因为他们似乎很少经历匮乏。但通常情况下，那些被过度保护和溺爱的人，很少有机会培养应对任何损失的自信。一旦察觉到自己可能面临匮乏，他们就会惊慌失措，并试图通过勒索来巩固自身。

This was definitely the case with Maria’s physician husband, Jay. I knew from my work with Maria that Jay was a man to whom everything had come easily. He’d flown through medical school, established himself as a wunderkind by pioneering a number of surgical procedures and moved easily in the most prestigious social circles. The word that came to my mind was entitlement.

玛丽亚的医生丈夫杰伊的情况正是如此。我从与玛丽亚的共事中了解到，杰伊是个一切都来得太容易的人。他轻松从医学院毕业，凭借开创的多项外科手术成为医学奇才，并在最负盛名的社交圈中游刃有余。我当时脑海中浮现的第一个词就是“自以为是”。

His childhood was incredible. No abuse, no trauma, nothing but adoration. His father was poor and the first one in his family to go to college. That man was amazing. He got through medical school with a combination of hard work, chutzpah and about two hours’ sleep a night. He had a part-time job as a waiter to earn enough money to take Jay’s mother out. He told me one of the things he’d promised himself was that Jay should never have to go through what he did. Jay was a golden child, no question. When he decided to become a doctor his parents spared no expense to see that he got chemistry sets and science camps. No part-time jobs for him. He got the world on a platter—along with tennis lessons, cashmere sports coats and, of course, lots of girls.

他的童年简直不可思议。没有虐待，没有创伤，只有无尽的宠爱。他的父亲家境贫寒，却是家中第一个上大学的人。他真是个了不起的人。他凭借着勤奋、胆识和每晚大约两小时的睡眠，完成了医学院的学业。为了挣钱带杰的母亲出去玩，他还兼职做服务员。他告诉我，他曾向自己许下诺言，绝不让杰经历他所经历的一切。杰无疑是个受宠的孩子。当他决定成为一名医生时，他的父母不惜一切代价，为他购买化学实验套装，并带他参加科学夏令营。他不需要做任何兼职。他拥有了一切——网球课、羊绒运动外套，当然，还有很多女孩。

Jay’s life had been more than privileged—it had been unreal. In trying to make sure that deprivation had no place in Jay’s life, his father had done little to prepare him for disappointments or setbacks.

杰伊的生活远不止是优渥——简直是天方夜谭。为了确保杰伊的人生中没有一丝贫困的滋味，他的父亲几乎没有让他做好面对失望或挫折的准备。

There are two down sides to this charmed existence. People who grow up in such a safe harbor develop unrealistic expectations, believing that whatever they want will fall into their laps. Even more damaging, they are deprived of the chance to develop the essential skills we all need for handling frustration. With what appeared to be the best of motives and intentions, Jay’s father had actually created a kind of emotional cripple.

这种看似美好的生活也有两个弊端。在如此安全的环境中长大的人容易产生不切实际的期望，认为想要的一切都会唾手可得。更糟糕的是，他们因此失去了培养应对挫折等基本技能的机会。杰伊的父亲看似出于好意，实际上却给杰伊造成了一种情感上的创伤。

When Maria challenged Jay’s belief that he was entitled to have it all—career, family, wife and mistress—she was the first person who mattered to him who threatened to take something important away from him. Jay was panic-stricken. Someone had changed the rules, and emotional blackmail was his means of regaining his accustomed position at the top of the heap.

当玛丽亚挑战杰伊“我理应拥有一切——事业、家庭、妻子和情妇”的信念时，她是第一个威胁要从他身边夺走重要之物的人。杰伊惊慌失措。有人改变了规则，而情感勒索成了他重新夺回昔日高位的手段。

INTIMATE STRANGERS

亲密陌生人

When Jay enlisted his parents to pressure Maria to stay with him, she couldn’t believe what they were saying to her:

当杰伊让他的父母去逼迫玛丽亚留在他身边时，她简直不敢相信他们跟她说的话：

My God—what am I dealing with here? People I loved and respected suddenly show themselves to be without any moral or ethical convictions whatsoever. Is keeping up appearances more important than feelings and basic human decency?

我的天哪——我这是在面对什么？我曾经爱戴和尊敬的人，突然间竟然毫无道德底线。难道维护体面比感情和基本的人性更重要吗？

Maria watched Jay change from the charmer who’d swept her off her feet to a devious, manipulative stranger. When people close to us resort to emotional blackmail, we’re struck by how their personalities seem to shift, a process that may be gradual or surprisingly fast. Much of the pain and confusion of emotional blackmail, in fact, arises from seeing people we care about and who we believe care about us become people who need to get their way so much that they are willing to ride roughshod over our feelings.

玛丽亚眼睁睁地看着杰伊从那个让她神魂颠倒的魅力男士变成了一个阴险狡诈、善于操纵的陌生人。当身边的人诉诸情感勒索时，我们会惊讶地发现他们的性格似乎发生了转变，这个过程可能是渐进的，也可能是出乎意料的迅速。事实上，情感勒索带来的痛苦和困惑，很大程度上源于我们看到那些我们关心、也以为关心我们的人，变成了为了达到目的不惜践踏我们感情的人。

Liz had a feeling of disorientation when Michael told her how brutally he’d punish her if she kept talking about leaving him.

当迈克尔告诉莉兹，如果她继续说要离开他，他会如何残酷地惩罚她时，莉兹感到一阵茫然。

He’s actually said: “The money you’ll have left when I get through with you won’t buy dog food. And kiss the kids good-bye. I’m thinking of taking them to Canada so they won’t have to listen to your lies about me.” And this is a man I’ve made love with and been naked with and bared my soul to. Who the hell is he?

他竟然说：“等我收拾完你，你剩下的钱连狗粮都买不起。还有，跟孩子们说再见吧。我打算带他们去加拿大，免得他们再听你编造关于我的谎言。” 而这个人，我曾和他做爱，和他赤身裸体，向他敞开心扉。他到底是谁？

Blaming, threatening, negative comparisons and other tools we’ve seen are obviously not what drew us into our close relationships, and they’re not what’s kept us there. These are people who share our lives, our work, our feelings and our secrets. Yet when emotional blackmail comes in, we quickly encounter some unappealing aspects of their personality—self-centeredness, overreaction, an insistence on short-term gains even if they result in long-term losses, and a need to win, no matter what.

指责、威胁、负面比较以及其他种种手段，显然并非我们建立亲密关系的初衷，也并非维系关系的根本。这些人与我们分享生活、工作、情感和秘密。然而，当情感勒索出现时，我们很快就会发现他们性格中一些令人反感的方面——自我中心、反应过度、为了短期利益而不惜牺牲长期利益，以及不择手段也要赢的执念。

IT’S ALL ABOUT THEM

一切都与他们有关

All the blackmailers we’ve seen are focused almost totally on their needs, their desires; they don’t seem to be the least bit interested in our needs or how their pressure is affecting us.

我们所见到的所有勒索者几乎都完全专注于他们自己的需求和欲望；他们似乎对我们的需求或他们的压力对我们造成的影响丝毫没有兴趣。

Blackmailers can be like steamrollers when we don’t satisfy them, becoming ruthless in their single-minded pursuit of their goals. It’s a strange kind of love that is so blind to the target’s feelings.

当我们无法满足勒索者的要求时，他们就像压路机一样横冲直撞，为了达到目的而不择手段。这是一种奇怪的爱，完全无视受害者的感受。

My nominee for the Narcissist Hall of Fame is Patty’s husband, Joe, who took to his bed with a contemporary version of the vapors when she told him they couldn’t afford a new computer. In a recent incident, his self-absorption was unparalleled:

我提名帕蒂的丈夫乔进入自恋名人堂。当帕蒂告诉他他们买不起新电脑时，他竟然装病卧床不起，简直像现代版的“精神错乱”。最近发生的一件事更是让他自我中心到了极点：

Joe makes good money, but he spends it faster than either one of us can make it, so we’re usually behind on everything. Last week the bills were really piled up, and he asked me to call my aunt and ask for a loan. My aunt is pretty well off, but she’d just had surgery for breast cancer. I told him there was no way I could bother her, and I couldn’t believe how he started to pressure me. “Here’s her number at the hospital,” he said. “You don’t even have to look it up. Call her now — it’s no big deal. She’s not in any pain and you’ve always been her favorite. Why can’t you do this one little thing for me?”

乔挣钱不少，但他花钱的速度比我们俩挣钱的速度都快，所以我们总是入不敷出。上周账单堆积如山，他让我打电话给我姑姑借点钱。我姑姑家境不错，但她刚做了乳腺癌手术。我告诉他我实在不好意思打扰她，没想到他居然开始逼我。“这是她在医院的电话号码，”他说，“你不用查，现在就打——没什么大不了的。她现在一点都不疼，而且你一直是她最喜欢的人。为什么你就不能帮我这个忙呢？”

Breast cancer? Hospital? Surgery? No problem for this blackmailer. After all, he wanted something. NOW. And at the moment of urgency, no one else existed on the face of the earth.

乳腺癌？住院？手术？对这个勒索者来说都不是问题。毕竟，他想要点什么。而且是现在就要。在如此紧急的时刻，这世上似乎只有他一个人。

Often blackmailers’ self-centeredness springs from a belief that the supply of attention and affection available to them is finite—and shrinking fast. Elliot is so self-centered that even when his girlfriend wants to take some classes to provide a backup career for herself, it’s about him. In his mind, giving to Eve robs him of security. What if he needs something while she’s gone? What if he gets bored or lonely? Who will take care of him? The universe revolves around him, just as it did when he was little. Once again, he’s the tyrannical five-year-old demanding total attention and satisfaction from the person he’s dependent on, and always wanting more.

勒索者的自我中心往往源于一种信念：他们所能获得的关注和关爱是有限的，而且正在迅速减少。埃利奥特就是如此自我中心，即使他的女友想去上一些课程，为自己储备一份职业，他也只关心自己。在他看来，给予伊芙会让他失去安全感。如果她不在的时候他需要什么怎么办？如果他感到无聊或孤独怎么办？谁来照顾他？整个世界都围绕着他转，就像他小时候那样。他又一次变成了那个专横跋扈的五岁小孩，要求他所依赖的人给予他全部的关注和满足，而且永远都想要更多。

MAKING MOUNTAINS OUT OF MOLEHILLS

小题大做

Emotional blackmailers often behave as though each disagreement is the make-or-break factor in the relationship. They feel such intense disappointment and frustration when they encounter resistance that they blow up even minor discord and allow it to color the whole relationship. Why would anyone make such a big deal out of your not wanting to have dinner with their parents, or attack you because you wanted to take a class or a fishing trip, or weren’t enthusiastic about their plans? The ferocity of their desire only makes sense when you realize that they are not reacting to the current situation but rather to what that situation symbolizes to them from the past.

情感勒索者常常把每一次分歧都看作是关系的生死攸关的大事。一旦遇到阻力，他们就会感到极度的失望和沮丧，甚至会把一些小摩擦无限放大，让这些负面情绪影响到整段关系。你不想和他们的父母共进晚餐，或者因为你想去上课、去钓鱼，又或者对他们的计划不太感兴趣，他们为什么会如此大惊小怪？只有当你意识到他们并非针对当下的情况做出反应，而是针对这种情况在他们心中象征的过往经历时，才能理解他们如此强烈的反应。

It became clear from some things Eve told me about Elliot’s background that he believed that a man can’t get what he needs from an independent woman.

从伊芙告诉我的关于艾略特的一些背景信息中，我清楚地了解到，他认为男人无法从独立女性那里得到他需要的东西。

I remember him telling me about his dad and how much he groused about being neglected. Elliot’s mother must have been a real pioneer in the business world. She ran a small children’s-clothing company, which was great—except for her husband, who hated it. Elliot said the thing he remembers most was his mother being gone a lot. She was loving when she was there, but then suddenly she’d be off on a business trip and he missed her terribly. His father was angry at her much of the time and was constantly saying things like, “These goddamn women — they can’t do enough for you when they need you, but they forget you exist if they start making it on their own.” I guess if you hear that enough it really sinks in.

我记得他跟我讲过他爸爸，还有他爸爸总是抱怨被冷落。埃利奥特的妈妈一定是商界的先驱。她经营着一家小型童装公司，生意很好——除了她丈夫，他丈夫很讨厌这份工作。埃利奥特说他印象最深的是妈妈经常不在家。妈妈在家的时候很慈爱，但突然之间她就出差了，他非常想念她。他爸爸经常对妈妈生气，总是说些类似这样的话：“这些该死的女人——她们需要你的时候对你百依百顺，但一旦她们开始独立生活，就把你忘得一干二净。”我想，这种话听多了，真的会让人印象深刻。

The message Elliot came away with was unambiguous: Women won’t be loving partners unless you make sure they’re with you all the time. He would probably deny holding that kind of belief, but his overreaction to Eve revealed that old demons were being stirred up. For Elliot, any sign of independence in a woman was threatening. Eve became a stand-in for his mother, the woman he was emotionally dependent on and fused with. She, too, would abandon him, as he perceived his mother had abandoned his father—and him—by being gone so much. Each time Eve tried to walk out the door, Elliot began to relive his old sense of deprivation.

埃利奥特从中得到的讯息非常明确：除非你确保她们时刻陪伴在你身边，否则她们不会成为你深爱的伴侣。他或许会否认自己持有这种观点，但他对伊芙的过激反应表明，他内心深处的旧日阴影正在被唤醒。对埃利奥特而言，女性身上任何独立的迹象都是一种威胁。伊芙成了他母亲的替代品，那个他情感上依赖并与之融为一体的女人。她也会像他母亲一样抛弃他，因为他觉得母亲因为经常不在家而抛弃了他的父亲——也抛弃了他自己。每当伊芙试图离开时，埃利奥特都会再次感受到那种被剥夺的痛苦。

As with all overreaction, a lot of noise and emotion are vented, but the real, underlying feelings are rarely expressed. Elliot is desperate for intimacy, but the barrage he directs at Eve almost guarantees that he won’t get it. Let’s look at what was expressed, and unexpressed, when Eve suggested that he might consider getting professional help for his anxiety.

就像所有过度反应一样，大量的喧嚣和情绪被宣泄出来，但真正深层的感受却很少表达出来。埃利奥特渴望亲密关系，但他对伊芙的猛烈抨击几乎注定让他无法如愿。让我们来看看，当伊芙建议他考虑寻求专业帮助来治疗焦虑症时，他表达了什么，又有哪些未表达的情感。

What Elliot says: “You’re gonna go out and do what you want and I’m gonna be alone—why should I live? You don’t care a bit about me.”

埃利奥特说：“你想做什么就做什么，而我却要孤身一人——我活着还有什么意义？你根本不在乎我。”

What Elliot means: “I’m scared because you’re changing. At the beginning, I was enough for you, but not anymore. If you go to school, I’m scared you’ll get a career of your own, and you won’t have time for me. I’m scared you’ll meet someone else. I’m scared you’ll get too independent. You won’t need me and you’ll leave me.”

埃利奥特的意思是：“我害怕，因为你变了。一开始，我就足够了，但现在不行了。如果你去上学，我害怕你会找到自己的事业，那样你就没时间陪我了。我害怕你会遇到别人。我害怕你会变得太独立。你不再需要我，你会离开我。”

But this kind of communication was not in Elliot’s repertoire. If it were, he wouldn’t need to resort to emotional blackmail. Perhaps, like many men, he was ashamed of his neediness and fears. The only option he saw for getting what he wanted was to rant and rave—overreacting to the slightest indication of Eve’s wish to improve herself.

但这种沟通方式并不在埃利奥特的考虑范围之内。如果他会，就无需诉诸情感勒索了。或许，像许多男人一样，他为自己的依赖和恐惧感到羞耻。在他看来，获得自己想要的东西的唯一途径就是大发雷霆——对伊芙想要提升自我的哪怕一丝一毫的迹象都反应过度。

Feelings from Another Time

来自另一个时代的感受

Roger, the screenwriter, was astounded at the furious assault Alice unleashed against him when he didn’t jump at her suggestion that they have a baby. When he appeared uncertain about what he wanted, she had a classic overreaction.

编剧罗杰对爱丽丝的猛烈抨击感到震惊，因为他没有欣然接受她生孩子的提议。当他表现出对自己想要什么犹豫不决时，她做出了典型的过激反应。

You never really cared about me. How can you call this love when you don’t want to take any steps that will bring us closer. I don’t trust you anymore. I’m not even sure I love you anymore! You have some pretty serious problems, and you really need help!

你从来就没真正关心过我。你都不愿意采取任何措施拉近我们之间的距离，这怎么能称之为爱呢？我不再信任你了。我甚至不确定自己是否还爱你！你真的有很多严重的问题，你需要帮助！

However, one night at their AA meeting, Roger was able to gain important insights into the fears behind Alice’s desperate push to get a long-term commitment from him. She told the group:

然而，在一次匿名戒酒互助会（AA）的会议上，罗杰终于了解到爱丽丝为何如此迫切地想要从他那里得到一份长期的恋爱关系，而她内心深处的恐惧也正是源于此。她告诉了互助小组：

I don’t believe in anything but right now. I dive into the present and hold on tight. My father was a compulsive gambler. He was really glamorous in my eyes. But what it really means is that one day you’re rich and the next day you’re shopping at the Salvation Army and you can’t answer the phone because it’s a collection agency. Everything I had as a kid was up for grabs — baby-sitting money, gifts from people, anything you could pawn. Even my father came and went. Sometimes he would be gone for weeks. Is it so wrong to want some security, some commitment? That feels like good values to me. What’s wrong with love ?

我只相信当下。我全身心投入现在，紧紧抓住它。我父亲是个赌徒。在我眼里，他魅力四射。但现实是，你可能今天还富甲一方，明天就得去救世军商店买东西，电话也打不通，因为是催债公司打来的。我小时候拥有的一切都可能被拿去典当——保姆费、别人送的礼物，任何能当的东西。就连我父亲也总是来来去去，有时一走就是好几个星期。想要一些安全感，一些承诺，难道错了吗？我觉得这才是美好的价值观。爱又有什么错呢？

Alice had spent years dreading that what she had would suddenly disappear, so it was no surprise that she wanted guarantees for the future. But like most blackmailers, she used a heavy-handed style of attempting to get around her target’s resistance.

多年来，爱丽丝一直害怕自己拥有的一切会突然消失，所以她想要未来的保障也就不足为奇了。但像大多数勒索者一样，她采取了一种强硬的手段，试图绕过目标的抵抗。

Her overreactiveness, which took the form of a scathing verbal attack on Roger, came from a place inside her that was full of hungers and fears. No matter how much she bound Roger to her, he couldn’t fill that place for her, even if he wanted to.

她对罗杰的过激反应，表现为尖刻的言语攻击，源于她内心深处的渴望和恐惧。无论她如何依附罗杰，即使他想，也无法填补她心中的空缺。

Through her work in AA, Alice was able to see how she was trying to handcuff Roger and to realize that she would have a difficult time with any relationship until she did some work on herself. She has since been able to significantly reduce the pressure on Roger and to give the relationship time to evolve naturally.

在参加匿名戒酒互助会（AA）的过程中，爱丽丝意识到自己一直在试图束缚罗杰，并且明白如果她不先解决自身的问题，任何关系对她来说都难以维系。此后，她大大减轻了罗杰的压力，也让这段关系有时间自然发展。

WINNING THE BATTLE, LOSING THE WAR

赢得战役，却输掉战争

Blackmailers frequently win with tactics that create an insurmountable rift in the relationship. Yet the short-term victory often appears to be enough of a triumph—as if there were no future to consider.

勒索者常常使用一些手段，在双方关系中制造无法弥合的裂痕，从而达到目的。然而，短期的胜利似乎就足以让他们感到满足——仿佛他们根本不需要考虑未来。

Most blackmailers operate from an I-want-what-I-want-when-I-want-it mind-set. They seem to have a childlike inability to connect behavior to consequences, and they don’t appear to give any thought to what they will be left with once they’ve gotten the target’s compliance.

大多数勒索者都抱着“我想要什么就一定要得到”的心态。他们似乎像孩子一样，无法将行为与后果联系起来，而且他们似乎根本不考虑在获得目标人物的顺从之后，自己会剩下什么。

It’s hard to believe that Michael, Elliot, Alice, Jay, Stephanie or any of the blackmailers we’ve seen so far could think they would have anything worthwhile left if their targets gave in to their threats and pressure. What kind of relationship does Josh’s father expect to have with his son if Josh provides the victory his father is demanding by giving up his lover? Margaret, whose husband, Cal, pressured her to take part in group sex, gave in to her husband’s emotional blackmail, but it was the death knell for the marriage.

很难相信，迈克尔、艾略特、爱丽丝、杰伊、斯蒂芬妮，或者我们目前为止见到的任何其他勒索者，会认为如果他们的目标屈服于他们的威胁和压力，他们还能剩下什么有价值的东西。如果乔什为了满足父亲的要求，交出情人，他父亲还指望和儿子维持怎样的关系？玛格丽特的丈夫卡尔强迫她参与群交，她最终屈服于丈夫的情感勒索，但这却成了这段婚姻的丧钟。

Liz bought herself time to regroup by appearing to give in to Michael’s threats. As Liz said,

莉兹假装屈服于迈克尔的威胁，以此为自己争取时间重整旗鼓。正如莉兹所说，

I called my lawyer and told him to hold off on doing anything. I keep hoping now that Michael’s calmed down he’ll at least start a rational dialogue with me. He’s really being sweet because he thinks he’s got me where he wants me and that ultimately I’ll come around and kiss and make up. The truth is, I’m just going through the motions. I’m living with a man I don’t even like anymore, let alone love.

我给我的律师打了电话，让他先别采取任何行动。现在迈克尔冷静下来了，我还是抱着一丝希望，希望他至少能和我理性地谈谈。他现在这么温柔体贴，是因为他觉得我已经完全掌控了我，最终我会回心转意，和好如初。但事实上，我只是在敷衍了事。我跟一个我根本不喜欢，更别提爱的男人住在一起。

Any logic or ability to see the consequences of their actions is obscured by the urgency blackmailers feel to hold on to what they have. They’re in a FOG of their own that makes them oblivious to how much they alienate other people with their bullying. All that matters is finding immediate relief from their deprivation fears—whatever that relief costs.

勒索者急于保住自己所拥有的东西，这种迫切感蒙蔽了他们的理智，也让他们看不到自己行为的后果。他们深陷于自己的迷雾之中，丝毫没有意识到自己的欺凌行为会给他人带来多大的伤害。对他们而言，最重要的就是尽快摆脱被剥夺的恐惧——无论代价是什么。

THE PAYOFFS OF PUNISHING

惩罚的回报

When we look at how intensely blackmailers fear deprivation, a more complete picture begins to take shape and it’s easier to fathom why they act as they do. But one question continues to nag most of the people I talk to about this subject: Why do they need to punish us? “OK,” they say. “I see why they nag or pressure us or even make threats, but why on earth do they need to hurt us if we don’t give them their way?”

当我们了解勒索者对失去东西的恐惧有多么强烈时，一幅更完整的图景便开始浮现，我们也更容易理解他们为何如此行事。但有一个问题始终萦绕在我与大多数人谈论这个话题时：他们为什么要惩罚我们？“好吧，”他们会说，“我明白他们为什么纠缠、施压甚至威胁我们，但如果我们不顺从他们，他们究竟为什么要伤害我们？”

Many times it does seem as though the goal of emotional blackmail is not only to make the blackmailer feel good but to make the target feel bad. Blackmailers demand—and they demean. In their attempts to show the rightness of what they want, they cast aspersions on our character and question our motives. Even when their threats of punishment are directed more against themselves than us, they target us by drowning us in guilt.

很多时候，情感勒索的目的似乎不仅在于让勒索者自我感觉良好，更在于让受害者感到痛苦。勒索者不仅提出要求，还会贬低受害者。为了证明自己要求的合理性，他们会诋毁我们的人格，质疑我们的动机。即使他们威胁惩罚的对象更多是自己而非我们，他们也会通过让我们深陷罪恶感来达到目的。

One obvious reason is the difference between what blackmailers tell themselves about what they’re doing and why they’re doing it—the “spin” we saw in the last chapter—and the actual effect of their behavior on us. Punishers don’t see themselves as punishing, but rather as maintaining order or keeping a firm hand on things or doing “what’s right” or letting us know they can’t be pushed around. They see themselves as strong and in charge. If their behavior hurts us, so be it. The end justifies the means.

一个显而易见的原因是，勒索者对自己行为及其动机的自我辩解——也就是我们在上一章看到的“粉饰”——与他们的行为对我们的实际影响之间存在差异。惩罚者并不认为自己是在惩罚，而是在维护秩序、掌控局面、做“正确的事情”，或者让我们知道他们不容欺凌。他们认为自己强大且掌控一切。如果他们的行为伤害了我们，那就这样吧。在他们看来，目的可以证明手段的正当性。

And as we’ve seen, many punishers see themselves as victims. In fact, the more abusive the blackmailers, the more they twist reality. Their extreme sensitivity and self-centeredness magnify the hurts they feel and help them justify retaliating against us for what they see as deliberate attempts to thwart them.

正如我们所见，许多施暴者都把自己视为受害者。事实上，勒索者越是肆意妄为，就越是扭曲现实。他们极度的敏感和自我中心放大了他们所感受到的伤害，并以此为借口，对我们进行报复——在他们看来，我们这样做是故意阻挠他们的。

Punishment also allows blackmailers to take an active, aggressive stance that makes them feel powerful and invulnerable. This is an extremely effective way for them to calm any perceived threat of deprivation and head it off at the pass. After all, if someone is yelling, threatening, slamming doors or refusing to speak to you, there’s not much spare time to deal with feelings.

惩罚还能让勒索者采取积极主动的姿态，让他们感觉自己强大无比、刀枪不入。这是一种极其有效的手段，可以消除任何潜在的损失威胁，防患于未然。毕竟，如果有人对你大喊大叫、威胁恐吓、摔门或拒绝与你交谈，你哪有时间去顾及自己的感受呢？

It’s a truism that what we don’t talk out, we act out. If punishers were to allow themselves a few moments of introspection, they would probably be revolted by the fears and vulnerabilities they would discover. It’s one of the most fascinating paradoxes of human behavior that angry, punitive people are really very frightened, but they rarely confront or diminish those fears. Instead they lash out at others when they are frustrated to prove how strong they are. They create so much unhappiness with their behavior that they often cause people to leave them, thereby ensuring that the thing they fear the most will happen.

俗话说，我们不说出口的话，就会用行动表达出来。如果那些喜欢惩罚别人的人能抽出一点时间反省一下，他们或许会对自己发现的恐惧和脆弱感到厌恶。人类行为中最令人着迷的悖论之一，就是那些愤怒、喜欢惩罚别人的人其实内心非常恐惧，但他们很少直面或消除这些恐惧。相反，当他们感到沮丧时，他们会攻击他人，以此来证明自己的强大。他们的行为造成了如此多的不快，以至于人们常常离开他们，从而确保了他们最害怕的事情最终发生。

CUTTING THEIR LOSSES

止损

The most punitive blackmailers are often those who have lost or fear losing someone important to them because that person is withdrawing emotionally or because of a separation, divorce or major rift in the relationship.

最残忍的勒索者往往是那些失去或害怕失去对他们来说重要的人的人，因为那个人在情感上疏远了他们，或者因为分居、离婚或关系出现重大裂痕。

Remember Sherry and Charles, the married man she worked for who threatened to fire her if she ended their affair?

还记得雪莉和查尔斯吗？查尔斯是她工作的已婚男人，他威胁说如果她结束这段婚外情就要解雇她。

One minute I’m the most beautiful, exciting, interesting woman in the world, but as soon as I tell him I feel like I’m on a dead-end street and I have to get off so I can move on with my life, I’m a cold-hearted witch who doesn’t care about all the stress he’s under and how much he’s trying to work things out. Now he’s telling me that all he does is give, give, give, and all I do is take, take, take—which is a total 180 on what’s been happening. Oh—and suddenly he’s finding fault with everything I do at work. If he’s trying to make my life miserable, he’s doing a good job of it. How could he turn on me like this?

前一秒我还觉得自己是世界上最美丽、最迷人、最有趣的女人，可当我告诉他我觉得自己走上了一条死胡同，必须离开才能继续生活时，他就把我当成了冷血无情的巫婆，根本不在乎他承受的压力，也不在乎他为了解决问题付出了多少努力。现在他却说他一直在付出，而我一直在索取——这跟之前的情况完全相反。哦，对了，他突然又开始挑剔我工作上的每件事。如果他真的想让我痛苦，那他做得也太成功了。他怎么能这样对我呢？

Faced with the loss of his young lover, and seeing that his threats weren’t working, Charles did something to ease his pain—he devalued her. If he could make her less desirable, less valuable, then he wasn’t losing so much, and his deprivation would be considerably alleviated. After all, damaged goods are easier to part with. He could also justify firing her by devaluing her work. Double devaluation, double punishment.

面对失去年轻情人的痛苦，眼见威胁无效，查尔斯决定采取措施减轻自己的伤痛——贬低她。如果能让她变得不那么有吸引力、不那么有价值，那么他的损失就不会那么大，痛苦也会大大减轻。毕竟，残次品更容易割舍。他还可以借此贬低她的工作表现，为解雇她找到借口。双重贬低，双重惩罚。

Devaluation is a common tactic for angry blackmailers. It softens the sting of confrontation and enables them to downplay their feelings of loss. But as they do this, they give their targets confusing double messages. It’s as if they were saying “You’re no good, but I’ll do everything in my power to hold on to you”—a further illustration of how desperate they’re feeling.

贬低是愤怒的勒索者常用的伎俩。它能减轻对抗的冲击，让他们淡化自己的损失感。但这样做，却会给目标对象传递出令人困惑的双重信息。就好像他们在说“你一无是处，但我会不惜一切代价留住你”——这进一步暴露了他们的绝望。

Even though the last thing in the world they want is to end a relationship, they will often initiate the breakup on their own if they sense that their partner is serious about leaving. Their aggressive stance will let them stay in control, the old face-saving strategy that goes “Let me quit before I get fired.”

即使他们最不想做的就是结束一段感情，但如果他们感觉到伴侣真的想离开，他们往往也会主动提出分手。这种强势的态度能让他们保持掌控权，这是一种老套的保全颜面的策略，也就是“与其被炒鱿鱼，不如先辞职”。

TEACHING US A LESSON

给我们上了一课

Like parents who believe that punishment will mold a child’s character, blackmailers may convince themselves that they’re helping us with their punishments. Instead of feeling guilt or remorse about hurting someone they care so much about, they can actually feel pride. They’re making better people of us, they reason.

就像有些父母认为惩罚能塑造孩子的品格一样，勒索者也可能说服自己，他们的惩罚是在帮助我们。他们非但不会对伤害自己如此在乎的人感到内疚或悔恨，反而会感到自豪。他们认为自己是在让我们变得更好。

Alex, the tantalizer we met in Chapter 2 , believed that by promising his girlfriend Julie help and contacts but withholding his offers unless she “measured up,” he was doing her a great favor.

我们在第二章中遇到的那个爱捉弄人的亚历克斯认为，他答应给女友朱莉提供帮助和人脉，但除非她“达到标准”，否则不会兑现承诺，这样他就是在帮她一个大忙。

He told me that sending my son off to my ex’s would be the best thing for me. Everything was in terms of “You’re holding yourself back” and “I just want to see you reach your potential,” when what he really wanted was to have me to himself without my little boy around. Right, he was really generous.

他跟我说，把儿子送到前夫家对我来说是最好的。他满嘴都是“你在自我设限”和“我只是想看到你发挥出全部潜力”之类的话，其实他真正想要的只是没有儿子在身边，能独占我一个人。真是够慷慨的。

Insults and infantilizing are similarly explained away with the “It’s for your own good” rationale. There’s generally much less malice here than you might think. Most blackmailers believe they really are teaching us valuable lessons. Charles was absolutely in earnest when he told Sherry, “You need to learn about loyalty. It’s the most important thing in this business.”

侮辱和幼稚化行为通常都会用“这都是为了你好”的理由来解释。实际上，这里面的恶意远比你想象的要少。大多数勒索者都相信他们真的在给我们上宝贵的一课。查尔斯对雪莉说“你需要学习忠诚。在这个行当里，忠诚是最重要的”时，他是真心实意的。

Lynn and Jeff, who blackmailed each other, also thought they were trying to improve each other’s character. “She’s got to learn that she can’t treat people like that,” Jeff told me after one of their fights, sincerely believing that he was teaching Lynn to be “less of a shrew.” And Lynn saw her actions as training, too. “Maybe if I humiliate him enough, he’ll get off his ass and get a part-time job,” she said. “Sometimes it takes a kick in the pants to get someone moving.”

琳恩和杰夫互相勒索，却都认为自己是在帮助对方改过自新。“她得明白不能那样对待别人，”杰夫在一次争吵后告诉我，他真心相信自己是在教琳恩“别那么泼妇”。琳恩也把自己的行为看作是一种训练。“也许我把他羞辱得够呛，他就会振作起来，找份兼职工作，”她说。“有时候，得有人狠狠地踹他一脚，他才会行动起来。”

It’s fairly apparent, especially to the person on the receiving end, that punishment doesn’t produce the results the blackmailer believes it will, yet there are attractive payoffs to clinging to this erroneous idea of punishment as training. Blackmailers can live with almost anything if they can make their targets seem like dunces. In this way they can avoid any introspection or hint that something in them is driving off the love or connection they so desperately want.

很明显，尤其对于受害者而言，惩罚并不能达到勒索者预期的效果，然而，坚持这种将惩罚视为训练的错误观念却能带来诱人的回报。如果勒索者能让受害者看起来像个傻瓜，他们几乎可以容忍任何事情。这样一来，他们就能避免受害者进行任何反思，也不会让受害者意识到自身某些特质正在阻碍他们渴望的爱或情感联结的产生。

OLD BATTLES, NEW VICTIMS

旧战，新受害者

As we’ve seen, sometimes current stresses in the blackmailer’s life reopen old wounds, and the blackmailer strikes out at a target who has become a stand-in for a figure from the past. When this happens, a blackmailer’s punishment can be overblown, and may feel completely uncalled-for.

正如我们所见，勒索者当前生活中的压力有时会揭开旧伤疤，导致其攻击的目标成为过去某个人物的替代品。在这种情况下，勒索者受到的惩罚可能过重，甚至显得完全没有必要。

Michael, perhaps the most blatant punisher we’ve met, began to seem like a monster to Liz, who felt almost shell-shocked in the face of his tirades. When I asked her why she thought he was being so mean to her, she was silent for a moment, then responded:

迈克尔或许是我们见过的最肆无忌惮的惩罚者，在莉兹眼里，他简直像个怪物，莉兹几乎被他的咆哮吓得魂飞魄散。当我问她为什么觉得他要对她这么刻薄时，她沉默了一会儿，然后回答说：

You know, when I really think about it, I think that Michael was like a powder keg that was ready to blow. He’s been working hard since he was about 14 in his family’s business. They sell office equipment, and they’ve been pretty successful. Michael never got to be a kid, really. He was great at sports — he’s still pretty athletic—but Mom and Pop never let him play. He had to do inventory or sweep the store or mind the register.

你知道，仔细想想，我觉得迈克尔就像个随时会爆炸的火药桶。他从十四岁左右就开始在自家公司辛苦干活。他们卖办公设备，生意做得相当不错。迈克尔根本没机会真正享受童年。他运动天赋很好——现在也依然很擅长——但他爸妈从来不让他玩。他只能负责盘点库存、打扫店铺或者看收银。

When we were first dating, we took a trip to Chicago and he knew everything about the buildings. And he told me his big dream was to go study architecture. But they never let him go, and he let it drop. He’s so responsible. I know he’s mad at them, though he’s never said a word and never will. But I don’t think that means he has to take it all out on me.

我们刚开始交往的时候，一起去了趟芝加哥，他对那里的建筑了如指掌。他告诉我，他最大的梦想是去学建筑。但是学校没让他去，他也放弃了。他真是个很有责任感的人。我知道他心里很生气，虽然他一句话也没说，以后也不会说。但我认为他没必要把所有的气都撒在我身上。

I told Liz that she was right, there’s no excuse for the kind of verbal attacks and threats Michael had leveled at her. But it was important for her to understand that Michael’s criticisms of her and his anger at her supposed flaws had nothing to do with her, even though it was difficult not to take them personally. When Liz got fed up and threatened to leave him, the punishments reached a fever pitch. His fear of being without her had ignited the stored-up frustrations Liz had seen.

我告诉莉兹，她是对的，迈克尔对她进行的那种言语攻击和威胁是绝对不可原谅的。但重要的是，她要明白，迈克尔对她的批评以及他对她所谓缺点的愤怒与她无关，尽管很难不往心里去。当莉兹忍无可忍，威胁要离开他时，惩罚达到了顶峰。他害怕失去她，这点燃了莉兹早已见识过他积压已久的挫败感。

If Michael had had the ability to express what he was feeling, he might have told her: “Please don’t take my dreams away again. I’ve been disappointed, hurt and deprived since I was a teenager, and I never really got what I wanted. No one cared about me, and that really hurts. How could my parents have destroyed everything I loved and forced me into this job I hate? And now you want to leave? I can’t stand to see this happen again. How much disappointment do you think I can handle?”

如果迈克尔能够表达自己的感受，他或许会告诉她：“求你别再夺走我的梦想了。从青少年时期起，我就饱受失望、伤害和剥夺，我从未真正得到过自己想要的东西。没有人关心我，这真的让我很痛苦。我的父母怎么能毁掉我所爱的一切，强迫我做这份我讨厌的工作？现在你又要离开？我无法忍受这一切再次发生。你觉得我能承受多少失望？”

That’s a speech full of emotions that rightfully deserve to be directed at his parents, but having been controlled by them all his life, he’s never felt safe or strong enough to make it. All the sadness and anger that Michael had stuffed didn’t disappear. It blew up into his life. He confused Liz, whom he loved, with the parents he had grown to resent.

那番话饱含深情，理应倾诉给他的父母，但由于一生都被他们掌控，他从未感到安全，也从未强大到足以表达出来。迈克尔压抑已久的悲伤和愤怒并没有消失，反而爆发了出来。他把深爱的莉兹和自己日渐怨恨的父母混淆了。

MAINTAINING A STRONG CONNECTION

保持紧密联系

Odd as it seems, punishment keeps a blackmailer in a strong emotional connection with you. In creating a highly charged atmosphere, blackmailers know they are activating the target’s feelings for them, and even if the feelings are negative, they’ve created a tight bond. You may resent or even hate the blackmailer, but as long as your focus is on them, they haven’t been abandoned or discarded with indifference. Punishment keeps a lot of passion and heat in a fractured relationship.

听起来或许很奇怪，但惩罚确实能让勒索者与你保持强烈的情感联系。勒索者通过营造紧张的气氛，知道他们正在激发目标对象对他们的感情，即使这种感情是负面的，他们也已经建立起了一种牢固的纽带。你或许会怨恨甚至憎恨勒索者，但只要你关注着他们，他们就不会被你冷落或抛弃。惩罚能让一段破裂的关系保持激情和活力。

Allen’s ex-wife, Beverly, continued to punish him in the most painful way possible—by using their children as a weapon. Allen and Beverly had had an acrimonious divorce. Even though their marriage had been a source of unhappiness and stress for both of them, it was a divorce that he wanted and she didn’t. And Beverly fought him tooth and nail. They had made a few attempts to reconcile, and even tried counseling, but to no avail.

艾伦的前妻贝弗莉继续用最痛苦的方式惩罚他——利用他们的孩子作为武器。艾伦和贝弗莉的离婚闹得沸沸扬扬。尽管他们的婚姻给两人都带来了痛苦和压力，但离婚是艾伦想要的，而贝弗莉却不肯。贝弗莉拼死抵抗。他们曾多次尝试和好，甚至接受过婚姻咨询，但都无济于事。

She knew what those kids mean to me. I don’t think a lot of people really understand what it’s like for a man not to be able to be with his kids every day, especially while they’re growing up. I had to divorce Beverly, but I didn’t want to divorce my kids. At first she threatened that if I left her I’d never see them again. She’d move out of the state, maybe even out of the country. I was panicked. I couldn’t think straight. I’ve known women who’ve done that — hell, I’ve known men who’ve done it to their ex-wives.

她知道那些孩子对我有多重要。我觉得很多人并不真正理解一个男人不能每天陪伴孩子是什么滋味，尤其是在他们成长的过程中。我不得不和贝弗莉离婚，但我不想和孩子们断绝关系。起初她威胁我说，如果我离开她，我就再也见不到孩子们了。她会搬到外州，甚至可能搬到国外。我当时慌了，脑子一片混乱。我认识一些女人这样做过——说实话，我也认识一些男人这样对待他们的前妻。

Everyone finally settled down, and ultimately Allen was given liberal visitation rights. He and Beverly managed to be civil to each other, and she honored the court order. But his remarriage to Jo started the blackmail up again.

一切最终平静下来，艾伦也获得了较为宽松的探视权。他和贝弗莉勉强维持着礼貌的关系，贝弗莉也遵守了法院的判决。但他与乔的再婚又引发了勒索。

Now that I’ve got someone I really care about in my life, she can’t stand it. I guess as long as I was single she figured there was still a chance. I know she’s still pretty bitter. So she’s getting back at me again through the kids. If I’m ten minutes late picking them up, she’ll have taken them out somewhere. It’s almost an hour’s drive to where they live, and I can’t always get there on the dot. Last week I had to wait almost an hour and a half. When she pulled into the driveway she said, “I’m not going to wait around for you. How did I know you’d even show up?” She expects me to take it and not complain. But if I need to reschedule something, she goes ballistic. And if the child-support payments are a day late, she’s on the phone threatening to take me back to court to get my visitation reduced. Christ, we’re talking more now than we did when we were married!

现在我生命中有了真正爱的人，她就受不了了。我猜只要我还是单身，她就觉得还有机会。我知道她现在还耿耿于怀。所以她又开始利用孩子来报复我了。如果我接孩子晚了十分钟，她就会带他们出去玩。去他们家开车要将近一个小时，我不可能每次都准时到。上周我等了将近一个半小时。她把车开进车道时说：“我才不会等你呢。我怎么知道你会来？”她希望我忍气吞声，不抱怨。但如果我需要改期，她就会大发雷霆。如果抚养费晚交一天，她就会打电话威胁要告我，减少我的探视时间。天哪，我们现在说话比结婚时还多！

Allen’s ex clearly hasn’t let go of him or the marriage. And like many divorced blackmailers, both women and men, she’s using the most powerful weapon in her arsenal—their children—to keep an emotional connection with him. Allen and Beverly are legally divorced, but the psychological divorce is still pending.

艾伦的前妻显然没有放下他，也没有放下这段婚姻。和许多离异的勒索者一样，无论男女，她都在利用自己最强大的武器——孩子——来维系与艾伦的情感联系。艾伦和贝弗莉在法律上已经离婚，但心理上的“离婚”尚未结束。

The use of children as a weapon against the noncustodial parent is one of the oldest and cruelest forms of emotional blackmail. There are no higher stakes. It’s especially effective because of the intensity of the emotions involved. It keeps people who once cared about each other locked in a terrible battle in which everyone loses.

利用孩子作为武器来对付非监护方父母，是最古老、最残酷的情感勒索手段之一。没有比这更危险的了。这种手段之所以如此有效，正是因为其中牵涉到强烈的情感。它让曾经彼此关爱的人陷入一场可怕的争斗，最终所有人都是输家。

IT’S NOT ABOUT YOU

这跟你无关。

The most important thing to take away from our tour of the blackmailer’s psyche is that emotional blackmail sounds like it’s all about you and feels like it’s all about you, but for the most part it’s not about you at all. Instead, it flows from and tries to stabilize some fairly insecure places inside the blackmailer. Much of the blaming, spin and self-righteousness that have made us feel so bad about ourselves—often bad enough to give in to the blackmailer’s pressure—is not valid. It’s fear-based. Anxiety-based. Insecurity-based. And those fears, anxieties and insecurities reside inside the blackmailer. Many times emotional blackmail has more to do with the past than with the present, and it’s more concerned with filling the blackmailer’s needs than with anything the blackmailer says we did or didn’t do.

从我们对勒索者心理的剖析中，最重要的一点是：情感勒索听起来好像一切都与你有关，感觉也好像一切都与你有关，但实际上，它大多与你无关。相反，它源于勒索者内心深处一些相当不安全的地方，并试图以此来稳定这些地方。很多让我们自我感觉糟糕的指责、歪曲事实和自以为是——这些糟糕到足以让我们屈服于勒索者的压力——都是站不住脚的。它们源于恐惧、焦虑和不安全感。而这些恐惧、焦虑和不安全感，恰恰存在于勒索者的内心深处。很多时候，情感勒索更多地与过去有关，而非与现在有关；它更关注的是满足勒索者的需求，而不是勒索者所说的我们做了什么或没做什么。

That’s not to say we don’t play a pivotal role in the blackmail process. After all, it couldn’t happen without our compliance. Now it’s time examine the factors inside us that allow blackmail to take hold.

这并非意味着我们在勒索过程中不扮演关键角色。毕竟，没有我们的配合，勒索根本不可能发生。现在是时候审视一下我们自身哪些因素使得勒索有机可乘了。

# ↩

6

It Takes Two

需要两个人

Blackmail takes two. It’s a duet, not a solo performance, and it cannot work without the target’s active participation.

勒索需要双方配合。这是一场双人合作，而不是单打独斗，而且没有目标对象的积极参与，勒索就无法成功。

I know that often that’s not how it feels, and I know how natural it is to become defensive about our own behavior. It’s always more comfortable to concentrate on what the other person is doing rather than to acknowledge what we bring to the table. But in order to break up the blackmail partnership, you’ll have to turn your attention inward and look at the elements that have led you, often unknowingly, to participate in emotional blackmail.

我知道很多时候并非如此，我也知道为自己的行为感到防卫是多么自然。我们总是更倾向于关注对方的所作所为，而不是反思自身的不足。但要想打破这种勒索关系，你必须反省自身，审视那些常常让你在不知不觉中卷入情感勒索的因素。

Please remember that when I talk about participating in blackmail, I’m not suggesting that you provoke or cause it, but rather that you give it permission to occur. You may not even realize that someone’s demands are unreasonable. It may seem that you’re just being a good wife or a good employee or a good son or daughter—accepting another person’s preferences almost unquestioningly because you’ve been taught that’s what you’re supposed to do.

请记住，我所说的参与勒索，并非指你挑起或促成勒索，而是指你默许勒索的发生。你甚至可能没有意识到别人的要求是不合理的。你或许觉得自己只是在做一个好妻子、好员工、好儿子或好女儿——几乎不加质疑地接受他人的意愿，因为你从小就被教导应该这样做。

Or you may be well aware of the blackmail but feel as though you can’t resist it, because the blackmailer’s pressure sets off almost programmed responses in you, and you’re reacting automatically or impulsively. Keep in mind that not everyone responds to blackmail attempts with compliance. If you do, I want to help you get a handle on how and why. As a start, please think about and answer the following questions.

或许你很清楚对方是在勒索，但却感觉无法抗拒，因为勒索者的压力触发了你几乎是本能的反应，让你不由自主地、冲动地做出反应。请记住，并非所有人都会对勒索行为屈服。如果你屈服了，我想帮助你了解其中的原因和过程。首先，请思考并回答以下问题。

When faced with blackmailers’ pressure do you:

面对勒索者的压力，你会怎么做？

  • Constantly berate yourself for giving in to their demands?
    你是否因为屈从于他们的要求而不断自责？
  • Often feel frustrated and resentful?
    经常感到沮丧和怨恨吗？
  • Feel guilty and believe that you’re a bad person if you don’t give in?
    如果不屈服，你会感到内疚，觉得自己是个坏人吗？
  • Fear that the relationship will fall apart if you don’t give in?
    害怕如果不让步，这段关系就会破裂？
  • Become the only one they turn to in a crisis, even though there are others who could help?
    在危机时刻，即使有其他人可以提供帮助，你却成为他们唯一求助的对象？
  • Believe the obligation you have to them is greater than the one to yourself?
    你是否认为你对他们的义务大于你对自己的义务？

If you answered yes to even one of these questions, your responses to pressure are helping to create an ideal climate for blackmail.

如果你对以上任何一个问题的回答是肯定的，那么你对压力的回应就助长了勒索的滋生。

HOT BUTTONS

热点话题

Why is it that some people, no matter how smart or together they are, seem to be so vulnerable to emotional blackmail, while others can brush it off? The answer lies in our hot buttons, the sensitive bundles of emotional nerves that form inside all of us. Each hot button is like a power cell charged with our unfinished psychological business—stored-up resentments, guilt, insecurities and vulnerabilities. These are our soft spots, shaped by our basic temperament and sensitivities along with our experiences from the time we were little. Each spot, if probed, would reveal vivid layers of our personal history—how we were treated, what self-image we carry inside and how we’ve been marked by impressions from our past.

为什么有些人，无论多么聪明或成熟，似乎都极易受到情感勒索，而有些人却能轻松应对？答案就在于我们的“敏感点”，也就是我们每个人内心深处那些敏感的情感神经束。每个“敏感点”都像一个能量电池，储存着我们未完成的心理问题——积压的怨恨、内疚、不安全感和脆弱。这些是我们脆弱的弱点，由我们的基本性格和敏感性，以及童年经历塑造而成。如果深入探究，每个弱点都会揭示我们个人历史的鲜活层面——我们曾遭受的对待，我们内心深处的自我认知，以及过往经历如何在我们身上留下印记。

The feelings and memories stored in our hot buttons can be searing, and when events in our current lives remind us of something we’ve kept buried inside, they can bring up reactions that override thought or logic, tapping pure emotion that has been stored and gaining power for a long time.

我们内心深处的情感和记忆可能非常强烈，当当前生活中的事件让我们想起一些我们一直深埋心底的事情时，它们会引发超越思考或逻辑的反应，激发出长期储存并积聚力量的纯粹情感。

We may not always remember the incidents that led to the formation of our hot buttons, and when it comes to the complexities of why we do the things we do, cause and effect can be elusive. But if you’ve ever wondered where “stuffed” feelings and experiences go, your hot buttons are a good place to look.

我们可能并不总是记得导致我们情绪敏感点形成的那些事件，而且当我们谈到我们行为背后的复杂原因时，因果关系往往难以捉摸。但如果你曾经好奇那些“压抑”的情绪和经历最终去了哪里，那么你的情绪敏感点或许是一个很好的切入点。

Providing a Map for the Blackmailer

为勒索者提供地图

Over the years our emotional landscape may become studded with these hot buttons, and many of us design portions of our lives to navigate around them. In fact, the most common strategy for people attempting to deal with these hot areas can be summed up in four words: avoid at all costs. We may not realize what we’re doing, but as we take this path of avoidance, we reveal ourselves more clearly than we know. As we tiptoe around our hot buttons, we’re practically drawing a map of where they are, which those who know us well can’t fail to see.

多年来，我们的情感世界可能会布满这些敏感点，许多人都会刻意安排生活中的某些部分来避开它们。事实上，人们应对这些敏感点最常见的策略可以用四个字概括：不惜一切代价地回避。我们或许没有意识到自己在做什么，但当我们选择回避时，我们反而比自己意识到的更清晰地暴露了自己。当我们小心翼翼地避开这些敏感点时，实际上就是在绘制它们的分布图，而那些真正了解我们的人一眼就能看穿。

We all know what the people around us are sensitive to; it’s no secret when a friend is afraid of anger or tends to soak up blame. But for the most part, we’re fairly compassionate and don’t use that knowledge to our own ends. When our blackmailers are feeling safe, they don’t either. But faced with resistance, their fears of deprivation flare up. They drop the compassion and use every bit of information they have about us to ensure that they prevail.

我们都知道身边的人对什么敏感；朋友害怕生气或者总是替别人背锅，这都不是什么秘密。但大多数情况下，我们都相当有同情心，不会利用这些了解来达到自己的目的。勒索者感到安全的时候，他们自己也不会。但一旦遇到反抗，他们害怕失去的恐惧就会爆发。他们会抛弃同情心，利用一切掌握的信息来确保自己得逞。

THE TRAITS THAT MAKE US VULNERABLE TO BLACKMAIL

使我们容易受到勒索的特质

To insulate ourselves against having our hot buttons activated, we develop a number of specific personality traits. They’re so much a part of us that it may not be apparent at first that they’re defenses against what we fear. But as we look at them more closely, you’ll see that all are deeply related to our hot buttons. Ironically, it is these “protective” qualities that open us up to emotional blackmail. They are:

为了避免触及我们的敏感点，我们发展出一些特定的性格特征。这些特征如此根深蒂固，以至于我们一开始可能不会意识到它们是我们抵御恐惧的防御机制。但当我们仔细观察这些特征时，就会发现它们都与我们的敏感点密切相关。讽刺的是，正是这些“保护性”特质让我们更容易受到情感勒索。这些特质包括：

  • An excessive need for approval
    对审批的过度需求
  • An intense fear of anger
    对愤怒的强烈恐惧
  • A need for peace at any price
    不惜一切代价追求和平。
  • A tendency to take too much responsibility for other people’s lives
    一种倾向于承担他人生活过多责任的倾向
  • A high level of self-doubt
    高度的自我怀疑

None of these traits is harmful—in moderation. In fact, some are viewed as positive, and even rewarded, when they’re not taken to extremes. But when they control us and go to war with the intelligent, confident, assertive and thoughtful parts of ourselves, we’re setting ourselves up for major manipulation.

这些特质本身并无害处——只要适度即可。事实上，有些特质如果运用得当，甚至会被视为积极的，并带来益处。但当它们控制我们，与我们自身聪明、自信、果断和深思熟虑的部分对抗时，我们就很容易被他人操控。

As we examine these traits and the behavioral styles they give rise to, notice how much of the target’s behavior is actually a response to feelings from the past. Notice, too, how often targets are betrayed by the very responses they believe will protect them.

当我们审视这些特质及其所导致的心理行为模式时，请注意，受害者的很多行为实际上是对过往情感的一种回应。还要注意的是，受害者往往被他们自认为能够保护自己的那些回应方式所背叛。

THE APPROVAL JUNKIE

渴望认可的人

It’s perfectly normal to want the people we care about to approve of us—we all want their goodwill. But when we must have it, and it becomes a drug we cannot do without, we aim a spotlight at a hot button that a blackmailer can easily zero in on.

我们都希望得到身边人的认可，这完全正常——我们都渴望他们的好感。但当我们非要得到认可不可，它变成一种无法割舍的瘾时，我们就触及了一个敏感点，而勒索者很容易就能找到这个弱点。

In the introduction, I talked about my client Sarah, who constantly had to prove herself to her boyfriend Frank. Each time she passed one of his tests, she basked in the glow of his approval. But each time she protested, he took it away, and she felt miserable. So she tried to maintain an uninterrupted flow of approval by giving in to his pressure—even when what he wanted went against the grain for her.

在引言中，我提到了我的客户莎拉，她总是需要向男友弗兰克证明自己。每次她通过他的考验，都会沉浸在他的认可之中。但每次她提出异议，他就会收回这份认可，让她感到痛苦不堪。所以，为了维持源源不断的认可，她只能屈服于他的压力——即使他想要的与她的意愿背道而驰。

I can’t stand it when he’s upset with me. When I said that painting the cabin was not how I had expected to spend the weekend, he just shook his head and went out on the porch. I followed him out there, and he said he couldn’t believe how spoiled and infantile I was being. I felt scared, and really shaky. So I went in and put on some old clothes and grabbed a brush. Then I got that great smile of his and a hug, and I could breathe again.

我受不了他生我气的样子。我说粉刷小木屋并不是我原本计划的周末安排，他只是摇了摇头，走到门廊上去了。我跟着他出去，他说他简直不敢相信我竟然这么任性幼稚。我当时很害怕，浑身发抖。于是我回到屋里，换上旧衣服，拿起刷子。然后，他露出了灿烂的笑容，给了我一个拥抱，我才终于松了一口气。

She’d gotten her “fix.” There’s nothing wrong with wanting approval, or asking for it. But approval junkies need a constant supply, and judge that they’ve failed if they can’t get it. They believe they’re not OK unless someone else says they are, and their sense of security depends almost entirely on outside validation. The approval junkie’s motto is “If I’m not getting approval, I’ve done something wrong.” Or worse yet, “If I’m not getting approval there’s something wrong with me.”

她已经得到了“满足”。渴望获得认可，或者主动寻求认可，这本身并没有错。但“认可成瘾者”需要源源不断的认可，如果得不到认可，他们就觉得自己失败了。除非别人肯定他们，否则他们觉得自己不够好，他们的安全感几乎完全依赖于外界的认可。“认可成瘾者”的座右铭是：“如果我得不到认可，那肯定是我做错了什么。”或者更糟糕的是，“如果我得不到认可，那肯定是我自身有问题。”

Sarah’s description of how devastated she felt when Frank was upset with her indicated a driving need for approval and a terror of what would happen if she didn’t regain it. This fear directly parallels that of a young child. In the child’s fantasy, the consequences of losing approval are catastrophic. “I did something Daddy (or Mommy) didn’t like. Daddy’s upset with me. Daddy doesn’t love me anymore. Maybe Daddy will get rid of me. I’ll be alone and I’ll die.”

萨拉描述弗兰克生她气时她有多么难过，这表明她极度渴望得到认可，并且害怕如果得不到认可会发生什么。这种恐惧与幼童的恐惧如出一辙。在孩子的幻想中，失去认可的后果是灾难性的。“我做了爸爸（或妈妈）不喜欢的事。爸爸生我的气了。爸爸不再爱我了。也许爸爸会抛弃我。我会孤零零地死去。”

Sarah discovered that her tendency to link approval with survival came not so much from her parents but from her grandmother, who had taken care of her while they worked.

莎拉发现，她将获得认可与生存联系起来的倾向，与其说是来自她的父母，不如说是来自她的祖母，祖母在她父母工作时照顾她。

God, she was formidable! She lived in a downstairs apartment my parents had set up for her, and that’s where I went every day after school. She was always critical—she told me I was too loud and that I was lazy. She said God didn’t like lazy girls, and sometimes they got sent away. I don’t think she meant to be mean, and I’m sure somebody told her something ridiculous like that when she was little. But it scared the hell out of me. She taught me a rhyme that I don’t think I ever put out of my mind. “Good, better, best. / Never let it rest, / Until good is better / And better is best.”

天哪，她真是个厉害角色！她住在我父母给她安排的楼下公寓里，我每天放学都去她家。她总是很挑剔——说我太吵闹，说我懒惰。她说上帝不喜欢懒惰的女孩，有时候她们会被赶走。我觉得她不是故意要伤害我，而且我肯定她小时候也听过类似荒唐的话。但这真的把我吓坏了。她教了我一首童谣，我至今都忘不了：“好，更好，最好。/永不停歇，/直到好变成更好，/更好变成最好。”

Sarah learned many lessons from her grandmother, whom she adored and with whom she spent many hours in her formative years. Some have worked well for her, others less well. She learned that if she behaved in a way that got her grandmother’s approval, she was a good girl, and therefore safe. But she also learned that what she did was never quite good enough for her perfectionistic grandma, and that the elusive “best” was always just out of reach.

莎拉从她敬爱的祖母那里学到了很多东西，在她成长的岁月里，她和祖母一起度过了许多时光。有些方法对她很有效，有些则不然。她明白，如果她的行为能得到祖母的认可，她就是个好女孩，因此也很安全。但她也明白，她所做的一切永远都无法让完美主义的祖母满意，而那遥不可及的“最好”总是近在咫尺。

The feelings that Sarah describes with Frank—her compulsion to please and a fear of disapproval that seem almost to take on a life of their own—are familiar to all approval junkies, and a sure sign that someone has pressed a hot button.

莎拉对弗兰克的描述——她渴望取悦他人，害怕被他人否定，这种感觉几乎有了自己的生命——对于所有渴望得到认可的人来说都很熟悉，而且这无疑是有人触碰到了他们的敏感点的迹象。

When we’re little, we need the approval of the powerful giants who care for us, and the ghosts of that need can haunt us long after we learn to take care of ourselves. In the home where Sarah had grown up, love was given and withdrawn based on how she “performed,” and she developed a voracious need for someone else’s OK. Frank tapped into that need when he withheld his “applause” and affection. Sarah knew intellectually that she couldn’t please everyone 100 percent of the time—but she felt she had to try.

小时候，我们需要那些照顾我们的大人的认可，这种需求的阴影会在我们学会照顾自己之后依然挥之不去。在莎拉长大的家庭里，爱的给予和收回都取决于她的“表现”，这让她对别人的认可产生了强烈的渴求。弗兰克正是利用了她的这种需求，他拒绝给予她“赞赏”和关爱。莎拉理智上明白自己不可能永远让每个人都满意——但她觉得自己必须尽力而为。

Sarah was primarily focused on Frank’s approval. Maria, who was trying to withstand her husband’s pressure to stay in their marriage even after she’d learned he was seeing other women, found herself dominated by a somewhat different concern: What will people think?

萨拉主要关注的是弗兰克的认可。玛丽亚在得知丈夫与其他女人交往后，努力抵制丈夫让她维持婚姻的压力，但她却发现自己被另一种略有不同的担忧所主导：别人会怎么想？

Divorce is not done in my family, or among the people I’m closest to. If that sounds old-fashioned, well, it is. I’m old-fashioned, and I’m proud of it. I can’t stand the idea that I can’t make this marriage work. And I can’t begin to think about what would happen if I decided to leave Jay. What will people think? My life will fall apart at the seams. My parents will be upset with me, and his parents, and my kids, and my minister. They’ll think I didn’t have the guts to hang in there and fight for my marriage.

在我的家庭里，在我最亲近的人当中，离婚是不可接受的。如果这听起来很老派，那确实如此。我就是老派，而且我为此感到自豪。我无法忍受这段婚姻无法维系的想法。我甚至不敢想象，如果我决定离开杰伊，会发生什么。人们会怎么想？我的生活会彻底崩溃。我的父母会生我的气，他的父母会生我的气，我的孩子会生我的气，我的牧师也会生我的气。他们会觉得我没有勇气坚持下去，没有勇气去挽救我的婚姻。

As Maria made her best case for remaining with Jay, it seemed that the weight of family tradition, history and community was pressing upon her, and she was sure that she had no choice but to stay. She was certain that she would be abandoning her principles if she considered a divorce. But as we worked together, Maria began to realize that the beliefs she held so strongly had been imposed on her—the ideas she defended so fiercely weren’t even her own—and her definition of what makes a good family or a good marriage was far broader and deeper than “one that stays together no matter what.”

当玛丽亚竭尽全力争取和杰伊继续在一起时，似乎家庭传统、历史和社区的重担压在她身上，她确信自己别无选择，只能留下。她确信，如果考虑离婚，就等于背弃了自己的原则。但随着我们一起努力，玛丽亚开始意识到，她如此坚定的信念其实是被强加的——她如此激烈地捍卫的那些想法甚至都不是她自己的——而她对美好家庭或美满婚姻的定义，远比“无论如何都要在一起”要宽广深刻得多。

For Maria, this discovery felt liberating, yet she was reluctant to explore or express the genuine beliefs she was uncovering in herself because she so needed to maintain the approval of her relatives, friends and church community. This woman, who held down a good job, ran a household, raised two terrific kids and managed an active church and social life, became a helpless child when she imagined the disapproval of people she cared about. As we dug for the roots of her approval hunger, a process that took many weeks, Maria remembered what she had always thought of as a “minor incident” that had taken place when she was a junior in high school.

对玛丽亚来说，这一发现让她感到解脱，但她却不愿探索或表达自己内心深处的真实想法，因为她太需要获得亲戚、朋友和教会的认可。这位拥有体面工作、操持家务、养育两个优秀孩子、同时兼顾教会和社交生活的女性，一旦想到自己在乎的人会不认可她，就会变得像个无助的孩子。在我们深入挖掘她渴望被认可的根源时——这个过程持续了数周——玛丽亚想起了一件她一直认为是“小事”的事情，那件事发生在她高二的时候。

I’d always been a Goody Two-shoes, but one day toward the end of the school year, my boyfriend, Danny, who was the love of my life, said no one would even know if we skipped last period and went to the beach. So we did, and I put it out of my mind. But a couple of days later, my father started asking me if I had anything I wanted to tell him. When I said I couldn’t think of anything, he said he couldn’t believe a daughter of his would lie to him, so he’d ask me again. Did I have anything to tell him?

我一直是个乖乖女，但学年快结束的时候，我的男朋友丹尼——我生命中最爱的人——说，如果我们翘掉最后一节课去海滩，没人会知道。于是我们就去了，我也把这件事抛在了脑后。但几天后，我父亲开始问我有没有什么想告诉他的。我说我想不出什么，他说他不敢相信自己的女儿会骗他，所以他要再问我一次。我到底有什么要告诉他的吗？

My heart started pounding, but I couldn’t confess. I just kept still. Then, in a very quiet tone of voice, Daddy told me that the school had called, and he knew what I’d done. I’d embarrassed him and our family, and I’d have to apologize to everyone at dinner that night and prepare a lesson for his adult Sunday school class that week on why it’s important to tell the truth.

我的心开始狂跳，但我说不出话来。我只是一动不动。然后，爸爸用很轻的声音告诉我，学校打电话来了，他知道我做了什么。我让他和我们全家都丢脸了，那天晚上吃饭的时候我得向所有人道歉，而且下周还要为他成人主日学班准备一堂课，讲讲为什么说真话很重要。

I was mortified. I did what he said, but I’ll never forget the humiliation and the sense of isolation I felt. It was like I’d been branded with a scarlet letter L for liar, and I felt as though no one treated me the same for weeks after that. That may be the last time I ever really stepped out of line.

我当时羞愧难当。我照他说的做了，但我永远也忘不了那种屈辱和孤立无援的感觉。就好像我被烙上了“骗子”的耻辱印记，之后好几个星期，感觉没人像以前那样对待我。那或许是我最后一次真正越轨了。

The well-intentioned attempt to show Maria the consequences of skipping school and violating the rules of the school and her family registered as:

出于好意，想让玛丽亚明白逃学和违反学校及家庭规定的后果，但结果却令人失望：

The support I have from my family and community is fragile. It can be withdrawn in a moment if I don’t please them. I have to earn their approval.

我从家人和社区得到的支持很脆弱。如果我不能让他们满意，他们随时都可能撤回这份支持。我必须赢得他们的认可。

This was not the intended or the appropriate message, yet it’s what Maria carried through her life, measuring her success by the approval of others. Before she could consider standing up to Jay’s pressure, she had to unlearn the lesson—now more than three decades old—that did not serve her and change her repertoire of responses to other people’s disapproval.

这并非玛丽亚的本意，也不恰当，但她却一直秉持着这种观念，以他人的认可来衡量自己的成功。在能够反抗杰的压力之前，她必须先摒弃这个三十多年前就已根深蒂固的错误观念，并改变自己应对他人批评的方式。

The most sensitive of approval junkies are reluctant to take any action that might be in their own best interests if they’d risk incurring anyone’s disdain. Eve, for example, could hardly stand a frown from a store clerk and, as most of us have done on occasion, would agree to keep items she’d gone to return if the person behind the counter made her feel guilty about it. She couldn’t risk even a stranger’s disapproval.

那些极度渴望被认可的人，即使采取任何可能对自己有利的行动，也不愿冒着招致他人鄙视的风险。例如，伊芙几乎无法忍受店员的皱眉，而且就像我们大多数人偶尔都会做的那样，如果柜台后面的人让她感到内疚，她甚至会同意留下原本打算退货的商品。她连陌生人的不满都承受不起。

THE ANGER AVOIDER/PEACEMAKER

避免愤怒/和平缔造者

Many of us live as though there were an 11th Commandment—“Thou shalt not get angry”—and a 12th—“Thou shalt not get other people angry with you.” At the first sign of disagreement, many of us jump to make peace, putting out the fire we fear will blaze out of control.

我们许多人的生活方式仿佛还有第十一条诫命——“不可动怒”——以及第十二条诫命——“不可使别人生你的气”。一旦出现分歧，我们许多人便急于求成，试图扑灭我们害怕会失控的怒火。

The peacemakers’ desire to provide a measure of calm and rationality in difficult situations can be problematic when it becomes a rigid belief that nothing is worse than a fight. That makes them afraid to argue, even with a friend, fearing that the relationship will break irreparably in two. After all, they tell themselves, surrender is a temporary concession to achieve a greater good.

和平缔造者希望在困境中带来一丝平静和理性，但如果他们固执地认为争吵是最糟糕的，那就可能适得其反。这让他们害怕争论，即使是和朋友争论，也担心关系会彻底破裂。毕竟，他们会告诉自己，妥协只是为了实现更大利益而做出的暂时让步。

The Voice of Reason

理性之声

Liz, who is grappling with the punishing blackmail of her husband, Michael, has the soothing voice of a late-night FM DJ and a manner so placid that it’s hard for someone who doesn’t know her to see that she’s upset. When I remarked on that, she laughed.

莉兹正饱受丈夫迈克尔的勒索之苦，她有着深夜电台DJ般温柔的嗓音，举止也十分平静，以至于不认识她的人很难看出她内心的痛苦。当我提到这一点时，她笑了。

Oh, that’s my camouflage. When I was a kid I realized watching my brothers and sisters that the ones who yelled back at my mom when she was raging got hit or punished, and the ones who didn’t got ignored. I think I must’ve figured out that you can calm people like you can calm an animal, just by stroking them and talking to them in a gentle way, never getting upset. On my job evaluations they always used to say things like “unflappable” and “great under pressure,” and I feel like I have this real talent for defusing tension—like the bomb squad. I like that about myself. For one thing, it makes me totally unafraid of anger, because I know I can handle it and keep it from getting out of control.

哦，这就是我的伪装。小时候，我看着我的兄弟姐妹们，发现那些在妈妈发火时顶嘴的孩子会被打或惩罚，而那些不顶嘴的孩子则会被忽略。我想我一定是领悟到了，安抚人就像安抚动物一样，只要温柔地抚摸他们，轻声细语地和他们说话，自己不要生气。在我的工作评估中，他们总是会提到“沉着冷静”、“抗压能力强”之类的评价，我觉得自己确实有化解紧张气氛的天赋——就像拆弹小组一样。我喜欢自己这一点。首先，这让我完全不害怕生气，因为我知道自己能够控制它，不让它失控。

When Liz described herself this way, she was pretty convincing because “calming,” “soothing,” “unflappable” and “great under pressure” had become part of her self-definition. They’re qualities she seemed to radiate. But obviously her situation with Michael was far from calm.

莉兹这样描述自己时，确实很有说服力，因为“冷静”、“抚慰人心”、“沉着冷静”和“抗压能力强”已经成为她自我定义的一部分。这些特质似乎由内而外地散发出来。但显然，她和迈克尔之间的关系远非平静。

I think I fell in love with Michael because he and I are so different. He’s outgoing and energetic and direct—he has a real passionate side, a lot of fire. And I’m softer, more in the background. I guess I always knew that he might have a temper, but I never saw it for the longest time, and like I said, I know how to handle anger. That sounds ridiculous, doesn’t it? Here I’m married to this raging maniac who threatens me, and I’m scared out of my mind of him and I’m saying I can handle anger. Well, I thought I could. And then it all spun out of control, and so did I. Everything I did, all the stroking and soothing and apologizing, seemed to make him madder. I don’t get it. What went wrong?

我想我爱上迈克尔是因为我们性格迥异。他外向、精力充沛、直率——他热情似火，充满活力。而我则比较温柔，更倾向于默默无闻。我想我一直都知道他脾气可能不太好，但很长一段时间我都没亲眼见过。而且就像我说的，我知道如何控制自己的怒气。听起来很荒谬，不是吗？我嫁给了这样一个暴躁易怒、威胁我的疯子，我害怕得要命，却还说自己能控制怒气。好吧，我当时是这么认为的。然后一切都失控了，我也失控了。我做的所有事，所有的安慰、抚慰和道歉，似乎都让他更加生气。我不明白。到底哪里出了问题？

Liz had spent most of her life refining a style of relating to people that seemed to work for her, one that is highly valued—our volatile society respects people who can rein in tempers. Her soothing voice, manner and approach had been so successful at defusing anger that she erroneously saw herself as a person who didn’t fear anger at all—because she knew how to neutralize it. She believed for a long time that if she could just keep the peace, Michael would be nice and she’d be able to reason things out with him. There’s no reason to get upset, she told herself. And even when he demonstrated that he was a bully, she resorted to reason, her time-tested tool.

莉兹一生都在努力磨练一套与人相处的技巧，这套技巧似乎对她行之有效，而且备受推崇——在我们这个动荡的社会里，能够控制脾气的人总是受到尊重。她温和的语气、举止和方法在化解怒火方面如此成功，以至于她错误地认为自己根本不惧怕愤怒——因为她知道如何化解它。她一直坚信，只要能维持表面的和平，迈克尔就会和蔼可亲，她就能和他讲道理。她告诉自己，没有理由生气。即使他表现出欺凌弱小的一面，她也依然诉诸理性，这是她屡试不爽的法宝。

When her well-honed techniques didn’t work on him, she felt defenseless and increasingly frustrated. Confronting his escalating pressure and threats had activated a hot button she didn’t think was still there, which had its genesis in a childhood full of anger and conflict. As a child she had resolved: “Don’t make an angry person angrier. Calm them down or they’ll hurt you, or worse, leave you. Don’t be the one who upsets them.” This decision dramatically limited the options available to Liz, and she’d never learned to express her own anger in an appropriate way. When her calming techniques failed, and she wound up unleashing her own stores of rage and frustration, a crisis quickly mounted.

当她精心磨练的技巧对他失效时，她感到无助，也越来越沮丧。面对他不断升级的压力和威胁，她内心深处一个她以为早已消失的敏感点被激活了，而这个敏感点源于她充满愤怒和冲突的童年。小时候，她就下定决心：“不要让生气的人更生气。要让他们冷静下来，否则他们会伤害你，甚至更糟，离开你。不要成为惹他们生气的那个人。”这个决定极大地限制了莉兹的选择，她也从未学会如何恰当地表达自己的愤怒。当她的安抚技巧失效，最终只能释放自己积压的愤怒和挫败感时，一场危机迅速爆发。

Until she revisited her fear of anger and broadened the ways in which she allowed herself to respond to it, she would always be vulnerable to blackmailers like Michael and startling eruptions of her own pressurized emotions.

除非她重新审视自己对愤怒的恐惧，并拓宽自己应对愤怒的方式，否则她将始终容易受到像迈克尔这样的勒索者的伤害，以及自己被压抑的情绪突然爆发的威胁。

The Other Face of Anger

愤怒的另一面

My client Helen, the literature professor we met in Chapter 1 , thought that she’d found the perfect man in her boyfriend Jim. She knows she’s sensitive to anger, and that’s shaped her thinking about the kinds of people, especially romantic partners, she’d like to be around.

我的客户海伦，也就是我们在第一章中遇到的那位文学教授，她认为她的男友吉姆就是她心目中的完美伴侣。她知道自己对愤怒很敏感，这影响了她对理想伴侣，尤其是恋爱对象的看法。

I wouldn’t ever consider seeing a man who raised his voice to me. My mom and dad gave me my fill of that when I was growing up. Pop’s a rebel, which made him exactly the wrong kind of guy to choose a career in the military. He couldn’t get promoted to save his life, so he wasn’t much more than a file clerk for 20 years. He couldn’t stand seeing stupid jerks—his words—being promoted over him just because they were good at conforming, and he was frustrated. He’d come home and yell at Mom, and she’d yell back, and they’d slam doors, bang pots and pans around in the kitchen—it was pretty scary for us kids. I knew nothing was going to happen, but my brother would run into his room and start to cry, and we’d push his bed against the door for protection—so the screamers couldn’t come in, I guess. When it got really bad, Dad would storm off and stay away for a couple of days. It was no big trauma, but you know, I don’t need that kind of drama in my life anymore. Been there. Done that. It really turns me off.

我绝对不会考虑见一个对我大声吼叫的男人。我爸妈在我成长过程中已经让我受够了这种事。我爸是个叛逆者，这让他根本不适合当兵。他升职无望，所以二十年来他几乎一直都是个档案管理员。他受不了那些蠢货——用他的话说——仅仅因为会服从就升职，这让他很沮丧。他回家后会冲着我妈大吼大叫，我妈也会回吼，然后他们会摔门，在厨房里敲锅碗瓢盆——这对我们小孩来说挺吓人的。我知道不会有什么事发生，但我弟弟会跑进房间哭起来，我们会把他的床推到门边保护自己——大概是为了防止那些大喊大叫的人进来吧。如果情况真的很糟糕，爸爸就会怒气冲冲地离开，好几天都不回来。那倒不是什么大事，但你知道，我不需要生活中再有那种狗血剧情了。经历过了，真的让我很反感。

Helen’s adult strategy for avoiding anger—“I prefer not to be around people who get angry”—echoed her childhood strategy—run away and hide till it blows over, or hide in a place where it will never find you. What hadn’t figured in Helen’s plan was that anger is a normal human emotion, and no matter how diligently she tries to find a place where it doesn’t exist, or a person who doesn’t express it, she’s bound to fail.

海伦成年后逃避愤怒的策略——“我宁愿不和容易生气的人待在一起”——与她童年的策略如出一辙：要么逃跑躲藏，直到怒气消散；要么躲到怒气永远找不到的地方。海伦的计划中没有考虑到的是，愤怒是人类正常的情绪，无论她多么努力地寻找一个没有愤怒的地方，或者一个不会发怒的人，她都注定会失败。

When I met Jim, I thought I was in heaven. He’s quiet and gentle, and he’s always writing me notes and making up songs for me—a real romantic. From the moment I met him, I couldn’t imagine him yelling or ever making a scene. Sold! I’ll take him! But you know that saying, “Be careful what you wish for because you might get it?” Well, now I know what it means.

遇见吉姆的那一刻，我感觉自己仿佛置身天堂。他安静又温柔，总是给我写小纸条，还为我创作歌曲——真是个浪漫的人。从见到他的那一刻起，我就无法想象他会大吼大叫或者闹事。就他了！我就要他！不过，你听过那句谚语吗？“小心你的愿望，因为它可能会成真。” 嗯，现在我终于明白它的意思了。

You’d think that the way to get to me would be to yell—that makes sense. But Jim is the opposite, and when he gets mad, he gets more quiet. He won’t tell me what’s wrong—he won’t say anything. I almost wish he’d start yelling so I’d know what I was up against. This is the worst. When he withdraws, I just die inside. It’s like I’m totally cut off—like I’m on an ice floe in the middle of the Arctic Ocean. I can’t stand it when he gets mad in that quiet, icy way. I have to get him out of that shell, even if I have to stand on my head.

你可能会觉得，要让我生气就应该大吼大叫——这很合情理。但吉姆恰恰相反，他生气的时候反而会更安静。他不会告诉我发生了什么——他什么也不说。我甚至希望他开始吼叫，这样我才能知道自己面对的是什么。这太糟糕了。他沉默不语的时候，我的内心就像被撕裂了一样。感觉就像我完全与世隔绝——就像我身处北冰洋中央的一块浮冰上。我无法忍受他用那种安静、冰冷的方式生气。我必须让他走出那层壳，哪怕为此我得倒立。

Or, as had been happening more and more, give in to emotional blackmail.

或者，就像越来越常见的情况一样，屈服于情感勒索。

I helped Helen reconsider choices she’d made, most of them as a child, about how to cope with anger—and then we worked on making a place for it in her life. She was able to make major improvements in her life with Jim, a process we’ll see in the chapters that follow.

我帮助海伦重新审视她过去做出的选择，其中大部分是在童年时期，关于她如何应对愤怒——然后我们一起努力，在她的生活中为愤怒找到一个合适的位置。她和吉姆的关系也因此有了显著的改善，我们将在接下来的章节中看到这个过程。

None of us likes anger, but if we believe that it’s always up to us to avoid it, or to squelch it to keep peace at any price, the range of actions available to us is about as wide as a tightrope: we can back down, give in, placate—all the things that tell blackmailers how to get what they want from us.

我们都不喜欢生气，但如果我们认为总是应该避免生气，或者不惜一切代价压制生气以维持和平，那么我们可采取的行动范围就如同走钢丝一样狭窄：我们可以退缩、让步、安抚——所有这些都会告诉勒索者如何从我们身上得到他们想要的东西。

THE BLAME-TAKER

推卸责任者

I encourage people to take responsibility for what they do. But many of us think that we have to take the blame for every problem that comes along in our lives or others’, even though we had little or nothing to do with creating it. Blackmailers, of course, feed this notion. In fact, they demand that we buy into it. If they’re displeased, we’re the problem. And our compliance with them is the solution.

我鼓励人们为自己的行为负责。但我们很多人却认为，生活中或他人遇到的每一个问题，即使与我们无关，也必须由我们来承担责任。当然，敲诈勒索者正是利用了这种观念。事实上，他们要求我们接受这种观念。如果他们不高兴，那就是我们的问题。而我们的顺从，就成了解决问题的办法。

Bizarre Blaming

离奇的指责

Eve’s world fell apart when Elliot took an overdose of prescription drugs after one of their fights. Elliot was kept under observation in a nursing facility for several weeks, and when he returned home, he blamed Eve for his pain, his problems and all of his fears.

在一次争吵后，埃利奥特服用了过量的处方药，伊芙的世界从此崩塌。埃利奥特在疗养院接受了数周的观察，出院回家后，他将自己的痛苦、问题和所有恐惧都归咎于伊芙。

He went off the deep end and he wouldn’t stop telling me that everything was all my fault. He said, “See, now they’re going to put me in a mental hospital and I’m going to have to kill myself, and you can thank yourself for that. Now I’ve got this record, and they’re going to put me away, and I’m going to be dead because of it.” It was horrible. I felt like I was causing him to suffer just for being who I am, and I didn’t know what to do.

他彻底疯了，不停地跟我说一切都是我的错。他说：“你看，现在他们要把我送进精神病院，我最后只能自杀，这都是你自找的。现在我有了案底，他们要把我关起来，我肯定会因此丧命。” 太可怕了。我觉得仅仅因为我的存在，我就让他受苦，我不知道该怎么办。

By any objective standards, Elliot’s behavior was ludicrous and his accusations far-fetched. It seems almost inconceivable that a bright young woman like Eve would take him seriously. Yet she did believe him. She was sure that what he predicted would probably happen—and all the blame would be hers.

客观来说，埃利奥特的行为荒谬可笑，他的指控也牵强附会。像伊芙这样聪慧的年轻女子竟然会认真对待他，这简直令人难以置信。然而，她却相信了他。她确信他预言的事情很可能会发生——而所有的罪责都将由她承担。

When I asked Eve if she had any idea why she was buying into all this blame peddling, she immediately went to her relationship with her father and we struck oil the first time out.

当我问伊芙是否知道自己为什么会相信这种互相指责的论调时，她立刻提到了她和父亲的关系，我们一语中的。

“My father was always talking about dying,” she said. “I think he was obsessed with it.” Then she described an incident that took place when she was eight years old.

“我父亲总是谈论死亡，”她说。“我觉得他对此很着迷。”然后她讲述了她八岁时发生的一件事。

I’ll never forget that day. I can see it like it was yesterday. I was in the front seat of our huge old Pontiac with my father, driving down the street. We were stopped at a crosswalk, and I was looking out the window at some little kids playing in their yard. Daddy turned to me and said, “You don’t know anything important, do you?”

我永远不会忘记那天。那情景仿佛就在昨天。我坐在我们那辆老旧的庞蒂亚克轿车的前排，和父亲一起沿着街道行驶。我们在人行横道前停了下来，我望着窗外，看到几个小孩在院子里玩耍。爸爸转过头对我说：“你什么重要的事都不懂，是吗？”

I looked at him. “If I had a heart attack right now, you wouldn’t know what to do, would you?” he said. “You wouldn’t know what to do, and I would die right in front of you. “Then he started the car up again and we drove on. He didn’t say anything, and I didn’t say anything. I just counted the dots on the skirt of my dress and tried not to think about anything at all.

我看着他。“如果我现在心脏病发作，你不知道该怎么办，对吧？”他说。“你不知道该怎么办，我会死在你面前。”说完，他又发动了车子，我们继续往前开。他什么也没说，我也没说话。我只是数着裙子上的点，努力不去想任何事情。

But of course, little Eve did think about what she perceived as her father’s indictment of her: You’re eight years old, you should be able to save me, and you can’t. Eve believed that she was responsible for keeping her father alive— shouldn’t she be able to do that?—and would therefore be to blame if he died. For a child, the family is the world, and to let them down is to let the world fall into pieces, carrying everyone with it.

当然，小伊芙也想到了她认为父亲对她的指责：你才八岁，你应该能救我，可你却做不到。伊芙认为她有责任让父亲活下去——难道她不应该做到吗？——所以如果父亲死了，她就是罪魁祸首。对孩子来说，家庭就是整个世界，让家人失望就等于让整个世界分崩离析，连累所有人。

“The most true thing in the world in my family was ‘If you don’t be nice to Daddy, he’ll die,’” Eve said. “I really believed it.” Eve’s father’s behavior was bizarre, and to a child it was terrifying. How could she objectively evaluate Elliot’s behavior when the bizarre was the norm for her?

“我家最真切的一句话就是‘如果你不好好对待爸爸，他就会死’，”伊芙说。“我真的深信不疑。”伊芙的父亲行为怪异，对一个孩子来说，这简直太可怕了。当怪异成为她习以为常的事情时，她又怎么能客观地评价埃利奥特的行为呢？

Her experience with her father planted the seeds of a style of blame-taking that has carried through strongly to the present. Though you can’t always make such direct connections between a person’s childhood and their adult difficulties with blame-taking and emotional blackmail, in Eve’s case the similarities were blatant.

她与父亲的相处经历在她心中埋下了推卸责任的种子，这种习惯一直延续至今。虽然我们不能总是将一个人的童年经历与其成年后推卸责任和情感勒索的问题直接联系起来，但在伊芙的例子中，相似之处却显而易见。

The Atlas Syndrome

阿特拉斯综合征

People with the Atlas syndrome believe that they alone must solve every problem, putting their own needs last. Like Atlas, who carried the world on his shoulders, they weigh themselves down with the burden of fixing everyone else’s feelings and actions, hoping to atone for past or future transgressions.

患有阿特拉斯综合症的人认为所有问题都必须由自己解决，把自己的需求放在最后。就像肩负世界重担的阿特拉斯一样，他们背负着修复他人感受和行为的重担，希望以此弥补过去或未来的过错。

Karen, the nurse we met earlier, developed the Atlas syndrome as a teenager, when her father and mother divorced.

我们之前遇到的护士凯伦，在她十几岁时父母离异后患上了寰椎综合征。

When Dad left, Mom was almost completely alone, and I was supposed to make up for the loss. Her family was all back in New York, and we were in California, and she only had one or two close friends out here and she depended on me.

爸爸离开后，妈妈几乎完全孤身一人。我本该弥补她的空缺。她的家人都在纽约，而我们身在加州，她在这里只有一两个亲密的朋友，她很依赖我。

I remember when I was 15 or so, I had a chance to go out on my first New Year’s Eve date with a friend. My mother and I had planned to go out to dinner that night, and then a movie, but around Christmas a friend of mine called and said she had a blind date for me, and we could double-date. I was so excited, I really wanted to go, but I felt a little guilty. So I talked over the situation with an aunt of mine who told me, “Frances can’t possibly expect you to stay with her when you have a chance like this — go!”

我记得大概十五岁的时候，我和朋友第一次有机会一起过新年。那天晚上我和妈妈计划先吃晚饭，然后去看电影，但圣诞节前后，一个朋友打电话来说她给我安排了一次相亲，我们可以一起去。我当时特别兴奋，真的很想去，但又有点内疚。于是我和一位阿姨聊了聊这件事，她对我说：“弗朗西丝不可能指望你待在她身边，你明明有这么好的机会——去吧！”

I got up all my courage and told my mother that I wanted to go out on this date. And she was so hurt, her eyes filled with tears and she said, “Well, what am I going to do on New Year’s Eve?” I did go out, and I had a good time, but when I got home, my mother was in bed with a migraine, practically screaming in pain, and I knew it never would’ve happened if I hadn’t gone. I felt so guilty I could hardly stand it. I didn’t want to give up my whole life, but I didn’t want to hurt her any more than I had already.

我鼓起勇气告诉妈妈我想出去约会。她伤心极了，眼泪盈眶，说：“那我跨年夜怎么办？” 我还是出去了，玩得很开心。但回家后，妈妈却因为偏头痛卧床不起，疼得几乎要尖叫。我知道如果我没去，这一切都不会发生。我感到无比愧疚，几乎无法承受。我不想放弃自己的一切，但也不想再让她伤心了。

Karen was only 15, but she had learned to let her mother depend on her. If she didn’t take care of her mother, after all, who would? It never occurred to her that her mom could take care of herself. Besides, if she angered her, or “harmed” her by not doing what she wanted, her mother might leave, too.

凯伦只有十五岁，但她已经学会了让母亲依赖自己。毕竟，如果她不照顾母亲，谁来照顾呢？她从未想过母亲可以照顾自己。再说，如果她惹母亲生气，或者因为不顺从母亲而“伤害”了母亲，母亲也可能离开。

At first, I didn’t know what to do for her, but one day I knew what would help. I got out a pencil and paper, and I wrote out a contract: “I hereby promise my mother that when I grow up, I will see that her life is wonderful. I will see that she has lots of interesting friends and fun things to do. Love, Karen.” I gave it to her one afternoon, and she smiled at me and said I was a good girl.

起初，我不知道该如何帮助她，但有一天，我突然明白了什么才是对她真正有帮助的。我拿出纸笔，写了一份“契约”：“我在此向妈妈承诺，长大后，我一定会让她过上美好的生活。我一定会让她结交许多有趣的朋友，并让她享受各种有趣的事情。爱你的，凯伦。”一天下午，我把契约交给了她，她对我微笑，说我是个好孩子。

Many of us take on the task of maintaining another person’s well-being, an overwhelming responsibility that nonetheless carries its own rewards. Karen had found a way to feel powerful. She had discovered how to make her mother happy—and make sure that her own world didn’t fall apart.

我们许多人都肩负着维护他人福祉的重任，这是一项艰巨的责任，但同时也带来了丰厚的回报。凯伦找到了让自己感到强大的方法。她发现了如何让母亲开心——同时也确保了自己的世界不会崩塌。

It’s hard to ignore someone’s Atlas tendencies. Karen’s daughter, who was blackmailing her by reminding her of the pain she’d suffered in a car accident years ago, had seen the way her mother responded to her grandmother—and most of the other people in her life. It was a snap for Melanie to activate the responsibility hot button.

很难忽视一个人身上那种“阿特拉斯式”的倾向。凯伦的女儿梅兰妮，用多年前车祸的痛苦来勒索她，她亲眼目睹了母亲对待祖母——以及她生命中大多数其他人——的态度。对梅兰妮来说，触发母亲的责任感简直易如反掌。

Melanie and I are close, and I know how hard it is for her to work the Program and hold on to her sobriety. If not for the accident, the scars, she would’ve been stronger. I’m a nurse, and I know the face of pain. I wish I could’ve spared her from it, and since I couldn’t, I have to protect her now. It’s my duty as a mother. I don’t like the pressure she puts on me, but I want her to have what I didn’t. I love her and my grandchildren so much! Do you know she threatens to not let me see them when she’s upset with me? Our family needs to be together, and if I’m the one who has to pull us together, I will.

我和梅兰妮关系很亲密，我知道她参加戒瘾项目、保持清醒有多么不容易。如果不是那场意外和那些伤疤，她会更坚强。我是一名护士，我了解痛苦的滋味。我多么希望我能让她免受这一切，既然我做不到，我现在就必须保护她。这是我作为母亲的责任。我不喜欢她给我的压力，但我希望她能拥有我曾经没有拥有的东西。我非常爱她和我的孙辈们！你知道吗？她生我的气的时候会威胁说不让我见他们。我们一家人需要在一起，如果必须由我来维系我们，我也会这么做。

Like many people with the Atlas syndrome, Karen had no idea where her responsibility for other people began and ended, because she’d long been told that she was supposed to take care of everyone but herself.

和许多患有寰椎综合征的人一样，凯伦不知道她对其他人的责任从哪里开始，到哪里结束，因为她从小就被告知她应该照顾所有人，唯独不应该照顾自己。

Blame and responsibility are closely allied, and it’s hard to see the boundaries between them. As I worked with Karen to disconnect her automatic “You’re right—I’m to blame. I owe you reparations,” she began to define, for the first time in her adult life, how to make room in her world for her own needs, and just what degree of responsibility she wanted to take for those around her.

责备和责任往往紧密相连，二者之间的界限难以划分。我帮助凯伦摆脱她那种下意识的“你说得对——都是我的错。我应该赔偿你”的想法后，她开始在成年生活中第一次明确，如何在自己的生活中为自己的需求留出空间，以及她究竟想为身边的人承担多大的责任。

THE BLEEDING HEART

流血的心

Compassion and empathy inspire kindness, even noble deeds, and we have little respect for people who lack them. It’s hard to imagine how these traits could be troublesome. But compassion can turn to a sense of pity so overwhelming that it moves us to renounce our own well-being for the sake of another person. How many times have we said “I can’t leave him because I feel so sorry for him” or “She looks at me with the tears running down her face and I’ll do whatever she wants” or “I’m always giving in to her, but she’s had such a terrible life . . .”? We get caught up in the other person’s emotional needs and lose the ability to assess problems and see how we can do the most good.

同情和共情能够激发善意，甚至促成高尚的行为，而我们往往对缺乏这些品质的人缺乏尊重。很难想象这些特质会带来什么麻烦。然而，同情心有时会演变成一种强烈的怜悯之情，驱使我们为了他人而牺牲自身的福祉。我们有多少次说过“我不能离开他，因为我太同情他了”、“她泪流满面地看着我，我愿意为她做任何事”、“我总是迁就她，但她的人生太悲惨了……”？我们被他人的情感需求所左右，失去了评估问题的能力，也失去了思考如何才能最大程度地帮助他人的能力。

What gives some people the ability to feel empathy for problems or suffering and offer appropriate help, while others, the bleeding hearts, feel compelled to fly in like Superman and give their all to stop the suffering—even if they have to sacrifice their self-respect or health? As we’ve seen so far, where there’s a compulsion to act and an automatic response that may rebound against us, there’s often a hot button at the root.

是什么让一些人能够对他人的问题或痛苦感同身受，并提供恰当的帮助，而另一些人，那些“心软的人”，却感觉自己必须像超人一样飞身而出，竭尽全力去阻止痛苦——即使这意味着牺牲自尊或健康也在所不惜？正如我们目前所看到的，当存在一种行动的冲动和可能对我们自身产生反作用的自动反应时，其根源往往在于某个敏感点。

The Power of Pity

怜悯的力量

My client Patty, the government worker we met in Chapter 2 , grew up in a house that was none too happy for most of her childhood years. Her mother suffered from what seemed to be a deep depression and often disappeared into her bedroom for hours or even days at a time. Patty often jokes, “My mother slept through my whole childhood,” but she remembers always being conscious of her mother’s presence and her needs, trying to play quietly so as not to disturb her.

我的客户帕蒂，也就是我们在第二章中遇到的那位政府工作人员，她的童年大部分时间都生活在一个并不幸福的家庭里。她的母亲似乎患有严重的抑郁症，经常把自己关在卧室里几个小时甚至几天。帕蒂经常开玩笑说：“我妈妈在我整个童年时期都在睡觉。”但她记得自己一直都意识到母亲的存在和需求，总是尽量安静地玩耍，以免打扰她。

I’ve always been independent, but I was worried about her. Other people’s moms weren’t sick all the time, but the slightest disruption would send my mother to bed. I really tuned in to her—I could tell by the sound behind the door of her room if she was awake or sleeping, and I could tell if she was sleeping well or if she was restless. If she was sound asleep, I’d look in on her, and I listened to her breathing to be sure she was OK. It was part of my job when my dad wasn’t around.

我一直都很独立，但我很担心她。别人的妈妈不会总是生病，但我妈妈哪怕最轻微的动静都会让她卧床不起。我特别留意她——我能从她房门后的声音判断她是醒着还是睡着，也能分辨她睡得好不好。如果她睡得很沉，我会进去看看，听听她的呼吸，确保她没事。爸爸不在家的时候，这算是我的职责之一。

It was a tailor-made training ground for a bleeding heart. When we’re in close quarters with a parent or another important person who is physically or emotionally needy, we become ultrasensitive to their cues. Every flutter of the eye, small sigh or change of voice becomes freighted with meaning, and we even tune in, as Patty did, to the nuances of a sleeping person’s breathing. A child like Patty can’t do anything to help, however.

这简直是培养一颗多愁善感的心的绝佳场所。当我们与身心需要关爱的父母或其他重要人物近距离相处时，我们会变得异常敏感，对他们的任何细微举动都格外在意。每一次眼皮的颤动、一声轻叹、一次语调的变化，都仿佛被赋予了某种意义，我们甚至会像帕蒂一样，去留意熟睡之人呼吸的细微变化。然而，像帕蒂这样的孩子却无能为力。

As we’ve seen, many of us resolve as children to make things better when we’re adults, and it’s common for us to reenact scenes from our childhood to make sure they come out right, now that we have the power to fix them.

正如我们所看到的，许多人在孩提时代就立志长大后要让事情变得更好，而且我们常常会重演童年时的场景，以确保事情能够正确解决，因为我们现在有能力弥补过去的错误。

You know that cliché “You marry your father”? I married my mother! Joe obviously isn’t as depressed as my mother was—in fact, what I love about him is how energetic he is when he’s happy. But he’s so moody—up and down. He has the same way of sighing, even going off to lie down in his room when he’s upset, that my mom did, and when he does, all that old training of mine kicks in. Joe talks about how he thinks I can read his mind. When he starts to look so sad, I seem to be able to figure out what the problem is or bring it to the surface the way no one else can. When we first got together, I liked the feeling that we clicked and I could make him happy. But he started to expect me to be a mind reader and it’s getting old.
