In return, she wanted an apology from Charles for bullying her and an agreement from him to keep their interactions civil.

雪莉的老板兼情人查尔斯威胁说，当她决定结束这段恋情时，就要解雇她。于是，她决定向查尔斯提出三项条件，以此作为对双方都有利的交换：首先，她绝不会再和查尔斯发生性关系，这是她最基本的原则。其次，她提出可以继续留在公司，直到完成手头的项目，并帮助查尔斯招聘和培训她的接替者。作为交换，她希望查尔斯为欺凌她的行为道歉，并承诺以后两人之间保持礼貌的互动。

I was really afraid that he was going to fire me on the spot, but I’d done a lot of practicing to be sure I knew what I wanted to say, and I think he was surprised that I wasn’t scared of him. At first, he really seemed to be saying “No sex, no job,” but when I said I could not compromise on that point, he backed down. He told me, “I don’t know if I could handle seeing you every day. I have feelings, too—this hasn’t just been a roll in the hay.” So I said maybe we could try it out and see how it feels, and he said we could do that. I think it helped that I had something to offer, and that I didn’t go in there ready to duke it out with him. I’m working on some things that it would be hard to hand off to a new person, and I think he knew that he’d be better off letting me finish than firing me.

我当时真的很害怕他会当场解雇我，但我事先做了很多练习，确保自己知道该说什么，我想他很惊讶我竟然不怕他。一开始，他似乎真的在说“不发生性关系，就没工作”，但当我表示在这点上我无法妥协时，他退缩了。他告诉我：“我不知道我能不能忍受每天都见到你。我也有感情——这不仅仅是一夜情。”所以我说也许我们可以试试看，看看感觉如何，他也同意了。我觉得我能为他做点什么，而且我没有一开始就准备和他正面冲突，这对他很有帮助。我正在做一些工作，很难交给新人，我想他也明白，让我完成这些工作比解雇我更有利。

But Charles’s behavior did not reflect the agreement he made with Sherry.

但查尔斯的行为并没有履行他与雪莉达成的协议。

Things have really turned difficult. He’s been really critical of me in front of clients, and he doesn’t miss a chance to get a dig in at me or put me down. He’s not keeping up his part of the bargain, and I don’t know what to do.

事情变得非常棘手。他在客户面前对我百般挑剔，总是抓住机会挖苦我、贬低我。他没有履行承诺，我不知道该怎么办。

I told Sherry that the only thing to do in her situation was to go back to Charles and let him know that he wasn’t doing what he’d promised to. Words aren’t enough. They have to be backed up by action. Many emotional blackmailers find it easy to apologize and say they’ll make changes but much harder to deliver on their promises. It’s important to remind them with words such as “We had an agreement, and I’d really appreciate it if you kept your part of the bargain.”

我告诉雪莉，她现在唯一能做的就是去找查尔斯，让他知道他没有履行承诺。光说不做是不够的，必须付诸行动。很多情感勒索者很容易道歉并承诺会改正，但真正兑现承诺却难上加难。所以，要提醒他们，比如可以说：“我们之前有约定，如果你能遵守约定，我会非常感激。”

Sherry confronted Charles in a gentle, nondefensive way:

雪莉以温和、不带防御性的方式与查尔斯对质：

I told him, “You may not even be aware of how hurtful your comments have been, but I’d like them to stop.” And of course he didn’t have to ask what comments—he knew what I was talking about. And then he half-smiled and said, “You were such a nice person before you went into therapy. . . .”

我告诉他：“你可能根本没意识到你的话有多伤人，但我希望你别再说了。” 当然，他不用问我具体是哪些话——他知道我在说什么。然后他微微一笑，说：“你以前是个很好的人，后来才去接受治疗……”

Even in a case like Sherry’s, in which the ultimate goal is to extricate yourself from a difficult situation, it’s important to be vigilant and to hold the other person to his or her agreements with you as long as you are with them.

即使像雪莉这样的情况，最终目标是让自己摆脱困境，只要你和对方在一起，保持警惕并要求对方遵守与你达成的协议也是很重要的。

STRATEGY 4: USING HUMOR

策略四：运用幽默

In a relationship that’s basically good, humor can be an effective tool for pointing out to the other person how their behavior looks to you. Let me give you a couple of examples.

在一段基本良好的关系中，幽默可以有效地帮助对方指出你如何看待他们的行为。让我举几个例子。

One day when Patty was complaining to me about Joe’s suffering, she blurted out: “God, someone should give the man an Oscar: best sufferer in a leading role.”

有一天，帕蒂向我抱怨乔的痛苦时，她脱口而出：“天哪，应该给这个人颁个奥斯卡奖：最佳主角受苦奖。”

“Why don’t you?” I asked her.

“你为什么不呢？”我问她。

She liked the idea so much that she went to a trophy shop and bought a replica of an Oscar. And the next time Joe went into his sulking and sighing routine, she gave him a big smile, applauded and presented him with his award. “‘That was brilliant,’ I told him. Then I said, ‘I especially liked the little sigh at the end.’” The situation suddenly seemed so ridiculous, Patty reported, that both of them burst out laughing—and Joe hasn’t been able to suffer effectively since.

她太喜欢这个主意了，于是去了奖杯店，买了一个奥斯卡奖杯的复制品。下次乔又开始闷闷不乐、叹气的时候，她就冲他咧嘴一笑，鼓掌，然后把奖杯颁给他。“‘太棒了！’我告诉他。然后我又说，‘我特别喜欢你最后那声叹息。’”帕蒂说，当时的情景突然变得如此滑稽，以至于他们俩都哈哈大笑起来——从那以后，乔就再也没能有效地装出一副苦瓜脸了。

Sarah’s relationship with Frank was fraying but intact, and she decided that humor might get his attention. She took out an old hula hoop that had been sitting in the coat closet, and the next time Frank set up a condition for their marriage, she said, “Could you hold this while I jump through it?”

莎拉和弗兰克的关系虽然日渐疏远，但仍然维系着。她觉得幽默或许能引起他的注意。她从衣橱里拿出一个旧呼啦圈，等弗兰克下次再提出结婚条件时，她就说：“你能帮我拿着这个，让我跳过去吗？”

“What’s this all about?” he asked.

“这到底是怎么回事？”他问道。

“Well, honey,” she said, “I’ve kind of noticed how you like to keep me jumping through hoops to prove myself to you. Do you think we could talk about it?”

“亲爱的，”她说，“我注意到你总是喜欢让我费尽心思证明自己。我们能谈谈这件事吗？”

“What are you talking about? I don’t do that,” Frank said.

“你在说什么？我不会那样做。”弗兰克说。

“I’m sure you don’t realize you do, and I know you love me, but it’s felt like a never-ending series of tests to me.”

“我知道你没有意识到这一点，我也知道你爱我，但对我来说，这感觉就像是一场永无止境的考验。”

“Hoops, huh?” he said. “OK, let’s talk about it.”

“篮球啊？”他说。“好吧，那我们来聊聊吧。”

Then, Sarah reported, “He broke into that grin I just adore and said, ‘But before we get serious, do you think you could jump through that little hoop for me first.’ It really took the edge off.”

然后，莎拉说：“他露出了我最喜欢那种笑容，说道：‘但在我们认真交往之前，你能不能先帮我跳过那个小圈？’这真的让我放松了不少。”

There’s nothing more intimate than sharing a private joke with someone. Humor is a bond between people, and recalling humorous experiences can be part of the fabric of a strong relationship. Using humor to make a point with a blackmailer can put you both in a relaxed state that lets you remember how much you enjoy each other’s company—and gives you a strong reminder of what it feels like to feel comfortable with each other. Humor is healing. It lowers the blood pressure, and it can take the heat right out of a potentially fiery encounter with someone you’ve been having difficulties with.

没有什么比和心爱的人分享一个只有彼此才懂的笑话更亲密的了。幽默是人与人之间的纽带，回忆那些有趣的经历可以成为牢固关系的重要组成部分。用幽默来回击勒索者，可以让你们双方都放松下来，想起彼此相处的乐趣——也能让你们再次感受到自在舒适的感觉。幽默具有疗愈作用。它能降低血压，也能化解与某个让你感到棘手的人之间可能出现的激烈冲突。

If humor is part of your regular vocabulary and you’re comfortable with it, it’s a wonderful way to express yourself. I can’t guarantee that it’ll work all the time, but it’s bound to make you feel a lot less grim.

如果你平时就习惯用幽默表达自己，并且能坦然接受，那么这是一种绝佳的自我表达方式。我不能保证它每次都奏效，但它肯定能让你感觉好很多。

EVALUATING THE RESULTS

评估结果

There’s no way of knowing how the other person will respond until you express your feelings and define the limits you need to set in your relationship. As over the years I’ve worked with targets who came in for consultations with their blackmailers, I’ve often been surprised by who responded to requests for change. Often people I’ve expected very little from, because they seemed angry or hard or mean, were actually quite willing to participate in making their relationships stronger. And sometimes those who seemed friendly and flexible turned out to be closed, defensive and not at all sensitive to their targets’ needs.

在你表达自己的感受并明确关系中的界限之前，你无法预知对方会作何反应。多年来，我曾与许多前来咨询的受害者合作，他们都曾遭受勒索者的骚扰。我常常惊讶于那些愿意做出改变的人。有些人我原本并不抱太大期望，因为他们看起来愤怒、冷漠或刻薄，但实际上他们非常愿意努力改善彼此的关系。而有些看似友好和善的人，最终却表现得封闭、防备，对受害者的需求漠不关心。

A Positive Outcome

积极的结果

Michael was a dramatic example of someone who responded in a way exactly the opposite of what I had expected. Though Liz had feared an explosion when she presented her conditions to him, she was thrilled by their actual exchange.

迈克尔的反应完全出乎我的意料，这真是一个戏剧性的例子。莉兹当初向他提出条件时，原本担心会引发一场冲突，但他们的实际交流却让她欣喜不已。

I thought a lot about what to do after I wrote that letter. Should I hand it to him and leave the house for a while, or go to his office and drop it off, or just leave it where he could find it? I finally decided that the most comfortable thing for me, because I’m not physically afraid of him, was to sit with him and ask him to hear me out while I read the letter to him.

写完那封信后，我一直在想该怎么办。我应该把信交给他然后离开家一会儿，还是去他的办公室把信送过去，或者就放在他容易看到的地方？最后，我决定对我来说最自在的做法是，因为我并不害怕他，所以就坐在他旁边，请他听我把信读给他听。

A couple of times he tried to interrupt, but something really must’ve touched him because he got very quiet and I could see that he was listening hard. For just a brief moment, I could see the guy I fell in love with sitting across from me instead of that controlling bully. Then his defenses went up and he went after me. He said, “None of this would’ve happened if you hadn’t threatened to get a divorce. Things never would have gotten to this point if you hadn’t turned on me like that.” I felt like yelling back at him, but I said, “Michael, I’m not willing to take more than 50 percent of the responsibility.”

他几次试图打断我，但似乎有什么事触动了他，他突然安静下来，我能看出他在认真倾听。那一瞬间，我仿佛看到了我爱上的那个男人，而不是那个控制欲极强的恶霸。然后他立刻竖起了防备，开始攻击我。他说：“如果你当初没有威胁要离婚，这一切都不会发生。如果你当初没有那样对我，事情也不会发展到今天这个地步。” 我当时真想冲他吼回去，但我还是说：“迈克尔，我最多只愿意承担一半的责任。”

And he calmed down and said, “I guess I didn’t want to see that I was hurting you. Why didn’t you tell me?” I’m not a Pollyanna, and I know this will take some time to work out, but the most exciting thing is that he’s agreed to go to therapy. His hair-trigger temper is a real problem, and I think he sees that his “Me Tarzan, you Jane” routine isn’t going to work anymore.

他冷静下来后说：“我想我是不想承认我伤害了你。那你为什么不告诉我呢？” 我不是个盲目乐观的人，我知道这需要时间才能解决，但最令人欣慰的是他同意接受心理治疗。他一点就着的脾气确实是个问题，我想他也意识到他那套“我是泰山，你是简”的把戏已经行不通了。

Michael, like a lot of blackmailers, was surprised by how hurt and scared Liz was. I’ve often heard people who resort to emotional blackmail say “Why didn’t she tell me?” or “If I’d only known how much my behavior was hurting him, we could’ve salvaged things before they got so bad.” This isn’t prevarication. Blackmailers are often unaware of how painful their behavior and pressure have been, because targets have been too frightened, angry or discouraged to let them know, believing that it wouldn’t do any good. In other words, you may not have been saying “Ouch” loudly enough.

和许多勒索者一样，迈克尔也对莉兹的受伤和恐惧感到惊讶。我经常听到那些诉诸情感勒索的人说：“她为什么不告诉我？”或者“如果我早知道我的行为对他伤害这么大，我们就能在事情变得这么糟糕之前挽回局面了。”这并非撒谎。勒索者往往意识不到自己的行为和压力造成了多大的伤害，因为受害者往往因为恐惧、愤怒或沮丧而不敢开口，认为说了也没用。换句话说，你可能只是没有足够大声地表达你的痛苦。

We often inhibit ourselves with admonitions like “Don’t be a complainer” or “Don’t feel sorry for yourself.” Some people, men in particular, want to look strong and confident and don’t want to seem easily bruised. So we don’t express our feelings. We don’t say “You’re hurting me. Please stop.”

我们常常用“别抱怨”或“别自怜自艾”之类的告诫来约束自己。有些人，尤其是男性，想要看起来坚强自信，不想显得容易受伤。所以我们不表达自己的感受。我们不说“你弄疼我了，请停下来”。

Don’t be surprised, then, by the other person’s surprise at your feelings. No matter what their response, resolve to keep talking, expressing yourself honestly and using nondefensive communication. Then watch to see what the other person does with the new information you’ve offered.

所以，当对方对你的感受感到惊讶时，你也不要感到意外。无论他们的反应如何，都要坚持继续沟通，坦诚地表达自己，并采用不带防御性的沟通方式。然后观察对方如何应对你提供的新信息。

Sorry Isn’t Enough

道歉远远不够

As I told Liz, after a forthright exchange with the other person we need information that only time can give us. “I know this is a hopeful time for you,” I told her, “and I’m excited for you and pleased that Michael is going to go into therapy. I hope this isn’t just a honeymoon period, and to be sure things are on the right track, we’ll need to keep reevaluating things.”

正如我告诉莉兹的那样，在与对方坦诚交流之后，我们需要一些只有时间才能提供的信息。“我知道这对你来说是一个充满希望的时期，”我告诉她，“我为你感到兴奋，也很高兴迈克尔要去接受治疗。我希望这不仅仅是蜜月期，为了确保一切朝着正确的方向发展，我们需要不断地重新评估情况。”

Many times we get very excited by the other person’s initial response and believe that a conflict is resolved because he or she has verbally agreed to our terms. But in time we may notice that promises are forgotten and old habits reemerge. We don’t want to turn into watchdogs and scorekeepers in our relationships, but we need to look realistically at what’s changing and how it fits with what we’ve decided we want and need.

很多时候，我们会被对方最初的反应所吸引，误以为对方口头答应了我们的条件，冲突就此解决。但随着时间的推移，我们可能会发现承诺被遗忘，旧习重现。我们不想在人际关系中变成斤斤计较的监督者和记分员，但我们需要客观地审视正在发生的变化，以及这些变化是否符合我们自身的需求和愿望。

That’s why it’s so important to make a decision not to decide on a final course of action until you see what the other person does. When you’re making an important decision about the future of a relationship, give the other person time—I suggest 30 to 60 days—and watch for behavioral as well as verbal responses. It’s not enough for someone to say, “I’m sorry—now let’s not talk about it anymore.”

这就是为什么在决定最终行动方案之前，不要急于做出决定如此重要，直到你看到对方的行动为止。当你在为一段关系的未来做出重要决定时，要给对方时间——我建议30到60天——并观察对方的行为和言语反应。仅仅一句“对不起，我们以后别再谈这件事了”是不够的。

What is enough?

什么才算足够？

  1. Accepting responsibility for using fear, obligation and guilt to get their way.
    他们承认自己利用恐惧、责任和愧疚感来达到目的。
  2. An acknowledgment that there are better ways to ask for what they want and a commitment that they will learn those ways.
    他们承认有更好的方式来表达自己的需求，并承诺会学习这些方式。
  3. An acknowledgment that their tactics have been unloving and have caused you pain.
    承认他们的做法缺乏爱心，给你带来了痛苦。
  4. An agreement to work with you on negotiating a healthier relationship, which may involve getting some sort of outside help if you are unable to work out a problem between you.
    双方同意共同努力，建立更健康的关系，如果你们之间无法解决问题，可能需要寻求外部帮助。
  5. A willingness to acknowledge your right to think, feel and behave differently than they do, and an agreement that differently does not mean “wrong” or “bad.”
    愿意承认你有权拥有与他们不同的思考、感受和行为方式，并同意不同并不意味着“错误”或“坏”。
  6. A commitment to work on eliminating the FOG-producing tactics they’ve used in the past (i.e., no more negative comparisons, no more threats to leave if they don’t get their way, no more guilt-peddling and so on).
    承诺努力消除他们过去使用的产生 FOG 的策略（即不再进行负面比较，不再威胁如果不如愿就离开，不再利用内疚感等）。

Changing entrenched behavior—both the blackmailer’s and your own—takes time and effort. Give yourself, and the other person, the gift of time.

改变根深蒂固的行为——无论是勒索者的还是你自己的——都需要时间和精力。给自己，也给对方一些时间吧。

YOU WILL BE STRONGER

你会变得更强大

It’s scary, telling another person “This is who I am. This is what I want.” Scarier still is standing by the truth of ourselves—our integrity—as we must when we give the other person a choice to accept or not accept our decisions and differences. We may feel as though expressing our needs is akin to making demands, but remember that what we’re asking of the blackmailer is absolutely reasonable: we want the other person to stop manipulating us. We’re not asking for anything that will harm us or them.

告诉别人“这就是我，这就是我想要的”是件令人恐惧的事。更可怕的是，当我们让对方选择接受或不接受我们的决定和分歧时，我们必须坚守真实的自我——我们的正直。我们或许会觉得表达需求就像是在提出要求，但请记住，我们对勒索者的要求是完全合理的：我们只是希望对方停止操纵我们。我们并没有要求任何会伤害我们或对方的事情。

Many of us delay presenting our decisions to the other person because we’re so afraid of what will happen. But step back for a moment and ask yourself, What’s the worst thing that can happen? A common fear is that the relationship will split in two irreparably. But the consequences of not standing up for yourself are worse because you will split in two. As time goes on, you’ll know less and less of who you are, what you want and what you believe in. Your core will become as thin as a leaf.

我们很多人之所以迟迟不愿向对方坦白自己的决定，是因为我们害怕后果。但请稍作停顿，问问自己：最糟糕的情况是什么？一种常见的恐惧是关系彻底破裂。但如果你不坚持自己的立场，后果会更糟，因为你会因此而分裂。随着时间的推移，你会越来越不了解自己，不知道自己想要什么，也不知道自己相信什么。你的内心会变得像一片树叶一样脆弱。

If the survival of any relationship depends on your constantly giving in to emotional blackmail, you have to ask yourself if the relationship is worth your well-being. If you get stronger, healthier and more confident and the other person doesn’t like it, what does that say about the quality of the relationship that you’re trying so hard to save? What is it based on?

如果一段关系的维系依赖于你不断屈服于情感勒索，那么你必须扪心自问，这段关系是否值得你牺牲自己的幸福。如果你变得更强大、更健康、更自信，而对方却不高兴，这说明你如此努力想要挽救的这段关系质量如何？它又建立在什么之上？

In this chapter, we’ve looked at several relationships that got better and some that ultimately didn’t survive. But in each case, blackmail targets pulled free from blackmail to gain a firmer grip on their priceless integrity. No one can predict what will happen as you begin to change, but I promise you that if you use these strategies and face emotional blackmail rather than capitulating to it, you will, no matter what the outcome, be a stronger, healthier person.

在本章中，我们探讨了一些关系好转的案例，以及一些最终破裂的案例。但无论哪种情况，被勒索者最终都摆脱了勒索的束缚，重新夺回了他们无比珍贵的尊严。没有人能够预知当你开始改变时会发生什么，但我向你保证，如果你运用这些策略，勇敢地面对情感勒索而不是屈服，无论结果如何，你都会变得更加强大、更加健康。

# ↩

11

Cutting Through the FOG

穿透迷雾

If you have begun to use the tools I gave you in the last chapter , you are developing effective new ways of communicating and behaving. Now I’m going to show you how to disconnect your most important hot buttons.

如果你已经开始运用上一章我教你的工具，你就正在培养有效的新沟通和行为方式。现在，我将向你展示如何消除你最敏感的情绪触发点。

You may have had some success already in resisting someone’s pressure, and you may be seeing changes both in yourself and the relationship. You’re tasting the satisfaction and the renewed sense of strength that come from reconnecting with your integrity. But you may have noticed that many of the same old feelings of fear, obligation and guilt that plagued you in the past are still very much with you. It’s as though a shiny new building is going up in place of an old one, but the unwelcome tenants who’ve always lived in the basement won’t leave.

你或许已经在抵制他人压力方面取得了一些成功，并且可能已经感受到自身和人际关系的变化。你正在品尝到重拾自我正直所带来的满足感和力量感。但你也可能注意到，过去困扰你的许多恐惧、责任感和内疚感依然挥之不去。这就好比一座崭新的大楼拔地而起，取代了旧楼，但那些一直住在地下室的不速之客却始终不肯离开。

There’s nothing to be concerned about. Feeling states don’t change as quickly as we would like them to. Those feelings have been with you a long time. They took years to become hot buttons, and they’re not going to let you evict them without putting up a battle. But it’s a battle you’re going to win. I’m going to show you direct, practical ways to diminish the lingering hurts and sensitivities that have made you vulnerable to emotional blackmail.

没什么好担心的。情绪状态不会像我们希望的那样迅速改变。这些情绪已经伴随你很久了。它们花了数年时间才变成你的敏感点，而且它们不会轻易让你摆脱，你会为此付出代价。但这是一场你终将胜利的战斗。我会向你展示一些直接有效的方法，帮助你减轻那些挥之不去的伤痛和敏感，这些伤痛和敏感让你容易受到情感勒索。

Remember: Even though I illustrate most of these strategies through my work with other people, all the exercises, role-playing, homework assignments and visualizations are designed for you to do on your own.

请记住：虽然我通过与其他人合作来说明这些策略中的大多数，但所有的练习、角色扮演、家庭作业和可视化练习都是为你自己设计的。

OLD FEELINGS, NEW RESPONSES

旧情复燃，新回应

To those of you who are familiar with my other books, especially Toxic Parents, it may come as a surprise that the work we’ll be doing here does not in every case involve traveling back to the experiences that are at the root of many of your vulnerabilities. Instead we’ll concentrate on changing your responses to those experiences. Certainly we all bear the marks of our pasts. Most of us have at least some awareness of how we were hurt and who hurt us. If we have done some work on ourselves, we have often made the important connection between our emotional scars and the way we behave in our relationships with other people.

对于那些熟悉我其他著作，尤其是《有毒的父母》的读者来说，我们即将开展的工作并非总是需要追溯那些造成你诸多脆弱性的根源经历，这或许会让你感到惊讶。相反，我们将专注于改变你对这些经历的反应。当然，我们每个人都带有过往的印记。我们大多数人至少都意识到自己曾受到怎样的伤害，以及是谁伤害了我们。如果我们曾进行过一些自我反思，我们往往会发现，我们情感上的创伤与我们在人际关系中的行为方式之间存在着重要的联系。

But what keeps some of us vulnerable to blackmail is the way we “favor” our injuries. We sabotage ourselves by giving in to blackmail to avoid uncomfortable feelings rather than learning to manage them. It’s very much like spraining your ankle and continuing to limp long after you need to because you’re afraid of the pain you might feel if you try to walk normally again. I’ll be referring to certain childhood experiences, as I have in previous chapters. But what I’d like to help you do here is to learn new responses to old feelings by staying in the present and dealing with the people who evoke those feelings in you now.

但让我们中的一些人容易受到勒索的原因在于我们“偏袒”自己的伤痛。我们为了逃避不适感而屈服于勒索，而不是学会如何应对，这无异于自毁前程。这很像扭伤了脚踝，却因为害怕再次正常行走时可能感受到的疼痛而继续跛行，即使已经可以正常行走了。我会像前几章那样，提及一些童年经历。但我在这里真正想帮助你们的是，通过活在当下，并与那些此刻会唤起你们这些感受的人相处，来学习如何以新的方式应对旧有的感受。

Note: Before we begin this work I need to reiterate an important point. There are several conditions that mandate some form of professional help. If you are struggling with recurrent depression, crippling anxieties, substance abuse or the aftermath of childhood physical, sexual or emotional abuse, there are many medical, psychological and biochemical interventions that do not require a great investment of time or money. Short-term interactive psychotherapy, the new antidepressant medications, support groups, 12-Step programs and personal growth seminars have changed the face of traditional psychotherapy in the past decade. There is help out there for anyone who truly wants it.

注：在开始之前，我需要重申一个重要的观点。有些情况需要寻求专业帮助。如果您正饱受反复抑郁、严重焦虑、药物滥用或童年时期遭受身体、性或情感虐待的后遗症困扰，那么有很多医疗、心理和生化干预措施无需投入大量时间和金钱。短期互动式心理治疗、新型抗抑郁药物、互助小组、十二步疗法和个人成长研讨会，在过去十年中彻底改变了传统心理治疗的面貌。只要真心需要帮助，总能找到办法。

LET’S START WITH THE FEELINGS

让我们从感受开始

Chances are, you know what you do when your hot buttons get pushed. Maybe you’re a people pleaser. Or you read about the Atlas syndrome and say, “That’s me.” Perhaps you avoid anger like the plague. As we begin this vital work of burning off the FOG, I want you to focus on which element or elements of the FOG you’re most sensitive to. Take a quick inventory by checking the items below that apply to you.

很有可能，你知道当别人触及你的痛点时你会怎么做。也许你是个讨好型人格。或者你读过关于阿特拉斯综合症的文章，然后说：“这说的就是我。”也许你像躲避瘟疫一样躲避愤怒。在我们开始这项至关重要的“驱散迷雾”工作时，我希望你专注于你对迷雾中的哪些元素最为敏感。请快速盘点一下，勾选以下符合你情况的选项。

When I give in to someone who’s pressuring me, I do it because:

当我屈服于他人的压力时，我这样做是因为：

  1. I’m afraid of their disapproval.
    我害怕他们的反对。
  2. I’m afraid of their anger.
    我害怕他们的愤怒。
  3. I’m afraid they won’t like/love me anymore and may even leave me.
    我担心他们会不再喜欢/爱我，甚至会离开我。
  4. I owe it to them.
    我亏欠他们。
  5. They’ve done so much for me, I can’t say no.
    他们为我做了这么多，我不能拒绝。
  6. It’s my duty.
    这是我的职责。
  7. I’ll feel too guilty if I don’t.
    如果我不这么做，我会感到非常内疚。
  8. I’ll feel selfish/unloving/greedy/mean if I don’t.
    如果我不这样做，我会觉得自己很自私/冷漠/贪婪/卑鄙。
  9. I won’t be a good person if I don’t.
    如果我不这样做，我就不是一个好人。

You’ll notice that the first three statements relate to fear, the second three to obligation and the last three to guilt. It may be that most, or even all, of these statements ring true for you. They did for Eve, who felt afraid of other people’s disapproval if she tried to extricate herself from Elliot’s smothering dependency, obligated to him because he had given her a place to live and paid her bills, and overwhelmed with guilt at the thought of abandoning him.

你会注意到，前三句话与恐惧有关，中间三句与责任有关，最后三句与内疚有关。或许这些话大部分，甚至全部，都能引起你的共鸣。伊芙就是如此，她害怕如果试图摆脱埃利奥特令人窒息的依赖，会遭到别人的反对；她觉得有义务照顾他，因为他给了她住处，还帮她支付账单；而一想到要抛弃他，她就感到无比内疚。

In other people, hot buttons tend to be wired to one dominant feeling, although there may be a good deal of overlap among the three feeling states. For example, Liz didn’t feel particularly obligated or guilty, but she was afraid of Michael’s anger. The statements above will help you figure out which hot button is front and center for you and which element—or elements—of FOG you need to work on for deep and lasting change to take hold.

对另一些人来说，情绪触发点往往与一种主导情绪相关，尽管三种情绪状态之间可能存在相当多的重叠。例如，莉兹并不觉得特别有义务或内疚，但她害怕迈克尔的愤怒。以上描述将帮助你找出对你而言最主要的情绪触发点，以及你需要着手解决的“情绪迷雾”（FOG）中的哪些因素，才能实现深刻而持久的改变。

DISCONNECTING THE FEAR BUTTON

解除恐惧按钮

Fear is a basic survival mechanism that’s designed to move us out of harm’s way. It is both an instinctive and a learned response to danger. If two guys in ski masks are demanding your money, you’re going to be afraid. If your husband or wife threatens to take the kids if you leave, you’re going to be afraid.

恐惧是一种基本的生存机制，旨在让我们远离危险。它既是对危险的本能反应，也是后天习得的反应。如果两个戴着滑雪面罩的人向你索要钱财，你会感到害怕。如果你的丈夫或妻子威胁说，如果你离开他们就带走孩子，你也会感到害怕。

But a lot of the fears we experience in emotional blackmail come up as we anticipate dangers that may or may not exist. The blackmailers in our lives intuitively play on those fears and magnify them. Catastrophic images snowball in our minds, becoming so vivid they seem absolutely real. So we adjust our actions to ward off the emotional blows we’re sure are coming. Dealing effectively with fear involves training ourselves to put aside our obsessive worst-case scenarios and develop positive options. You’ve been letting your imagination work against you. Now let it work for you.

但我们在情感勒索中体验到的许多恐惧，都源于我们对可能存在也可能不存在的危险的预判。生活中的勒索者会本能地利用这些恐惧，并将其放大。灾难性的画面在我们脑海中不断累积，变得如此生动逼真，仿佛触手可及。于是，我们调整自己的行为，以抵御那些我们确信即将到来、却无动于衷的情感打击。有效应对恐惧的关键在于训练自己放下那些挥之不去的极端假设，并制定积极的应对方案。你一直在让你的想象力与你作对。现在，让它为你所用吧。

Fear of Disapproval

害怕被否定

This fear may sound insignificant, but believe me, for many people it is excruciating. The fear of disapproval is much deeper than cringing if someone goes “Tsk-tsk” over something you’ve said or done. It is interwoven with our basic sense of self-worth. If we allow other people’s approval or disapproval to define us, we set ourselves up to believe that there is something fundamentally wrong with us whenever we incur displeasure.

这种恐惧听起来或许微不足道，但相信我，对很多人来说，它却痛苦不堪。害怕被否定远比别人对你的言行发出“啧啧”声而感到尴尬要深刻得多。它与我们最基本的自我价值感紧密相连。如果我们允许他人的认可或否定来定义我们，那么每当我们感到不快时，我们就会让自己相信，我们自身存在着根本性的缺陷。

We all love approval and praise from others, and it can sometimes seem like an absolute essential. Many years ago, before I went back to school to become a therapist, I made my living as an actress. I loved it when my efforts were greeted with applause and approval, and I rode the roller coaster to the depths when they weren’t. I gauged how well I was doing on the basis of how other people responded to me. But as I’ve gotten older, I have made a wonderful discovery. I’ve taken many risks in my life, and I’ve found that I can tolerate the thundering silence of someone’s disapproval or even harsh criticism as long as I stay connected to my integrity.

我们都渴望得到他人的认可和赞扬，有时甚至觉得这是绝对必要的。很多年前，在我重返校园成为一名心理治疗师之前，我曾是一名演员。我喜欢我的努力得到掌声和认可，也喜欢没有得到认可时那种跌入谷底的痛苦。我常常根据别人对我的反应来衡量自己的表现。但随着年龄的增长，我有了一个美好的发现。我一生中承担过许多风险，我发现，只要我坚守自己的原则，即使面对他人的不赞同，甚至是严厉的批评，我也能承受得住。

I know it’s not easy to hold on to that connection when people you value tell you you’re wrong, but it can be done.

我知道，当你重视的人告诉你你错了的时候，要维持这种关系并不容易，但这并非不可能。

Sarah’s relationship with Frank had been improving steadily since she’d made him aware of how much he’d been making her pass little tests to earn the right to marry him.

自从莎拉让弗兰克意识到他为了让她赢得嫁给他的权利而让她通过了多少小考验之后，莎拉和弗兰克的关系就一直在稳步改善。

The talks we’re having are helping a lot, but I still can’t shake off the idea that I can’t feel good about myself or my decisions unless he says they’re OK. I keep trying to tell myself to grow up and get over it, but it’s not working. I don’t want to wind up like my mother, who couldn’t even cross the street without getting my father’s permission.

我们之间的谈话很有帮助，但我仍然无法摆脱这种想法：除非他认可，否则我无法对自己或自己的决定感到满意。我一直告诉自己要成熟起来，别再纠结了，但这根本行不通。我不想变成我母亲那样，连过马路都要征得父亲的同意。

A SPECIAL KIND OF COURAGE

一种特殊的勇气

Freeing yourself from the fear of disapproval involves knowing which values and judgments belong to you and which have been imposed from the outside. It means knowing what you value about yourself and then having the courage to stand up to disapproval and hold on to your own beliefs and desires.

摆脱对他人反对的恐惧，意味着要明白哪些价值观和判断源于自身，哪些是外在强加的。这意味着要了解自己珍视的品质，然后鼓起勇气面对反对，坚持自己的信念和愿望。

Sarah was full of excitement when she reported how she had done just that.

莎拉兴奋地汇报了她是如何做到这一点的。

You asked me to think about the best parts of me, and what I put at the top of the list were my spirit and my loving a challenge. My business is the way I feed both of those, and I didn’t have to think hard to know that I had to move ahead with expanding it. I love Frank, but he’s not my whole life. I told him that if he would take some time to think about it, he’d see that I’ll be a lot more fun to live with if I’m truly excited about what I’m doing. He mumbled and grumbled a little bit, but I kept using the nondefensive phrases, and he saw I wasn’t going to back down. He’s fine with it now. I feel like it’s Christmas!

你让我想想自己身上最棒的品质，我把活力和热爱挑战放在首位。我的事业正是我滋养这两点的途径，我毫不犹豫地意识到我必须继续拓展它。我爱弗兰克，但他不是我生活的全部。我告诉他，如果他能花点时间好好想想，就会明白，如果我真的对自己的事业充满热情，和我一起生活会更有趣。他嘟囔了几句，但我坚持用不带防御性的措辞，他明白我不会退缩。现在他接受了。感觉就像过圣诞节一样！

Eve’s circumstances were different from Sarah’s. Sarah had a successful career and a potentially solid relationship. Eve was facing many unknowns—and the job of rebuilding her life—but she too was starting to calm her fear of disapproval.

伊芙的境遇与莎拉截然不同。莎拉事业有成，感情生活也看似稳定。而伊芙则面临着诸多未知，还要重建自己的生活，但她也开始慢慢平复内心对他人不认可的恐惧。

I’ve had all these voices coming at me for so long: “You’re a cold-hearted bitch.” “You’re unfeeling.” “What a moronic thing to do.” “Everything you do is silly.” But I’m not going to worry so much about what people think, because what people think in this world can be pretty weird. There are people who think the Holocaust never happened!

长久以来，我一直被各种各样的声音包围着：“你是个冷血的婊子。”“你毫无感情。”“你做的真是蠢透了。”“你做的每件事都很愚蠢。”但我不会太在意别人的想法，因为这世上的人想法真是千奇百怪。竟然有人认为纳粹大屠杀从未发生过！

On the other side of the fear of disapproval is the freedom to imagine and create a life that really belongs to you. I’m not going to pretend it’s easy, but every time you make the commitment to steer your own ship, as Sarah and Eve did, you take a giant step toward shaping a life that reflects what you know and what you believe is right for you—no matter what anyone else may think or say. When you do that, you’ll be able to kick your addiction to approval.

克服了对他人反对的恐惧之后，你将拥有自由去想象和创造真正属于自己的生活。我不会假装这很容易，但每当你像莎拉和夏娃那样，下定决心掌控自己的人生航向时，你就朝着塑造一个反映你所知所信、真正适合自己的生活迈出了重要一步——无论别人怎么想怎么说。当你做到这一点时，你就能摆脱对他人认可的依赖。

Fear of Anger

对愤怒的恐惧

Michael made good on his promise to work on his anger, but it didn’t take Liz long to see that he wasn’t the only one who needed to deal with that emotion. She said:

迈克尔信守承诺，努力控制自己的愤怒情绪，但莉兹很快就意识到，需要处理这种情绪的并非只有他一人。她说：

The other night he tripped on a toy one of the kids had left out, and he started to swear and yell. I was in the other room and he wasn’t even yelling at me, but just the sound of his voice made my heart race. He’s really been trying to change, and I thought everything would be fine once he got a handle on his anger, but I’m still so sensitive. . . . I don’t want to go through life going into a panic every time somebody raises their voice.

那天晚上他被孩子们留下的玩具绊倒了，开始破口大骂。我当时在另一个房间，他甚至都没冲我吼，但光是听到他的声音就让我心跳加速。他一直在努力改变，我以为只要他能控制住自己的脾气，一切都会好起来，但我还是那么敏感……我不想以后每次有人提高嗓门就惊慌失措。

Liz wasn’t afraid that Michael would physically harm her. Certainly there had been verbal abuse, but she insisted there was never even a hint that he would go any further. So what was it that was creating such a strong visceral reaction in her?

莉兹并不害怕迈克尔会对她进行身体上的伤害。当然，他确实对她进行过言语虐待，但她坚称他从未有过任何进一步伤害她的迹象。那么，究竟是什么让她产生了如此强烈的本能反应呢？

I asked her three questions:

我问了她三个问题：

  1. What are you afraid of?
    你害怕什么？
  2. What’s the worst thing that could happen?
    最糟糕的情况会是什么？
  3. What’s your fantasy of what could happen?
    你幻想接下来会发生什么？

I guess I’m afraid that he’ll lose control and run right over me. It’s hard to explain. I get this sense of being about two years old and totally helpless. When he’s mad, it’s like this engulfing, devouring heat. . . .

我猜我害怕他会失控，直接撞到我身上。很难解释。我感觉自己像个两岁小孩，完全无助。他生气的时候，就像一股吞噬一切的热浪……

The sound of Michael’s yelling transports Liz through time. She’s no longer a 35-year-old adult; she becomes a little girl who hears only danger in a raised voice. That’s hardly a surprise given that she grew up in a volatile family where yelling was a cue to duck and take cover. But like many blackmail targets who bend over backward to calm or avoid anger, she kept getting the past mixed up with the present. I told Liz that at some point it would be a good idea to talk to her father and brother about how afraid she used to feel, but for now I wanted her to focus on dealing with Michael’s “slips.”

迈克尔的吼叫声仿佛将莉兹带回了过去。她不再是35岁的成年人，而是变成了一个小女孩，听到提高的嗓门就觉得危险。考虑到她成长在一个动荡不安的家庭，吼叫声意味着要赶紧躲起来，这也就不足为奇了。但就像许多被勒索的对象一样，为了平息或避免愤怒而百般讨好，她总是把过去和现在混淆起来。我告诉莉兹，她最好找个时间和父亲、哥哥谈谈她过去感受到的恐惧，但现在我希望她先集中精力应对迈克尔的“失言”。

No one teaches us how to deal with another person’s anger, and most of us have a limited repertoire of responses. The first thing you need to do with a yeller is to choose a calm moment and put them on notice. Say to that person: “I’m not willing to be yelled at, and the next time you yell at me I’m going to walk out of the room.” Right away you’ve taken a strong position and become proactive on your own behalf. Then you need to follow through the next time it happens so the other person will take you seriously.

没有人教过我们如何应对他人的愤怒，而且我们大多数人能做的也十分有限。遇到大吼大叫的人，首先要做的就是找个安静的时机，警告对方。你可以对对方说：“我不允许别人对我大吼大叫，下次你再对我大吼大叫，我就走出房间。” 这样，你就立刻表明了自己的立场，并主动维护了自己的权益。下次再发生类似的事情时，你一定要说到做到，这样对方才会认真对待你。

At the same time you are removing yourself from the conflict, say any of the following in a strong, clear voice: “Stop it!” or “Knock it off!” or, my personal favorite, “Put a sock in it!” Liz looked at me with astonishment. “I can really do that?” she asked.

在你让自己置身冲突之外的同时，用坚定清晰的声音说以下任何一句话：“住手！”或“别闹了！”或者，我个人最喜欢的，“闭嘴！”莉兹惊讶地看着我。“我真的可以这么做吗？”她问。

“Why not?” I told her. “You have my permission.”

“为什么不行？”我告诉她，“我允许你这么做。”

We often imagine other people’s yelling escalating to the point where they lose control and resort to violence. (If you truly fear that another person will harm you, you don’t belong in a relationship with them.) But most of us have rarely imagined what would happen if we responded in a more powerful, confident way. Once you step out of the role of fearful little girl or boy and behave like the adult you are now, you’re on your way to conquering the fear of anger that triggers so much compliance.

我们常常想象别人的叫喊声不断升级，最终失控诉诸暴力。（如果你真的害怕别人会伤害你，那么你就不应该和他们保持关系。）但我们大多数人很少想象，如果我们以更强大、更自信的方式回应，会发生什么。一旦你不再扮演胆怯的小女孩或小男孩的角色，而是像一个成熟的成年人那样行事，你就走上了克服对愤怒的恐惧之路，而这种恐惧正是导致你过度顺从的原因。

REWRITING HISTORY

改写历史

An exercise that I have found invaluable for helping blackmail targets handle anger more confidently involves replaying a recent incident when you gave in to someone because you were afraid.

我发现，对于帮助勒索受害者更自信地处理愤怒情绪，一个非常有价值的练习是：重温最近一次因为害怕而向某人屈服的事件。

Close your eyes. Rerun the words they said, listen to what you said, and conjure up the memories—the anxiety, the pounding heart, the weak knees, the catastrophic images that ran through your mind as you imagined their anger getting loose and coming at you.

闭上眼睛。回想他们说过的话，听听你说过的话，回忆起那些记忆——焦虑、怦怦直跳的心、发软的双腿，以及想象着他们的怒火爆发并向你袭来时，脑海中浮现的灾难性画面。

Now play the scene again, but this time, when you see the other person’s anger rising, rewrite the scene. Firmly and clearly say, “No. I’m not giving in! Stop pressuring me!” Repeat these phrases until they’re convincing—most people start out very tentatively. Listen to how the words sound, and feel how much stronger you are. Yes, you can say that, and yes, the words do empower you.

现在再演练一遍，但这次，当对方的怒气开始升腾时，改写一下场景。坚定而清晰地说：“不！我不会让步！别再逼我了！”反复说这些话，直到你觉得它们很有说服力——大多数人一开始都会很犹豫。听听这些话听起来如何，感受一下你的力量增强了多少。是的，你可以这么说，而且这些话确实能赋予你力量。

Rewrite as many blackmail scenes from your life as you like, as often as you like, unleashing your imagination to experience what it’s like to reclaim your personal power. It’s especially important to do this exercise if you’ve been dealing with punishers because they can be so frightening to us. Fear is their modus operandi.

尽情重写你生活中遭遇勒索的场景，次数不限，释放你的想象力，体验重获个人力量的感觉。如果你曾与施暴者打过交道，这项练习尤为重要，因为他们会让我们感到恐惧。恐惧是他们的惯用伎俩。

PLAYING THE BLACKMAILER

扮演勒索者

“One reason I’m so scared of the anger,” Liz told me, “is that when I feel it coming at me, it’s like the person behind it just disappears. There’s no Michael anymore—just this blast of yelling.”

“我如此害怕愤怒的原因之一，”莉兹告诉我，“就是当我感觉到愤怒袭来时，愤怒背后的那个人就好像消失了一样。迈克尔不见了——只剩下一阵怒吼。”

I told Liz that I wanted her to step into the role of “The Yeller” and give me an imitation of Michael at his worst.

我告诉莉兹，我想让她扮演“爱叫的人”，模仿迈克尔最糟糕的样子。

“You’re kidding, right?” she said. “I can’t do that.”

“你在开玩笑吧？”她说道，“我做不到。”

“Just push past the self-consciousness and give it a try,” I said. “Some interesting things might happen. Standing in the blackmailer’s shoes for a few minutes can be very revealing.”

“克服一下自己的不自在，试一试，”我说。“也许会发生一些有趣的事情。设身处地地站在勒索者的角度思考几分钟，可能会让你豁然开朗。”

Liz began hesitantly, but warmed up to the task and launched into an approximation of Michael on the warpath.

莉兹一开始有些犹豫，但很快就进入状态，开始模仿迈克尔在战争中的气势。

If you think you’re walking out on me you’ve got another thing coming. You’re not breaking up this family, and if you try, I’m going to make you regret it! You won’t get a penny, and I’m not going to let you take the kids! Do you hear me?

你要是以为能一走了之，那就大错特错了。你休想拆散这个家，要是你敢这么做，我会让你后悔莫及！你一分钱也别想拿到，孩子们也别想带走！听见了吗？

When Liz stopped she was very quiet for a moment. Then she said,

莉兹停下脚步，沉默了一会儿。然后她说：

It was the strangest thing. I didn’t feel powerful at all saying those things. I felt scared and almost helpless, like someone was trying to take something away from me that I really wanted, and the only way I could keep from crying was to yell and scream. I felt like a kid having a tantrum — I didn’t have the right words to say, so I just made a lot of noise.

那感觉真是太奇怪了。说出那些话的时候，我一点也不觉得有力量。我感到害怕，几乎无助，好像有人要从我身边夺走我真正想要的东西，而我唯一能忍住不哭的方法就是大喊大叫。我感觉自己像个耍脾气的孩子——我不知道该说什么，所以就胡乱叫喊。

If the blackmailer in your life expresses anger silently, get into the sullen, withdrawn mode and tune into what’s going on inside you. See if you can get in touch with how afraid you are of anger and how ineffectual you feel.

如果生活中勒索你的人默默地表达愤怒，那就让自己变得阴郁、孤僻，仔细感受自己内心的情绪。看看你是否能体会到自己对愤怒的恐惧以及无力感。

Whatever kind of anger you portray, you’ll realize that the person you have seen as powerful and in charge is really something of an emotional coward—that’s what bullying is all about. Confident, secure people don’t need to push others around to get what they want or to prove how strong they are. You may know this intellectually, but “becoming” that person will allow you to experience that awareness physically and emotionally as well.

无论你表现出怎样的愤怒，你都会意识到，你一直视为强大掌控一切的人，实际上却是一个情感上的懦夫——这就是霸凌的本质。自信、有安全感的人不需要通过欺凌他人来获得自己想要的东西，也不需要通过这种方式来证明自己的强大。你或许在理智上明白这一点，但“成为”那样的人，会让你在身心两方面都真正体验到这种觉悟。

It is an awareness that can go a long way toward helping you deal with anger, whether you ultimately decide to continue in a relationship with this person or not. Loud, angry punishers and passive-aggressive sulkers are really frightened little kids inside. That doesn’t make their behavior any less unacceptable—but it can make it less scary.

这种意识能极大地帮助你应对愤怒，无论你最终是否决定继续与这个人保持关系。那些大声咆哮、愤怒地惩罚别人，以及消极攻击、闷闷不乐的人，内心其实都是害怕的小孩。这并不能减轻他们的行为的恶劣程度，但至少能让他们的行为不那么可怕。

Fear of Change

害怕改变

Nobody likes to make major life changes. What’s familiar is comfortable, and even though it may be making us miserable, at least we know what’s expected of us and what to expect from other people.

没有人喜欢做出重大的生活改变。熟悉的事物令人感到舒适，即使它可能让我们痛苦，但至少我们知道别人对我们的期望是什么，以及对其他人的期望是什么。

Maria was firm in her decision to leave Jay, but she dreaded what lay ahead for her.

玛丽亚决心离开杰伊，但她害怕未来的路会如何。

I’m afraid, Susan. I’m afraid to be a divorced woman out in the world again. I’m afraid of the pain and the grief. I’m afraid of the uncertainty. I’m afraid of having to start over. I’m afraid I won’t know how to make my kids feel safe and secure when it’s just me and them. I’m afraid of what people will think—that it was my failure, that I had everything and I blew it. There’s such a temptation to call the divorce off and go back to my familiar unhappiness—at least I know how to do that.

苏珊，我很害怕。我害怕再次成为一个离异女人，重新踏入社会。我害怕痛苦和悲伤。我害怕前途未卜。我害怕一切都要重新开始。我害怕当只有我和孩子们相依为命时，我不知道该如何让他们感到安全和安心。我害怕别人会怎么想——他们会觉得这是我的失败，觉得我曾经拥有一切，却最终搞砸了。我多么想取消离婚，回到我熟悉的痛苦之中——至少我知道该怎么做。

Maria could play her assigned role of dutiful wife and mother like a pro, and she knew how to behave in the context of familiar situations. But that comfort, of course, was the problem—it was hard to give up. As soon as we contemplate making any kind of major change, almost all of us feel some degree of panic. And it’s that panic that the more destructive blackmailers feed on. So we stay in our old behavior patterns and often cling to harmful relationships and situations to assuage the anxiety and insecurities that threaten to overwhelm us.

玛丽亚能像个老手一样扮演好贤妻良母的角色，她也懂得在熟悉的环境中如何得体行事。但这种舒适感恰恰是问题所在——放弃它并非易事。几乎所有人都会在考虑做出任何重大改变时感到某种程度的恐慌。而正是这种恐慌，被那些更具破坏性的勒索者所利用。因此，我们固守旧有的行为模式，常常为了缓解那些几乎要将我们吞噬的焦虑和不安，而紧紧抓住那些有害的关系和环境不放。

I told Maria that I had stayed in a bad marriage for years longer than I should have because I had been afraid of all the same things she was.

我告诉玛丽亚，我之所以在一段糟糕的婚姻中待了那么久，是因为我害怕和她一样的事情。

“It really helps to know that,” she said, “and it helps to know that I’m not some kind of freak or weirdo because I feel this way.”

“知道这一点真的很有帮助，”她说，“知道我这样想并不是因为我是个怪胎或异类，这很有帮助。”

The fear of change is universal, and blackmailers often exploit that fear with statements like:

人们普遍害怕改变，而勒索者常常利用这种恐惧，说出诸如此类的话：

  • You’re going to be really lonely without me.
    没有我，你会非常孤独的。
  • You’ll be sorry, and then it will be too late.
    你会后悔的，到那时就太晚了。
  • It’s really rough out there for single women.
    单身女性的日子真的不好过。
  • How can you do this to the kids?
    你怎么能这样对待孩子？
  • You’re just not thinking clearly—you don’t know what you want.
    你现在思路不清——你不知道自己想要什么。
  • Look at all the miserable divorced people out there.
    看看外面那些痛苦的离婚人士吧。

It’s perfectly OK to acknowledge your fears to them, but as you do, also reiterate your commitment to change. Say something like “You may be right, and I know it won’t be easy, but I’m still going to get a divorce.” Or if it’s another type of relationship you might say, “I appreciate your concern”—and nothing further. If others persist in painting a gloomy picture of the future to which you’ve doomed yourself, go back to your nondefensive communication and say, “I choose not to discuss this anymore.” Remember: You have as much right to talk about or not talk about something as they do!

向他们坦诚你的恐惧完全没问题，但同时，也要重申你改变的决心。你可以说：“你说的或许有道理，我知道这并不容易，但我还是会离婚。”或者，如果是其他类型的关系，你可以说：“感谢你的关心”，然后就不要再说别的了。如果对方执意描绘你注定要面对的悲观未来，那就回到你平和的沟通方式，说：“我不想再讨论这件事了。”记住：你和他们一样，都有权利选择谈论或不谈论某件事！

When you decide to leave or cut off from an important person in your life, you enter a state of crisis—a time of intense emotional upheaval and uncertainty. But crisis is not just a time of danger. When managed thoughtfully and with courage, crisis is also a marvelous opportunity for personal growth and a better life.

当你决定离开或断绝与生命中重要之人的联系时，你便进入了危机状态——一段充满强烈情绪波动和不确定性的时期。但危机并非仅仅是危险的时刻。如果能够深思熟虑、勇敢应对，危机也能成为个人成长和通往更美好生活的绝佳契机。

This is a good time to find some kind of group or seminar with people in similar situations. To find one, start by asking friends and people you feel comfortable with to recommend programs you know have worked for them. Community colleges and universities have many adult evening programs, and churches and synagogues have formed many support groups that are open to the public. The YWCA or YWHA and women’s centers will have a list of resources, and you can call the American Psychological Association for a referral. You don’t have to tough it out all by yourself. You need to make sure, however, that the group you’ve joined is one in which people are working on changing and not just sitting around saying “Ain’t it awful” and telling war stories. There is a wonderful healing energy that emanates from people supporting each other through rough times and working toward rebuilding their confidence so that change can become a challenge and not an enemy.

现在正是寻找一些与你处境相似的人组成的互助小组或研讨会的好时机。你可以先询问朋友和你信任的人，让他们推荐一些对他们有效的项目。社区学院和大学有很多面向成人的晚间课程，教堂和犹太教堂也成立了许多面向公众的互助小组。基督教女青年会（YWCA）或基督教女青年会（YWHA）以及妇女中心通常会提供资源清单，你也可以致电美国心理学会寻求推荐。你无需独自承受一切。但是，你需要确保你加入的小组是大家共同努力改变的，而不是只是坐在那里抱怨“真是太糟糕了”，讲述各自的“苦难经历”。当人们在困境中互相扶持，努力重建自信时，会散发出一种奇妙的治愈能量，让改变成为一种挑战，而不是敌人。

Fear of Abandonment

害怕被抛弃

The fear of abandonment might be the mother of all fears. Some experts believe it’s encoded in our genes and is the endpoint of all our relationship fears, including the fear of disapproval and the fear of anger. I really don’t think it matters whether it’s an instinctive or learned fear or a combination of the two. The bottom line is that we all feel it. Some people manage it pretty well, but for others, this fear is profound. When the fear of abandonment causes us to capitulate repeatedly in a self-defeating way, it’s as if we were saying “I’ll do anything—just don’t leave me.”

被抛弃的恐惧或许是所有恐惧之母。一些专家认为它根植于我们的基因，是我们所有关系恐惧的最终归宿，包括害怕被否定和害怕被愤怒。我认为，这种恐惧是本能的、后天习得的，还是两者兼而有之，其实并不重要。关键在于，我们每个人都能感受到它。有些人能很好地应对，但对另一些人来说，这种恐惧却根深蒂固。当被抛弃的恐惧驱使我们一次又一次地做出自我挫败的妥协时，就好像我们在说：“我什么都愿意做——只要你别离开我。”

Lynn took great comfort when Jeff agreed not to walk out on her during an argument without letting her know where he was and when he would be back. But her fear of abandonment, which had been part of her for many years, didn’t disappear overnight.

杰夫同意不会在争吵时一声不响地离开，不告诉琳恩他在哪里，什么时候回来，这让琳恩感到很欣慰。但她多年来一直存在的被抛弃的恐惧并没有在一夜之间消失。

This really keeps me stuck. If someone gets upset with me, I know they’ll wind up leaving me, so I’ll just do what they want. I know it’s the coward’s way out, but I don’t care.

这真的让我很纠结。如果有人生我的气，我知道他们最终会离开我，所以我只能照他们说的做。我知道这是懦夫的做法，但我不在乎。

It’s a big and not too logical jump from “You get mad at me” to “You’ll leave me alone forever,” but negative thinking isn’t logical, and it can easily escalate, turning a simple disagreement into the first step into the abyss.

从“你生我的气”到“你会永远离开我”，这是一个很大的、不太合乎逻辑的跳跃，但消极的想法是不合逻辑的，而且很容易升级，将简单的分歧变成坠入深渊的第一步。

If, like Lynn, you get pulled into a whirlpool of calamitous thoughts, one of the best ways to escape is to actively limit the amount of time and attention you give them.

如果你像琳恩一样陷入了灾难性想法的漩涡中，那么摆脱这种漩涡的最好方法之一就是主动限制你给予这些想法的时间和注意力。

THOUGHT-STOPPING

令人深思

For the next week I’d like you to set aside some time to focus on your negative thoughts of abandonment. Feel free to turn on the doomsday machine and let the fearsome images pour out. But here’s the trick: You have to set a timer for five minutes and confine your negative thinking to that period only.

接下来的一周，我希望你抽出一些时间，专注于那些关于被抛弃的负面想法。你可以尽情地想象那些可怕的画面，让它们涌上心头。但关键在于：你必须设定一个五分钟的计时器，并将你的负面想法限制在五分钟之内。

You only need to do this once a day. Think of it as your fret-and-worry time. When your five minutes are up, tell your thoughts, as you would any unwelcome guest, that they need to leave. If they come back during the day, tell them they’ve had their time, and you’ll see them tomorrow. Reduce the time period each day until by the fifth day you’re down to one minute. I know this sounds simplistic, but remember: Feelings are triggered by thoughts, no matter how fleeting. We energize our fears by constantly feeding them with mental attention. This thought-stopping technique allows you to interrupt the thought/feeling/behavior continuum at its source and puts you back in the driver’s seat.

你每天只需做一次。把它当作你的“焦虑担忧时间”。五分钟结束后，就像对待不速之客一样，告诉你的思绪该离开了。如果它们在白天再次出现，就告诉它们，它们已经待够了，明天再见。每天逐渐缩短时间，直到第五天缩短到一分钟。我知道这听起来很简单，但请记住：情绪是由想法触发的，无论这些想法多么转瞬即逝。我们不断地用注意力去滋养恐惧，从而强化了恐惧。这种思维阻断技巧能让你从源头上打断想法/情绪/行为的连续体，让你重新掌控自己的命运。

THE BLACK HOLE

黑洞

Thought-stopping during the week helped keep Lynn from spiraling into emotional tailspins, but she still had not confronted the fear of what she called “the black hole,” the place she would fall into—and never be able to get out of—if Jeff left her. Lynn was not the first person to use that term. I’ve heard it many times from people who are terrified of abandonment. It seems to be some universally imagined hell.

一周的“思维阻断”训练帮助琳恩避免陷入情绪的漩涡，但她仍然无法直面她所谓的“黑洞”——如果杰夫离开她，她就会坠入其中，永远无法逃脱。琳恩并非第一个使用这个词的人。我曾多次听到那些害怕被抛弃的人这样形容。这似乎是某种人人都能想象到的地狱。

The black hole had been an image for Lynn as long as she could remember. She was intimately familiar with the dread that surrounded it, and she did not want to cross the threshold and enter. But that, I told her, was what she must do.

黑洞的景象在琳恩的记忆中一直萦绕着她。她对围绕着它的恐惧感无比熟悉，她不想跨过那道门槛，走进去。但我告诉她，那是她必须做的。

“I don’t know if I can,” she said hesitantly.

“我不知道我能不能做到，”她犹豫地说。

“If not today, when?” I asked her. “I want you to take my hand and walk into the black hole with me. What do you see?”

“如果不是今天，那又是什么时候呢？”我问她。“我想让你牵着我的手，和我一起走进黑洞。你会看到什么？”

“It’s dark, and it’s really cold. No human contact. Just isolation with no one to talk to. I’m totally cut off. The days are so long without company . . . The walls close in . . . No one loves me or cares about me or even knows I exist.”

“天黑了，而且非常冷。没有人与人接触。只有孤独，没有人可以说话。我完全与世隔绝了。没有陪伴的日子如此漫长……四面墙壁向我逼近……没有人爱我，没有人关心我，甚至没有人知道我的存在。”

Who wouldn’t choose capitulation when the only other choice seems to be falling into the bleak, depressed state Lynn describes? And how vulnerable to manipulation you are if you pin your emotional survival on one person!

谁会在面临其他选择，似乎只能陷入琳恩所描述的那种凄凉、沮丧的状态时，选择屈服呢？如果你把自己的情感生存寄托在一个人身上，你又是多么容易被操纵啊！

“OK,” I said to Lynn. “You took me in here. Now I want you to find a way out.”

“好吧，”我对琳恩说，“是你收留了我。现在我希望你能想办法出去。”

“Yeah, right,” said Lynn. “I’ll just wave my magic wand and the terror will disappear.”

“是啊，没错，”琳恩说，“我只要挥动魔法棒，恐惧就会消失。”

“You can get out of here, you know.”

“你知道，你可以离开这里。”

“Only Jeff can get me out,” she replied.

“只有杰夫才能救我出去，”她回答说。

“No—this one you have to do by yourself or it won’t mean anything. I’m not discounting how much Jeff means to you, but he’s only one of the elements that enrich your life. Let’s start some creative thinking here. What’s the opposite of the black hole for you?”

“不——这件事你必须自己做，否则毫无意义。我不是说杰夫对你有多重要，但他只是丰富你生活的众多元素之一。咱们来发挥一下创造力。对你来说，黑洞的反义词是什么？”

Lynn shut her eyes. “I’m thinking of the other people in my life that I care about—my folks, my friends, some really neat people at work . . . things I love to do—wait, there’s a special day I remember. I’m about 12 and my dad got me my first horse—a beautiful palomino. I couldn’t believe it! He was all mine. I remember the smell of the hay, the sun on my face . . . I think that’s the closest to complete happiness I’ve ever been.”

琳恩闭上眼睛。“我在想我生命中其他我关心的人——我的父母、我的朋友、一些很棒的同事……还有我喜欢做的事情——等等，我记得一个特别的日子。我大概12岁的时候，爸爸给我买了我的第一匹马——一匹漂亮的帕洛米诺马。我简直不敢相信！它完全属于我了。我记得干草的味道，阳光洒在脸上的感觉……我想那是我最接近完全幸福的时刻。”

“And you can go back to that place whenever you feel yourself panicking,” I told her. “You can recapture all the sensual pleasures and the excitement anytime you choose. And you can have other days like that. You have a husband and other people who love you, and a good career, and the capacity to feel things deeply. What wonderful gifts! You see—you found your way out of the black hole by yourself!”

“每当你感到恐慌时，你都可以回到那个地方，”我告诉她。“你可以随时重拾所有感官上的愉悦和兴奋。而且你以后还会有那样的日子。你有丈夫，有爱你的人，有不错的事业，还有感受事物深刻的能力。多么美好的礼物啊！你看——你自己找到了走出困境的方法！”

The kind of visualization that Lynn did is one we can all do when we feel frightened. Sit down, close your eyes, and take four or five deep breaths. Now remember one of the best days of your life. It might be a day in childhood when you didn’t have a care in the world. Or maybe you’ll want to return to a beautiful place you visited where all your senses were acute and absorbing the romance and beauty of what surrounded you. Fill up your mind and body with that day, the sights and sounds, the feel of the air, the perfume of flowers or fresh-cut grass. Let yourself fully experience that day until the memories calm you. Remember that you can always use this visualization as a way of bringing light to the black hole.

琳恩做的这种冥想练习，我们每个人在感到害怕的时候都可以做。坐下来，闭上眼睛，深呼吸四五次。现在，回想一下你生命中最美好的日子之一。也许是童年时无忧无虑的一天。又或许，你想回到曾经去过的某个美丽的地方，在那里，你的所有感官都异常敏锐，沉浸在周围的浪漫与美好之中。让你的身心都充满那一天的景象、声音、空气的气息、花香或青草的芬芳。让自己完全沉浸在那一天，直到回忆抚平你的伤痛。记住，你可以随时运用这种冥想练习，为内心的黑暗带来光明。

The fear of abandonment that we feel in love relationships is the adult version of the fear of abandonment we felt as children, when we couldn’t survive if we were left alone. Unfortunately, many adults still believe they will face some sort of psychological death if someone they are bonded to leaves them. But the black hole exists only in the imagination. It is a lie masquerading as the truth.

我们在恋爱关系中感受到的被抛弃的恐惧，其实是童年时期那种害怕被抛弃的恐惧的成人版——那时我们害怕如果被独自留下就无法生存。不幸的是，许多成年人仍然相信，如果自己所依恋的人离开，他们就会经历某种心理上的死亡。但这种“黑洞”只存在于想象之中，它不过是伪装成真相的谎言。

The joyful, precious people and experiences that nourish us tend to fall from our minds when we are frightened. But they’re available to all of us both in reality and through our memory and imagination. If fear is like a dark river running through you, you can create stepping stones in the midst of that darkness to help yourself across.

那些滋养我们、令我们快乐珍贵的人和事，在我们恐惧时往往会被我们遗忘。但它们其实触手可及，既存在于现实之中，也存在于我们的记忆和想象之中。如果恐惧如同黑暗的河流在你体内奔涌，你可以在这片黑暗中筑起阶梯，帮助自己渡过难关。

DISCONNECTING THE OBLIGATION BUTTON

断开义务按钮

I wish somebody could assign us to obligation brackets the way the government assigns us to tax brackets. Wouldn’t it simplify our lives if we had a formula for figuring out how much we owe to other people instead of constantly having to wrestle with this dilemma on our own? Wouldn’t it be great if there were clear guidelines for knowing how much giving is too much or not enough, figuring out when giving is helpful and when it’s harmful or determining how to balance our obligations to others with our very real and vitally important obligations to ourselves?

我真希望有人能像政府划分税级那样，把我们划分到不同的义务等级。如果我们能有一个公式来计算我们欠别人多少，而不是总是独自为此苦恼，那该多好啊！如果能有明确的指导方针，告诉我们付出多少才算合适，付出何时有益何时有害，以及如何在对他人的义务和我们对自己至关重要的义务之间找到平衡，那该多好啊！

We are not born with a concept of obligation. We learn it from our parents, in school, from religion and politics and the culture at large. And to complicate matters further, we get bombarded with new rules all the time. For many years, sacrifice and altruism were seen as desirable. Then came the “Me Generation,” with its mantra of “Do your own thing.” Then the pendulum swung back toward a more compassionate and caring way of relating to others. No wonder we’re confused.

我们并非生来就具备义务的概念。我们从父母、学校、宗教、政治以及整个文化中学习义务。更复杂的是，我们不断受到各种新规则的冲击。多年来，牺牲和利他主义被视为美德。随后，“自我一代”兴起，其信条是“做你自己”。之后，风向又转向了更富有同情心和关怀的待人方式。难怪我们会感到困惑。

It’s not easy to sort out where we came by the beliefs about obligation that we’ve made our own. And in the long run, it doesn’t matter. What matters is that you have them—and some of them may be making you vulnerable to blackmail. If you operate from the belief that everyone else’s needs are automatically more important than yours, and if you’ve fallen into a pattern of habitually putting yourself last in any relationship until you exhaust yourself physically, mentally, emotionally, spiritually and financially, it’s time to examine—and change—those beliefs.

要弄清楚我们根深蒂固的关于义务的信念究竟源自何处并不容易。从长远来看，这并不重要。重要的是你拥有这些信念——而其中一些可能让你容易受到勒索。如果你一直认为其他人的需求自动比你的需求更重要，如果你已经习惯性地在任何关系中都把自己放在最后，直到身心俱疲，甚至经济拮据，那么是时候审视并改变这些信念了。

Where Is It Written?

哪里写着？

One of the best ways to start changing some of the beliefs you have about the obligations that are making you feel resentful and stressed out is to see them in black and white. Then you can begin to challenge them.

改变你对那些让你感到怨恨和压力重重的义务的固有观念，最好的方法之一就是把它们看得清清楚楚，然后你就可以开始质疑它们了。

Start by making a list of what the other person expects from you. Here are some suggestions to get you started:

首先列出对方对你的期望。以下是一些建议，可以帮助你入门：

________________ [name] assumes/expects/demands that I will:

[姓名] 认为/期望/要求我将：

  • Drop everything to help them
    放下一切去帮助他们
  • Come running when they call
    一听到呼唤就跑过去
  • Take care of them physically/emotionally/financially
    在身体、情感和经济上照顾他们
  • Always do what they want during holidays, vacations or leisure time
    在节假日、假期或休闲时间，总是满足他们的愿望。
  • Listen to their problems no matter how I’m feeling
    无论我心情如何，我都会倾听他们的问题。
  • Always bail them out of trouble
    总是帮他们摆脱困境。
  • Put my work, interests, friends and activities last
    把我的工作、兴趣、朋友和活动放在最后
  • Never leave them even if they make me miserable
    即使他们让我痛苦，也永远不要离开他们。

Now, rewrite each statement by preceding it with the phrase “WHERE IS IT WRITTEN” in capital letters. Notice how different “WHERE IS IT WRITTEN that I’m not allowed to enjoy the holidays because I have to be with my husband’s family?” sounds, looks and feels from “My husband expects that we’ll always go to his family for the holidays.” WHERE IS IT WRITTEN that everyone else’s needs are more important than yours? WHERE IS IT WRITTEN that you are supposed to sacrifice your well-being to take care of a demanding parent who is perfectly capable of taking care of herself? WHERE IS IT WRITTEN? These seemingly immutable rules, which are keeping you from treating yourself even half as well as you treat other people, are not etched in stone. They exist only in the belief system that is seared into your mind about how you are supposed to be in the world.

现在，请在每句话前面加上大写的“哪里写着呢？”。注意一下，“哪里写着我不能享受假期，因为我必须和丈夫的家人在一起？”和“我丈夫期望我们总是去他家过节”听起来、看起来和感觉起来有多么不同。哪里写着别人的需求比你的需求更重要？哪里写着你应该牺牲自己的幸福去照顾一个完全有能力照顾自己的、却又要求苛刻的父母？哪里写着呢？这些看似不可更改的规则，让你无法像对待别人那样善待自己，但它们并非铁律。它们只存在于你脑海中根深蒂固的关于你应该如何在这个世界上生存的信念体系中。

Commuting Your Sentence

减刑

Karen had a difficult time letting go of her deeply ingrained “I-owe-my-daughter-anything-she-wants-because-she’s-had-such-a-hard-time-and-it’s-all-my-fault” litany of self-flagellation. She needed to deal with her feelings of obligation on an emotional as well as an intellectual level.

凯伦很难摆脱根深蒂固的“我欠女儿的一切，她想要什么我都给她，因为她受了很多苦，这都是我的错”这种自我责备的念头。她需要在情感和理智层面都处理好这种责任感。

Karen had been judge and jury and sentenced herself to “obligation jail” for a crime she didn’t even commit—the car accident that took her husband’s life. I asked her to look up the word accident in the dictionary in my office.

凯伦既当法官又当陪审团，把自己判进了“义务监狱”，罪名是她根本没犯的——那场夺走她丈夫生命的车祸。我让她在我办公室的字典里查一下“事故”这个词的意思。

“It means ‘unforeseen, unexpected and . . .,’” she stopped for a moment and I saw her eyes become teary, “and unintended!”

“它的意思是‘不可预见的、意想不到的……’”她停顿了一下，我看到她的眼睛里噙满了泪水，“而且是无意的！”

“That’s right,” I said. “ Unintended. ” I told her to repeat that word often to herself. She hadn’t wanted what happened to happen, she hadn’t planned it, and she had nothing to do with it. I told her that everyone except some murderers who get life imprisonment without possibility of parole gets out of jail sooner or later. How come she was still there?

“没错，”我说，“是无意的。”我告诉她要经常默念这个词。她不想发生这样的事，她没有计划过，这件事也与她无关。我告诉她，除了少数被判终身监禁且不得假释的杀人犯之外，每个人迟早都会出狱。为什么她还待在那里？

I knew that Karen had a rich spiritual life. She attended Al-Anon meetings regularly, often went away on retreats, was an avid student of yoga and meditated daily. Yet Karen had not been able to cross the threshold to self-forgiveness.

我知道凯伦的精神生活非常丰富。她定期参加匿名戒酒互助会（Al-Anon）的会议，经常参加静修活动，热衷于瑜伽，并且每天都冥想。然而，凯伦始终无法跨越自我宽恕的门槛。

I asked her to conjure up a figure that would have the power to let her out of obligation jail, a figure that she could play in a scene with herself. “Well . . . I don’t think I’d feel comfortable playing God, but I do believe I have a guardian angel out there—I could play her.”

我请她想象一个能让她摆脱义务束缚的人物，一个她可以和自己一起扮演的人物。“嗯……我觉得扮演上帝不太自在，但我相信我有一个守护天使——我可以扮演她。”

“Great” I said. “You be your guardian angel. Put Karen in the empty chair and get her out of this lousy jail once and for all! And I want you to start by saying ‘I forgive you.’”

“太好了，”我说。“你就做你自己的守护天使吧。把凯伦放到空椅子上，让她彻底离开这该死的监狱！我希望你先对她说‘我原谅你’。”

The tears that had filled Karen’s eyes rolled down her face as she began.

卡伦开口说话时，她眼中的泪水顺着脸颊滚落下来。

I forgive you, Karen. You didn’t have anything to do with Pete’s death. It was an accident. You’ve been a good mother, you’ve been protective and loving to both your kids, you’ve been a good daughter, a wonderful nurse. You really care about other people— it’s time to start giving to yourself. I forgive you, sweetie—I forgive you, I forgive you.

凯伦，我原谅你。皮特的死跟你一点关系都没有，那只是一场意外。你一直是个好妈妈，对两个孩子都呵护备至、关爱有加；你也是个好女儿，一位出色的护士。你真的很关心别人——现在是时候好好爱自己了。亲爱的，我原谅你——我原谅你，我原谅你。

These were things Karen had not been able to say to herself, but in the role of her guardian angel, she could give herself the validation and release she so desperately needed. I urge you to try this exercise. If the guardian angel concept doesn’t work for you, you can do it by playing the role of any genuinely loving person in your life. The important thing is to focus on where you got stuck in obligation jail and to get yourself out.

这些话凯伦一直无法对自己说出口，但扮演守护天使的角色，她可以给予自己迫切需要的肯定和解脱。我强烈建议你也试试这个练习。如果守护天使的概念对你不起作用，你可以扮演生活中任何一位真正爱你的人。重要的是，你要专注于自己是如何陷入责任的牢笼，并设法挣脱出来。

That session was a real turning point for Karen. Toward the end of our hour together she said, “So WHERE IS IT WRITTEN that I’m supposed to dig into my retirement account because my daughter has to have a house right now?”

那次谈话对凯伦来说是一个真正的转折点。在我们谈话快结束时，她说：“到底哪条规定说我应该动用我的退休账户，因为我女儿现在需要一套房子？”

I told Karen I thought it would be just fine if she wanted to help Melanie financially as long as she was genuinely able to and did it out of love and generosity rather than out of fear of reprisals from her daughter. She acknowledged that the $5,000 that Melanie wanted was too much for her to handle right now, but that she would feel fine with $1,500.

我告诉凯伦，如果她真心实意地想在经济上帮助梅兰妮，并且是出于爱和慷慨，而不是害怕女儿的报复，我觉得完全没问题。她承认梅兰妮要的5000美元对她来说现在太多了，但她觉得1500美元就足够了。

“And if Melanie squawks about it?” I asked her.

“如果梅兰妮对此大吵大闹呢？”我问她。

Karen smiled and took a deep breath. “Well . . . she’s squawked before, and I’m sure she’ll squawk again at some future date. I’ll just say it’s the best I can do and if you want to get mad at anyone, get mad at Susan—she’s the one who’s responsible for the changes I’ve made.”

凯伦笑了笑，深吸了一口气。“嗯……她以前就抱怨过，我相信以后肯定还会再抱怨。我就说这是我能做的最好的了，如果你想找人发火，那就去找苏珊吧——她才是造成我这些改变的罪魁祸首。”

People grow up and evolve, but sometimes their beliefs don’t change along with them. Like Karen, you are entitled to live by the codes and beliefs that you accept freely as an adult instead of the ones that you assumed automatically and unquestioningly long ago.

人会成长，会改变，但有时他们的信念却不会随之改变。就像凯伦一样，你有权按照你成年后自由接受的准则和信念生活，而不是继续遵循你很久以前不假思索、想当然地接受的那些。

How Much Can You Give?

你能捐多少？

Eve knew that she had to leave Elliot, but all the FOG elements were immobilizing her.

伊芙知道她必须离开艾略特，但迷雾的所有元素都让她动弹不得。

He needs me so much. I do everything for him. And I owe him so much. I just can’t get my foot out that door.

他太需要我了。我为他做了一切。我欠他太多了。我就是迈不出那扇门。

This lovely, talented young woman had given up so much of herself to be Elliot’s caretaker that she was living on an emotional overdraft with practically nothing in the psychological bank. She had cut herself off from friends, had no fun time or activities that gave her pleasure, had submerged her career aspirations to his and had narrowed her world to a thin sliver.

这位美丽而才华横溢的年轻女子为了照顾埃利奥特，牺牲了太多自己，以至于她的情感早已透支，心理储备几乎耗尽。她与朋友断绝了联系，没有了任何娱乐消遣，放弃了自己的事业，将世界缩小到只剩一小块。

The more resources you have, the more you can give. It’s that simple. If you have a lot of riches in your life—people you love and who love you, emotional and professional satisfaction, friends, fun, enough money—you can probably give a great deal without diminishing your own well-being. Conversely, if you’re going through a divorce, having trouble at work and scraping to make ends meet, it will be much harder for you to expend a lot of time and energy to meet someone else’s demands. It’s a hard lesson to learn, but the truth is that you can’t save somebody from drowning if you can barely keep your own head above water.

你拥有的资源越多，你能给予的就越多。就这么简单。如果你生活中拥有很多财富——你爱的人和爱你的人，情感和事业上的满足感，朋友，快乐，足够的金钱——你或许可以在不损害自身福祉的情况下给予很多。反之，如果你正在经历离婚，工作不顺，勉强维持生计，你就会很难抽出大量时间和精力去满足别人的需求。这是一个难以接受的教训，但事实是，如果你自己都难以自保，又怎能去救溺水的人呢？

THE GUILT BUTTON

内疚按钮

Guilt draws much of its power over us from the fact that most of us have real difficulty telling appropriate guilt from undeserved guilt. We believe that if we’re feeling guilty, it’s always because we’ve done something bad.

内疚感之所以能如此强烈地控制我们，很大程度上是因为我们大多数人很难区分合理的内疚感和不应有的内疚感。我们认为，如果我们感到内疚，那一定是因为我们做了坏事。

Allen’s euphoria at being able to talk calmly with Jo and come up with a plan for taking his business trip lasted for about five minutes. Almost immediately, he was squeezed between knowing he was doing the right thing and feeling intensely uncomfortable about making such a huge change in the way he related to his wife.

艾伦终于能和乔冷静地商量出差计划，这种欣喜之情只持续了大约五分钟。几乎立刻，他就陷入了两难的境地：一方面，他知道自己做的是对的；另一方面，他又因为要彻底改变与妻子相处的方式而感到极度不安。

I know Jo agreed to stay home and didn’t seem too upset, but I feel guilty as hell. I get this picture of her in the house alone, curled up on the sofa in front of the TV crying and jumping at every sound she hears. Guilt doesn’t come up for no reason, Susan. I’m many things, but I’m not a man who likes to see his wife suffer.

我知道乔同意待在家里，而且看起来也不太难过，但我还是内疚得要命。我脑海里总是浮现出她独自在家，蜷缩在沙发上看电视，哭个不停，听到一点动静就吓得跳起来的画面。苏珊，内疚感不会无缘无故地涌上心头。我有很多缺点，但我绝不是那种喜欢看到妻子受苦的男人。

I told Allen that by answering a few questions he would quickly be able to evaluate if his guilt was appropriate or excessive for the situation. I asked him:

我告诉艾伦，只要回答几个问题，他就能很快判断自己的罪责是否恰当，或者是否过重。我问他：

  • Is what you did or want to do malicious?
    你所做的事情或你想做的事情是恶意的吗？
  • Is what you did or want to do cruel?
    你所做的事情或你想做的事情是残忍的吗？
  • Is what you did or want to do abusive?
    你所做或想要做的事情是否构成虐待？
  • Is what you did or want to do insulting, belittling or demeaning?
    你所做或想要做的事情是否具有侮辱性、贬低性或侮辱性？
  • Is what you did or want to do truly harmful to the other person’s well-being?
    你所做或想要做的事情真的会对他人的福祉造成伤害吗？

If you answer yes to any of the questions, the guilt you’re feeling is appropriate as long as it creates feelings of remorse and not self-hatred. Honoring your integrity will mean taking responsibility for your behavior and making amends. It doesn’t mean you’re a moral monster.

如果你对任何问题回答“是”，那么你所感受到的内疚是合理的，只要它让你感到懊悔而不是自我憎恨。维护你的正直意味着为你的行为负责并做出弥补。这并不意味着你是一个道德败坏的怪物。

But if, like Allen, you’re doing something healthy for yourself and not trying to harm or diminish another person, then your guilt is undeserved and needs to be confronted. Unless we do confront it, excessive guilt can become so entrenched that it becomes like wallpaper—the backdrop for our daily lives.

但是，如果你像艾伦一样，只是在做对自己有益的事情，而不是试图伤害或贬低他人，那么你的内疚感就是不必要的，需要正视。如果我们不正视它，过度的内疚感就会根深蒂固，最终像墙纸一样，成为我们日常生活的背景。

Allen answered no to all of the questions, but he was still full of ambivalence when he went on his business trip to San Francisco without Jo.

艾伦对所有问题都回答“不”，但当他独自一人前往旧金山出差时，心中仍然充满矛盾。

The first night was the hardest. Just as I’d feared, she was crying on the phone when we spoke in the evening. My first instinct was to make a lot of suggestions about what she could do—see friends, go out, visit her family—but I realized that the only way to help her was to stop telling her what to do and let her figure it out for herself. So I told her I missed her, the trip was going well, and I’d talk to her the next night.

第一晚最难熬。正如我所担心的，晚上我们通电话时，她正在哭。我的第一反应是给她提很多建议——见见朋友、出去走走、探望家人——但我意识到，唯一能帮到她的办法就是停止告诉她该怎么做，让她自己去想办法。所以我告诉她我很想她，旅途一切顺利，第二天晚上再聊。

The second day was a real turning point for me. When I called her, she wasn’t there. I was worried, so I left a message, and when she called back she said she’d been to a movie with her friend Linda. She sounded just fine. It was like—all that worrying for nothing. She was kind of up and down through the week, but she found things to do, and she coped just fine. I’m not saying all this was easy, but we both got by. And it’s going to make it a hell of a lot easier the next time.

第二天对我来说是个真正的转折点。我打电话给她，她不在。我很担心，就留了言。她回电说和朋友琳达去看电影了。听起来她一切都很好。感觉就像——之前的担心都是多余的。她那周情绪有点起伏，但她总能找到事情做，也挺过来了。我不是说这一切都很容易，但我们俩都挺过来了。而且下次肯定会轻松得多。

Use the questions I’ve listed above to help you whenever your sense your guilt, like Allen’s, may be way out of proportion to the event that is triggering it. A healthy conscience will create the amount of guilt that’s commensurate with the deed. There should be guilt if you sleep with your best friend’s husband, and the questions certainly aren’t intended to let anyone off the hook for criminal acts. But you don’t deserve to feel guilty because you burned the toast or suggested a movie that turns out to be a turkey. And certainly not because you want to do something to enrich your life—even if the other person doesn’t like it.

当你像艾伦一样，感到内疚感与引发内疚的事件严重不成比例时，不妨参考我上面列出的问题。健康的良知会让你产生与行为相称的内疚感。如果你和闺蜜的丈夫发生了关系，当然应该感到内疚，这些问题也绝非为了让任何人逃脱罪责。但你不应该因为烤焦了吐司或者推荐了一部烂片而感到内疚。更不应该因为你想做一些让自己生活更美好的事情——即使对方不喜欢——而感到内疚。

Opinions, Not Facts

观点，而非事实

The people in our lives who resort to emotional blackmail don’t discriminate when it comes to guilt. They will push just as much guilt at us over the small things as the big ones. And oh how willingly we open the door and let the guilt in.

生活中那些动辄诉诸情感勒索的人，在制造愧疚感方面毫不挑剔。无论大事小事，他们都会让我们背负同样的愧疚感。而我们又是多么心甘情愿地敞开心扉，让愧疚感涌入心头啊！

Leigh had told her mother how much the negative comparisons with her cousin had hurt her, and her mother appeared to be receptive. But old habits die hard, and when her mother wanted something that Leigh resisted, she used a different form of pressure.

莉告诉母亲，和表妹的负面比较让她多么难过，母亲似乎也接受了她的说法。但旧习难改，当母亲想要莉做她不愿意做的事情时，她就换了一种施压方式。

She wanted me to go down to San Diego with her for the weekend so she could visit my brother and his family, but I have a date and theater tickets, and it just wouldn’t work out. I told her she was a big girl and she could get there by herself. I know it was bitchy, but I suggested she go with Caroline. Well, she didn’t do the comparison routine, but she did launch into “I guess you’re just too busy to spend time with me — you’re so wrapped up in your own life you don’t care about anyone else. I can’t believe you turned out this way!” I know it’s manipulative and she’s playing the martyr to the hilt, but dammit, I still feel guilty—not as much as before, but more than I want to. I even toyed with the idea of breaking my date and giving my tickets away—but I didn’t, so I guess that’s progress.

她想让我周末跟她去圣地亚哥，这样她就可以去看望我哥哥一家，但我已经有约会了，而且还有戏票，实在去不了。我跟她说她是个成年人了，自己去完全没问题。我知道这样说有点刻薄，但我还是建议她跟卡罗琳一起去。结果她没跟我比较，而是开始抱怨：“看来你太忙了，没时间陪我——你只顾着自己，根本不在乎别人。真不敢相信你竟然变成这样！”我知道她这是在耍手段，而且装得特别可怜，但该死，我还是觉得内疚——虽然没有以前那么强烈，但还是比我想象的要多。我甚至想过取消约会，把票也送人——但我忍住了，所以我想这算是进步吧。

Of course that was progress. Despite the pressure Leigh had changed her behavior, and like so many of us she wasn’t giving herself enough credit, because she expected her feelings to change as quickly. One of the things she could do to speed the process of diminishing her undeserved guilt was to learn how to separate her mother’s negative labels from fact.

当然，这算是一种进步。尽管承受着压力，莉还是改变了自己的行为，但和我们很多人一样，她并没有充分肯定自己的进步，因为她期望自己的感受也能如此迅速地改变。为了更快地减轻自己不应有的内疚感，她可以做的其中一件事就是学会区分母亲的负面评价和事实。

I told Leigh to bring in a list of the most critical things her mother had called her through the years when she was upset with her. I predicted that her labels would probably be familiar to a lot of emotional blackmail targets.

我让莉列一张清单，写下这些年来她母亲生气时对她最恶毒的辱骂之词。我预感，这些词语对很多情感勒索的目标来说可能都很熟悉。

Here are some items from Leigh’s list:

以下是莉的清单中的一些项目：

  • Uncaring
    冷漠
  • Selfish
    自私
  • Thoughtless
    不顾后果
  • Clumsy
    笨拙
  • Pig-headed
    固执的
  • Mean
    意思是
  • Unreasonable
    不合理
  • Rude
    粗鲁的

Sticks and stones may indeed break our bones, and names like these coming from someone we are close to can hurt us. But these labels are not the truth. They are someone else’s opinions. Often we cloak our blackmailers in a mantle of wisdom. They know us better than we know ourselves, we believe, and when they define us in negative ways, we’re often quick to buy into these definitions of ourselves, especially if they resonate with what others have told us in the past. In this way we turn another person’s opinion into fact. “You are selfish” mutates inside us into “ I am selfish.” It’s the same way a child who is told “You are bad” internalizes that message into “ I am bad.”

棍棒和石头的确会伤人，来自亲近之人的这样评价也会让我们感到痛苦。但这些标签并非事实，它们只是他人的看法。我们常常会用智慧的外衣来掩盖那些诋毁我们的人。我们总觉得他们比我们更了解自己，所以当他们用负面的方式定义我们时，我们往往会很快接受这些定义，尤其当这些定义与过去别人对我们说过的话产生共鸣时。就这样，我们把别人的意见变成了事实。“你很自私”这句话在我们心中悄然演变成“我很自私”。这就像一个孩子被告知“你很坏”后，会将这句话内化成“我很坏”。

To help Leigh separate fact from fiction, I had her take her list and opposite each item write the phrase “OPINION, NOT FACT!” in capital letters. Her list then began to look like this:

为了帮助莉莉区分事实和虚构，我让她把清单上的每一项都用大写字母写上“观点，非事实！”。之后，她的清单看起来是这样的：

  • Uncaring: OPINION, NOT FACT!
    漠不关心：这只是观点，不是事实！
  • Selfish: OPINION, NOT FACT!
    自私：这只是观点，不是事实！
  • Thoughtless: OPINION, NOT FACT!
    轻率之举：这只是观点，并非事实！

I’m sure you get the idea. It’s important that you absorb this concept.

我相信你明白我的意思了。理解这个概念很重要。

Sometimes, of course, we are uncaring and thoughtless, and it’s important to examine the validity of the other person’s label. The questions I had Allen answer will help you do that. But most of the time when you’re dealing with emotional blackmailers, their name-calling is opinionated, biased and a product of their own self-serving agenda. This is particularly hard to see if the blackmailer is a parent, as in Leigh’s case, because we spent our early years believing they were always right. But as you’ve seen consistently throughout this book, blackmailers are operating out of their own fears and frustrations, and often the very things they accuse you of are the traits and behaviors they evidence themselves. They have projected these flaws onto you, expecting you to take them in. Let’s send them back.

当然，有时候我们也会冷漠无情、考虑不周，这时就需要仔细审视对方贴的标签是否合理。我让艾伦回答的那些问题就能帮到你。但大多数时候，当你遇到情感勒索者时，他们的谩骂都带有强烈的个人偏见，是出于自身利益的考量。如果勒索者是父母，比如莉的遭遇，这一点就更难看清，因为我们从小就被灌输父母永远是对的观念。但正如你在本书中反复看到的，勒索者往往出于自身的恐惧和挫败感而行事，他们指责你的那些特质和行为，往往正是他们自己所表现出的。他们把这些缺点投射到你身上，希望你接受。让我们把这些缺点反弹回去。

Return to Sender

退回寄件人

The unconscious pays a lot of attention to symbolic rituals and ceremonies. One of the most exciting parts of my work has been creating simple rituals to help clients confront their demons in new and interesting ways. Here’s one for guilt that can really help disconnect this hot button.

潜意识非常重视象征性的仪式和庆典。我工作中最大的乐趣之一就是创造一些简单的仪式，帮助客户以新颖有趣的方式面对内心的恐惧。这里有一个针对内疚感的仪式，它能真正帮助你摆脱这种敏感的情绪。

Find a small box with a lid, like a shoe box. Make it your Guilt Box. Every day for a week jot down the guilt-inducing statements or names that someone uses to pressure you and that you know are unfair and manipulative. Write each one down on a separate piece of paper and put it in the box.

找一个带盖的小盒子，比如鞋盒。把它当作你的“愧疚盒”。连续一周，每天都记下别人用来给你施加压力、让你感到愧疚的话语或称呼，你知道这些话语或称呼是不公平的、带有操控性的。把每一条都写在一张纸上，然后放进盒子里。

At the end of the week, wrap the box as if you were going to mail it, put the return address of the guilt-peddler(s) on the upper left-hand corner and your own name and address in the center. In large letters, preferably red, write “RETURN TO SENDER” across the front. Then, with as much ceremony as you like, dispose of the box in a way that feels good to you. You can bury it in the backyard, burn it and scatter the ashes, drop it in a Dumpster, put it out with the trash cans or run over it with your car. The point is to stop accepting delivery of the guilt that doesn’t really belong to you. It’s not yours. Don’t let it in.

一周结束时，把盒子像寄出去一样包好，在左上角写上寄件人的地址，中间写上你自己的姓名和地址。用醒目的大字，最好是红色，在正面写上“退回寄件人”。然后，用你喜欢的方式，以任何你觉得舒服的方式处理掉这个盒子。你可以把它埋在后院，烧掉后撒灰，扔进垃圾箱，扔到垃圾桶旁边，或者开车碾过去。关键是要停止接收那些不属于你的愧疚感。它不是你的。别让它进入你的生活。

An Exercise in Paradox

悖论练习

Despite all the demons that were pulling at her, Eve did find the courage to leave Elliot in the most compassionate way possible. She set a specific date when she would be leaving and stayed on long enough to help him find a personal assistant to take over much of the work she had been doing for him. She also alerted his family members to how depressed he was and got several to agree to stay in close touch with him and try to get him to seek professional help.

尽管内心充满挣扎，伊芙最终还是鼓起勇气，以最体贴的方式离开了埃利奥特。她定下了具体的离开日期，并留了一段时间，帮助他找到了一位私人助理，接手了她之前为他做的大部分工作。她还告知埃利奥特的家人他情绪低落的情况，并说服了几位家人与他保持密切联系，努力劝说他寻求专业帮助。

But I knew Eve was not going to get rid of her mountain of undeserved guilt easily, even though she had made dramatic progress. She had moved in with her mother temporarily, which was working out quite well, and had made some attempts to find a job. But every time Elliot called her and broke down on the phone, she was thrown back into the FOG.

但我知道，即使伊芙取得了显著的进步，她也无法轻易摆脱那堆积如山的、不应承受的罪恶感。她暂时搬去和母亲同住，一切都很顺利，她也尝试找工作。但每次埃利奥特打电话给她，在电话里崩溃大哭时，她都会再次陷入那层迷雾之中。

I put an empty chair in front of Eve and asked her to imagine Elliot sitting in it. Then I asked her to get down on her knees in front of the chair and say, “I know you can’t make it without me so I will never leave your side. I’m coming back and I will never leave you again. I will give up all my dreams, my aspirations, my very life for you. I will ask for nothing for myself. Inever known anyone will take care of you forever.”

我把一把空椅子放在伊芙面前，让她想象埃利奥特坐在上面。然后我让她跪在椅子前，说：“我知道没有我你活不下去，所以我永远不会离开你。我会回来的，我再也不会离开你了。我会为你放弃我所有的梦想、我的抱负，甚至我的生命。我什么都不求。我从未想过会有人永远照顾你。”

Eve looked at me as if I were crazy. “Are you kidding?” she shrieked. “I would never say anything like that!”

伊芙看着我，仿佛我是个疯子。“你在开玩笑吧？”她尖叫道，“我怎么可能说出那样的话！”

“Indulge me,” I said.

“请您体谅一下，”我说。

Eve reluctantly did as I asked. About halfway through she stopped and said, “Wait a minute! I feel ridiculous. I know I’m a soft touch but I’m not a total idiot! I’m not going back! I’m going to have a life! I didn’t make him the way he is—why should I have to fix him?”

伊芙很不情愿地照做了。做到一半，她停下来，说道：“等等！我觉得自己好荒唐。我知道自己心软，但我又不是傻子！我不回去了！我要好好过日子！他变成现在这样又不是我造成的——我为什么要改变他？”

This kind of work is called paradoxical therapy. A paradox is a contradiction and refers to something that may seem absurd or ridiculous on the surface but that actually turns out to contain some basic truths. Paradox therapy is wonderfully effective. As we saw, Eve’s spirit was activated by the absurdity of what I had asked her to say, and she rebelled. Even though she may never have said those actual words to Elliot, until recently her behavior had been saying them for her. Paradox let her take her guilt to a ridiculous extreme and see just how undeserved it was. Once she’d done that, she was on her way to breaking free.

这种方法被称为悖论疗法。悖论是一种矛盾，指的是表面上看似荒谬可笑，实则蕴含着一些基本真理的事物。悖论疗法非常有效。正如我们所见，我要求伊芙说出的那些话荒谬至极，这激发了她的内心，她开始反抗。尽管她可能从未对艾略特说过那些话，但直到最近，她的行为一直在替她表达这些话。悖论疗法让她将自己的内疚感推向一个荒谬的极端，让她看清自己是多么不该承受这些。一旦她意识到这一点，她就走上了挣脱束缚的道路。

A few weeks later, Eve announced she had found an entry-level job in an advertising agency. She sounded very different from the trapped, hopeless young woman I had first met five months earlier. I asked her if she remembered telling me she was convinced she would “die of guilt” if she ever left Elliot.

几周后，伊芙宣布她在一家广告公司找到了一份入门级工作。她听起来和五个月前我第一次见到她时那个被困住、绝望的年轻女子判若两人。我问她是否还记得自己曾说过，如果离开埃利奥特，她会“愧疚而死”。

“Well, I’ve never known anyone to die of guilt, and I don’t intend to be the first,” she said. “I just have to make myself strong and financially independent. I have enough skills to support myself, and all I need is a one-bedroom apartment and a running car. Running water and a running car. I can accomplish that and I’m OK.”

“嗯，我从没见过有人因为内疚而死，我也不想成为第一个，”她说。“我只需要让自己变得坚强，经济独立。我有足够的技能养活自己，我需要的只是一套一居室的公寓和一辆能开的车。有自来水和能开的车就行了。我能做到这些，我就没事了。”

She certainly was.

她的确是。

Fighting Guilt with Imagination

用想象力对抗内疚

Jan was confused when she came to see me after telling her sister that she couldn’t lend her money.

简告诉她姐姐她不能借钱给她，然后她来找我，显得很困惑。

I know it was the right thing , but I can’t shake the idea that I really did something terrible. She’s in dire straits. When I think about this, all those old clichés keep coming up: your family is all you have, forgive and forget, blood is thicker than water, the past is the past. Bottom line, she’s my sister, she’s in trouble and I don’t feel good about just leaving her hanging out there.

我知道我做的是对的，但我始终无法摆脱那种觉得自己做了件很糟糕的事的感觉。她现在处境非常危险。每当我想起这件事，那些老生常谈的道理就浮现在我的脑海里：家人是你的一切，宽恕和遗忘，血浓于水，过去的事就让它过去吧。说到底，她是我妹妹，她现在身处困境，我实在不忍心就这么把她丢下不管。

Jan was waging an inner battle between what she knew and what she couldn’t help hoping for. It was as though the hard-won and painful wisdom that had come from years of dealing with Carol couldn’t penetrate deeply enough to challenge her guilt.

简内心正经历着一场挣扎，一边是她所认知的，一边是她无法抑制的渴望。仿佛多年来与卡罗尔相处所积累的痛苦而深刻的智慧，也无法彻底触动她内心的愧疚。

When the unconscious is resisting healthy change, I’ve found that it’s effective to reach it through metaphors and stories instead of traditional talk therapy. To help Jan do this, I asked her to write a fairy tale about her relationship with her sister. “That’s really going to be a Grimm fairy tale,” she said sardonically. “So how do I do this?”
